parts.latex: Which inequality gives the domain of $y=\sqrt{2x-3}$?

dif.r: one inequality: radicand >= 0

solutions.latex:
The expression under the square root cannot be negative:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3&\ge 0\\ x&\ge \dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The function $f(x)=x^3$ is transformed to $g(x)=(x-2)^3+5$ by a horizontal translation of 2 units followed by a vertical translation of 5 units.

Which row of the table shows the directions of the translations?

dif.r: one translation pair: read x-2 right, +5 up

solutions.latex: Replacing $x$ by $x-2$ moves the graph 2 units to the right; adding $5$ moves it 5 units up.

parts.latex:
John recently did a class test in each of three subjects. The class scores on each test were normally distributed.

The table shows the subjects and John's scores as well as the mean and standard deviation of the class scores on each test.

\extable{Tp307_1}

Relative to the rest of the class, which row of the table below shows John's strongest subject and his weakest subject?

dif.r: MCQ: compare three z-scores, direct formula

solutions.latex:
Compare the $z$-scores, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{French: } z&=\dfrac{82-70}{8}=1.5\\ \text{Commerce: } z&=\dfrac{80-65}{5}=3\\ \text{Music: } z&=\dfrac{74-50}{12}=2\end{aligned}$$
The highest $z$-score is Commerce and the lowest is French.

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int e+e^{3x}\,dx$?

dif.r: MCQ: e is constant, direct exponential primitive

solutions.latex:
$e$ is a constant, so its primitive is $ex$, and $\displaystyle\int e^{3x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}$:
$$\int e+e^{3x}\,dx=ex+\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}+c$$

parts.latex: Which of the following could represent the graph of $y=-x^2+bx+1$, where $b>0$?

dif.r: concavity, intercept and sign of axis b/2 combined

figures.cap: option A parabola
option B parabola
option C parabola
option D parabola

solutions.latex:
The coefficient of $x^2$ is negative, so the parabola is concave down (graphs C or D), and the $y$-intercept is $1$.

The axis of symmetry is $x=\dfrac{b}{2}>0$, so the vertex is to the right of the $y$-axis: graph C.

parts.latex: Which interval gives the range of the function $y=5+2\cos 3x$?

dif.r: MCQ: range of 5+2cos3x by scaling and shifting [-1,1]

solutions.latex:
Start from the range of cosine, then build up $y$ one step at a time:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \cos 3x\le 1\\ -2&\le 2\cos 3x\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ 3&\le 5+2\cos 3x\le 7 &&(\text{add } 5)\end{aligned}$$
So $3\le y\le 7$: the range is $[3,7]$.

dif.r: MCQ: signed areas of trapezia, semicircle, triangle below axis

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): line segments and semicircle, 0 to 12

solutions.latex:
Add the signed areas between the graph and the $x$-axis (the semicircle has radius $2$; the area below the axis counts as negative):
$$\begin{aligned} 0\le x\le 4:&\quad 4\times3=12\\ 4\le x\le 8:&\quad 4\times3+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(2)^2=12+2\pi\\ 8\le x\le 10:&\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times3=3\\ 10\le x\le 12:&\quad -\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times3=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{12} f(x)\,dx&=12+(12+2\pi)+3-3\\ &=24+2\pi\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: signs plus f'(1)<f(1) via chord gradient comparison

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: increasing concave-down curve through O with point at x=1

solutions.latex:
At $x=1$ the curve is above the axis, increasing and concave down, so $f(1)>0$, $f'(1)>0$ and $f''(1)<0$.

The curve starts at the origin and its gradient is decreasing, so the gradient at $x=1$ is less than the gradient of the chord from $O$, which is $\dfrac{f(1)}{1}$. So $f'(1)<f(1)$:
$$f''(1)<0<f'(1)<f(1)$$

parts.latex:
Suppose the weight of melons is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma$.

A melon has a weight below the lower quartile of the distribution but NOT in the bottom 10% of the distribution.

Which of the following most accurately represents the region in which the weight of this melon lies?

dif.r: MCQ: locate quartile and 10% cut-offs in sigma units, interpret

can_use: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: normal curve, option A shaded region
normal curve, option B shaded region
normal curve, option C shaded region
normal curve, option D shaded region

solutions.latex:
Below the lower quartile means $z<-0.67$ approximately; not in the bottom 10% means $z>-1.28$ approximately.

So the weight lies between about $\mu-1.3\sigma$ and $\mu-0.7\sigma$: the narrow region just either side of $\mu-\sigma$, graph C.

parts.latex:
The graph shows two functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$.

\exfigure{34_q10_1}

Define $h(x)=f\big(g(x)\big)$.

How many stationary points does $y=h(x)$ have for $1\le x\le 5$?

dif.r: chain rule on composite read from graphs; count g(x)=c solutions

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: graphs of y=f(x) and y=g(x)

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule,
$$h'(x)=f'\big(g(x)\big)\,g'(x)$$
$h'(x)=0$ when $g'(x)=0$, which happens once, at $x=3$; or when $f'\big(g(x)\big)=0$, that is, when $g(x)$ equals the $x$-value of the maximum of $f$ (about $0.7$). On $1\le x\le5$, $g$ falls to $0$ and rises again, so $g(x)\approx0.7$ twice.

So $y=h(x)$ has $3$ stationary points.

questions.stem: There are two tanks on a property, Tank $A$ and Tank $B$. Initially, Tank $A$ holds 1000 litres of water and Tank $B$ is empty.

parts.label: a

dif.r: plot a given linear model

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Tank $B$ remains empty until $t=15$ when water is added to it at a constant rate of 30 litres per minute.

By drawing a line on the grid on the previous page, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when the two tanks contain the same volume of water.

dif.r: build delayed model 30(t-15), then intersect lines

can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

can: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities
A.note: by graph or otherwise

can: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

Simultaneous equations.reason: Assumed-algebra skill used only as an optional algebraic check of the graph reading.

Piecewise-defined functions.reason: Only the t>=15 linear piece is used to find the intersection; the piecewise rule itself is not needed.

Equations of straight lines.evidence: Tank B: V=30(t-15) for t>=15 ... drawn on the grid
Equations of straight lines.reason: Writing and graphing the Tank B line earns the first mark.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Using the graphs drawn, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ (where $t>0$) when the total volume of water in the two tanks is 1000 litres.

dif.r: set up total-volume equation from both models, check validity

can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: blank grid: V (litres) 0-1100 vs t (minutes) 0-55

solutions.latex: \exfigure{33_q11_1}

Tank $B$: $V=30(t-15)$ for $t\ge15$. This line starts at $(15,0)$ and rises $30$ litres each minute; drawn on the grid in part (a), it meets the Tank $A$ line at $t=29$.

\exfigure{33_q11_1}

Check algebraically:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000-20t &= 30(t-15)\\ 1000-20t &= 30t-450\\ 1450 &= 50t\\ t &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The tanks hold the same volume after $29$ minutes.
criteria: Draws the graph of volume for tank $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $t\ge15$, the total volume is
$$\begin{aligned} (1000-20t)+30(t-15) &= 1000\\ 10t-450 &= 0\\ t &= 45 \end{aligned}$$
(For $0<t<15$ the total is $1000-20t<1000$.) Tank $A$ is not yet empty at $t=45$ ($V=100$), so the model still applies.

$\therefore$ $t=45$ minutes.

questions.stem:
Mr Ali, Ms Brown and a group of students were camping at the site located at $P$. Mr Ali walked with some of the students on a bearing of $035^\circ$ for 7 km to location $A$. Ms Brown, with the rest of the students, walked on a bearing of $100^\circ$ for 9 km to location $B$.

parts.label: a

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{33_q15_1}

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of the curve $y=-x^3+3x^2-1$, labelling the stationary points and point of inflection. Do NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve.

dif.r: routine cubic: stationary points, nature, inflection, sketch

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 1 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3x^2 + 6x \\ &= 3x(2 - x) \end{aligned}$$
When $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, we have $3x(2-x) = 0$.
$$x = 0, \qquad x = 2$$
$$y = -1 \qquad y = -2^3 + 3(2)^2 - 1 = 3$$
Stationary points are $(0, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -6x + 6$$
When $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, we have $6(1-x) = 0$.
$$x = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1^3 + 3\times 1^2 - 1 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The point of inflection is $(1, 1)$.

\exfigure{33_q16_1}
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the point of inflection, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative of the function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{4+x^2}\,dx$.

dif.r: f prime over f with constant adjustment

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{x}{4 + x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{2x}{4 + x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(4 + x^2\right) + c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an anti-derivative involving the log function, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{2x}(2x+1)$.

dif.r: product rule then factorise

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(x+1)e^{2x}\,dx$.

dif.r: reverse differentiation; must match factor 4(x+1), scale by 1/4

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=2x+1\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{2x}(2x+1)\right] &= 2e^{2x}(2x+1) + 2e^{2x} \\ &= 2e^{2x}(2x + 2) \\ &= 4e^{2x}(x + 1) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} &\int (x+1)e^{2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int 4(x+1)e^{2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}e^{2x}(2x+1) + c \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\sec\theta-\cos\theta=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.

dif.r: routine identity proof: reciprocal, common denominator, Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
$$\sec\theta - \cos\theta = \sin\theta\tan\theta$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - \cos\theta \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \tan\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows that the LHS is equal to $\dfrac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Hot tea is poured into a cup. The temperature of tea can be modelled by $T=25+70(1.5)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the tea, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after it is poured.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the temperature of the tea 4 minutes after it has been poured?

dif.r: substitute t=4 into given model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what rate is the tea cooling 4 minutes after it has been poured?

dif.r: differentiate a^(-0.4t) needing ln 1.5, then substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: How long after the tea is poured will it take for its temperature to reach $55^\circ\text{C}$?

dif.r: rearrange exponential model, solve with logs

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} T &= 25 + 70(1.5)^{-0.4\times 4} \\ &= 61.5891\ldots \\ &\approx 61.6^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = 70(1.5)^{-0.4t}(-0.4)\ln(1.5)$$
When $t = 4$,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 70(1.5)^{-1.6}(-0.4)\ln(1.5) \\ &= -5.934\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore at $t = 4$ the tea is cooling at $5.9^\circ\text{C}$ per minute.
criteria: Finds the derivative of $T$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 55 &= 25 + 70(1.5)^{-0.4t} \\ \dfrac{30}{70} &= 1.5^{-0.4t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.5) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)}{0.4\ln(1.5)} \\ &\approx 5.22 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ it takes approximately $5.22$ minutes.
criteria: Uses the log function to solve the equation
Makes $1.5^{-0.4t}$ the subject of the equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x & \text{for } 0\le x\le k\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

dif.r: integral of pdf equals 1, solve cos k = 0

B.note: cos k = 0 solved for k

Trigonometric equations.reason: Must solve cos k = 0 on the domain to find k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(X\le 1)$. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.

dif.r: one direct definite integral of given pdf

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k \sin x\,dx &= 1 \\ \Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^k &= 1 \\ -\cos k + \cos 0 &= 1 \\ \cos k &= 0 \\ k &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an equation involving a definite integral set equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \le 1) &= \int_0^1 \sin x\,dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^1 \\ &= -\cos 1 + 1 \\ &\approx 0.4597 \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $P=2x+\dfrac{72}{x}$.

dif.r: build area and perimeter with quarter-circle, eliminate y

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the smallest possible perimeter of the garden bed, showing why this is the minimum perimeter.

dif.r: P given; standard derivative, second-derivative test, evaluate

figures.cap: rectangle x by y attached to quarter-circle

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} xy + \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x^2 &= 36 \\ xy &= 36 - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x^2 \\ y &= \dfrac{36}{x} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 2y + 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\times 2\pi x \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{36}{x} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x\right) + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= \dfrac{72}{x} - \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= 2x + \dfrac{72}{x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression for the perimeter in terms of $x$ and $y$ and finds a correct expression for $y$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit
Writes an expression for a perimeter in terms of $x$ and $y$ which includes the curved length of a quadrant, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 2 - \dfrac{72}{x^2}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 0$, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{72}{x^2} \\ x^2 &= 36 \\ x &= 6 \quad (\text{since } x > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{144}{x^3}$$
When $x = 6$,
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{144}{6^3} \text{ which is greater than zero.}$$
$\therefore$ $P$ is a minimum when $x = 6$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{The minimum perimeter} &= 2\times 6 + \dfrac{72}{6} \\ &= 12 + 12 \\ &= 24 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Verifies that at $x = 6$ there is a minimum turning point, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{34_q27_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y=-10.6063+bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
parts.note: Least-squares regression with box-plot data: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

dif.r: Combines box-plot median, mean shift and regression through means; several unprompted steps.

figures.cap: box-plot of temperature data, 13 to 28 degrees Celsius

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= 22 - 0.525 \\ &= 21.475 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &= \dfrac{684}{20} \\ &= 34.2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ into the regression equation, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063 + b(21.475) \\ \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} &= b \\ b &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 19$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063 + 2.08644\ldots \times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 29 chirps are expected.
criteria: Finds value of $b$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ into the regression equation, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ or $\bar{y}$ or the median of the temperature, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=c\ln x$, $c>0$.

\exfigure{34_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the equation of the tangent to $y=c\ln x$ at $x=p$, where $p>0$, is

$$y=\dfrac{c}{p}x-c+c\ln p.$$

dif.r: routine tangent derivation but parametric show-that

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $c$ such that the tangent from part (a) has a gradient of 1 and passes through the origin.

dif.r: two conditions on tangent, solve c ln c - c = 0

figures.cap: graph of y = c ln x crossing x-axis at 1

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= c\ln x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{c}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x = p$ is $\dfrac{c}{p}$.

At $x = p$, $y = c\ln p$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}(x - p) \\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c \\ y &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c + c\ln p \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent at $x = p$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{c}{p} = 1 \quad (\text{since the tangent has a gradient of } 1)$$
$$\therefore\ c = p$$
$$-c + c\ln p = 0 \quad (\text{since the tangent passes through the origin})$$
$$\begin{aligned} -c + c\ln c &= 0 \\ c(-1 + \ln c) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$c = 0 \text{ or } \ln c = 1$$
$$\therefore\ c = e \quad (\text{as } c > 0)$$
criteria: States that $\dfrac{c}{p} = 1$ or $-c + c\ln p = 0$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows two parabolas $y=4x-x^2$ and $y=ax^2$, where $a>0$. The two parabolas intersect at the origin, $O$, and at $A$.

\exfigure{34_q30_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{4}{a+1}$.

dif.r: solve parametric intersection by factorising out x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ such that the shaded area is $\dfrac{16}{3}$.

dif.r: area with parametric bound, set equal, solve for a

figures.cap: parabolas y=4x-x^2 and y=ax^2 with shaded region between O and A

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} ax^2 &= 4x - x^2 \\ (a+1)x^2 - 4x &= 0 \\ x\left[(a+1)x - 4\right] &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$x = 0 \text{ or } (a+1)x - 4 = 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} (a+1)x &= 4 \\ x &= \dfrac{4}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{4}{a+1}$.
criteria: Attempts to solve a quadratic equation to find the $x$-coordinate of $A$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} \left(4x - x^2 - ax^2\right)dx &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \int_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} \left(4x - (a+1)x^2\right)dx &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \left[2x^2 - \dfrac{(a+1)x^3}{3}\right]_0^{\frac{4}{a+1}} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{2\times 16}{(a+1)^2} - \dfrac{(a+1)}{3}\times\dfrac{64}{(a+1)^3} - 0 &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{32}{(a+1)^2} - \dfrac{64}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{96 - 64}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ \dfrac{32}{3(a+1)^2} &= \dfrac{16}{3} \\ (a+1)^2 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = \sqrt{2} - 1 \qquad (\text{since } a > 0)$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes the limits into the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit
Finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit
Writes an expression for the area involving an integral of the difference between two functions, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The population of mice on an isolated island can be modelled by the function

$$m(t)=a\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}t\right)+b,$$

where $t$ is the time in weeks and $0\le t\le 52$. The population of mice reaches a maximum of 35 000 when $t=13$ and a minimum of 5000 when $t=39$. The graph of $m(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{34_q31_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What are the values of $a$ and $b$?

dif.r: amplitude and centre line from given max and min

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
On the same island, the population of cats can be modelled by the function

$$c(t)=-80\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}(t-10)\right)+120.$$

Consider the graph of $m(t)$ and the graph of $c(t)$.

Find the values of $t$, $0\le t\le 52$, for which both populations are increasing.

dif.r: sketch shifted -cos model, intersect increasing intervals of two graphs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the rate of change of the mice population when the cat population reaches a maximum.

dif.r: locate cat maximum from phase shift, differentiate mice model, evaluate

figures.cap: graph of m(t) for 0<=t<=52, max 35000, min 5000

criteria: Provides the correct value of $a$ or the correct value of $b$, or equivalent merit

criteria: Finds the values of $t$ when the population of mice increases and the values of $t$ when the population of cats increases
Finds the values of $t$ when the population of mice increases, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cat population reaches a maximum at $t = 36$.
$$m'(t) = \dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 15\,000\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}t\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} m'(36) &= \dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 15\,000\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 36\right) \\ &= -642.7\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the mice population is decreasing at 643 mice per week.

parts.latex:
There are 8 chocolates in a box. Three have peppermint centres (P) and five have caramel centres (C).

Kim randomly chooses a chocolate from the box and eats it. Sam then randomly chooses and eats one of the remaining chocolates.

A partially completed probability tree is shown.

What is the probability that Kim and Sam choose chocolates with different centres?

dif.r: tree without replacement: two products added

figures.cap: partially completed probability tree, first branches 3/8 P and 5/8 C

solutions.latex:
After Kim eats one chocolate, 7 remain.

Different centres means peppermint then caramel, or caramel then peppermint:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= \dfrac{3}{8}\times\dfrac{5}{7} + \dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{3}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{56} + \dfrac{15}{56} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{28} \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: combine three graph facts: concavity, f'=0, sign of f

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: cubic-like curve with local minimum at x=-2 and local maximum at x=3

solutions.latex:
Read each value from the graph:

$x = -2$ is a local minimum, so the curve is concave up there: $f''(-2) > 0$.

$x = 3$ is a stationary point: $f'(3) = 0$.

The curve is below the $x$-axis at $x = 0$: $f(0) < 0$.

$$\therefore\ f(0) < f'(3) < f''(-2)$$

dif.r: read single/triple roots and end behaviour sign

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

figures.cap: quartic graph with single root on negative x-axis and horizontal point of inflection on positive x-axis

solutions.latex:
From the graph: the curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -1$ (a single root) and has a horizontal point of inflection on the $x$-axis at $x = 2$ (a triple root, factor $(x-2)^3$ or $(2-x)^3$).

Both ends of the graph go down, so the quartic has a negative leading coefficient.

$y = (x+1)(2-x)^3$ has roots $-1$ and $2$ (triple), and its leading term is $x\cdot(-x)^3 = -x^4$, which is negative.

Options A and D have roots at $1$ and $-2$; option B has a positive leading coefficient.

parts.latex:
Let $h(x)=f(g(x))$ where the function $f(x)$ is an odd function and the function $g(x)$ is an even function.

The tangent to $y=h(x)$ at $x=k$, where $k>0$, has the equation $y=mx+c$.

What is the equation of the tangent to $y=h(x)$ at $x=-k$?

dif.r: abstract parity of composite, then tangent symmetry argument

solutions.latex:
$g$ is even, so $h(-x) = f\big(g(-x)\big) = f\big(g(x)\big) = h(x)$: $h$ is an even function.

The graph of an even function is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$h(-k) = h(k) = mk + c \qquad\text{and}\qquad h'(-k) = -h'(k) = -m$$
Tangent at $x = -k$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - (mk + c) &= -m(x + k) \\ y &= -mx - mk + mk + c \\ y &= -mx + c \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: tangent through origin; reason m=-sin a=cos a/a, bound by graph

A.note: graph-based tangent reasoning, no differentiation in solution

B.note: tangent through origin: m = cos a / a, then graphical/concavity reasoning; no differentiation needed in the given solution

Concavity and points of inflection.reason: Concavity is only read informally from the diagram; no sign of f'' or inflection point is needed.

figures.cap: graph of y=cos x with line y=mx through O tangent at x=a

solutions.latex:
The tangent passes through the origin and the point $(a, \cos a)$, so
$$m = \dfrac{\cos a}{a}$$
From the diagram $\cos a < 1$, so $m < \dfrac{1}{a}$.

At $x = 2\pi$ the curve has $\cos 2\pi = 1$. The tangent touches the curve where it is concave down, so near the peak at $2\pi$ the line lies above the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} m(2\pi) &> 1 \\ m &> \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{2\pi} < m < \dfrac{1}{a}$$

parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 5000, varies according to the formula

$$P=5000b^{\frac{-t}{10}},$$

where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t\ge 0$.

The population is 1250 after 20 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 30 people per year.

dif.r: find b, differentiate b^(-t/10), solve with logs

solutions.latex:
$$P = 5000b^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
When $t = 20$, $P = 1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1250 &= 5000\,b^{-2} \\ b^{-2} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ b &= 2 \quad (b > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 5000(2)^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 5000\times\ln 2\times\dfrac{-1}{10}\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -30$:
$$\begin{aligned} -30 &= -500\times\ln 2\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{500\ln 2}{30} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= 11.55\ldots \\ \dfrac{t}{10}\ln 2 &= \ln 11.55\ldots \\ t &= 35.3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Equates $-30$ to a correct derivative, with $b = 2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $b$ and provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit
Provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} y(t) &= -5t^2 + 70t + 100 \\ y'(t) &= -10t + 70 \end{aligned}$$
When $y'(t) = 0$,
$$\begin{aligned} -10t + 70 &= 0 \\ t &= 7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y &= -5(7)^2 + 70(7) + 100 \\ &= 345 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

To find when the particle hits the ground, we solve
$$\begin{aligned} -5t^2 + 70t + 100 &= 0 \\ t^2 - 14t - 20 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{14 \pm \sqrt{196 + 80}}{2} \\ &= 7 \pm \sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$t = 7 + \sqrt{69}$, since $t > 0$
$$\begin{aligned} y'(7+\sqrt{69}) &= -10(7+\sqrt{69}) + 70 \\ &= -10\sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ a = -10$ and $b = 69$

parts.latex: By considering the equation of the tangent to $y=x^2-1$ at the point $(a,a^2-1)$, find the equations of the two tangents to $y=x^2-1$ which pass through $(3,-8)$.

dif.r: general tangent at (a,a^2-1) through external point gives quadratic in a

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{226_q31_1}
$$y = x^2 - 1$$
$$y' = 2x$$
Gradient of tangent at $x = a$ is $2a$.

$\therefore$ Equation of tangent at $(a, a^2 - 1)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y - \left(a^2 - 1\right) &= 2a(x - a) \\ y - a^2 + 1 &= 2ax - 2a^2 \\ y &= 2ax - a^2 - 1 \end{aligned}$$
Since the tangent passes through $(3, -8)$, then
$$\begin{aligned} -8 &= 6a - a^2 - 1 \\ a^2 - 6a - 7 &= 0 \\ (a-7)(a+1) &= 0 \\ a &= 7 \text{ or } a = -1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The equations of the two tangents are:

When $a = 7$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2(7)x - 7^2 - 1 \\ y &= 14x - 50 \end{aligned}$$
and when $a = -1$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2(-1)x - (-1)^2 - 1 \\ y &= -2x - 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitute $(3, -8)$ into the equation of the tangent at $x = a$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores of people are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.

It has been observed that the puzzle is generally completed more quickly by people with a high IQ.

It is known that 80% of people with an IQ greater than 130 can complete the puzzle in less than two hours.

A person chosen at random can complete the puzzle in less than two hours.

solutions.latex:
$$\int_0^6 \dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{A}{2}\left[\ln\left(x^2+4\right)\right]_0^6 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}(\ln 40 - \ln 4) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}\left(\ln\dfrac{40}{4}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{A}{2}\ln 10 &= 1 \\ A &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 10} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the anti-derivative of $\dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{A\left(x^2+4\right) - Ax(2x)}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{Ax^2 + 4A - 2Ax^2}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{4A - Ax^2}{\left(x^2+4\right)^2} = 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ 4A - Ax^2 &= 0 \\ Ax^2 &= 4A \\ x^2 &= 4 \\ x &= 2 \quad (x > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The mode of $X$ is 2.
criteria: Finds the correct derivative of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X < 2) &= \int_0^2 \dfrac{Ax}{x^2+4}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}\left[\ln\left(x^2+4\right)\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}(\ln 8 - \ln 4) \\ &= \dfrac{A}{2}\ln 2 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 10}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\ln 2 \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 10} \\ &= \log_{10} 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} &P(\text{IQ} > 130) \\ &= P\left(\dfrac{\text{IQ} - 100}{15} > \dfrac{130 - 100}{15}\right) \\ &= P(Z > 2) \\ &= 2.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} &P\left(\text{IQ} > 130 \;\middle|\; \text{Time to complete} < 2\right) \\ &= \dfrac{P\left(\text{IQ} > 130 \cap \text{Time to complete} < 2\right)}{P\left(\text{Time to complete} < 2\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2.5\%\times 80\%}{\log_{10} 2} \\ &= 0.06643\ldots \\ &= 0.066 \text{ (three decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to find the conditional probability, or equivalent merit

dif.r: GP sum condition gives r^(n+1)=2r-1, then E(X) general show-that

solutions.latex:
$$r + r^2 + \cdots + r^n = 1$$
Sum of GP with $a = r$, common ratio $= r$, number of terms $= n$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \dfrac{r\left(r^n - 1\right)}{r - 1} &= 1 \\ r^{n+1} - r &= r - 1 \\ r^{n+1} &= 2r - 1 \qquad (*) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum xP(X = x) \\ &= r\times r^n + r^2\times r^{n-1} + \cdots + r^n\times r \\ &= r^{n+1} + r^{n+1} + \cdots + r^{n+1} \\ &= r^{n+1}\times n \\ &= nr^{n+1} \\ &= n(2r - 1) \qquad \text{from } (*) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows $E(X) = nr^{n+1}$ and attempts to find the sum of probabilities using sum of GP formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is the range of the function $f(x)=x^2-1$?

solutions.latex:
$x^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, so
$$f(x) = x^2 - 1 \ge -1$$
and $f(x)$ takes every value from $-1$ upwards (the minimum $-1$ is at $x = 0$).
$$\therefore\ \text{range} = [-1, \infty)$$

Quotient rule:
$$h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{\big(g(x)\big)^2}$$
At $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} h'(1) &= \dfrac{4\times 8 - 2\times 12}{8^2} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{64} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{(2x+1)^2}\,dx$?

Write the integrand as a power of $(2x+1)$; the reverse chain rule divides by the inner derivative $2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int (2x+1)^{-2}\,dx &= \dfrac{(2x+1)^{-1}}{(-1)\times 2} + C \\ &= \dfrac{-1}{2(2x+1)} + C \end{aligned}$$

($\dfrac{3}{2\pi}$ is the height of the maximum, not the mode.)

parts.latex:
Liam is playing two games. He is equally likely to win each game. The probability that Liam will win at least one of the games is $80\%$.

Which of the following is closest to the probability that Liam will win both games?

dif.r: work backwards from P(at least one) to p, then p squared

solutions.latex:
Let $p$ be the probability Liam wins a game. Losing both is the complement of winning at least one:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - (1-p)^2 &= 0.8 \\ (1-p)^2 &= 0.2 \\ 1 - p &= \sqrt{0.2} \approx 0.447 \\ p &\approx 0.553 \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{wins both}) = p^2 \approx 0.553^2 \approx 0.31 = 31\%$$

dif.r: composite graph from two sketches: asymptotes, evenness, signs

figures.cap: graphs of y=f(x) (parabola through origin) and y=g(x) (hyperbola-like curve with vertical asymptote right of the y-axis)
option A graph
option B graph
option C graph
option D graph

solutions.latex:
Let $c > 0$ be the $x$-value of the vertical asymptote of $y = g(x)$.

$g(f(x))$ is undefined where $f(x) = x^2 = c$, so it has vertical asymptotes at $x = \pm\sqrt{c}$. $f$ is even, so $g(f(x))$ is even: the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

For $|x| > \sqrt{c}$: $f(x) > c$, where $g$ is positive and tends to $0$, so $y > 0$ and $y \to 0$ as $x \to \pm\infty$.

For $|x| < \sqrt{c}$: $0 \le f(x) < c$, where $g$ is negative (except $g(0) = 0$), so the graph passes through the origin and drops towards $-\infty$ near both asymptotes.

Graph B is the only graph with these features.

Arithmetic series
$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big)$$
with $a = 3$, $d = 3$
$$\begin{aligned} S_{12} &= \dfrac{12}{2}(2 \times 3 + 11 \times 3) \\ &= 234 \end{aligned}$$

There are 23 rows.

parts.latex:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is translated $m$ units to the right, dilated vertically by a scale factor of $k$ and then translated 5 units down. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=3x^2-12x+7$.

Find the values of $m$ and $k$.

dif.r: build k(x-m)^2-5 from description, then equate coefficients or complete square

B.note: Alternative: completing the square on g(x)

Translations of graphs.reason: Shifting m right and 5 down must be applied to write g.

Dilations of graphs.evidence: g(x) = k(x - m)^2 - 5 ... By inspection k = 3
Dilations of graphs.reason: The vertical dilation by k must be applied and recognised.

Combined transformations.reason: A translation, a dilation and a translation are applied in sequence to form g.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= k(x - m)^2 - 5 \\ &= k\left(x^2 - 2xm + m^2\right) - 5 \\ &= kx^2 - 2mkx + m^2k - 5 \end{aligned}$$
By inspection $k = 3$.

By equating coefficient of $x$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2mk &= 12 \\ 6m &= 12 \\ m &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternate solution
$$g(x) = k(x - m)^2 - 5$$
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= 3x^2 - 12x + 7 \\ &= 3\left(x^2 - 4x\right) + 7 \\ &= 3\left(x^2 - 4x + 4\right) + 7 - 12 \\ &= 3(x - 2)^2 - 5 \end{aligned}$$
So $k = 3$ and $m = 2$.
criteria: Writes $g(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $k$, and finds value of $k$, or equivalent merit
Writes $g(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $k$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the rate of increase in the number of bacteria 24 hours after starting the experiment?

dif.r: differentiate ae^{kt} and substitute

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} N(0) &= 200e^{0} \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} N(24) &= 200e^{0.013 \times 24} \\ &= 273.23\ldots \\ &\approx 273 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 200 \times 0.013 \times e^{0.013t}$$
When $t = 24$,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= 0.013 \times 273 \quad \text{(from part (b))} \\ &= 3.55 \end{aligned}$$
Rate of increase $= 3.55$ bacteria/hour.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=\sin(2x)$.

Find the value of $x$, for $0<x<\pi$, for which $f'(x)=-\sqrt{3}$ AND $f''(x)=2$.

dif.r: two double-angle trig equations, common solution in domain

A.note: Two conditions must be combined; marks split between differentiating and solving.

B.note: Marks split between differentiating sin 2x twice and solving cos 2x and sin 2x equations; equation solving taken as primary.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sin 2x \\ f'(x) &= 2\cos 2x \\ f''(x) &= -4\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
When $f'(x) = -\sqrt{3}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 2x &= -\sqrt{3} \\ \cos 2x &= \dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
When $f''(x) = 2$,
$$\begin{aligned} -4\sin 2x &= 2 \\ \sin 2x &= \dfrac{-1}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ for } 0 < x < \pi$$
criteria: Finds the values of $x$, $0 < x < \pi$, for each derivative equation
Attempts to find a value for $x$ that solves $f'(x)$ or $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points where $f'(x) = 0$
$$(1 - 2x)e^{-2x} = 0$$
$$x = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \text{since } e^{-2x} \neq 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{-1} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= 4 \times -\dfrac{1}{2} \times e^{-1} \\ &= -2e^{-1} \\ &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2e}\right) \text{ is a local maximum.}$$
criteria: Finds the $x$ value of the stationary point

solutions.latex:
Possible point of inflection where $f''(x) = 0$
$$4(x - 1)e^{-2x} = 0$$
$$\therefore\ x = 1, \qquad \text{since } e^{-2x} \neq 0$$
\extable{Ts212_1}

Changes concavity at $x = 1$.

$\therefore$ Inflection point at $x = 1$
$$\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 1e^{-2 \times 1} \\ &= e^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
$\left(1, \dfrac{1}{e^2}\right)$ is an inflection point.

As $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to 0$

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x = y = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{a}{b} - 1 \\ \therefore\ \dfrac{a}{b} &= 1 \\ \therefore\ a &= b \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x = y = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \dfrac{a}{b - 1} - 1 \\ 1 &= \dfrac{a}{a - 1} - 1 \\ \dfrac{a}{a - 1} &= 2 \\ a &= 2a - 2 \\ \therefore\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b = 2$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area under curve (hyperbola)} &= \int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{2}{2 - x} - 1\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-2\ln(2 - x) - x\Big]_0^1 \\ &= -2\ln 1 - 1 + 2\ln 2 - 0 \\ &= 2\ln 2 - 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area} &= 2\ln 2 - 1 + \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 2\ln 2 + \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{3}{2} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases} 1 & x>e^3 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{k}\ln x & 1\le x\le e^3 \\[6pt] 0 & x<1 \end{cases}.$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=3$.

dif.r: F(e^3)=1, one substitution

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that $P(X<c)=2P(X>c)$, find the exact value of $c$.

dif.r: turn P(X<c)=2P(X>c) into F(c)=2/3, solve log

solutions.latex:
We need $F\left(e^3\right) = 1$, since $F(x)$ is a CDF.
$$\begin{aligned} F\left(e^3\right) &= \dfrac{1}{k}\ln e^3 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{k} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{3}{k} = 1$.
$$\therefore\ k = 3$$

$$P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} P(X < c) &= 2\left[1 - P(X < c)\right] \\ 3P(X < c) &= 2 \\ P(X < c) &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(c) = \dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\ln c &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ \ln c &= 2 \\ c &= e^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises that $P(X > c) = 1 - P(X < c)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A line passes through the point $P(1,2)$ and meets the axes at $X(x,0)$ and $Y(0,y)$, where $x>1$.

\exfigure{268_q31_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $y=\dfrac{2x}{x-1}$.

dif.r: collinearity/gradient set-up then algebra

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the minimum value of the area of triangle $XOY$.

dif.r: form area x^2/(x-1), quotient rule, justify minimum

figures.cap: line through P(1,2) meeting axes at X(x,0) and Y(0,y); triangle XOY shaded

solutions.latex:
$$\text{Gradient } XP = \text{gradient } PY$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{0 - 2}{x - 1} &= \dfrac{y - 2}{0 - 1} \\ (x - 1)(y - 2) &= 2 \\ y - 2 &= \dfrac{2}{x - 1} \\ y &= \dfrac{2}{x - 1} + 2 \\ &= \dfrac{2 + 2x - 2}{x - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{2x}{x - 1} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Equates the two expressions for the gradients, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$A = \dfrac{x^2}{x - 1} \qquad \left[\text{from } A = \dfrac{1}{2}xy \text{ and } y = \dfrac{2x}{x - 1}\right]$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{(x - 1)2x - x^2(1)}{(x - 1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2 - 2x - x^2}{(x - 1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - 2x}{(x - 1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x - 2)}{(x - 1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$ when $x = 0$ or $x = 2$.

Discard $x = 0$ since $x > 1$ (from question).

\extable{Ts222_1}

Slope changes from negative to positive, so $x = 2$ is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{4}{2 - 1} \\ \therefore\ \text{Minimum area} &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$ and determines the nature of the stationary point at $x = 2$
Attempts to find the area in terms of $x$

solutions.latex:
From the graph: the curve crosses the $x$-axis once at a negative value and touches it (a double root) at a positive value. It does not pass through the origin, so the equation is $y = -(x-b)(x-c)^2$, not $y = -x(x-b)(x-c)$.

The single root $b$ is negative and the double root $c$ is positive: $b < 0$, $c > 0$.

(The leading coefficient is negative, matching the curve rising on the left and falling on the right.)

The diagram shows the graph $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is an odd function.

The shaded area is 1 square unit.

What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx$?

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: graph of odd function with shaded area between x=0 and x=1, points -a and a marked

solutions.latex:
The shaded region between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ is below the $x$-axis with area $1$:
$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = -1$$
$f$ is odd, so $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$, and
$$\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$$
By odd symmetry, $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx = -\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = 0$.
$$\therefore\ \int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx = 0 + (-1) = -1$$

dif.r: match derivative sign table to graph, horizontal inflection

option B sketch
option C sketch
option D sketch

solutions.latex:
Read the table at each $x$-value:
$$\begin{aligned} &x = -2: &&f' > 0,\ f'' < 0 &&\text{increasing, concave down}\\ &x = 0: &&f' = 0,\ f'' = 0 &&\text{horizontal point of inflection}\\ &x = 2: &&f' > 0,\ f'' > 0 &&\text{increasing, concave up} \end{aligned}$$
Graph C is the only sketch that is increasing and concave down at $x = -2$, flat with a change of concavity at the origin, and increasing and concave up at $x = 2$.

It is given that $y=f\big(g(x)\big)$, where $f(1)=3$, $f'(1)=-4$, $g(5)=1$ and $g'(5)=2$.

dif.r: chain rule with given values; must evaluate f' at g(5)

solutions.latex:
Chain rule:
$$y' = f'\big(g(x)\big)\,g'(x)$$
At $x = 5$, with $g(5) = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'(5) &= f'(1)\times g'(5) \\ &= -4\times 2 \\ &= -8 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be any function with domain all real numbers.

Which of the following is an even function, regardless of the choice of $f(x)$?

dif.r: test f(-x) on abstract expressions, reject others

solutions.latex:
Let $h(x) = f(x)f(-x)$. Replacing $x$ by $-x$:
$$h(-x) = f(-x)f(x) = h(x)$$
so $h$ is even for every function $f$.

The others depend on $f$: for example, with $f(x) = x$, the functions $2f(x) = 2x$ and $f\big(f(x)\big) = x$ are odd, and with $f(x) = x + 1$, $\big(f(-x)\big)^2 = (1-x)^2$ is not even.

The fourth term of a geometric sequence is 48.

solutions.latex:
Let $a$ be the first term and $r$ the common ratio.

Then
$$ar^3=48 \qquad (1)$$
and
$$ar^7=\dfrac{3}{16} \qquad (2)$$
Dividing (2) by (1),
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{ar^7}{ar^3}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{16}}{48}\\\therefore\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{256}\\\therefore\ r&=\pm\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
If $r=\dfrac{1}{4}$,
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3&=48\\\therefore\ a&=3072\end{aligned}$$
If $r=-\dfrac{1}{4}$,
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3&=48\\\therefore\ a&=-3072\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}50&=(x-2)(y-1)\\\dfrac{50}{x-2}&=y-1\end{aligned}$$
So $y=\dfrac{50}{x-2}+1$ as required.

Area of concrete path is $2y+x-2$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\left(\dfrac{50}{x-2}+1\right)+x-2\\A&=2\left(\dfrac{50}{x-2}\right)+2+x-2\\A&=\dfrac{100}{x-2}+x\\&=100(x-2)^{-1}+x\end{aligned}$$

Since $x$ is a distance, discard $-8$.

Stationary point at $x=12$.

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-6x-8$$
Tangent at $(-1,6)$ is $y=x+7$.

Slope of tangent is 1.

Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$, i.e.
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x-8&=1\\3x^2-6x-9&=0\\3(x^2-2x-3)&=0\\3(x-3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So the $x$-coordinate of $R$ is 3.

When $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-6x-8$,
$$y=x^3-3x^2-8x+k$$
and when $x=-1$, $y=6$.

When $x=3$,
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^3-3x^2-8x+2\\&=27-27-24+2\\&=-22\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Coordinates of $R$ are $(3,-22)$.

solutions.latex:
Mode of $X$ will be when $f(x)$ has a maximum.
$$f(x)=12x^2-12x^3,\qquad0\le x\le1$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=24x-36x^2\\&=12x(2-3x)\end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)=0$ when $x=0$ and when $2-3x=0$, $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Discard $x=0$ since $f(0)=0$, so the mode of $X$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x12t^2(1-t)\,dt\\&=\int_0^x\left(12t^2-12t^3\right)dt\\&=\left[4t^3-3t^4\right]_0^x\\&=4x^3-3x^4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses $F(x)$ as an integral of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$,
$$\begin{aligned}4x^3-3x^4&=4\times\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)-3\times\left(\dfrac{16}{81}\right)\\&=0.59\end{aligned}$$
The probability of the variable being less than $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is greater than 0.5, therefore the mode is greater than the median.
criteria: Substitutes the mode from part (a) into their cumulative distribution function, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The curves $y=e^{-2x}$ and $y=e^{-x}-\dfrac{1}{4}$ intersect at exactly one point as shown in the diagram. The point of intersection has coordinates $\left(\ln 2,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$. (Do NOT prove this.)

\exfigure{296_q32_1}
questions.review_note: AUDIT audit-v1: ok

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area bounded by the two curves and the y-axis, as shaded in the diagram, is $\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2-\dfrac{1}{8}$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the values of $k$ such that the curves $y=e^{-2x}$ and $y=e^{-x}+k$ intersect at two points.

dif.r: quadratic in e^{-x}, needs both roots positive: insight

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

figures.cap: curves y=e^{-2x} and y=e^{-x}-1/4 touching at (ln 2, 1/4), region shaded near y-axis

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Shaded area}&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left[e^{-2x}-\left(e^{-x}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\right]dx\\&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(e^{-2x}-e^{-x}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}+e^{-x}+\dfrac{1}{4}x\right]_0^{\ln2}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2\ln2}+e^{-\ln2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+1+0\right)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\ln\left(2^{-2}\right)}+e^{\ln\left(2^{-1}\right)}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{8}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides an antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Provides an integral expression for the area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
We want the equation $e^{-2x}=e^{-x}+k$ to have 2 solutions.

i.e. $e^{-2x}-e^{-x}-k=0$ has 2 solutions

i.e. $\left(e^{-x}\right)^2-\left(e^{-x}\right)-k=0$ has 2 solutions.

Using the quadratic formula,
$$e^{-x}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$$
For two real solutions we want $1+4k>0$, i.e. $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

But for two solutions for $e^{-x}$, both the real solutions to the quadratic must be positive.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \sqrt{1+4k}&<1\\\therefore\ 1+4k&<1\\\therefore\ k&<0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{4}<k<0$$
criteria: Uses the discriminant to find $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Suppose the graph of $y=f(x)$ has an $x$-intercept at 1, a $y$-intercept at 2, a minimum turning point $(5,\,-5)$ and a single horizontal asymptote $y=-4$.

What can you say is definitely true about the graph of $y=-f(x-2)$?

dif.r: reflection plus shift tracked through turning point and asymptote

Translations of graphs.evidence: f(x−2) shifts the graph 2 units right: the minimum moves to (7,−5)
Translations of graphs.reason: Translation needed for correct option C

Combined transformations.reason: −f(x−2) is a horizontal shift plus vertical reflection; order does not matter, so counts_when not met

Reflections of graphs.evidence: −f(x−2) reflects that in the x-axis: minimum becomes a maximum (7,5)
Reflections of graphs.reason: Reflection needed for correct option C

options.label: C
options.latex: It has a maximum turning point at $(7,\,5)$.

options.label: D
options.latex: Its horizontal asymptote cannot be determined.

solutions.latex:
Draw a possible $y=f(x)$ with the given features, then apply the two transformations.

\exfigure{408_q7_s1}

$y=f(x-2)$ shifts the graph $2$ units right: the minimum moves to $(7,-5)$, the $x$-intercept to $3$, the asymptote stays $y=-4$.

$y=-f(x-2)$ reflects that in the $x$-axis: the minimum $(7,-5)$ becomes a maximum $(7,5)$ and the asymptote becomes $y=4$.

The $y$-intercept of $y=-f(x-2)$ is $-f(-2)$, which is not given, so B cannot be confirmed; A is wrong ($x$-intercept $3$) and D is wrong (asymptote $y=4$).

$\therefore$ It has a maximum turning point at $(7,5)$.

parts.latex: A bag contains six white socks and eight black socks. Two socks are selected at random without replacement. Given the two selected socks are the same colour, which of the following is the closest to the probability that they are both black?

dif.r: conditional on compound event same colour, without replacement

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both black} \mid \text{same colour}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{both black and same colour})}{P(\text{same colour})} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{8}{14}\times\frac{7}{13}}{\frac{8}{14}\times\frac{7}{13}+\frac{6}{14}\times\frac{5}{13}} \\ &\approx 65\% \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: f' graph: read inflection from min of f'

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

options.label: A
options.latex: $f(x)$ has a minimum turning point at $x=a$.

options.label: B
options.latex: $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=b$.

options.label: C
options.latex: $f(x)$ has a maximum turning point at $x=c$.

options.label: D
options.latex: $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=c$.

figures.cap: graph of y=f'(x) with x-values a, b, c marked

solutions.latex:
Read the features of $f(x)$ from the graph of $y=f'(x)$:

At $x=a$, $f'(x)=0$ and changes from positive to negative, so $f(x)$ has a maximum turning point there (A is false).

At $x=b$, $f'(x)$ has a minimum turning point, so $f''(x)=0$ and $f''(x)$ changes from negative to positive: the concavity of $f(x)$ changes, so $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=b$.

At $x=c$, $f'(x)=0$ and changes from negative to positive, so $f(x)$ has a minimum turning point there, not a maximum or a point of inflection (C and D are false).

$\therefore$ $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=b$.

parts.latex: The function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\cos(\alpha-2x)$ is odd. Its graph also increases in the interval of $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. What is a possible value of $\alpha$?

dif.r: MCQ: odd condition fixes cos(alpha)=0, then test increasing on interval

solutions.latex:
Since $f$ is odd, $f(0) = \sqrt{3}\cos\alpha = 0$, so $\cos\alpha = 0$.

$\therefore$ eliminate B and C.

If $\alpha = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2x\right) \\ &= -\sqrt{3}\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
which decreases on $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (sketch).

If $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
which increases on $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (sketch).

$\therefore\ \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.stem:
Recycled plastic materials can contain bacteria from previous usage. To ensure the plastic is clean and safe for recycling, it is heated to $135^\circ\text{C}$ for a certain period to kill the bacteria present.

The number of bacteria $N$ in the plastic after $t$ minutes at $135^\circ\text{C}$ is given by:
$$N(t)=4800e^{-0.3t}, \quad t\ge 0$$

parts.label: a

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b

$$N(t) = 50\%\times 4800 = 2400$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4800e^{-0.3t} &= 2400 \\ e^{-0.3t} &= 0.5 \\ -0.3t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln(0.5)}{0.3} \\ &= 2.310\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ t \approx 2$ minutes $19$ seconds.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= 4800(-0.3)e^{-0.3t} \\ &= -1440e^{-0.3t} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= -1440\times e^{-1.5} \\ &\approx -321 \text{ bacteria/min} \end{aligned}$$
The number decreases at $321$ bacteria/min.

questions.stem: Consider the geometric series: $\sin^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^4\theta+\cdots$, where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the limiting sum of the series.

dif.r: a/(1-r) then Pythagorean identity gives 1

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is $r = \cos^2\theta$.

Since $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 < \cos\theta &< 1 \\ 0 < \cos^2\theta &< 1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ |r| < 1$, so the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x^2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$. You do NOT need to check the nature of the stationary points.

dif.r: product and chain rule, solve 1-2x^2=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Without using any further calculus, sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, showing stationary points, any intercepts and asymptotes.

dif.r: sketch from stationary points; odd function, limit to zero

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2xe^{-x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= x\left(-2xe^{-x^2}\right) + e^{-x^2} \\ &= (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} &= 0 \\ 1 - 2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
When $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
$\therefore$ The stationary points are
$$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$
and
$$\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) = \dfrac{x}{e^{x^2}} &\to 0^+ &&\text{as } x \to \infty\\ f(x) = \dfrac{x}{e^{x^2}} &\to 0^- &&\text{as } x \to -\infty \end{aligned}$$

$f(x)$ is an odd function.

parts.latex:
The lamp shown in the diagram below can move along the vertical line $OB$ using a pulley system. The point $A$ lies on the horizontal line $OA$ at a distance of $d$ from $O$. The intensity $I$ of light from the lamp at point $A$ is inversely proportional to the square of its distance $r$ from the lamp. The intensity $I$ is also directly proportional to $\sin\phi$, where $\phi$ is the angle of elevation from $A$ to the lamp. Hence, the formula for $I$ can be expressed as:
$$I=\dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}, \quad \text{where } C \text{ is a positive constant.}$$
Determine the height $h$ of the lamp above the line $OA$ that maximizes the intensity of light at the point $A$. Express your answer in terms of $d$.

\exfigure{408_q31_1}

dif.r: build I=kh/(h^2+d^2)^(3/2) from geometry then maximise

figures.cap: lamp at B above O, right triangle OAB with height h, base d, hypotenuse r, angle phi at A

solutions.latex:
The lamp is $h$ above $O$ and $A$ is $d$ from $O$, so $O$, $A$ and the lamp form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$r^2 = h^2 + d^2$$
$\phi$ is the angle at $A$, and the side opposite it is $h$:
$$\sin\phi = \dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$$
Substitute both into $I = \dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}$ to write $I$ in terms of $h$ only:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= C\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{h^2+d^2}\right) \\ &= Ch(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dh} &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} + Ch\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)(2h)(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}} \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}\left[(h^2+d^2) - 3h^2\right] \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}(d^2 - 2h^2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $C>0$ and $(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}>0$, $\dfrac{dI}{dh}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 - 2h^2 &= 0 \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} \\ h &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d \quad (h>0) \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dh}$ is the sign of $d^2-2h^2$. Test either side:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{d}{2}: & d^2-2\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} > 0 \\ h &= d: & d^2-2d^2 &= -d^2 < 0 \end{aligned}$$
$I$ increases then decreases, so the stationary point is a maximum.

$\therefore$ The intensity at $A$ is greatest when $h = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d$.
criteria: Makes a suitable substitution, $\sin\phi=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$, or equivalent merit

For the $y$-intercept, $x = 0$: $h(0) = b - 1$.

For the $x$-intercept:

solutions.latex:
$$\int_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \left(-3^{-x} + b\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[\dfrac{3^{-x}}{\ln 3} + bx\right]_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + 0\right) - \left(\dfrac{3^{\log_3 b}}{\ln 3} - b\log_3 b\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b \end{aligned}$$
LHS = RHS:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= 0 \\ b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$
Since $b \ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \dfrac{\ln b}{\ln 3} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \ln b &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b = e$$

The region is between the curve and the $y$-axis, from $y = 1$ ($x = 0$) to $y = 4$ ($x = 2$).

It is the rectangle $0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le 4$ minus the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$:

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the distance between the maximum and minimum:
$$\text{Amplitude} = \dfrac{5 - (-1)}{2} = 3$$
The period of $\cos 6x$ is
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
For the phase, factor the $6$ out of the angle:
$$6x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 6\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$$
so the phase is $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

A bricklayer is building a wall in the shape of a triangle where each row contains 3 bricks less than the row immediately below.

The bottom row of the wall contains 150 bricks.

If it takes the bricklayer 10 seconds to install each brick, how many rows of the wall will be completed after 6 hours?

dif.r: Model bricks as arithmetic series, convert time, test bounding n.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
In 6 hours the bricklayer lays
$$\dfrac{6\times 60\times 60}{10} = 2160 \text{ bricks}$$
The rows form an arithmetic series with $a = 150$ and $d = -3$:
$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times 150 + (n-1)(-3)\big) = \dfrac{n}{2}(303 - 3n)$$
$$\begin{aligned} S_{17} &= \dfrac{17}{2}(303 - 51) = 2142 \le 2160 \\ S_{18} &= 9(303 - 54) = 2241 > 2160 \end{aligned}$$
So 17 rows are completed.

parts.latex: For what values of $b$ is the function $y=x^4+bx^3-3x^2$ concave up and decreasing at the point where $x=1$?

dif.r: Combine first and second derivative sign conditions into parameter inequality.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 + 3bx^2 - 6x \\ y'' &= 12x^2 + 6bx - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Decreasing at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 + 3b - 6 &< 0 \\ b &< \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Concave up at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12 + 6b - 6 &> 0 \\ b &> -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1 < b < \dfrac{2}{3}, \text{ that is } b \in \left(-1, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$$

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

dif.r: integrate, find C from rest times, sign of v to graph x

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

parts.latex:
Katrina runs a business refurbishing old computers.

The cost, $C$ dollars, of refurbishing $n$ computers is given by $C=3n^2+100$.

The income, $I$ dollars, received from selling $n$ computers is given by $I=80n$.

dif.r: Set up profit inequality, solve quadratic, interpret integer bounds.

solutions.latex:
Solve $3n^2+100=80n$.

$$\begin{aligned}3n^2-80n+100&=0\\ n&=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{(-80)^2-4\times 3\times 100}}{2\times 3}\\ n&=1.315,\ 25.352\end{aligned}$$

Katrina will make a profit when $I>C$ and this occurs for $2\le n\le 25$, where $n$ represents the number of computers refurbished and sold.

Hence, the minimum number is 2 and the maximum number is 25 in order to make a profit.

solutions.latex:
Sum of probabilities equals 1: $$\begin{aligned}0.05+p+p+q+0.01&=1\\ 2p+q&=0.94\quad(1)\end{aligned}$$

$E(X)=2.08$: $$\begin{aligned}(0\times 0.05)+(1\times p)+(2\times p)+(3\times q)+(4\times 0.01)&=2.08\\ 3p+3q&=2.04\\ p+q&=0.68\quad(2)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The shoe size of women in a town is normally distributed with a mean size of 8 and a standard deviation of 1.

A shoe shop in the town sells women's shoes ranging from size 5 to size 10.

Given that there are 4000 women in the town, how many would be expected to find shoes that fit them in this shop?

dif.r: z-scores and empirical rule halves combined, scaled to population.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
$z$-score corresponding to size 5: $$z=\dfrac{5-8}{1}=-3$$

$z$-score corresponding to size 10: $$z=\dfrac{10-8}{1}=2$$

By the empirical rule, the area under the standard normal curve from $z=-3$ to $z=2$ is $$\dfrac{99.7\%}{2}+\dfrac{95\%}{2}=97.35\%$$

$$4000\times 97.35\%=3894$$

3894 women in the town can be expected to buy shoes that fit them.
criteria: Uses empirical rule to determine the percentage corresponding to the range of sizes, or equivalent merit
Finds $z$-scores corresponding to size 5 and size 10, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=2x-\sin x$.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.

dif.r: Routine check f(-x)=-f(x) using sin odd.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Use odd symmetry to double area integral, avoiding cancellation.

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Show that $-f(x)=f(-x)$.

$$-f(x)=-2x+\sin x$$

$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=2(-x)-\sin(-x)\\ &=-2x-(-\sin x)\\ &=-2x+\sin x\\ &=-f(x)\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore\ f(x)$ is an odd function.

Using the symmetry property of $f(x)$ from part (a):

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_0^{\pi}(2x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=2\Big[x^2+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi}\\ &=2\big((\pi^2+\cos\pi)-(0^2+\cos 0)\big)\\ &=2(\pi^2-2)\\ &=2\pi^2-4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Determines the definite integral without considering the signed area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Ashford ($A$), Brookdale ($B$) and Carlton ($C$) are three country towns.

Brookdale is 85 km east and 33 km north of Ashford.

Carlton is on a bearing of $026^\circ$ from Ashford and $321^\circ$ from Brookdale.

Jo completes a cross-country drive which starts and finishes in Ashford and passes through Brookdale and Carlton.

Calculate the total distance that Jo travelled, correct to the nearest kilometre.

\exfigure{510_q22_1}

dif.r: Multi-step bearings: derive triangle angles, then sine rule twice for perimeter

figures.cap: bearing diagram of towns A, B, C with 85 km and 33 km

solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem: $$AB=\sqrt{85^2+33^2}=91.181\ldots$$

$$\text{Angle }DAB=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{33}{85}\right)=21^\circ 13'$$

$$\text{Angle }CAB=90^\circ-26^\circ-21^\circ 13'=42^\circ 47'$$

$$\text{Angle }ACB=(360^\circ-321^\circ)+26^\circ=65^\circ\quad\text{(angles at a point and alternate angles)}$$

$$\text{Angle }ABC=180^\circ-65^\circ-42^\circ 47'=72^\circ 13'\quad\text{(angle sum of triangle }ABC\text{)}$$

By the sine rule: $$AC=\dfrac{\sin 72^\circ 13'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=95.800$$

$$BC=\dfrac{\sin 42^\circ 47'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=68.335$$

Alternatively, $BC$ may be determined using the cosine rule: $$BC=\sqrt{91.181^2+95.800^2-2\times 91.181\times 95.800\times\cos 42^\circ 47'}=68.335$$

Perimeter of triangle $ABC$: $$91.181+95.800+68.335=255.316$$

The total distance travelled is 255 km, correct to the nearest kilometre.
criteria: Determines the length of the other sides of triangle $ABC$ using sine or cosine rule
Finds all angles in triangle $ABC$ and distance $AB$ or equivalent merit
Finds both distance $AB$ and angle $DAB$, or equivalent merit
Finds either distance $AB$ or angle $DAB$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the cosine-rule line used $68.335$ in place of $95.800$.

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right), & \text{for } 0\le x\le\pi \\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}.$$
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images | AUDIT audit-v1: ok

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$.

dif.r: Standard pdf normalisation; integrate sec squared with linear inner function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the median of $X$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Median from cumulative integral, solving tan equation with inverse

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

req: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

Cumulative distribution functions.reason: Sets F(t)=0.5; not_when says median from F(m)=0.5 also gets Median, i.e. both; kept when unsure

Trigonometric equations.reason: Must solve tan of a linear argument for t

solutions.latex:
Solve for $k$:

$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx&=1\\ 3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{\pi}&=1\\ 3k\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\ 3k\times\sqrt{3}&=1\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: States correct equation and attempts to solve for $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), solve for $t$: $$3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}=0.5,\text{ where }k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

$$\begin{aligned}3\times\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}&=0.5\\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)&=0.5\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)&=0.5\times\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t=3\tan^{-1}(0.5\times\sqrt{3})=2.14\text{ (correct to two decimal places)}$$
criteria: States correct equation attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x-2}}$.

Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Quotient rule with surd, messy simplification, then nature test

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=\sqrt{x-2}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{4x}{2\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Solve $f'(x)=0$ to find any stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{x-2}-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}&=0\\ 4(x-2)-2x&=0\\ 4x-8-2x&=0\\ 2x&=8\end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=4$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{4\times 4}{\sqrt{4-2}}=8\sqrt{2}$$
A stationary point exists at $(4,8\sqrt{2})$.

Using a table of gradients to determine the nature of the stationary point:

\extable{Ts418_1}

Hence the stationary point is a local minimum.
criteria: Finds the location of the stationary point, or equivalent merit
Finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The rate of fuel consumption of a particular vehicle may be modelled by the formula

$$R=5+4e^{-0.5t},$$

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

In the first hour of travel, the vehicle consumed 25 litres of fuel.

Determine the amount of fuel consumed after 4 hours of travel, correct to the nearest litre.

dif.r: Integrate rate model, find constant from non-zero condition, interpret context

solutions.latex:
The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=1$, the vehicle has consumed 25 litres of fuel since the start of the journey.

Finding the constant of integration, $c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25 &= 5(1)-8e^{-0.5(1)}+c \\ 20 &= -8e^{-0.5}+c \\ c &= 20+8e^{-0.5} \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=4$, the amount of fuel the vehicle consumed is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F &= 5(4)-8e^{-0.5(4)}+20+8e^{-0.5} \\ &= 43.7695\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ After 4 hours of travel, the vehicle has consumed 44 litres of fuel.
criteria: Finds the value of the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Correctly integrates expression representing rate of fuel consumption, or equivalent merit

questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images; Question is crossed out by hand with a large X on the scanned paper (possibly removed from this sitting); confirm whether it should be kept.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Maroun is going to withdraw \$7500 at the end of each month, starting from the end of the sixth month.

The recurrence relation $A_n=A_{n-1}\times 1.003-7500$ models this situation, where $A_n$ is the balance in the retirement fund at the end of the $n$th month.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Maroun is offered an alternative retirement fund, where interest is paid at 3.2% per annum, compounded daily.

By calculating the effective annual rate of interest for both retirement funds, or otherwise, determine whether Maroun should remain with the current retirement fund or change to the alternative retirement fund.

dif.r: Compute two effective annual rates and compare

figures.cap: incomplete retirement fund table (crossed out by hand)

solutions.latex:
Balance at the end of the fourth month:
$$496994.00+1490.98-3800=494684.98$$

$\therefore$ Balance at the end of the fourth month is $\$494\,684.98$.

Interest earned at the end of the fifth month:
$$494684.98\times 0.003=1484.05$$

$\therefore$ Interest earned at the end of the fifth month is $\$1484.05$.

Amount Maroun withdrew at the end of the fifth month:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Balance} &= P+I-M \\ M &= P+I-\text{Balance} \\ &= 494684.98+1484.05-491969.03 \\ &= 4200 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ Maroun withdrew $\$4200$ at the end of the fifth month.
criteria: Finds the interest earned at the end of the fifth month, or equivalent merit
Finds the balance at the end of the fourth month, or equivalent merit
Determines the balance at the end of the sixth month, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Effective annual rate of interest for the current retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} (1+0.003)^{12}-1 &= 0.036599\ldots \\ &\approx 3.66\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$

Effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(1+\dfrac{0.032}{365}\right)^{365}-1 &= 0.032516\ldots \\ &\approx 3.25\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$

The effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund is less than Maroun's current retirement fund, hence Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund.

Alternatively, compare the future value (FV) of one dollar invested in both funds.

Current fund:

questions.stem:
A rocket is returning back to Earth after completing a space mission.

Its distance from Earth can be modelled by the equation

$$S=55000\times 3^{-0.182t},$$

where $S$ is the distance from Earth in kilometres at time $t$ hours after it begins its return journey.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images | AUDIT audit-v1: ok

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the speed of the rocket after 2 hours on its return journey.

dif.r: Differentiate base-3 exponential, substitute, take magnitude for speed

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
When the rocket reaches a distance of 1000 km from Earth, a parachute is released.

How long, in hours, after the rocket begins its return journey does it release its parachute? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation using logarithms

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(t)=\dfrac{dS}{dt} &= -0.182\times\ln 3\times 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182t} \end{aligned}$$

Speed of the rocket at time $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(2) &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182\times 2} \\ &= -7372.3576\ldots \\ \text{speed} &= |S'(2)| \approx 7372 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The speed of the rocket 2 hours after it begins its return journey is $7372 \text{ km/h}$.
criteria: Correctly differentiates to find an equation for speed, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: an absolute value was set equal to a negative number.

solutions.latex:
Let $S=1000$ and solve the equation for $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ \dfrac{1}{55} &= 3^{-0.182t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right) &= -0.182t\times\ln 3 \\ t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right)\div(-0.182\times\ln 3) \\ &= 20.0419\ldots \\ &\approx 20.04 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The rocket deploys its parachute 20.04 hours after it begins its return journey.
criteria: Attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule plus exact integral, then difference; two routine techniques

figures.cap: curve y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4 with trapezia, heights 4, 5.125, 13

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$

Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$

$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$

$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using either the trapezoidal rule or integration, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A ball is dropped from a height $H$ metres above the ground. Each time it strikes the ground, it rebounds to a lower height which is $q\%$ of its previous height.

Let $h_n$ be the height reached by the ball after the $n$th bounce.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images; Question is crossed out by hand with a large X on the scanned paper (possibly removed from this sitting); confirm whether it should be kept.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that, after the second bounce, the ball rebounds to a height given by

$$h_2=\dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2}.$$

dif.r: Translate percentage rebound into geometric terms symbolically

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

A.note: percentage rebound; could be Applications

req: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences
B.note: bouncing ball GP

Applications of arithmetic and geometric.evidence: Attempts to model height of bounce as a geometric progression
Applications of arithmetic and geometric.reason: Identifying a GP from a bouncing-ball context earns the first mark.

Geometric growth and decay.reason: A bouncing ball is a worded AP/GP application, not population/depreciation growth; covered by Applications.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the total distance, $D$, travelled by the ball is given by

$$D=\dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q}.$$

dif.r: General show-that: model up-and-down distance as limiting sum, symbolic algebra

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Initial height of the ball is $H$ metres.

The height after the $n$th bounce is the $n$th term of the geometric progression with first term $a=\dfrac{qH}{100}$ (the first rebound) and common ratio $r=\dfrac{q}{100}$, $0<q<100$.

Height after the second bounce:
$$\begin{aligned} h_n &= T_n=ar^{n-1} \\ h_2 &= \dfrac{qH}{100}\times\dfrac{q}{100} \\ &= \dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to model height of bounce as a geometric progression, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the first term was given as $H$, which would make $h_2=\dfrac{qH}{100}$.

solutions.latex:
Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to simplify the expression involving the limiting sum, or equivalent merit
Correctly models the total distance involving the limiting sum, or equivalent merit
