solutions.latex:
At a critics' score of $7.2$ the regression line gives a public's score of about $6.65$, so the new point $(7.2,\ 6)$ lies well below the line at the left end of the data.

Including it pulls the left end of the line down, so the gradient of the least-squares regression line increases (the line becomes steeper) and the $y$-intercept decreases.

meta.check: Re-fitted a least-squares line to the 23 points read from the scatterplot with and without (7.2, 6): gradient 0.53 to 0.57, intercept 2.82 to 2.42.
meta.concern: Open-ended 'identify ONE effect': increased gradient, decreased y-intercept (or weaker fit) should all be acceptable; solution names gradient increase as the main effect.

The process of decay can be modelled by the function

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=7-3x$ and $y=-x^2+x+12$. The graphs intersect at two points.

\exfigure{1632_q18_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the two points of intersection are $x=-1$ and $x=5$.

dif.r: equate, solve factorising quadratic

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the area enclosed by the line $y=7-3x$ and the parabola $y=-x^2+x+12$.

dif.r: standard area between curves, bounds given

figures.cap: parabola with x-intercepts -3 and 4 and a decreasing line

solutions.latex:
At the points of intersection the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 7-3x&=-x^2+x+12\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-1 \text{ or } x=5$$
criteria: Equates the two functions to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Substituted x=-1 (y=10 both) and x=5 (y=-8 both).

solutions.latex:
Between $x=-1$ and $x=5$ the parabola is above the line (at $x=0$: $12>7$), so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{5}\big((-x^2+x+12)-(7-3x)\big)\,dx\\ &=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{125}{3}+50+25\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\ &=\dfrac{100}{3}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\ &=36\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=36 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes a correct integral for the area, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Antiderivative evaluated by hand; cross-checked with the parabola-chord formula (b-a)^3/6 = 6^3/6 = 36.

dif.r: derivative sketch: max of f' at inflection, asymptote to zero

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

req: Graphs of f, f′ and f″
Graphs of f, f′ and f″

Asymptotes and limiting behaviour.evidence: As x→∞, f(x)→5 (horizontal asymptote), so f'(x)→0
Asymptotes and limiting behaviour.reason: Non-hyperbola horizontal asymptote/limit needed for f' behaviour as x→∞.

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: concave up for x<5 and concave down for x>5, so f' increases
Concavity and points of inflection.reason: Criterion needs maximum of f' at the point of inflection; requires concavity/POI meaning.

Stationary points and their nature.reason: Criterion 1 mark: shows f'(2)=0 at the local minimum.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with minimum at x=2, inflection at x=5, asymptote y=5
blank axes with x marks 2 and 5
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)$ is the gradient of $y=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le x<2 &&f \text{ decreasing}\\ f'(2)&=0 &&\text{local minimum}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x>2 &&f \text{ increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$f$ is concave up for $x<5$ and concave down for $x>5$, so $f'$ increases up to $x=5$ and then decreases: $f'(x)$ is greatest at the point of inflection $x=5$.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to5$ (horizontal asymptote), so $f'(x)\to0$ from above: the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote of $y=f'(x)$.

figures.cap: probability tree: walk/not walk then correct/not correct uniform

solutions.latex:
Walks and not wearing the correct uniform (multiply along the branches):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{3}{10}\times\dfrac{1}{10}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{100}\end{aligned}$$

From (a), each student independently walks and is not wearing the correct uniform with probability $\dfrac{3}{100}$, so the probability that a student does not is $\dfrac{97}{100}$.

At least one is the complement of neither:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one})&=1-\left(\dfrac{97}{100}\right)^2\\ &=1-\dfrac{9409}{10\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{591}{10\,000}\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the first derivative of $g(x)=\dfrac{x}{\ln x}$ is $g'(x)=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}$.

dif.r: direct quotient rule with ln x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the global maximum of $g(x)$ on the interval $[2,5]$?

dif.r: stationary point is a minimum; maximum must be at endpoint

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=\dfrac{1\cdot\ln x-x\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Numerical derivative at x=3 matches formula.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points: $g'(x)=0$ when $\ln x-1=0$, so $x=e$, which lies in $[2,5]$.

The denominator $(\ln x)^2>0$, so the sign of $g'(x)$ is decided by $\ln x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 2\le x<e &&\text{decreasing}\\ g'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } e<x\le5 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=e$ is a local minimum, and the global maximum is at an endpoint:
$$\begin{aligned} g(2)&=\dfrac{2}{\ln2}\approx2.885\\ g(5)&=\dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.107\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the global maximum is } \dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.11 \text{ (at } x=5)$$
criteria: Shows $x=e$ is a minimum and evaluates $g$ at an endpoint, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point at $x=e$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Evaluated g on a fine grid over [2,5]: max at x=5, 3.1067.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+2}{x+1}&=\dfrac{(x+1)+1}{x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}$$

From (a), $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$.

Replacing $x$ by $x+1$ in $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$: a translation $1$ unit to the left.

Adding $1$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$: a translation $1$ unit up.

$\therefore$ Translate the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ $1$ unit to the left and $1$ unit up.

questions.stem:
Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: 75% decayed means 25% remains; solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $t$ when the rate of change of $A$ is $-9.48$ g/year, correct to the nearest year.

dif.r: differentiate exponential, set rate, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $A=1000e^{kt}$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-9.48$ with $k=-0.1315$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(-0.1315)e^{-0.1315t}&=-9.48\\ e^{-0.1315t}&=\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\\ -0.1315t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\right)\\ t&\approx20.0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx20 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$ and equates it to $-9.48$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Solved with rounded and unrounded k: t = 19.9987 and 19.9961, both 20.

parts.latex:
The weights of watermelons produced by a certain farm are normally distributed with a mean of 4.82 kg. Long-term quality control data show that when a watermelon from this farm is randomly selected, the probability that it weighs less than 3.75 kg is $0.116$.

A watermelon is labelled as being the ideal size if it weighs between 4.82 kg and 5.89 kg.

What is the probability that a watermelon selected at random is the ideal size?

dif.r: spot symmetric distances about mean, subtract from 0.5

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The normal distribution is symmetric about the mean $4.82$, and $3.75$ and $5.89$ are the same distance from it:
$$4.82-3.75=1.07=5.89-4.82$$
So, by symmetry, $P(X>5.89)=P(X<3.75)=0.116$.

Half of the distribution lies above the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(4.82<X<5.89)&=0.5-P(X>5.89)\\ &=0.5-0.116\\ &=0.384\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses symmetry to obtain $P(X>5.89)=0.116$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Symmetry argument; cross-checked with z-score: P(Z<-z)=0.116 gives z=1.195, P(0<Z<1.195)=0.384.

questions.stem:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: At what value(s) of $t$ does the particle change direction in this interval?

dif.r: v changes sign where graph crosses axis

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

req: Particles at rest and changing direction
Particles at rest and changing direction
B.note: 1 mark: t=0.5 can be read from the given v-t graph or found by solving e^{cos(pi t)}=1, cos(pi t)=0.

Trigonometric equations.evidence: cos(pi t) = 0, pi t = pi/2 (0<=pi t<=1.25pi)
Trigonometric equations.reason: Solving cos of linear argument on restricted domain.

Exponential equations.reason: Unknown in an index solved by equal bases / logs.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0.5$.

dif.r: chain rule on e^{cos(pi t)}, substitute

parts.label: c

dif.r: trapezoidal rule but distance needs |v| over sign change

B.note: Distance needs |v| across the sign change at t=0.5.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph v(t) for 0<=t<=1.25

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=0\\ e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=1\\ \cos(\pi t)&=0\\ \pi t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&(0\le\pi t\le1.25\pi)\\ t&=0.5\end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $t$-axis there ($v<0$ before, $v>0$ after).
$$\therefore\ t=0.5$$

meta.check: Graph crosses at 0.5; cos(pi t)=0 has no other solution in [0,1.25pi].

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{f(t)}=f'(t)e^{f(t)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\ &=-\big(-\pi\sin(\pi t)\big)e^{\cos(\pi t)}\\ &=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)e^{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\\ &=\pi\times1\times e^0\\ &=\pi \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Distance is the area between the graph and the $t$-axis, so use $|v|$ ($v\le0$ for $0\le t\le0.5$ and $v\ge0$ for $0.5\le t\le1$):
$$\text{distance}=\int_0^1|v|\,dt$$
Four subintervals of $[0,1]$: $h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=0.25$, with $t=0,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.75,\ 1$ as in the table.

Trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(t_0)+2\big(f(t_1)+f(t_2)+f(t_3)\big)+f(t_4)\big]$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1|v|\,dt&\approx\dfrac{0.25}{2}\big[1.72+2(1.03+0+0.51)+0.63\big]\\ &=0.125\times5.43\\ &=0.67875\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}\approx0.68 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with $h=0.25$ to the table values (e.g. finds the displacement), or equivalent merit

meta.check: Hand sum 5.43 x 0.125; exact integral of |v| is 0.710, so the estimate is reasonable.
meta.concern: Distance (not displacement) needs |v|; since v=0 at the node t=0.5, applying the rule to |v| equals splitting at t=0.5. Rounding of final answer (0.68 vs 0.679) not specified.

parts.latex:
Maya plans to go on an overseas trip in 5 years’ time. Maya expects that the trip will cost \$14 000. To save for the trip, Maya began by contributing \$750 every 6 months into an annuity. After making a number of payments, Maya realised that the annuity would not reach \$14 000 in 5 years. Maya decides to double the contribution until the trip.

The interest rate was $2\%$ per annum compounding half yearly.

\exfigure{1632_q27_1}

What is the maximum number of \$750 contributions Maya could make before she will need to double her payments to reach \$14 000?
parts.note: Annuity future-value interest-factor table look-up (owner ruling: tables moved to Standard).

dif.r: Set up split annuity inequality, search table for periods

figures.cap: table: Future values of an annuity of $1, periods 2-12, rates 0.01-0.04 (diagonal split corner cell Rate/Period)

solutions.latex:
Contributions are every 6 months for 5 years, so $n=5\times2=10$ periods, at $r=\dfrac{2\%}{2}=1\%=0.01$ per period.

If all $10$ contributions were $\$750$, the future value (table: rate $0.01$, period $10$) would be
$$750\times10.4622=\$7846.65$$
Doubling a contribution adds another $\$750$, so if the last $m$ contributions are doubled, the extra amount is $\$750$ times the future value of an annuity of $\$1$ for $m$ periods, $\text{FV}_m$. We need
$$\begin{aligned} 7846.65+750\times\text{FV}_m&\ge14\,000\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge\dfrac{14\,000-7846.65}{750}\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge8.2045\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $\text{FV}_8=8.2857\ge8.2045$, while $\text{FV}_7=\dfrac{1.01^7-1}{0.01}\approx7.2135<8.2045$.

So at least the last $8$ contributions must be doubled, leaving at most $10-8=2$ contributions of $\$750$.

Check: $750\times10.4622+750\times8.2857=\$14\,060.93\ge\$14\,000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum number of } \$750 \text{ contributions}=2$$
criteria: Uses the table to find that at least $8$ contributions must be doubled, or equivalent merit
Forms a correct inequality or equation for the future value of the mixed contributions, or equivalent merit
Uses $r=0.01$ and $n=10$ with the table, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Python: total FV with n contributions of 750 then 1500: n=2 gives 14060.91, n=3 gives 13256.81 (end-of-period). Annuity-due timing also gives n=2.
meta.concern: Question wording (contributions at start or end of each period, whether 'number of payments' counts only the $750 ones) is slightly ambiguous; all readings tried give 2.

parts.latex:
Let $y=4x^3-3x^2-6x+d$, where $d$ is a real number.

Use differential calculus to find the values of $d$ for which this curve has exactly three $x$-intercepts. (Note: You do NOT need to find the $x$-intercepts.)

dif.r: three roots iff max above and min below axis

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12x^2-6x-6\\ &=6(2x+1)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} y\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=4\left(-\dfrac{1}{8}\right)-3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+3+d=d+\dfrac{7}{4}\\ y(1)&=4-3-6+d=d-5\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=24x-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-18<0 &&\text{local maximum}\\ x&=1: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=18>0 &&\text{local minimum}\end{aligned}$$
The cubic has exactly three $x$-intercepts when its local maximum is above the $x$-axis and its local minimum is below it:
$$\begin{aligned} d+\dfrac{7}{4}&>0 &&\text{so } d>-\dfrac{7}{4}\\ d-5&<0 &&\text{so } d<5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{7}{4}<d<5$$
criteria: Finds the $y$-values $d+\dfrac{7}{4}$ and $d-5$ at the stationary points and states one correct condition, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points at $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x=1$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: numpy roots: d=-1.74 and 4.99 give 3 real roots; d=-1.76 and 5.01 give 1.
meta.concern: At d=-7/4 or d=5 there are two intercepts (repeated root), so strict inequalities.

questions.stem:
A pyramid $MABCD$ has its vertex $M$ vertically above $O$, the centre of its square base $ABCD$, as shown. $AM=\ell$ cm and makes an angle of $\theta$ with the base.

\exfigure{1632_q30_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Let $V$ be the volume of the pyramid.

Show that $V=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D trig set-up; base area from half-diagonal; general show-that.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $\theta$, in radians, for which the volume of the pyramid is a maximum. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

dif.r: Product-rule trig derivative, solve tan²θ=1/2, justify maximum; heavy algebra.

figures.cap: square-based pyramid MABCD with AM = l cm at angle theta to base

solutions.latex:
In triangle $AOM$ (right angle at $O$, $\angle MAO=\theta$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned} MO&=\ell\sin\theta\\ AO&=\ell\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is the centre of the square, so the diagonal $AC=2AO=2\ell\cos\theta$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, a square with side $s$ has $s^2+s^2=AC^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{base area}=s^2&=\dfrac{(2\ell\cos\theta)^2}{2}\\ &=2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
The volume of a pyramid is $\dfrac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\times\ell\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the base area $2\ell^2\cos^2\theta$ and the height $\ell\sin\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Checked with l=1, theta=pi/4: half-diagonal 0.7071, side 1, height 0.7071, V=0.2357 = (2/3)(0.7071)(0.5).

solutions.latex:
Here $\ell$ is constant and $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos^2\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-2\cos\theta\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{d\theta}&=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\left(\cos^3\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta\left(\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\cos\theta\ne0$ when $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta&=0\\ \tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} &&(\tan\theta>0)\\ \theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\approx0.6155\end{aligned}$$
Nature: $\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ is decided by
$$\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\left(1-2\tan^2\theta\right)$$
that is, by $1-2\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0.5: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx0.40>0 &&V \text{ increasing}\\ \theta&=0.7: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx-0.42<0 &&V \text{ decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary point is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx0.62$$
criteria: Finds $\theta\approx0.62$ without justifying the maximum, or equivalent merit
Finds a correct factorised $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ and sets it equal to $0$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ using the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos 2x\,dx$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
It is given

$$\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\int \cos 2x\,dx$$

where $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)>0$ for all real $x$.

Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: recognise ln f, use condition, exponentiate; abstract function

B.note: ln f(x) = (1/2)sin 2x rewritten as f = e^{...}.

Integrals of trigonometric functions.evidence: ln f(x) = 1/2 sin 2x + C (primitive of cos 2x)

solutions.latex: $$\int\cos2x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x+C$$

The left side is a standard integral, $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$, and $f(x)>0$, so using (a):
$$\ln f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x+C$$
Using $f(0)=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln1&=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin0+C\\ C&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\ln f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x$, and
$$f(x)=e^{\frac{1}{2}\sin2x}$$
criteria: Obtains $\ln f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x+C$ and uses $f(0)=1$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Let

$$g(x)=\int_{x^3}^{1}\sqrt{\tan(t)}\,dt$$

The repayments are made at the end of each month after the interest is added to the account.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{final payment}&=A_{26}\times1.005\\ &\approx\$8295.68\end{aligned}$$

Let $A$ and $B$ be two independent events from a sample space.

If $P(A)=p$, $P(B)=p^2$, then which of the following is an expression for $P\left(\overline{A}\cup B\right)$?

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Using the addition rule, then independence of $A$ and $B$ (so $\overline{A}$ and $B$ are independent):
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(\overline{A}\cup B\right)&=P\left(\overline{A}\right)+P(B)-P\left(\overline{A}\cap B\right) \\ &=P\left(\overline{A}\right)+P(B)-P\left(\overline{A}\right)P(B) \\ &=(1-p)+p^2-(1-p)p^2 \\ &=1-p+p^2-p^2+p^3 \\ &=1-p+p^3 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The population of two towns Melbtown and Brisbay are given by $P_M=1200e^{0.04t}$ and $P_B=1500e^{0.025t}$ respectively, where $t$ is the number of years elapsed since January 2010.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: In which year will the population of Melbtown exceed 1500?

dif.r: exponential inequality with logs, convert to year

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In which year will the rate of growth of the population in Melbtown be double the rate of growth of Brisbay?

dif.r: differentiate two exponentials, solve ratio equation with logs

solutions.latex:
The population of Melbtown exceeds 1500 when
$$\begin{aligned}1200e^{0.04t}&>1500\\ e^{0.04t}&>\dfrac{5}{4}\\ 0.04t&>\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)\\ t&>5.57\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=5.57\ldots$ is during 2015.

$\therefore$ In 2015 the population will exceed 1500.

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style

solutions.latex:
Differentiate each population:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}&=0.04\times 1200e^{0.04t}\\ &=48e^{0.04t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}&=0.025\times 1500e^{0.025t}\\ &=37.5e^{0.025t}\end{aligned}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}=2\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}48e^{0.04t}&=75e^{0.025t}\\ e^{(0.04-0.025)t}&=\dfrac{75}{48}\\ e^{0.015t}&=1.5625\\ 0.015t&=\ln(1.5625)\\ t&=\dfrac{1}{0.015}\ln(1.5625)\\ &=29.75247\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=29.75\ldots$ is during 2039.

$\therefore$ During 2039 the rate of growth of Melbtown will be double that of Brisbay.

solutions.latex:
Consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence have a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=T_2-T_1\\ 4e^k-5&=5-4e^{-k}\\ 4e^k-10+4e^{-k}&=0\\ 2e^k-5+2e^{-k}&=0\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Multiply by $e^k$ to form a quadratic in $e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^k-5+\dfrac{2}{e^k}&=0\\ 2e^{2k}-5e^k+2&=0\end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2u^2-5u+2&=0\\ (2u-1)(u-2)&=0\\ u&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ e^k&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right),\ \ln 2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a rectangle $PQRS$ drawn in a sector $OAB$ of a circle with radius 6. $OR=x$, $QR=2x$ and $RS=y$. All units are in metres.

\exfigure{1369_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $(x+y)^2=36-4x^2$.

dif.r: spot right triangle OPS, Pythagoras

parts.label: b

Show that the perimeter, $L$, of the rectangle is given by

$$L=2x+2\sqrt{36-4x^2}$$

dif.r: perimeter algebra using (a)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of $x$ which gives the maximum perimeter of the rectangle.

dif.r: chain rule on surd, solve, justify maximum

figures.cap: rectangle PQRS in sector OAB, OP = 6

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OPS$ (right-angled at $S$), $OS=x+y$, $PS=QR=2x$ and $OP=6$ (radius), so by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned}(x+y)^2+(2x)^2&=6^2\\ (x+y)^2&=36-4x^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style

solutions.latex:
The rectangle has sides $QR=2x$ and $RS=y$:
$$\begin{aligned}L&=2x+2x+y+y\\ &=4x+2y\\ &=2x+2(x+y)\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $(x+y)^2=36-4x^2$ and $x+y>0$, so $x+y=\sqrt{36-4x^2}$.
$$\therefore\ L=2x+2\sqrt{36-4x^2}$$

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dL}{dx}&=2+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(36-4x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-8x)\\ &=2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}&=0\\ \dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}&=2\\ 8x&=2\sqrt{36-4x^2}\\ 4x&=\sqrt{36-4x^2}\\ 16x^2&=36-4x^2\\ 20x^2&=36\\ x^2&=\dfrac{36}{20}\\ x^2&=\dfrac{9}{5}\\ x&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Check the sign of $\dfrac{dL}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}$:

\extable{Ts750_1}

$\therefore$ Maximum $L$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}$ m.

$$g'(t)=\dfrac{33}{10}te^{-kt}.$$

where $k$ is a positive constant. The diagram below shows a sketch of $g'(t)$ against $t$.

parts.label: a

B.note: Max of g' means g''(7.5)=0.

A.note: Area under g' as total change in g.

solutions.latex:
$g'(t)$ has its greatest value at $t=7.5$, so $g''(7.5)=0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=e^{-kt}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-ke^{-kt}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}g''(t)&=\dfrac{33}{10}\left(e^{-kt}+t(-k)e^{-kt}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-kt}(1-kt)\end{aligned}$$
When $t=7.5$, $g''(t)=0$:
$$\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-7.5k}(1-7.5k)=0$$
Since $e^{-7.5k}\ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-7.5k&=0\\ 7.5k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{7.5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{15}\end{aligned}$$

Four sub-intervals on $0\le t\le 12$ give strip width $h=\dfrac{12-0}{4}=3$, so $t=0,3,6,9,12$:

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$A\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(x_0)+2\big(f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)\big)+f(x_4)\big]$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{12-0}{2\times 4}\left[0+\dfrac{33}{10}\times 12e^{-\frac{24}{15}}+2\times\dfrac{33}{10}\left(3e^{-\frac{6}{15}}+6e^{-\frac{12}{15}}+9e^{-\frac{18}{15}}\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}\times 56.9518\ldots\\ &=85.43\text{ u}^2\ \text{(2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}2\cos(d-1)+2&=0\\ 2\cos(d-1)&=-2\\ \cos(d-1)&=-1\\ d-1&=\pi\quad(\text{first solution})\\ d&=\pi+1\end{aligned}$$
The area of the window is the area under each piece of $h(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^1 4\left(1-(x-1)^2\right)dx+\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(2\cos(x-1)+2\right)dx\\ &=4\int_0^1\left(2x-x^2\right)dx+2\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(\cos(x-1)+1\right)dx\\ &=4\left[\dfrac{2x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1+2\Big[\sin(x-1)+x\Big]_1^{\pi+1}\\ &=4\left[\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\right]+2\left[\sin\pi+\pi+1-(\sin 0+1)\right]\\ &=\left(\dfrac{8}{3}+2\pi\right)\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

Correct integral expression for the area, or equivalent merit
Shows $d=\pi+1$ and makes some progress on the area, or equivalent merit

$$m_{AB}=\dfrac{-1.39}{\pi+1}$$
$AB$ touches the window at $C$, so the gradient of the curve at $C$ equals $m_{AB}$. For $x>1$, $h'(x)=-2\sin(x-1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2\sin(x-1)&=\dfrac{-1.39}{\pi+1}\\ \sin(x-1)&=\dfrac{1.39}{2(\pi+1)}\\ x-1&=0.1686\ldots\quad(\text{first solution})\\ x&=1.1686\ldots\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: There are 25 seats in the front row of an amphitheatre, 30 in the second row, 35 in the 3$^{\text{rd}}$ row and so on such that the number of seats in each row is 5 more than the row in front. How many seats are in the 50$^{\text{th}}$ row?

dif.r: MCQ: direct T_50

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The numbers of seats $25,\ 30,\ 35,\ \ldots$ form an arithmetic sequence with $a=25$ and $d=5$, and the 50th row is $n=50$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=a+(n-1)d\\ T_{50}&=25+(50-1)\times 5\\ &=270\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following correctly describes the order of the transformations of $y=\sin x$ to $y=3\sin(2x-1)$?

dif.r: MCQ: factor inside sine to order transformations

options.label: A
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of 3, horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, horizontal translation right 1.

options.label: B
options.latex: Horizontal translation right 1, horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, vertical dilation by a factor 3.

options.label: C
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, horizontal translation right $\dfrac{1}{2}$, vertical dilation by a factor of 3.

options.label: D
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, horizontal translation right 2, vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
Order of transformations from $y=f(x)$ to $y=kf(a(x+b))+c$:

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{a}$
\item Translate $b$ units left
\item Dilate vertically by a factor of $k$
\item Translate up $c$ units
\end{itemize}

Write the equation in this form:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3\sin(2x-1)\\&=3\sin\left(2\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The transformations are, in order:

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Horizontal translation right $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of 3
\end{itemize}

parts.latex: The weights of an Australian Cattle Dog are normally distributed with mean 25 kg and standard deviation 4 kg. Approximately what percentage of dogs will weigh between 29 kg and 33 kg?

dif.r: empirical rule band between 1 and 2 sd

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, $68\%$ of weights lie within one standard deviation of the mean, $25\pm 4$, that is between 21 kg and 29 kg.

$95\%$ lie within two standard deviations, $25\pm 2\times 4$, that is between 17 kg and 33 kg.

Between 29 kg and 33 kg is half of the difference:
$$\dfrac{95\%-68\%}{2}=13.5\%$$

parts.latex: How hot will the water be after 10 minutes?

$T_0$ is the room temperature, so $T_0=27$.

Initially ($t=0$), $T=95$:
$$\begin{aligned}95&=27+Ae^{k(0)}\\A&=68\end{aligned}$$
When $t=5$, $T=90$:
$$\begin{aligned}90&=27+68e^{5k}\\63&=68e^{5k}\\e^{5k}&=\dfrac{63}{68}\\5k&=\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\k&=\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\&=-0.01527459576\\&=-0.0153\ (3\text{ significant figures})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T=27+68e^{-0.0153t}\quad(\text{or equivalent})$$

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{x}{\tan x}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

dif.r: quotient rule with tan, evaluate, negative reciprocal

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\tan x-x\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=\dfrac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4}}{\tan^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1-\frac{\pi}{4}\times 2}{1}\\&=1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_N&=\dfrac{-1}{1-\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi-2}\\&=1.751938394\ldots\\&\approx 1.752\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Solve the two equations simultaneously:
$$\begin{aligned}x^3-3x^2+7&=4x+7\\x^3-3x^2-4x&=0\\x(x^2-3x-4)&=0\\x(x-4)(x+1)&=0\\x&=0,\ -1\text{ or }4\end{aligned}$$
Substitute each value into $y=x^3-3x^2+7$:
$$\begin{aligned}x=0:\quad y&=7\\ x=-1:\quad y&=(-1)^3-3(-1)^2+7=3\\ x=4:\quad y&=(4)^3-3(4)^2+7=23\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3x^2-6x\\3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }x=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=2^3-3\times 2^2+7\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
Determine the nature using $y''=6x-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=0:\quad y''&=-6<0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ x=2:\quad y''&=6>0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $(0,7)$ is a maximum turning point and $(2,3)$ is a minimum turning point.

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=5e^{-2t}$. Initially the particle is at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write an equation for the velocity.

dif.r: integrate exponential, C from rest

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why the particle is always speeding up for $t>0$.

dif.r: explain speeding up: v and a same sign

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
On the number plane below, sketch the graph of the particle's velocity as a function of time.

\exfigure{1356_q20_1}

dif.r: sketch v with horizontal asymptote 5/2

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

figures.cap: blank v-t axes
solution sketch: velocity curve from origin approaching asymptote v=2.5

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int 5e^{-2t}\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+c\end{aligned}$$
The particle is initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2(0)}+c\\c&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ v=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+\dfrac{5}{2}$$

$a=5e^{-2t}>0$ for all $t$, since $e^{-2t}>0$.

For $t>0$, $e^{-2t}<1$, so $v=\dfrac{5}{2}\left(1-e^{-2t}\right)>0$.

Velocity and acceleration are both positive for $t>0$, so the particle is always speeding up.

parts.latex: The function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ has a stationary point at $x=0.23$ and $x=1.80$ (correct to 2 decimal places). Find the point of inflection of the function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ for $0.23<x<1.80$.

dif.r: second derivative via repeated product rule, solve tan 2x

figures.cap: solution sketch: table of dy/dx and d2y/dx2 at x=1, 1.25, 1.7 with slope and concavity sketches

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x$$
Differentiate each term with the product rule again. For $-2e^x\sin 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-2e^x & v&=\sin 2x\\ u'&=-2e^x & v'&=2\cos 2x\end{aligned}$$
For $e^x\cos 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4e^x\cos 2x-2e^x\sin 2x-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x\\&=-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x&=0\\-e^x(3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x)&=0\\3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x&=0\quad\text{since } e^x>0\\3\cos 2x&=-4\sin 2x\\\dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\\\tan 2x&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
For $0.23<x<1.80$, $0.46<2x<3.60$, and $\tan 2x<0$, so $2x$ is in the second quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{reference angle}&=0.6435011088\\2x&=\pi-0.6435011088\\&=2.498091545\\x&=1.249045772\\&=1.25\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{1.249045772}\cos(2\times1.249045772)\\&=-2.789611172\\&=-2.79\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Check that the concavity changes either side of $x=1.25$:

\exfigure{1356_q21_s1}

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign, so there is a point of inflection at $(1.25,-2.79)$.
criteria: Correctly finds the reference angle, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds second derivative and equates to zero, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds first derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1356_q22_s1}

The bearing of $L$ from $W$ is $258^\circ$, so measured anticlockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NWL+258^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle NWL&=102^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $C$ from $W$ is $280^\circ$, so $\angle NWC=80^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CWL&=102^\circ-80^\circ\\&=22^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned}CL^2&=10^2+6^2-2\times 10\times 6\cos 22^\circ\\&=24.73793745\\CL&=4.973724706\\&\approx 4.97\text{ km}\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$ to find $\angle WLC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\angle WLC&=\dfrac{CL^2+WL^2-CW^2}{2\times CL\times WL}\\&=\dfrac{4.97\ldots^2+6^2-10^2}{2\times 4.97\ldots\times 6}\\&=-0.6578246162\\\angle WLC&=131.1341759^\circ\\&\approx 131^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\angle NWL=102^\circ$ (part (b)), and the north lines at $W$ and $L$ are parallel:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle WLN&=180^\circ-102^\circ\\&=78^\circ\quad(\text{co-interior angles})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NLC&=131^\circ-78^\circ\\&=53^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is $53^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-53^\circ\\&=307^\circ T\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle WLC$ using the cosine rule or the sine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\log_8 x+\log_4 x=5$.

dif.r: change of base to common base 2, combine fractions

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base 2:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_8 x+\log_4 x&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 8}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{3}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{2}&=5\\2\log_2 x+3\log_2 x&=30\\5\log_2 x&=30\\\log_2 x&=6\\x&=2^6\\&=64\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes $\log_a x$ the subject, or equivalent merit
Uses change of base law, or equivalent merit

dif.r: area between curves needs f'/f log primitive, exact form

figures.cap: curve y=4x/(x^2+3) and line y=x/3 with region between x=0 and x=3 shaded

solutions.latex:
The curve lies above the line for $0<x<3$, so the area is the integral of the difference:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^3\left(\dfrac{4x}{x^2+3}-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx\\&=2\int_0^3\dfrac{2x}{x^2+3}\,dx-\int_0^3\dfrac{x}{3}\,dx\\&=\left[2\ln(x^2+3)-\dfrac{x^2}{6}\right]_0^3\\&=\left(2\ln(3^2+3)-\dfrac{3^2}{6}\right)-\left(2\ln(0^2+3)-\dfrac{0^2}{6}\right)\\&=2\ln 12-\dfrac{9}{6}-2\ln 3\\&=2(\ln 12-\ln 3)-\dfrac{3}{2}\\&=2\ln 4-\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The number of hours of daylight ($H$) in Sydney can be modelled by the trigonometric function $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$ where $t$ is the number of days after 1$^{\text{st}}$ January, 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the maximum number of hours of daylight in Sydney in a year?

dif.r: centre plus amplitude

can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How quickly are the number of hours of daylight increasing when $t=10$?

dif.r: chain rule on sine model, substitute t=10

parts.label: c

dif.r: solve negative sine equation, interval above 12 h in context

figures.cap: graph of H against t for 0 to 600

solutions.latex:
$H$ is greatest when the sine term equals 1:
$$\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)=1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{Maximum number of daylight hours}&=2.3\times 1+13.1\\&=15.4\end{aligned}$$

Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}H&=2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))+13.1\\\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi t-265))\end{aligned}$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi\times 10-265))\\&=0.01416467195\\&\approx 0.0142\text{ hours/day}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the derivative of $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find when $H=12$:
$$\begin{aligned}2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))+13.1&=12\\2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))&=-1.1\\\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))&=\dfrac{-1.1}{2.3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\text{reference angle}=0.4986733471$$
The sine is negative, so the angle is in the third or fourth quadrant.

Third quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}0.005(\pi t-265)&=\pi+0.498\ldots\\\pi t-265&=728.0532001\\\pi t&=993.0532001\\t&=316.0986511\end{aligned}$$
Fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}0.005(\pi t-265)&=-0.498\ldots\\\pi t-265&=-99.73466941\\\pi t&=165.2653306\\t&=52.60558857\end{aligned}$$
From the graph, $H>12$ between these two values:
$$\therefore\ 53\le t\le 316$$
criteria: Correctly finds two values of $t$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the reference angle, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{x^2} & 2\le x\le 10\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ such that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

dif.r: integral of a/x^2 equals 1, solve a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(X>8)$

dif.r: one direct definite integral

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the median of $X$.

dif.r: F(x)=0.5 with rational CDF, solve linear

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{10}\dfrac{a}{x^2}\,dx&=1\\\int_2^{10}ax^{-2}\,dx&=1\\\Big[-ax^{-1}\Big]_2^{10}&=1\\\left[\dfrac{-a}{x}\right]_2^{10}&=1\\\dfrac{-a}{10}-\left(\dfrac{-a}{2}\right)&=1\\-a+5a&=10\\4a&=10\\a&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates $\dfrac{a}{x^2}$ with correct limits and equates to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $a=\dfrac{5}{2}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{2x^2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>8)&=\int_8^{10}\dfrac{5}{2x^2}\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-5}{2x}\right]_8^{10}\\&=\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 10}\right)-\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 8}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{16}\end{aligned}$$

The median $x$ satisfies $P(X\le x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^x\dfrac{5}{2t^2}\,dt&=0.5\\\left[-\dfrac{5}{2t}\right]_2^x&=0.5\\\left(-\dfrac{5}{2x}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{5}{2\times 2}\right)&=0.5\\\dfrac{-5}{2x}+\dfrac{5}{4}&=0.5\\-10+5x&=2x\\3x&=10\\x&=\dfrac{10}{3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly solves for $x$, or equivalent merit
Forms an expression for $F(x)-F(2)$, or equivalent merit

$$A=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx+\left|\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx\right|$$
Using the reverse chain rule with $f(x)=\sin 2x$, $f'(x)=2\cos 2x$ and $n=4$:
$$\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}2\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx+\left|\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx\right|\\&=\left[\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+\left|\left[\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 2x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right|\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 0+\left|\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{2}-\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{4}\right|\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Nila builds furniture to order. The amount of time that it takes between placing an order and it leaving the warehouse follows a normal distribution.

Nila knows that $2.5\%$ of all her orders are made and leave her warehouse within 10 days of being placed. In total, last year, Nila received 35 orders and customers waited a combined total of 1610 days for their orders to leave the warehouse.

Nila decides that she will give a discount to at most $5\%$ of her customers who have to wait a long time for their orders and would like to advertise this.

What is the minimum waiting time a customer must exceed in order to qualify for the discount? You may use the $z$-tables provided.

dif.r: mean from total, sd from 2.5%, inverse table for top 5%

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The mean waiting time is the total wait divided by the number of orders:
$$\begin{aligned}\mu&=\dfrac{1610}{35}\\&=46\end{aligned}$$
$2.5\%$ of orders leave within 10 days, and $2.5\%$ of a normal distribution lies below $z=-2$, so 10 days has a $z$-score of $-2$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\-2&=\dfrac{10-46}{\sigma}\\-2\sigma&=-36\\\sigma&=18\end{aligned}$$
The discount goes to the $5\%$ of customers who wait longest, so we need the score corresponding to a $z$-score of $1.65$:
$$\begin{aligned}1.65&=\dfrac{x-46}{18}\\29.7&=x-46\\x&=75.7\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Customers who wait more than 76 days will receive a discount.
criteria: Finds the mean and standard deviation, or equivalent merit
Finds the mean, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the $z$-score formula was written $z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma}$; it is $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

Sunya and Jonathan are playing a game. The spinner below is spun. If the hand lands on red then Sunya wins (and the game is over). If the hand lands on blue then Jonathan wins (and the game is over). If the hand lands on green then another spin is taken.

\exfigure{1356_q30_1}
questions.review_note: Spinner sector sizes are not printed; the guideline uses P(B)=3/10, P(R)=2/10, P(G)=1/2 (presumably read from the drawing). Check the figure supports these.

figures.cap: spinner with Blue (Jonathan wins), Green (Spin Again), Red (Sunya wins) sectors
solution sketch: tree diagram, three stages, branches B 3/10, R 2/10, G 1/2

solutions.latex:
From the spinner:
$$P(B)=\dfrac{3}{10}$$

Jonathan can win on the first, second, third, … spin; each extra green spin multiplies the probability by $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$P(\text{Jonathan wins})=\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{10}+\ldots$$
This is the limiting sum of a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{3}{10}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{10}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{5}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The common difference of an arithmetic sequence is $-4$. The sum of the first 30 terms is $23940$ and the sum of the last 30 terms is $-1980$. Find how many terms are in the sequence.

dif.r: non-routine: sum of last 30 terms, two-stage set-up

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $n=30$ and $d=-4$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{30}&=\dfrac{30}{2}\big(2a+(30-1)\times(-4)\big)\\23940&=15(2a-116)\\1596&=2a-116\\1712&=2a\\a&=856\end{aligned}$$
Let $n$ be the number of terms. The last 30 terms are
$$a+(n-1)d,\ a+(n-2)d,\ a+(n-3)d,\ \ldots,\ a+(n-30)d$$
and their sum is $-1980$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Sum}&=a+(n-1)d+a+(n-2)d+a+(n-3)d+\ldots+a+(n-30)d\\&=30a+30dn-d(1+2+3+\ldots+30)\\&=30a+30dn-d\times\dfrac{30}{2}(1+30)\\&=30a+30dn-465d\\-1980&=30\times 856+30\times(-4)n-465(-4)\\-1980&=27540-120n\\120n&=29520\\n&=246\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes a correct simplified expression (algebraic or numeric) for the sum of the last 30 terms, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct value for $a$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Ella borrows \$820 000 to purchase a house. She is being charged $8.4\%$ per annum and plans to making equal monthly repayments of \$6248 over 30 years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the amount owing after 10 years is \$724 960.57

dif.r: build recurrence unprompted, GP sum, evaluate A_120

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After paying the home loan off for 10 years, Ella gets a pay rise. Immediately after making the 120$^{\text{th}}$ payment, Ella makes a one-off payment to reduce the balance owing to \$720 000. She then increases her monthly repayments so that the loan is paid off 25 years after the initial loan. Calculate the amount of her new monthly payment.

dif.r: restart loan after lump sum, 180 months remaining, solve for M

criteria: Writes an expression for $A_{120}$, or equivalent merit
Establishes a pattern and writes an expression for $A_2$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
After the one-off payment the balance is $\$720\,000$. The loan is paid off 25 years after it began, so $25-10=15$ years, or $180$ months, remain. Let $M$ be the new monthly repayment.

After $n$ more months the amount owing is
$$A_n=1.007^n\times 720000-M-M\times 1.007-M\times 1.007^2-\ldots-M\times 1.007^{n-1}$$
The repayments form a GP with first term $M$ and ratio $1.007$, and the loan is repaid when $A_{180}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=1.007^{180}\times 720000-\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{1.007-1}\\0&=1.007^{180}\times 720000-\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{0.007}\\1.007^{180}\times 720000&=\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{0.007}\\1.007^{180}\times 720000\times 0.007&=M(1.007^{180}-1)\\M&=\dfrac{1.007^{180}\times 720000\times 0.007}{1.007^{180}-1}\\&=7047.983754\\&=\$7047.98\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression to find the monthly repayment, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find two expressions in terms of $\theta$, one expression for the time taken for the bus to travel from $S$ to $P$ and the other expression for the time taken by Lucas to cycle from $F$ to $P$.

dif.r: trig set-up of distances, time=distance/speed

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By considering the difference in the time taken for the bus and Lucas to travel to $P$, find the latest time that Lucas can leave home in order to catch the bus? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: maximise time difference with trig derivative, interpret clock time

figures.cap: farmhouse F 300 m from road at G; S 4000 m from G; angle GFP = theta
solution sketch: table of T' at theta = 0, 0.411..., 0.5 (40, 0, -47) with slope sketches

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle FGP$, $FG=300$ and $\angle GFP=\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{GP}{FG}\\&=\dfrac{GP}{300}\\GP&=300\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
The bus travels $SP=4000+GP$ at 20 m/s, and time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_B&=\dfrac{4000+300\tan\theta}{20}\\&=200+15\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
Lucas cycles $FP$ at 8 m/s:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{FG}{FP}\\&=\dfrac{300}{FP}\\FP&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_L&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\div 8\\&=\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the time taken for either the bus or Lucas to make their journey OR correctly writes an expression for $GP$ and $FP$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Lucas can leave home $T=T_B-T_L$ seconds after 8 am and still reach $P$ in time, so the latest departure is when this difference is a maximum.
$$T=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-1}\\T'&=15\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-2}\times(-\sin\theta)\\&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=15-\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta\\\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta&=15\\\sin\theta&=\dfrac{30}{75}\\\theta&=0.4115168461\end{aligned}$$
Check the sign of $T'$ either side of $\theta=0.411\ldots$:

\exfigure{1356_q33_s1}

$T'$ changes from positive to negative, so $T$ is a maximum when $\theta=0.411\ldots$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}\\&=165.6306823\text{ seconds}\\&=2\text{ minutes and }45\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Lucas must leave at 8:02 am at the very latest to catch the bus.
criteria: Recognises that $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2}{5}$ gives maximum value of $T$, or equivalent merit
Gives correct expression for $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}$, or equivalent merit
Recognises that $T=T_B-T_L$ has to be a maximum, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: 8:03 am was not awarded as Lucas would miss the bus by 15 seconds.

parts.latex: Which of the following represents an inverse variation relationship?

dif.r: recall form of inverse variation

solutions.latex:
Inverse variation is of the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$, where $k$ is the constant of variation.

Only $y=\dfrac{4}{x}$ has this form (with $k=4$); the others are direct variation or exponential.

dif.r: MCQ: compare z-scores across tests

dif.r: MCQ: direct a/(1-r)

solutions.latex:
This is a geometric series with first term $a=2\pi$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum is $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{2\pi}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=4\pi \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For which values of $k$ does the equation $x^2+(k+2)x+4=0$ have one solution?

dif.r: discriminant zero gives quadratic in k

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
One solution means equal roots, so the discriminant is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=(k+2)^2-4\times1\times4\\ &=k^2+4k-12 \end{aligned}$$
For equal roots, $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2+4k-12&=0\\ (k+6)(k-2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=-6\text{ or }k=2$$
criteria: Uses the discriminant correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^2-9x$ at the point $(1,-8)$.

dif.r: polynomial derivative, perpendicular gradient, normal equation

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-9$$
At $(1,-8)$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T&=2\times1-9\\ &=-7 \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}=\dfrac{1}{7}$.

Using the point–gradient formula $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(-8)&=\dfrac{1}{7}(x-1)\\ y&=\dfrac{x}{7}-\dfrac{57}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ for the two given terms:
$$\begin{aligned} a+9d&=29 &&\text{(1)}\\ a+14d&=44 &&\text{(2)} \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 5d&=15\\ d&=3 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $d=3$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a+27&=29\\ a&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=2,\ d=3$$
criteria: Finds the two equations, or shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]$ with $n=75$, $a=2$, $d=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{75}&=\dfrac{75}{2}\big(2\times2+(75-1)\times3\big)\\ &=8475 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the sum of the first 75 terms is $8475$.
criteria: Uses the formula for the sum of $n$ terms with one correct value, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+4x}{x+2}$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2+4x & v&=x+2\\ u'&=2x+4 & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{(2x+4)(x+2)-(x^2+4x)}{(x+2)^2}$$
criteria: Correctly differentiates $u$ or $v$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $f(x)=e^{x\sin 3x}$

dif.r: chain rule with product rule inside exponent

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$$
To find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$, use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin 3x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)=\sin 3x\,(1)+x\cdot 3\cos 3x$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x)$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solution sketch: sketch of cubic with (-1,-49), (0,0), (2,32), (4,16), (6,0), (7,7)

solutions.latex:
For the $y$ intercept, $x=0$, so $y=0$.

For the $x$ intercepts, $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=x^3-12x^2+36x\\ 0&=x(x^2-12x+36)\\ 0&=x(x-6)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $x$ intercepts are $x=0$ and $x=6$.
criteria: Finds the $x$ or $y$ intercepts, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct answer. 1: Finds the x or y intercepts

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=3x^2-24x+36\\ y''&=6x-24 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-24x+36&=0\\ x^2-8x+12&=0\\ (x-2)(x-6)&=0\\ x&=2\text{ or }x=6 \end{aligned}$$
For $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2^3-12(2)^2+36(2)\\ &=32\\ y''&=6(2)-24\\ &=-12<0 \end{aligned}$$
so the curve is concave down at $x=2$.

For $x=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=6^3-12(6)^2+36(6)\\ &=0\\ y''&=6(6)-24\\ &=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
so the curve is concave up at $x=6$.

$\therefore$ $(2,32)$ is a local maximum and $(6,0)$ is a local minimum.
criteria: Finds the location of the two stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and equates it to zero, or equivalent merit

Possible inflection when $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-24&=0\\ x&=4 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=4$, $y=16$.

parts.latex: Evaluate $256+128+64+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{8}$.

dif.r: GP analogue of 2020 Q12: n from last term then S_n

solutions.latex:
This is a geometric series with $a=256$, $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and last term $\dfrac{1}{8}$. Find $n$ using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 256\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}&=\dfrac{1}{2048}\\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{2048}}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}+1\\ &=12 \end{aligned}$$
Sum using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:

The diagram shows the graphs $y=2-\dfrac{3}{x}$ and $y=x-2$ for $x\ge 0$.

\exfigure{1363_q27_1}

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find in simplest exact form the area of the shaded region contained between.

dif.r: area between curves with 3/x log term

figures.cap: graphs of y=2-3/x and y=x-2 intersecting at P and Q with the region between shaded

solutions.latex:
At the intersections the $y$ values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} x-2&=2-\dfrac{3}{x}\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $x=1$ at $P$ and $x=3$ at $Q$.
criteria: Correct procedure with one error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 3$ the curve $y=2-\dfrac{3}{x}$ lies above the line $y=x-2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_1^3\left(2-\dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx-\int_1^3(x-2)\,dx\\ &=\int_1^3\left(\left(2-\dfrac{3}{x}\right)-(x-2)\right)dx\\ &=\int_1^3\left(4-\dfrac{3}{x}-x\right)dx\\ &=\left[4x-3\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3\\ &=4(3)-3\ln 3-\dfrac{3^2}{2}-\left(4(1)-3\ln 1-\dfrac{1^2}{2}\right)\\ &=4-3\ln 3\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Dan finished ahead of $84\%$ of competitors, so $84\%$ of times are greater than his.

By the empirical rule, $68\%$ of times lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so the percentage of times greater than $\mu-\sigma$ is
$$50\%+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 68\%=84\%$$
$\therefore$ Dan's completion time is $60-5=55$ minutes.

parts.latex: Prove that $\sin x+1+\cos x\cot x-\operatorname{cosec}x=1$

dif.r: routine identity: sin/cos form, common denominator, Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
Write everything in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, then use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\sin x+1+\cos x\cot x-\operatorname{cosec}x\\ &=\sin x+1+\cos x\times\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\sin x+\cos^2x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x+\sin x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x}\\ &=1\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes significant progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
$ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium, with three equal sides, $AD=DC=CB=12$ cm, as shown in the diagam below. The length of $BQ=x$.

\exfigure{1363_q31_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area of $ABCD$ is given by $A=(12+x)\sqrt{144-x^2}\text{ cm}^2$.

dif.r: find AB=12+2x, Pythagoras, trapezium area

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the value of $x$ when the area of the trapezium is a maximum.

dif.r: product rule with surd, solve quadratic, justify maximum

figures.cap: isosceles trapezium ABCD with DC=12 cm, height h from C to Q on AB, BQ=x; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled $\triangle BQC$ (hypotenuse $CB=12$, base $BQ=x$):
$$h=\sqrt{144-x^2}$$
The trapezium is isosceles, so $AB$ is $DC=12$ plus $x$ at each end:
$$AB=12+2x$$
Area of a trapezium, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{144-x^2}\times(12+12+2x)\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{144-x^2}}{2}(24+2x)\\ &=\sqrt{144-x^2}\times(12+x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Shows $h$ or $AB$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=12+x & v&=\sqrt{144-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{144-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\sqrt{144-x^2}-\dfrac{x(12+x)}{\sqrt{144-x^2}}$$
Stationary when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{144-x^2}&=\dfrac{x(12+x)}{\sqrt{144-x^2}}\\ 144-x^2&=x(12+x)\\ 144-x^2&=12x+x^2\\ 2x^2+12x-144&=0\\ x^2+6x-72&=0\\ (x+12)(x-6)&=0\\ x&=-12\text{ or }x=6 \end{aligned}$$
$x$ is a length, so $x>0$ and $x=6$.

Check the nature:

\extable{Ts913_1}

So there is a maximum turning point at $x=6$.

$\therefore$ the trapezium has its maximum area when $x=6$ cm.
criteria: Finds the correct stationary points from the correct derivative, or equivalent merit
Progresses to the correct derivative function, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x\ \text{ for }\ 0\le x\le\pi.$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function.

dif.r: integrate sin pdf to CDF

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the first quartile of the distribution.

dif.r: F(x)=0.25 gives cos x=1/2

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\big[\cos t\big]_0^x\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x),\qquad 0\le x\le\pi$$
criteria: Finds the integral $-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The first quartile $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.25$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x)&=0.25\\ 1-\cos x&=0.5\\ \cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
The first quartile is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: The population of a certain bacteria culture grows exponentially. At 12:00 pm, the population is 1000 bacteria. After 3 hours, the population reaches 2500 bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
The exponential function modelling the bacteria culture growth is of the form

$$P(t)=P_0a^t$$

where $P(t)$ is the population and $t$ is the time in hours since 12:00 pm.

$P_0$ and $a$ are constants.

Find the value of $P_0$ and $a$.

dif.r: P0 read off, a from cube root of 2.5

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the average rate of change of the population between $t=1$ hours and $t=4$ hours. Include units in your answer.

dif.r: average rate: two substitutions, chord gradient

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the instantaneous rate of change of the population at $t=2$ hours.

dif.r: derivative of a^t with ln a, substitute t=2

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Is the average rate of change constant over time in this scenario? Explain why or why not, based on the nature of exponential growth.

dif.r: explain non-constant rate from exponential growth in context

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ (12:00 pm) the population is 1000, so $P_0=1000$ and $P(t)=1000(a)^t$.

Given $P(3)=2500$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2500&=1000(a)^3\\ a^3&=2.5\\ a&\approx1.3572 \end{aligned}$$
So the function is $P(t)=1000(1.3572)^t$.
criteria: Correct substitution into the model, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} P(1)&=1000(1.3572)^1\\ &=1357.2\\ P(4)&=1000(1.3572)^4\\ &\approx 3392.93 \end{aligned}$$
The average rate of change is the gradient of the chord from $t=1$ to $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate}&=\dfrac{P(4)-P(1)}{4-1}\\ &\approx\dfrac{3392.93-1357.2}{3}\\ &\approx\dfrac{2035.73}{3}\\ &\approx 678.58\text{ bacteria/hour} \end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $P(4)=1000(1.3572)^4\approx3392.93$, not $3386$, so the average rate is $\approx678.58$ bacteria/hour, not $676.27$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right)=a^t\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(t)&=1000(1.3572)^t\\ P'(t)&=1000(1.3572)^t\ln 1.3572\\ P'(2)&=1000(1.3572)^2\ln 1.3572\\ &\approx 562.6 \end{aligned}$$
At 2 hours, the population is increasing at approximately $562.6$ bacteria/hour.
criteria: Correct differentiation of the function, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $\ln 13572$ (typo) replaced by $\ln 1.3572$, and $P'(2)=1000(1.3572)^2\ln 1.3572\approx562.6$, not $560.1$.

solutions.latex: No, the average rate of change is not constant. In exponential growth, the rate increases over time because the population grows by a constant percentage, not a constant amount.
criteria: States the rate is not constant, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Determine the least number of attempts that this player must make so that the probability of scoring at least one goal is greater than $0.8$.

dif.r: build 1-0.85^n>0.8, log inequality with sign reversal

solutions.latex:
$$\text{Probability (player misses in 1 attempt)}=1-0.15=0.85$$
$$\text{Probability (player misses in both attempts)}=(0.85)^2=0.7225$$

The player scores at least one goal unless every one of the $n$ attempts misses:
$$P(\text{at least one goal})=1-(0.85)^n$$
We need
$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.85)^n &> 0.8\\ (0.85)^n &< 0.2\end{aligned}$$
Taking logs (and dividing by $\ln(0.85)<0$ reverses the inequality):
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln(0.85) &< \ln(0.2)\\ n &> \dfrac{\ln(0.2)}{\ln(0.85)}\\ &\approx 9.90\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The player needs 10 attempts.
criteria: Provides the correct inequality, $(0.85)^n<0.2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=x^4-2x^3+2$ by first finding all stationary points, checking their nature, and finding the points of inflection.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1628_q19_s1}

Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^4-2x^3+2\\ y' &= 4x^3-6x^2\\ y'' &= 12x^2-12x\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^3-6x^2 &= 0\\ 2x^2(2x-3) &= 0\end{aligned}$$
$$x=0 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$
When $x=0$, $y=2$ and $y''=0$. Check concavity:

\extable{Ts556_1}

Concavity changes sign, $\therefore$ horizontal point of inflection at $(0,2)$.

When $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$, $y=\dfrac{5}{16}$ and $y''=9>0$.

$\therefore$ Local minimum at $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{5}{16}\right)$.

Possible points of inflection occur where $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-12x &= 0\\ 12x(x-1) &= 0\end{aligned}$$
$$x=0 \text{ or } x=1$$
$(0,2)$ is already found. When $x=1$, $y=1$. Check concavity:

\extable{Ts556_2}

Concavity changes sign, $\therefore$ point of inflection at $(1,1)$.

A second point $B$ is on a different bearing from the tower as shown. The angle of elevation to the top of the tower from $B$ is $30^\circ$. The points $A$ and $B$ are 100 metres apart.

\exfigure{1628_q20_1}

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the bearing of $B$ from $C$ to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: Tangent ratio, then cosine rule for angle, then convert to bearing in 3D setting

figures.cap: 3D diagram of tower TC with points A and B

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $TCA$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 35^\circ=\dfrac{40}{AC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 35^\circ}\\ &= 57.1259\ldots\\ &= 57.13 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

In right-angled triangle $TCB$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{40}{BC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ BC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 30^\circ}\\ &= 69.28 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ACB$, with $AC=57.13$ from part (a) and $AB=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle ACB &= \dfrac{57.13^2+69.28^2-100^2}{2\times(57.13)\times(69.28)}\\ &= -0.24462\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle ACB=104^\circ \quad (\text{nearest degree})$$
$A$ is due east of $C$ (bearing $090^\circ$), so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } B \text{ from } C &= 104^\circ+90^\circ\\ &= 194^\circ\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angle at $C$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graph of y=ln(1+x^2) with area shaded from x=-1 to x=1
solution sketch

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (quotient rule for $f'$):
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \ln\left(1+x^2\right)\\ f'(x) &= \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\\ f''(x) &= \dfrac{2\left(1+x^2\right)-2x(2x)}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}\\ &= \dfrac{2-2x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}\end{aligned}$$
The denominator is always positive, so $f''(x)>0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} 2-2x^2 &> 0\\ x^2 &< 1\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1628_q22_s1}
$$\therefore\ f''(x)>0 \text{ for } -1<x<1$$
So $f(x)$ is concave up for $-1<x<1$.
criteria: Finds the correct second derivative, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct first derivative, or equivalent merit

The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so the shaded area is twice the area from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

The table gives 4 strips on $[0,1]$, so
$$h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=0.25$$
Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\,dx\\ &\approx 2\times\dfrac{1-0}{2\times 4}\left[0+0.6931+2(0.0606+0.2231+0.4463)\right]\\ &= 0.538275\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the values from the table correctly in the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

questions.stem: Jack intends to deposit \$80 into a savings account on the first day of each month for 24 months. The interest rate during this time is 6\% per annum, compounded monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate how much money Jack will have in his account at the end of the 24 months.

dif.r: Set up geometric series for start-of-month deposits and sum correctly

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A table of future value interest factors could have been used to calculate how much money Jack would have in his account at the end of the 24 months.

Part of the table is shown.

\exfigure{1628_q24_1}

What is the value of $A$ in the table? Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up: Standard (2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only) · Standard: MST-12-S2-03

dif.r: Recognise table factor scales deposit; divide previous result by 80

figures.cap: partial table of future value interest factors with entry A

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{6\%}{12}=0.5\%$, so each month the balance is multiplied by $1.005$.

The first deposit accrues interest for 24 months.

$\therefore$ Its future value is $80(1.005)^{24}$.

The next deposit accrues interest for 23 months, and so on, down to 1 month for the last deposit.

Summing the geometric series ($a=1.005$, $r=1.005$, 24 terms):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 80(1.005)^{24}+80(1.005)^{23}+\cdots+80(1.005)^{1}\\ &= 80\left[(1.005)^1+(1.005)^2+\cdots+(1.005)^{24}\right]\\ &= 80\times(1.005)\left[\dfrac{(1.005)^{24}-1}{1.005-1}\right]\\ &= 2044.73\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Jack will have $\$2044.73$.
criteria: Sets up an appropriate series, or equivalent merit
Finds a correct term in the series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The future value of an annuity of \$1 for 24 periods is $A$, so the future value of \$80 per period is $80A$.
$$\begin{aligned} 80A &= 2044.73\\ A &= \dfrac{2044.73}{80}\\ &= 25.559\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A function $f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}0, & \text{for } x<0\\[6pt] 1-\dfrac{x}{h}, & \text{for } 0\le x\le h\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for } x>h\end{cases},$$

where $h$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $h$ such that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

dif.r: area of triangle equals 1

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By first finding a formula for the cumulative distribution function, sketch its graph.

dif.r: integrate to piecewise CDF and sketch all pieces

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of the median of the probability density function $f(x)$. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

dif.r: F(t)=1/2 gives quadratic, choose root in domain

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

figures.cap: solution sketch
solution sketch

criteria: Identifies that the area under the curve $=1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 2$, the cumulative distribution function is
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x \left(1-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt\\ &= \left[t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_0^x\\ &= x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & \text{for } x<0\\[6pt] x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}, & \text{for } 0\le x\le 2\\[6pt] 1, & \text{for } x>2\end{cases}$$
\exfigure{1628_q25_s2}
criteria: Finds the formula for the $CDF$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the integral of $1-\dfrac{t}{2}$ was written with $dx$; it is with respect to $t$.

solutions.latex:
The median $t$ satisfies $F(t)=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} t-\dfrac{t^2}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ t^2-4t+2 &= 0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4\times 1\times 2}}{2\times 1}\\ &= \dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{8}}{2}\\ &= 2\pm\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
The median lies in $0\le t\le 2$, so we need $t<2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ t &= 2-\sqrt{2}\\ &\approx 0.586\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\tan x\right) &= 2x\tan x+x^2\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$ and part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int (x\tan x+1)^2\,dx &= \int \left(x^2\tan^2 x+2x\tan x+1\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(x^2\left(\sec^2 x-1\right)+2x\tan x+1\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(x^2\sec^2 x+2x\tan x-x^2+1\right)dx\\ &= x^2\tan x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+x+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses the identity, $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Anna is sitting in a carriage of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $A(t)$, in metres above the ground of the top of her carriage is given by

$$A(t)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{24}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Anna's carriage first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1628_q28_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 39 metres and a smallest height of 3 metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $c$ and $k$.

dif.r: centre line and amplitude from max 39 and min 3

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many seconds does it take for one complete revolution of the Ferris wheel?

dif.r: period 2pi/(pi/24)

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Billie is in another carriage. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of the top of her carriage is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right),$$

where $c$ and $k$ are as found in part (a).

During each revolution, there are two occasions when Anna's and Billie's carriages are at the same heights. At what two heights does this occur? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: equate phase-shifted cosines; non-routine cos A=cos B cases

figures.cap: Ferris wheel with six carriages
solution sketch

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1628_q28_s1}

The centre line $c$ is midway between 39 and 3, and the amplitude $k$ is half the difference:
$$c=\dfrac{39+3}{2}=21$$
$$k=\dfrac{39-3}{2}=18$$
criteria: Finds the value of $c$ or $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{24}}=48$$
It takes 48 seconds.

The carriages are at the same height when $A(t)=B(t)$:
$$c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
$$\therefore\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
Two angles have equal cosines when they are equal, opposite, or add to $2\pi$ (within one revolution).

Equal angles:
$$\dfrac{\pi}{24}t=\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)$$
which is impossible.

Opposite angles:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}t-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{12}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ t &= 3\end{aligned}$$
Angles adding to $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{2\pi}{24}t &= -2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi t}{12} &= \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ t &= 27\end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{24}=4.37 \text{ m}$$
When $t=27$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{27\pi}{24}=37.63 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Makes correct use of the periodic nature of cosine function, or equivalent merit
Equates the appropriate trigonometric ratios, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the curve $y=ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\ne 0$.

At a particular point, the tangent and normal to the curve are given by $t(x)=2x+3$ and $n(x)=-\dfrac{1}{2}x-2$ respectively.

The curve has a minimum turning point at $x=-4$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: combine tangent-normal intersection, turning point and gradient into simultaneous equations

solutions.latex:
The tangent and normal meet where
$$\begin{aligned} 2x+3 &= -\dfrac{1}{2}x-2\\ \dfrac{5x}{2} &= -5\\ x &= -2\\ y &= 2(-2)+3\\ y &= -1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ They meet at $(-2,-1)$.

If $y=ax^2+bx+c$, then $y'=2ax+b$.

When $x=-4$, $y'=0$ (minimum turning point):
$$\begin{aligned} -8a+b &= 0\\ \therefore\ b &= 8a\end{aligned}$$
When $x=-2$, $y'=2$ (gradient of the tangent):
$$\begin{aligned} -4a+b &= 2\\ -4a+8a &= 2\\ \therefore\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ \therefore\ b &= 4\end{aligned}$$
When $x=-2$, $y=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a(-2)^2+b(-2)+c &= -1\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4+4\times(-2)+c &= -1\\ -6+c &= -1\\ \therefore\ c &= 5\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the values of $a$ and $b$, or equivalent merit
Finds a relevant equation linking $a$ and $b$, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-ordinate of the point of intersection of the tangent and normal, or equivalent merit
