parts.latex:
Suppose the geometric series $x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ has a limiting sum, $S$.

By considering the graph $y=-1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, or otherwise, find the range of possible values of $S$.

dif.r: limiting sum range via graph and domain restriction; real insight

figures.cap: solution sketch

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum of a geometric series with $a=x$, $r=x$ is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= x+x^2+x^3+\cdots\\ &= \dfrac{x}{1-x} \qquad \text{where } -1<x<1\end{aligned}$$
Rewriting the given function:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}=\dfrac{-(x-1)-1}{x-1}\\ &= \dfrac{-x}{x-1}=\dfrac{x}{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
So, the graph of $y=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$ is as shown.

\exfigure{1628_q30_s1}

When $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

From the graph, when $-1<x<1$, $y>-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\therefore\ S>-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
criteria: Shows that the graph given is equal to $S_\infty$, or equivalent merit
Finds the limiting sum $S$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Two circles have the same centre $O$. The smaller circle has radius 1 cm, while the larger circle has radius $(1+x)$ cm. The circles enclose a region $QRST$, which is subtended by an angle $\theta$ at $O$, as shaded.

The area of $QRST$ is $A\text{ cm}^2$, where $A$ is a constant and $A>0$.

\exfigure{1628_q31_1}

Let $P$ cm be the perimeter of $QRST$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By finding expressions for the area and perimeter of $QRST$, show that $P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$.

dif.r: sector area and arcs, eliminate theta using constant A

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that if the perimeter, $P(x)$, is minimised, then $\theta$ must be less than 2.

dif.r: minimise, back-substitute for theta, then bound it

A.note: minimise P then deduce theta<2 using area relation

B.note: Minimise P then deduce theta<2 from the constraint.

Area of a sector.reason: Area relation (1) comes from an earlier part; this part only substitutes it, never uses A=½r²θ.

figures.cap: concentric circles with shaded annular sector QRST

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is two arcs ($l=r\theta$) and two straight edges of length $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1\theta+(1+x)\theta+2x\\ &= (2+x)\theta+2x\end{aligned}$$
The area is the difference of two sectors ($A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1+x)^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1^2\theta\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left[1+2x+x^2-1\right]\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left(2x+x^2\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta x(2+x) \qquad (1)\end{aligned}$$
From (1):
$$(2+x)\theta=\dfrac{2A}{x}$$
Substituting into $P=(2+x)\theta+2x$:
$$\therefore\ P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$$
criteria: Finds correct expressions for the perimeter and area, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct expression for the perimeter or area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a stationary point, $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} P' &= 2-\dfrac{2A}{x^2}=0\\ x^2 &= A\\ x &= \sqrt{A} \quad (x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$P''=\dfrac{4A}{x^3}>0 \text{ when } x=\sqrt{A}$$
$\therefore$ This gives a minimum value.

Using (1) with $x=\sqrt{A}$:
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\theta\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)$$
$$\theta=\dfrac{2A}{\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)}=\dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{2+\sqrt{A}}$$
Since $2+\sqrt{A}>\sqrt{A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &< \dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{\sqrt{A}}\\ &= 2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ If $P(x)$ is minimised, $\theta<2$.
criteria: Expresses $\theta$ in terms of $A$, or equivalent merit
Shows $x=\sqrt{A}$ is a minimum, or equivalent merit

\extable{Tq574_1}

parts.label: e

The probabilities add to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.75+0.1+k&=1 \\ k&=0.15 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\times 0.1+1\times 0.2+2\times 0.25+3\times 0.3+4\times 0.15 \\ &= 2.2 \end{aligned}$$

Using $E(X)=2.2$ and $E(X^2)=6.3$ from parts (c) and (d):
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\mu^2 \\ &= 6.3-2.2^2 \\ &= 1.46 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: cubic with maximum (-3,4), inflexion (0,2), minimum (3,0), x-intercept -6

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{9}x^2-1 \\ 0&=\dfrac{1}{9}x^2-1 \\ x^2&=9 \\ x&=-3 \text{ or } x=3 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $y=\dfrac{1}{27}x^3-x+2$, the stationary points are $(-3,4)$ and $(3,0)$.

Nature, using $y''=\dfrac{2}{9}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-3)&=-\dfrac{2}{3}<0 &&\text{local maximum at } (-3,4) \\ y''(3)&=\dfrac{2}{3}>0 &&\text{local minimum at } (3,0) \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Possible points of inflection occur where $y''=\dfrac{2}{9}x=0$, so $x=0$ and the point is $(0,2)$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-1)&=-\dfrac{2}{9}<0 &&\text{concave down} \\ y''(1)&=\dfrac{2}{9}>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=0$.

$\therefore$ $(0,2)$ is a point of inflexion.

questions.stem: Alex takes out a loan at an interest rate of $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually. At the end of each year, interest is charged and then Alex makes a repayment.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Suppose Alex borrows $\$10\,000$ and he pays off the loan in $10$ years with regular annual repayments of $\$M$. Let $A_n$ be the amount Alex still owes by the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find $A_1$ and hence $A_2$ in terms of $M$.

dif.r: routine unrolling to A_1 and A_2

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find $A_n$ in terms of $M$ and $n$.

dif.r: generalise pattern to A_n, unsummed form accepted

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Find $M$ correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: sum GP, set A_10=0, solve for M

A.note: A_n formula from (ii) reused; solve A_10=0

B.note: uses A_n from (ii); A_10=0 solved for M

Geometric series.evidence: Sums the geometric series to obtain A_n=10000(1.05)^n−M×(1.05^n−1)/0.05

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If Alex only wants to repay $\$350$ each year in order to pay off his loan in $20$ years, what is the maximum amount he would be able to borrow under the same interest rate? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: reuse model with unknown principal, solve A_20=0

A.note: PV of repayments is an alternative

B.note: principal found from A_20=0; could be seen as present value

Geometric series.evidence: B = 20(350)(1.05^20 - 1)/1.05^20 (GP sum inside the loan formula)

solutions.latex:
Each year interest is added (multiply by $1.05$) and then $M$ is repaid:
$$A_1=10000(1.05)-M$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1(1.05)-M \\ &=\left[10000(1.05)-M\right](1.05)-M \\ &=10000(1.05)^2-M(1.05)-M \end{aligned}$$

Continuing the pattern from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=10000(1.05)^2-M(1+1.05) \\ A_n&=10000(1.05)^n-M\left(1+1.05+1.05^2+\cdots+1.05^{n-1}\right) \end{aligned}$$

The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.05$, $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=10000(1.05)^n-M\times\dfrac{1.05^n-1}{0.05} \\ &=10000(1.05)^n-20M(1.05^n-1) \end{aligned}$$
The loan is repaid after $10$ years, so $A_{10}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=10000(1.05)^{10}-20M(1.05^{10}-1) \\ M&=\dfrac{10000(1.05)^{10}}{20(1.05^{10}-1)} \\ &=\$1295.05 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sums the geometric series to obtain $A_n=10000(1.05)^n-M\times\dfrac{1.05^n-1}{0.05}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Suppose $f(x)=e^x(x+1)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the first derivative of $f(x)$.

dif.r: direct product rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the second derivative of $f(x)$.

dif.r: differentiate again, simplify

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By identifying a pattern, write down an expression for the $n$th derivative of $f(x)$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

dif.r: generalise derivative pattern to nth

A.note: pattern in repeated differentiation; no dot point for pattern spotting

B.note: nth derivative by pattern; no skill for higher derivatives/pattern spotting

Product rule.reason: Differentiating e^x(x+1) needs the product rule to find the pattern.

Second derivative.reason: Pattern for nth derivative requires computing higher derivatives.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=x+1 \\ u'&=e^x & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$$

Differentiate $f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$, using part (a) for the first term:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=e^x(x+1)+e^x+e^x \\ &=e^x(x+1)+2e^x \\ &=e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$

Each derivative adds another $e^x$: $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$, $f''(x)=e^x(x+3)$, so
$$\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}\,e^x(x+1)=e^x(x+n+1)$$

solutions.latex:
$4$ function values give $3$ strips:
$$h=\dfrac{10-1}{3}=3$$
so $x=1,\ 4,\ 7,\ 10$. By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{3}{2}\left[f(1)+2f(4)+2f(7)+f(10)\right] \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln 1+2\ln 4+2\ln 7+\ln 10\right] \\ &=13.45 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

The shaded area is the rectangle $10\times\ln 10$ minus the region between the curve and the $y$-axis for $0\le y\le\ln 10$. On the curve, $x=e^y$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=10\ln 10-\int_0^{\ln 10}e^y\,dy \\ &=10\ln 10-\Big[e^y\Big]_0^{\ln 10} \\ &=10\ln 10-(10-1) \\ &=10\ln 10-9 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the area bounded between the graphs of $y=\sqrt{x-1}$ and $y=x-1$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1374_q26_s1}

Intersections (square both sides):
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x-1}&=x-1 \\ x-1&=x^2-2x+1 \\ x^2-3x+2&=0 \\ (x-1)(x-2)&=0 \\ x&=1 \text{ or } x=2 \end{aligned}$$
The curve is above the line for $1<x<2$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_1^2\left(\sqrt{x-1}-(x-1)\right)dx \\ &=\int_1^2\left((x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-x+1\right)dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(x-1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_1^2 \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-2+2-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral for the area, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State the initial mass of the radioactive substance.

dif.r: read initial value

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the half-life of the radioactive substance. Give your answer as an exact value in terms of $k$.

dif.r: half-life with logs in terms of k

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dM}{dt}$.

dif.r: differentiate exponential

A.note: pure differentiation in a decay context; rule (c) would favour model

parts.label: d
parts.latex: A biomaterial is also decaying simultaneously, but at every instance in time its rate of decay is twice as fast as the radioactive substance. Find an expression for the mass of the biomaterial, in terms of $k$ and $t$, given that its initial mass is $3$ kg.

dif.r: interpret twice the rate, integrate, find C

solutions.latex: $2\text{ kg}$

Half-life: the mass halves to $1$ kg:
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=2e^{-kt} \\ e^{kt}&=2 \\ kt&=\ln 2 \\ t&=\dfrac{1}{k}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-2ke^{-kt}$

The biomaterial decays twice as fast, so $\dfrac{dB}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{dM}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt}&=-4ke^{-kt} \\ B&=\int -4ke^{-kt}\,dt \\ &=4e^{-kt}+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $B=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=4+C \\ C&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B=4e^{-kt}-1$$

questions.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time at which the particle is stationary.

dif.r: solve v=0

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when it is stationary.

dif.r: differentiate power of (t+1), substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The total distance travelled by the particle in the first two seconds is $\ln b$ metres, for some constant $b>0$. Find the value of $b$.

dif.r: distance over turnaround, combine logs to ln b

solutions.latex:
Stationary when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{t+1}-1&=0 \\ \dfrac{2}{t+1}&=1 \\ 2&=t+1 \\ t&=1\text{ second} \end{aligned}$$

Acceleration $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2(t+1)^{-1}-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-2(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=-\dfrac{2}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$ (from part (a)):
$$a(1)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ ms}^{-2}$$

$a<0$ for all $t$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$, so
$$\begin{aligned} v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right} \\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le 2 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1\right)dt&=\Big[2\ln|t+1|-t\Big]_0^1 \\ &=2\ln 2-1 \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the next second (velocity negative):
$$\begin{aligned} \Big[t-2\ln|t+1|\Big]_1^2&=2-2\ln 3-(1-2\ln 2) \\ &=1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Total distance:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\ln 2-1+1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2&=4\ln 2-2\ln 3 \\ &=\ln 2^4-\ln 3^2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Finds both distances, $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$ and $1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$ for $1\le t\le 2$, or equivalent merit
Finds the distance $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x$.

dif.r: single product rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.

dif.r: rearrange derivative from (a), integrate by subtraction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x\cos x\,dx$.

dif.r: substitute limits into primitive from (b)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x=\sin x+x\cos x$$

Integrate both sides of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int(\sin x+x\cos x)\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int\sin x\,dx+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ -\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x+\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

Using part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}x\cos x\,dx&=\Big[x\sin x+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: In early planetary models, planets orbit the sun in circular orbits. Suppose a planet completes its orbit of radius $r$ around the sun in time $T$, while moving at a constant speed $v$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Express $v$ in terms of $r$ and $T$ by using:

$$\text{constant speed}=\dfrac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time}}.$$

dif.r: distance is circumference 2 pi r, one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By examining astronomical data made in the 1600's, Kepler noticed that $r^3$ is always directly proportional to $T^2$ for all orbits, that is, $r^3=kT^2$, for some fixed positive constant $k$. By finding an appropriate derivative, determine whether planets further from the sun move faster or slower.

dif.r: eliminate T, express v(r), differentiate, interpret sign in context

solutions.latex:
In time $T$ the planet travels one circumference, $2\pi r$:
$$v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$$

Make $\dfrac{1}{T}$ the subject of $r^3=kT^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{T^2}&=\dfrac{k}{r^3} \\ \dfrac{1}{T}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{r^{\frac{3}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into part (a):
$$v=2\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dv}{dr}&=-\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\ &=-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{k}}{r\sqrt{r}} \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{dv}{dr}<0$ for $r>0$, so $v$ is a decreasing function of $r$.

$\therefore$ Planets further from the sun move slower.

meta.marker_note: Right conclusion based on correct derivative for last mark.
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct conclusion; right conclusion based on correct derivative for last mark

questions.stem: A patient is undergoing a treatment involving repeated injections of $M$ milliliters of medicine, separated by regular time intervals of $t$ hours. Let $A_n$ be the amount of medicine in the body immediately after the $n^{\text{th}}$ injection, so $A_1=M$. While in the body, the medicine decays exponentially such that the amount left in the body right before the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ injection is given by $A_ne^{-t}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression for $A_2$, and show that $A_3=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t})$.

dif.r: build A_2, A_3 from recurrence (like A_2 show)

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The patient is safe from side effects as long as the amount of medication in the body stays below $2M$ milliliters. Find the minimum value of $t$, to nearest minute, such that the patient is always safe as this treatment continues indefinitely.

dif.r: limiting amount 2M condition, solve for t, convert to minutes

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Before each injection the amount is multiplied by $e^{-t}$, then $M$ is added:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1e^{-t}+M \\ &=Me^{-t}+M \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3&=A_2e^{-t}+M \\ &=(Me^{-t}+M)e^{-t}+M \\ &=M+Me^{-t}+Me^{-2t} \\ &=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}) \end{aligned}$$

$A_n$ is increasing in $n$, so for the treatment to be always safe we need $A_\infty<2M$.

$A_\infty$ exists since $0<e^{-t}<1$ for $t>0$ (geometric series, $r=e^{-t}$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_\infty&=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}+e^{-3t}+\cdots) \\ &=M\times\dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}} \\ &=\dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}} \end{aligned}$$
We require $A_\infty<2M$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}}&<2M \\ \dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}}&<2 \\ \dfrac{e^t}{e^t-1}&<2 \\ e^t&<2e^t-2 \\ e^t&>2 \\ t&>\ln 2\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
In minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&>\ln 2\times 60 \\ &=41.588\cdots\text{ mins} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=42\text{ mins}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: "$0<e^{-t}<1$ for $t\ge 0$" should be $t>0$ ($e^{0}=1$).

questions.stem:
The Grammar timetable follows a six day cycle, with the days labelled $A$ to $F$. In a certain year, the first school day is Monday and is an A day. Part of the timetable is shown in the table below, with weeks 8 to 35 omitted. For simplicity we assume the entire school year consists of 40 weeks.

\extable{Tq593_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the probability that a randomly selected school day is an A day.

dif.r: count A days in six-day cycle over five-day weeks

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: When a school day is randomly selected, find the probability that the day is an A day, given that it is a Monday. Hence state, with justification, whether these two events are independent.

dif.r: count A Mondays from cycle pattern, test independence

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Suppose there are:

\begin{itemize}
\item $0$ periods of maths on A days.
\item $1$ period of maths on B days.
\item $2$ periods of maths on each of D, E and F days.
\item $3$ periods of maths on C days.
\end{itemize}

Let $X$ be the number of maths periods on a randomly chosen Monday. Find $E(X)$.

dif.r: build day-type distribution over Mondays, then E(X)

solutions.latex:
The six-day cycle runs across five-day weeks. There is an A day every week except weeks $6,12,18,24,30,36$, so $34$ A days in $200$ school days:
$$P(\text{A})=\dfrac{34}{200}=\dfrac{17}{100}=17\%$$

Of the $40$ Mondays, $7$ are A days:
$$P(\text{A}\,|\,\text{Monday})=\dfrac{|\text{A}\cap\text{Monday}|}{|\text{Mondays}|}=\dfrac{7}{40}=17.5\%$$
This is not equal to $P(\text{A})=17\%$ from part (a), so the events are not independent.

Day types on the $40$ Mondays:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{A}\,|\,\text{Mon})&=P(\text{D}\,|\,\text{Mon})=P(\text{E}\,|\,\text{Mon})=P(\text{F}\,|\,\text{Mon})=\dfrac{7}{40} \\ P(\text{B}\,|\,\text{Mon})&=P(\text{C}\,|\,\text{Mon})=\dfrac{6}{40}=\dfrac{3}{20}=15\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times\dfrac{7}{40}+1\times\dfrac{6}{40}+2\times\dfrac{7}{40}\times 3+3\times\dfrac{6}{40} \\ &=1.65 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct probabilities for each day type on a Monday, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
If $M$ is the midpoint of $AP$ then $\angle OMA=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. (Do NOT show this)

Find $AM$ in terms of $R$ and $\theta$.

dif.r: cosine in right triangle

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an expression, in terms of $v_1$ and $v_2$, for the angle $\theta$ which maximises $t$.

dif.r: arc via angle at centre, form t, maximise in v1, v2

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the condition on $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$ so that the minimum value of $t$ is achieved by only running.

dif.r: only maximum so minimum at endpoint; compare endpoints

figures.cap: circle centre O with diameter AB, chord AP with midpoint M, OM perpendicular to AP, arc PB in bold, angle PAB = theta

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle OMA$, $OA=R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{AM}{R} \\ AM&=R\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$

Swim $AP=2AM=2R\cos\theta$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $\angle POB=2\theta$ and arc $PB=2R\theta$:
$$t=\dfrac{2R\cos\theta}{v_1}+\dfrac{2R\theta}{v_2}$$
$$\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta+\dfrac{2R}{v_2}$$
Stationary when $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta&=\dfrac{2R}{v_2} \\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\cos\theta$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}\le 0$ on the whole domain, $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ is a local maximum.

It is the only turning point between the end points, so the maximum cannot occur at an end point.

$\therefore$ $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ gives the global maximum.
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$ to get $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$, or equivalent merit
Correct expression for $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct angle with justification of maximum

solutions.latex:
$t$ is concave down with only a maximum turning point, so the minimum occurs at an end point, $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0: &t&=\dfrac{2R}{v_1} &&\text{only swimming} \\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}: &t&=\dfrac{\pi R}{v_2} &&\text{only running} \end{aligned}$$
For the minimum to occur by only running:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi R}{v_2}&<\dfrac{2R}{v_1} \\ \dfrac{v_2}{v_1}&>\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $t$ at both end points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The parabola $g(x)=2(x-1)(x-3)$ is transformed into a concave up parabola with vertex is at the origin.

Which of the following transformations could have achieved this?

dif.r: complete square for vertex, then match translations

options.label: A
options.latex: Horizontal translation of 2 units to the left followed by a vertical translation of 2 units up

options.label: B
options.latex: Reflection in the $x$ axis followed by a translation 1 unit to the left

options.latex: Translation of 3 units to the right followed by a reflection in the $x$ axis

options.label: D
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ followed by a horizontal translation of 2 units to the right

solutions.latex:
Complete the square:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)&=2(x^2-4x+3)\\ &=2(x-2)^2-2 \end{aligned}$$
The vertex is $(2,-2)$ and the parabola is already concave up, so no reflection is needed.

Translating 2 units left gives $y=2x^2-2$.

Then translating 2 units up gives $y=2x^2$, with vertex at the origin.

questions.stem:
A bag contains 3 white and 4 black stones. Two stones are drawn out of the bag with the probability tree below showing the possibilities:

\exfigure{1370_q4_1}

parts.latex: If it is known that one of the stones is white, what is the probability that the stones are different colours?

dif.r: condition is at least one white; twin of 2024 Q9 trap

'At least one' probabilities.reason: Conditioning event is at least one white, found as 1 - P(none).

figures.cap: probability tree for drawing two stones: white 3/7, black 4/7, then 2/6, 4/6, 3/6, 3/6

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, $P(X\mid Y)=\dfrac{P(X\cap Y)}{P(Y)}$, where "one of the stones is white" means at least one white:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one white})&=1-\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{30}{42}\\ P(\text{different colours})&=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{6}+\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{24}{42} \end{aligned}$$
Different colours always includes one white stone, so
$$P(\text{different}\mid\text{one white})=\dfrac{24}{42}\div\dfrac{30}{42}=\dfrac{4}{5}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \log_b\sqrt{c}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log_b c\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2\log_c b}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\log_c b^2} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $y=8x^3-15x^2+5$ with a domain $x\epsilon[-1,2]$.

parts.latex: Which of the following is true for the function?

dif.r: stationary points plus endpoints on domain

options.label: A
options.latex: The maximum value of the function is 0 and the minimum value is $\dfrac{5}{4}$

options.label: B
options.latex: The minimum value is $\dfrac{5}{4}$ and the maximum value is 0

options.label: C
options.latex: The minimum value is $-\dfrac{45}{16}$ and the maximum value is 5

options.label: D
options.latex: The minimum value is $-18$ and the maximum value is 9

solutions.latex:
Find the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=24x^2-30x\\ &=6x(4x-5) \end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{5}{4}$, both inside the domain. Evaluate $y$ at the stationary points and the endpoints:
$$\begin{aligned} y(0)&=5\\ y\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{45}{16}\\ y(-1)&=-8-15+5=-18\\ y(2)&=64-60+5=9\end{aligned}$$
Comparing all values, the minimum is $-18$ and the maximum is $9$.

questions.stem:
Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$.

\exfigure{1370_q9_1}

parts.latex: At what value of $x$ is $f''(x)>f'(x)>f(x)$?

dif.r: near-twin of 2020 Q8: order f'', f', f from graph

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

req: Graphs of f, f′ and f″
Graphs of f, f′ and f″
B.note: reads signs of f, f', f'' from a graph of f

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: At x=b the curve is concave down, so f''(b)<0

Stationary points and their nature.evidence: f'(d)=0 stationary point; minimum turning point below the x-axis

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with maximum at x=b, x intercept c and minimum at x=d

solutions.latex:
At $x=b$ the curve is concave down, so $f''(b)<0=f'(b)$.

At $x=c$ the gradient is negative while $f(c)=0$, so $f'(c)<f(c)$.

At $x=d$ there is a minimum turning point below the $x$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned} f(d)&<0 &&\text{below the } x\text{-axis}\\ f'(d)&=0 &&\text{stationary point}\\ f''(d)&>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
Hence $f''(d)>f'(d)>f(d)$.

questions.stem:
The formula for the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of a series is given by

$$T_n=400n-2^n$$

parts.latex: What is the sum of the first 10 terms?

dif.r: MCQ: split into AP and GP sums

solutions.latex:
Split the sum into an arithmetic part and a geometric part:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=400(1+2+\cdots+10)-(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{10})\\ &=400\times 55-\dfrac{2(2^{10}-1)}{2-1}\\ &=22\,000-2046\\ &=19\,954 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Evaluate

$$\int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx$$

dif.r: split fraction into 2x - 1/x, definite with log

solutions.latex:
Split the integrand into separate terms:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx&=\int_2^4\left(2x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx\\ &=\Big[x^2-\ln|x|\Big]_2^4\\ &=(4^2-\ln 4)-(2^2-\ln 2)\\ &=12-\ln 4+\ln 2\\ &=12-2\ln 2+\ln 2\\ &=12-\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A particle moves along the $x$ axis with a displacement at time $t$ seconds given by

$$x=\dfrac{32}{(t+1)^2}+t-12$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the particle comes to rest when $t=3$.

dif.r: chain rule on power, solve v=0

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Find the total distance the particle travels in the first 5 seconds.

Answer correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: distance: positions at 0, 3, 5 with turnaround

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(0+1)^2}+0-12\\ &=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ initially the particle is 20 m to the right of the origin.

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten marking guidelines (scanned pages, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(-2)(32)(1)(t+1)^{-3}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1 \end{aligned}$$
At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1\\ (t+1)^3&=64\\ t+1&=4\\ t&=3 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle comes to rest when $t=3$.

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten marking guidelines (scanned pages, no text layer)
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct proof (solve $v=0$, or substitute $t=3$ and show $v=0$)
meta.marker_note: Either solve $v=0$, or substitute $t=3$ and show $v=0$.

solutions.latex:
At $t=3$ (at rest):
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(3+1)^2}+3-12\\ &=-7 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate $v$ to find the acceleration:
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-64(-3)(1)(t+1)^{-4}$$
At $t=3$, $a=\dfrac{192}{4^4}>0$, so the particle moves to the right after $t=3$.

At $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(5+1)^2}+5-12\\ &=-\dfrac{55}{9} \end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left from $x=20$ to $x=-7$, then right to $x=-\dfrac{55}{9}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance travelled}&=20+7+\left(7-\dfrac{55}{9}\right)\\ &\approx 27.9\text{ m (1 decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the location at $t=3$ or $t=5$, or equivalent merit

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)&=2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=x+2x\ln x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e x\ln x\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e 2x\ln x\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\big((2x\ln x+x)-x\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x^2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^e\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(e^2\ln e-\dfrac{e^2}{2}\right)-\left(1\ln 1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{e^2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{e^2+1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

\item 8 adults pay for neither

parts.label: c

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1370_q18_s1}

Let $x$ be the number who pay for TV only. The four regions total 40:
$$\begin{aligned} x+6+8+12&=40\\ x&=14 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{pay for TV})&=\dfrac{14+6}{40}\\ &=\dfrac{20}{40}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Two adults are chosen without replacement from all 40. Two adults who both pay for neither do not count, so they pay the same if both are TV only, both sport only, or both pay for both:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both TV only})&=\dfrac{14}{40}\times\dfrac{13}{39}=\dfrac{182}{1560}\\ P(\text{both sport only})&=\dfrac{12}{40}\times\dfrac{11}{39}=\dfrac{132}{1560}\\ P(\text{both TV and sport})&=\dfrac{6}{40}\times\dfrac{5}{39}=\dfrac{30}{1560} \end{aligned}$$
Adding the three cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both pay same})&=\dfrac{182+132+30}{1560}\\ &=\dfrac{43}{195} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
For $x\ge 0$, $|x|=x$; for $x<0$, $|x|=-x$:
$$x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\quad\text{or}\quad -x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$$
Multiply by 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=x+6 & -2x&=x+6\\ x&=6 & -3x&=6\\ & & x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=-2,\ 6$$

solutions.latex:
The region from $x=-2$ to $x=0$ (between the line and $y=-x$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-(-x)\right)dx\\ &=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{3}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{4}+3x\right]_{-2}^0\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{3(-2)^2}{4}+3(-2)\right)\\ &=3 \end{aligned}$$
(Or as a triangle, $A_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 2=3$.)

So $7$ square units more are needed for $x$ from $0$ to $k$.

The whole triangle from $x=0$ to $x=6$ has area $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6=9>7$, so $k<6$.

For $0\le x\le k$, the region lies between the line and $y=x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=\int_0^k\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-x\right)dx\\ 7&=\int_0^k\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ 7&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{4}x^2+3x\right]_0^k\\ 7&=-\dfrac{1}{4}k^2+3k\\ k^2-12k+28&=0\\ (k-6)^2&=8\\ k&=6\pm 2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
But $k<6$:
$$\therefore\ k=6-2\sqrt{2}$$

solutions.latex:
For the $y$ intercept, substitute $x=0$: $y=-3$.
$$y'=3x^2-12x+9$$
For stationary points, $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-12x+9&=0\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$, $y=-3$ or $x=1$, $y=1$.

The sign of $y''$ decides the nature:
$$y''=6x-12$$
When $x=3$, $y''=6(3)-12=6>0$ (concave up), so there is a minimum turning point at $(3,-3)$.

When $x=1$, $y''=6(1)-12=-6<0$ (concave down), so there is a maximum turning point at $(1,1)$.

For possible points of inflection, $y''=0$: $6x-12=0$, so $x=2$, $y=-1$.

Check for concavity:

\extable{Ts859_1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(2,-1)$.

questions.stem:
The tangent to $y=\tan x$ at the point where $x=c$, $c\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is drawn on the diagram below. The value $c$ is chosen so that the $y$ intercept of the tangent is $-c$.

\exfigure{1370_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the equation of the tangent is

$$y=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c$$

dif.r: parametric tangent show-that at x=c

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the gradient of this tangent can be simplified to $\dfrac{c^2+1}{c^2}$.

dif.r: use y-intercept -c, identity, deduce tan c=1/c, non-routine

A.note: use y-intercept to get tan c = 1/c then sec^2 c = 1+tan^2 c

figures.cap: graph of y=tan x with tangent at x=c meeting the y axis at -c

solutions.latex:
Differentiate, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x$:
$$y'=\sec^2 x$$
When $x=c$: $y=\tan c$ and $y'=\sec^2 c$.

Equation of the tangent, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-\tan c&=\sec^2 c\,(x-c)\\ y&=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $y=\tan c$ and the gradient $\sec^2 c$, or equivalent merit
Finds $y=\tan c$ or $y'=\sec^2 c$ at $x=c$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten marking guidelines (scanned pages, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
The tangent passes through $(0,-c)$; use $\sec^2 c=1+\tan^2 c$:
$$\begin{aligned} -c&=-c\sec^2 c+\tan c\\ -c&=-c(1+\tan^2 c)+\tan c\\ -c&=-c-c\tan^2 c+\tan c\\ c\tan^2 c-\tan c&=0\\ \tan c\,(c\tan c-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$\tan c=0$ gives $c=0$, not possible since $c\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. So $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}\\ 1+\tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}+1\\ \sec^2 c&=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{c^2+1}{c^2}$$
Alternative: from $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$ and the points $(0,-c)$, $(c,\tan c)$,
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{\tan c+c}{c-0}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{c}+c}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c}\times\dfrac{1}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Write $P$ with a negative power:
$$P(t)=200-44\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^{-1}$$
Chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P'(t)&=44\left(-2e^{-0.2t}\right)\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^{-2}\\ &=\dfrac{-88e^{-0.2t}}{\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Since $P'(t)<0$ for all $t\ge 0$, $P(t)$ is a decreasing function, so $P(t)$ is a maximum when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0)&=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^0}\\ &=196 \end{aligned}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.2t}\to 0$, so $P(t)\to 200-44=156$.
$$\therefore\ 156<P(t)\le 196$$
criteria: Correct lower bound $156<P(t)$ or upper bound $P(t)\le 196$, or equivalent merit

From (c), $P'(t)$ is a quadratic in $P$:
$$P'(t)=\dfrac{1}{220}(P-156)(P-200)$$
Its graph against $P$ is a concave-up parabola with $P$-intercepts $156$ and $200$, so the minimum value of $P'(t)$ (fastest decrease) occurs midway between them:
$$P=\dfrac{156+200}{2}=178$$
$\therefore$ the population is decreasing at the fastest rate when $P=178$.

parts.latex: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x) = e^{5x^3 - 10x}$ is increasing.

dif.r: chain rule on exponential, e^u>0, quadratic inequality with surds

solutions.latex:
The function is increasing where $f'(x) > 0$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{g(x)} = g'(x)e^{g(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= (15x^2 - 10)e^{5x^3 - 10x} \\ &= 5(3x^2 - 2)e^{5x^3 - 10x} \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{5x^3 - 10x} > 0$ for all $x$, only the factor $3x^2 - 2$ decides the sign, so we need
$$3x^2 - 2 > 0$$

questions.stem:
Finn is working in the garden when he has an accident and puts a hole in the bottom of his rainwater tank. At the time of the accident, the tank contained 10 200 litres of water.

In the first hour after the accident, Finn noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by 200 litres.

In the second hour, he noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by a further 250 litres.

Finn is concerned that the leak is growing, but he is not sure what will happen next. He wonders if the amount of water leaking from the tank each hour might form an arithmetic sequence or geometric sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If the amount of water that leaks out of the tank each hour forms an arithmetic sequence, how many hours will it take until the tank is empty?

dif.r: quadratic in n from S_n=10200

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the amount of water that leaks out of the tank each hour forms a geometric sequence, show that eight hours after the leak, over 60% of the water remains in the tank

dif.r: GP sum of leaks then compare to 60%

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The leak each hour is arithmetic with $a = 200$, $d = 50$, and the tank is empty when $S_n = 10\,200$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,200 &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(200) + (n-1) \times 50\right] \\ 20\,400 &= n(400 + 50n - 50) \\ 20\,400 &= 350n + 50n^2 \\ n^2 + 7n - 408 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{-7 \pm \sqrt{7^2 - 4 \times 1 \times (-408)}}{2} \\ &= -24 \text{ or } 17 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 17$.

$\therefore$ Tank empty after 17 hours.
criteria: Correct substitution into $S_n$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions copy (images, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
The leak each hour is geometric with $a = 200$, $r = \dfrac{250}{200} = 1.25$, $n = 8$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_8 &= \dfrac{200(1.25^8 - 1)}{1.25 - 1} \\ &= 3968.37 \text{ L has leaked out} \end{aligned}$$
$$10\,200 - 3968.37 = 6231.63 \text{ L}$$
$$\dfrac{6231.63}{10\,200} \times 100 = 61.09\%$$
$\therefore$ After 8 hours more than $60\%$ of water remains.
criteria: Correct substitution into $S_8$, or equivalent merit

Using $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin x)(1 - \sin x)}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x} = \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Multiplies numerator and denominator by $1 - \sin x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $P$ the curves meet:

The line lies above the parabola for $0 \le x \le 2k$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{2k} \left(kx - x(x - k)\right) dx \\ &= \int_0^{2k} \left(2kx - x^2\right) dx \\ &= \left[kx^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^{2k} \\ &= 4k^3 - \dfrac{1}{3} \times 8k^3 \\ &= \dfrac{4}{3}k^3 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral for the area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}$$

dif.r: prove quotient rule result with Pythagorean identity

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, or otherwise, show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\right]=\sec x$$

dif.r: rewrite sec+tan, use part (a) with f prime over f

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1+\sin x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x)-(-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}{\cos^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2 x+\sin x+\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes one mistake, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\sec x+\tan x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}$$
From part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x} \\ f'(x)&=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\times\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}=\sec x\end{aligned}$$
Hence proved.
criteria: Simplifies the expression, or equivalent merit

So $f'(x)<0$ when
$$(3x-7)(x-1)<0$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: routine cubic stationary points with second-derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the point of inflection of $f(x)$.

dif.r: cubic inflection: f''=0 and concavity check

dif.r: sketch cubic from features already found

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What is the maximum value of $f(x)$ for $-3\le x\le 5$?

dif.r: global max is an endpoint, not the local max

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=-x^3+6x^2-1 with min (0,-1), POI (2,15), max (4,31)

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=-3x^2+12x$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x^2+12x&=0\\ -3x(x-4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$f''(x)=-6x+12$$
At $x=0$, $f(0)=-1$, so the point is $(0,-1)$.
$$f''(0)=12>0 \text{ (concave up)}$$
$\therefore$ $(0,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=4$:
$$f(4)=-4^3+6\times4^2-1=31$$
$$f''(4)=-6\times4+12=-12<0 \text{ (concave down)}$$
$\therefore$ $(4,31)$ is a maximum turning point.
criteria: Calculates the two stationary points, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: f''(4) = -6 × 4 + 12 = -12 (source wrote -4 × 4 + 12 = -4); still < 0, so the conclusion is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Possible points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)=-6x+12&=0\\ -6x&=-12\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$f(2)=-(2)^3+6(2)^2-1=15$$
Check the concavity either side of $x=2$:

\extable{Ts1043_1}
$$\begin{aligned} f''(1)&=-6+12=6 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(3)&=-6\times3+12=-6 &&\text{concave down}\end{aligned}$$
Since the concavity changes at $x=2$, $(2,15)$ is a point of inflection.
criteria: Calculates the point of inflection, or equivalent merit

$$f(-3)=-(-3)^3+6(-3)^2-1=80$$
$$f(5)=-(5)^3+6(5)^2-1=24$$
For $-3\le x\le 5$ the maximum value of $f(x)$ is 80.

questions.stem:
The tide in a harbour can be modelled using the equation $d(t)=A\cos(Bt)+C$,

where $d$ represents the depth of the water in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours after 7:00 am.

High tide occurs at 7:00 am when the water's depth is 60 m.

Low tide occurs at 2:00 pm when the water's depth is 20 m.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$, and hence write the completed function $d(t)$.

dif.r: amplitude, centre, plus period from half-cycle timing

parts.label: b
parts.latex: A ship enters the harbour only if the height of the tide is at least 50 m. Find all the times between 7:00 am and 7:00 pm during which the ship is able to enter the harbour.

dif.r: solve cos equation, interval above 50 m as clock times

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of d(t): 60 at t=0, 20 at t=7 h (2 pm), 60 at t=14 h (9 pm)
solution sketch: ASTC quadrant diagram with 60 and 300 degree angles marked

solutions.latex:
The depth varies between 60 m and 20 m:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{60-20}{2}=20 &&\text{(amplitude)}\\ C&=\dfrac{60+20}{2}=40 &&\text{(centre)}\end{aligned}$$
High tide (7:00 am) to low tide (2:00 pm) is 7 hours, half a period, so the period is 14:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{B}&=14\\ B&=\dfrac{2\pi}{14}=\dfrac{\pi}{7}\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{644_q16_s1}
$$\therefore\ d(t)=20\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}+40$$
criteria: Makes one mistake, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The ship can enter while $d(t)\ge 50$. The boundary times are when $d(t)=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} 20\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}+40&=50\\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}&=\dfrac{10}{20}=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le t\le 12\\ 0&\le\dfrac{\pi t}{7}\le\dfrac{12\pi}{7} &&\left(\text{multiply by } \dfrac{\pi}{7}\right)\end{aligned}$$
($\dfrac{12\pi}{7}$ is $5.39$ radians or $308.57^\circ$.)

The related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{644_q16_s2}
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{7}=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{7}{\pi},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{7}{\pi}\\ &=2 \cdot \dot{3},\ 11.67\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ h 20 min or 11 h 40 min after 7:00 am, that is 9:20 am and 6:40 pm.

The depth starts at its maximum, 60 m, at $t=0$, so $d(t)\ge 50$ for
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le t\le 2 \cdot \dot{3} &&\text{7:00 am to 9:20 am}\\ 11.67&\le t\le 12 &&\text{6:40 pm to 7:00 pm}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $20\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}+40=50$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $q^2$ and then

translated 81 units down, the transformed function is given as

$$g(x)=q^2x^2-81$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When the transformed function $g(x)$ is translated $p$ units to the left, the resulting function is denoted as $h(x)$. Write an expression for $h(x)$.

dif.r: replace x with x+p for horizontal shift

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find all possible values of $p$ and $q$ if $h(x)=9x^2+36x-45$.

dif.r: match forms: complete square, q=+-3, p=2

solutions.latex:
Translating $p$ units to the left replaces $x$ with $x+p$:
$$h(x)=q^2(x+p)^2-81$$

Equate $h(x)$ from (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} q^2(x+p)^2-81&=9x^2+36x-45\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x-45+81\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x+36\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x^2+4x+4)\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$

Carlos decides that the aquarium is to be $s$ units high so that the volume of the aquarium can be found using $V=As$.

Calculate the value of $s$, such that the capacity of the water tank is a maximum.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: form V=As cubic, differentiate, solve stationary point

figures.cap: top view of aquarium: rectangle of width w and height s with a semicircle of diameter s on each end

solutions.latex:
The glass is the two semicircular arcs (together $\pi s$), the two sides of length $w$ and the two dividers of length $s$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2s+2w+\pi s&=200\\ 2w&=200-2s-\pi s\\ w&=100-s\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Creates an expression for the length of glass walls, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: creating an expression for the length of glass walls

solutions.latex:
The area is two semicircles of diameter $s$ (one circle) plus the rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right)^2+w\times s\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+s\left(100-s\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\\ &=100s+\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}-\dfrac{\pi s^2}{2}-\dfrac{2s^2}{2}\\ &=100s-\dfrac{\pi}{4}s^2-s^2\\ &=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right)\\ A&=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $V=As$ with part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} V&=s\left(100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\right)\\ &=100s^2-s^3\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{ds}=200s-3s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dV}{ds}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 200s-3s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)&=0\\ s\left(200-3s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$s=0$ gives no tank, so
$$\begin{aligned} 3s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)&=200\\ s&=\dfrac{200\times4}{3(\pi+4)}\\ &\approx 37.34\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{ds^2}=200-6s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)$$
At $s=37.34$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{ds^2}\approx-200<0$$
so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum turning point.

$\therefore$ $s=37.34$ will give maximum volume.
criteria: Calculates the value of $s$, or equivalent merit
Finds a correct volume expression, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Consider the curve $y=ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\ne 0$.

At a particular point, the tangent and normal to the curve are given by

$t(x)=5(x+1)$ and $n(x)=-\dfrac{x}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5}$ respectively.

The curve has a maximum turning point at $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the point of intersection of the tangent and the normal is $(-1,0)$

dif.r: solve two linear equations simultaneously

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: twin of 2024 Q29 but intersection scaffolded: simultaneous a,b,c

solutions.latex:
The tangent and normal meet where $t(x)=n(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5(x+1)&=-\dfrac{x}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5}\\ 5(5x+5)&=-x-1\\ 25x+25&=-x-1\\ 25x+x&=-1-25\\ 26x&=-26\\ x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$t(-1)=5(-1+1)=0$$
$\therefore$ the point of intersection of the tangent and the normal is $(-1,0)$.

$$\begin{aligned} y&=ax^2+bx+c\\ y'&=2ax+b\end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent and the curve is the same at $(-1,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2a(-1)+b&=5\\ -2a+b&=5 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The maximum turning point is at $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$, so $y'\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+b&=0\\ \dfrac{a}{2}+b&=0 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a}{2}+2a&=-5\\ \dfrac{5a}{2}&=-5\\ a&=-\dfrac{5\times2}{5}=-2\end{aligned}$$
From (2):
$$b=-\dfrac{a}{2}=1$$
For $c$, substitute the point $(-1,0)$, $a$ and $b$ into $y=ax^2+bx+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-2(-1)^2+1(-1)+c\\ c-1-2&=0\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=-2,\ b=1,\ c=3$$
criteria: Substitutes the point into the quadratic equation, or equivalent merit
Uses the gradient at the turning point, or equivalent merit
Uses the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

Since $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)}&=\sqrt{2}\\ \sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi\\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{7\pi}{3} &&\left(\text{add } \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\\ &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{11\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ x&=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{9\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{5\pi}{12} \text{ or } \dfrac{23\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A company produces resistors with resistance being normally distributed ($\mu=50\,\Omega$, $\sigma=2\,\Omega$).

Resistors below $48\,\Omega$ or exceeds $52\,\Omega$ are defective.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the percentage of defective resistors.

dif.r: empirical rule: outside 1 sd is 32%

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In a batch of 1000 resistors, how many are expected to be non-defective?

dif.r: scale percentage to 1000

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Defective resistors lie more than one standard deviation from the mean ($48=50-2$, $52=50+2$). By the empirical rule, $68\%$ lie within one standard deviation:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{defective}) &= P(X<48)+P(X>52)\\ &= 1-68\%\\ &= 32\% \end{aligned}$$

From (a), $100\%-32\%=68\%$ are non-defective:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(1-32\%) &= 1000\times 0.68\\ &= 680 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 680 resistors are expected to be non-defective.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right)=e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$$

dif.r: product rule then sec^2 = 1 + tan^2

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence evaluate

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)\,dx$$

dif.r: substitute limits into primitive from (a)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
Then, using $\sec^2 x=\tan^2 x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right) &= e^x\tan x+e^x\sec^2 x\\ &= e^x\left(\sec^2 x+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+1+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Sets up the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (a), $e^x\tan x$ is a primitive of $e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)dx &= \Big[e^x\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &= e^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-e^0\tan 0\\ &= \sqrt{3}\,e^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\overline{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the expression of $P(A\cap B)$ in terms of $k$.

dif.r: symbolic Venn decomposition of B

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.

dif.r: independence gives quadratic in k, reject k=0

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram with complement-of-A intersect B shaded

solutions.latex:
The events are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$. Using (a):
$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2 &= \dfrac{3k}{4}\cdot k\\ 4k-4k^2 &= 3k^2\\ 7k^2-4k &= 0\\ k(7k-4) &= 0\\ k &= 0 \text{ or } k=\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$k=0$ is not allowed since $0<k<1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$
criteria: Uses $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The amount of time for Opstra Telecom. to respond to a customer query follows the probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}, & x\ge 1\\[6pt] 0, & 0<x<1\end{cases}\qquad\text{where } x \text{ is time in hours.}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=20$.

dif.r: improper integral equals 1, show k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the median response time.

dif.r: F(m)=0.5 with rational CDF

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that the company spends more than 2 hours but less than 3 hours to respond to the customer query?

dif.r: one direct definite integral

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\int_1^{\infty}(5x-1)^{-2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\left[\dfrac{(5x-1)^{-1}}{-1\times 5}\right]_1^{\infty} &= 1\\ -\dfrac{k}{5}\left[0-\dfrac{1}{4}\right] &= 1\\ \dfrac{k}{20} &= 1\\ k &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the correct integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let the median be $m$. Half the probability lies below the median:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^m\dfrac{20}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ -4\left[\dfrac{1}{5x-1}\right]_1^m &= 0.5\\ -\dfrac{4}{5m-1}+1 &= 0.5\\ \dfrac{4}{5m-1} &= 0.5\\ m &= \dfrac{9}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median response time is $\dfrac{9}{5}$ hours ($1.8$ hours).
criteria: Writes the correct integral equation, or equivalent merit
Shows correct working, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the times(s) the particle is at rest.

dif.r: v=0 with e^{t^4}>0, one step

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the displacement function is $x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$.

dif.r: reverse chain rule integral with e^{t^4}, find C

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what time does the particle reach a displacement of 100 metres? (Give your answer to 2 d.p.)

dif.r: solve exponential equation with logs, fourth root

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$8t^3e^{t^4}=0$$
$e^{t^4}>0$ for all $t$, so $t^3=0$.
$$\therefore\ t=0$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity. The derivative of $t^4$ is $4t^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2\int 4t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2e^{t^4}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin: when $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^0+C &= 0\\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten line $2e^0+C=-2$ should read $2e^0+C=0$, which gives the stated $C=-2$.

solutions.latex:
Let $x(t)=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{t^4}-2 &= 100\\ e^{t^4} &= 51\\ t^4 &= \ln 51\\ t &\approx 1.41 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The mass of oranges at Fruit King farm are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

It is known that 25.78% of these oranges have mass more than 190 g and 34.46% of them have mass more than 180 g.

Using the table of z scores below, answer the following questions.

\extable{1358_q28_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

dif.r: two table z-values give simultaneous equations for mu, sigma

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Two oranges from Fruit King farm are chosen at random.

Given that the mass of both oranges is greater than 180 grams, what is the probability that both of them have a mass less than 194 g. Give your answer as a percentage to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: conditional on two independent oranges, squared ratio of areas

solutions.latex:
$25.78\%$ of oranges are heavier than 190 g, so $100\%-25.78\%=74.22\%$ are lighter. From the table, this corresponds to $z=0.65$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.65 &= \dfrac{190-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.65\sigma &= 190-\mu \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$
Similarly, $100\%-34.46\%=65.54\%$ corresponds to $z=0.4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4 &= \dfrac{180-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.4\sigma &= 180-\mu \quad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (2) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25\sigma &= 10\\ \sigma &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $\sigma=40$ into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4(40) &= 180-\mu\\ \mu &= 164 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The mean is 164 g and the standard deviation is 40 g.
criteria: Sets up two correct equations, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $100\%-25.75\%$ should be $100\%-25.78\%$ (the given percentage); the result $74.22\%$ is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
$z$-score for 194 g, using $\mu=164$ and $\sigma=40$ from (a):
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{194-164}{40}\\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, $77.34\%$ of the oranges have mass less than 194 g.

Let the mass of an orange be $X$. For one orange, by conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<194\mid X>180) &= \dfrac{P(180<X<194)}{P(X>180)}\\ &= \dfrac{77.34\%-65.54\%}{34.46\%}\\ &= 34.24\% \end{aligned}$$
The two oranges are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both}) &= (34.24\%)^2\\ &= 11.73\% \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the conditional probability $34.24\%$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: c

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: right-angled triangle ABC with right angle at B and a sequence of decreasing squares a1, a2, ... along BC touching hypotenuse AC
solution sketch: annotated triangle: a - a1 on AB, areas A1, A2, A3, BC = 2a

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1358_q29_s1}
$$\dfrac{AB}{BC}=\dfrac{a}{2a}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The small triangle above the first square (vertical side $a-a_1$, horizontal side $a_1$) is similar to $\triangle ABC$ (corresponding angles, both right-angled):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a-a_1}{a_1} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2a-2a_1 &= a_1\\ 2a &= 3a_1\\ a_1 &= \dfrac{2a}{3} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Each square sits on the one before in the same way as in (a), so
$$a_2=\dfrac{2}{3}a_1,\quad a_3=\dfrac{2}{3}a_2,\ \ldots$$
Using (a), the areas are
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= (a_1)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}a^2\\ A_2 &= (a_2)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_1\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\dfrac{4}{9}a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2\\ A_3 &= (a_3)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_2\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^3a^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The areas of the squares form a geometric sequence with $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$.
criteria: Shows successive areas, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The areas form a geometric series with first term $A_1=\dfrac{4}{9}a^2$ and $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{A_1}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\frac{4}{9}a^2}{1-\frac{4}{9}}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{5}a^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the limiting sum formula, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any stationary points of $f(x)$, determine their nature, and find any points of inflection.

dif.r: stationary point and inflection of (x+1)e^x, standard tests

Product rule.reason: Differentiating the product e^x(x+2) for f''.

Derivatives of exponential functions.evidence: Possible points of inflection occur when f''(x)=0: e^x(x+3)=0
Derivatives of exponential functions.reason: f'' of e^x(x+2) must be found.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch the curve $f(x)$, labelling any stationary points, points of inflection and intercepts with the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

\exfigure{1358_q30_1}

dif.r: sketch from found features plus asymptote y=0 to the left

figures.cap: blank grid with x and y axes and origin O for sketching
solution sketch: sketch of y=(x+1)e^x with (0,1), (-1,0), minimum (-2,-e^-2), inflection (-3,-2e^-3), x-axis asymptote on the left

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^x+(x+1)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
Again with the product rule, $u=x+2$, $v=e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^x+(x+2)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. From (a), $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$:
$$e^x(x+2)=0$$
$e^x>0$ for all $x$, so $x+2=0$, $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=(-2+1)e^{-2}=-e^{-2}$$
Nature: $f''(-2)=e^{-2}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

$\therefore$ $\left(-2,-e^{-2}\right)$ is a local minimum turning point.

Possible points of inflection occur when $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} e^x(x+3) &= 0\\ x &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(-3)=-2e^{-3}$$
Check the concavity either side of $x=-3$:

\extable{Ts1102_1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $\left(-3,-2e^{-3}\right)$.
criteria: Finds the stationary point and its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the two curves intersect at the point $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1+a}},\dfrac{a}{1+a}\right)$.

dif.r: parametric intersection, choose positive root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ such that the areas of the two regions are equal.

dif.r: equal areas with parameter a, set up and solve

figures.cap: region under L1 from x=0 to 1 split by the parabola L2 into S1 (left, against y-axis) and S2 (right)

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} -x^2+1 &= ax^2\\ (a+1)x^2 &= 1\\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{a+1}\\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}} \end{aligned}$$
$x\ge 0$ is given, so $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2\\ &= \dfrac{a}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $y=a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2=\dfrac{a}{a+1}$ (the factor $a$ was missing).

solutions.latex:
Method 1

$S_1+S_2$ is the area under $L_1$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_1+S_2 &= \int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\ &= \left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $S_1=S_2$, so $2S_1=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $S_1=S_2=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$S_1$ lies between $L_1$ (above) and $L_2$ (below), from $x=0$ to the intersection in (a):
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}(-x^2+1-ax^2)\,dx\\ &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\left(1-(1+a)x^2\right)dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{1+a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1+a}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)-0\\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $S_1=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^2(1+a)\\ (1+a)^2(1+a)-4(1+a)^2 &= 0\\ (1+a)^2(1+a-4) &= 0\\ a &= -1 \text{ or } a=3 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=3$.

Method 2

$S_2=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx-S_1$ and $S_1=S_2$, so
$$S_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx$$
then continue as in Method 1.

Method 3

From Method 1:
$$S_1=\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}$$
$S_2$ is the area under $L_2$ up to the intersection, plus the area under $L_1$ from the intersection to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_2 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}ax^2\,dx+\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[\dfrac{a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}+\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1\\ &= \dfrac{a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}+\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2+2a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} \end{aligned}$$
Equating $S_1$ and $S_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\\ \dfrac{2(1+a)}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= 1\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^3\\ (1+a)^2(a-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$a=-1$ is outside the domain.
$$\therefore\ a=3$$
criteria: Forms an equation in $a$, such as $\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{1+a}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the primitive for $S_1$, $\left[x-\dfrac{(1+a)x^3}{3}\right]$, or equivalent merit
Writes an integral for $S_1$ with limits $0$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}$, or finds $S_1+S_2=\dfrac{2}{3}$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: trapezium ABCD with AB at the bottom, DC at the top, P on DC near C, segment AP drawn; NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: trapezium annotated with feet E, H, F, height h, AE = BF = 1, DC = 2, AB = 4, angle 60 degrees

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1358_q32_s1}

The trapezium is symmetric ($AD=BC$, equal base angles), so $\triangle ADE\equiv\triangle BCF$ and
$$AE=BF=\dfrac{4-2}{2}=1 \text{ km}$$
In right-angled $\triangle ADE$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{1}\\ h &= \sqrt{3} \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled $\triangle APH$, using the sine ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{h}{AP}\\ AP &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the triangle with $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{1}$ is $\triangle ADE$, not $\triangle APE$.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle APH$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{h}{AH}\\ AH &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta} \end{aligned}$$
$DPHE$ is a rectangle, so $DP=EH$:
$$\begin{aligned} DP &= AH-AE\\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}-1 \end{aligned}$$

From (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} AP &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta}\\ PC &= CD-DP\\ &= 2-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}-1\right)\\ &= 3-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Total cost (\$ per km times km):
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 100\,000\,AP+80\,000\,PC\\ &= 100\,000\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta}+80\,000\left(3-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}\right)\\ &= 100\,000\sqrt{3}(\sin\theta)^{-1}+240\,000-80\,000\sqrt{3}(\tan\theta)^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating, using
$$\dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{\tan^2\theta}=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}\times\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}$$
$$\begin{aligned} C' &= \dfrac{-100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta}{\tan^2\theta}\\ &= \dfrac{-100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}}{\sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $C'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta+80\,000\sqrt{3} &= 0\\ \cos\theta &= \dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}}{100\,000\sqrt{3}}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta\approx 36.9^\circ$.

Check the sign of $C'$ either side:

\extable{Ts1108_1}

$\therefore$ The cost is a minimum when $\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}$.
criteria: Finds the derivative of the cost function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation: $|2x - 3| = 9x$

dif.r: absolute value equation, reject extraneous solution

solutions.latex:
$|2x-3|=9x$ means $2x-3=9x$ or $-(2x-3)=9x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x - 3 &= 9x & \qquad -2x + 3 &= 9x \\ -3 &= 7x & 3 &= 11x \\ x &= -\dfrac{3}{7} & x &= \dfrac{3}{11} \end{aligned}$$
Test the solutions in the original equation.

$x=-\dfrac{3}{7}$:
$$\left|2 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right) - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{7},\qquad 9 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right)=-\dfrac{27}{7}$$
These are not equal, so $x = -\dfrac{3}{7}$ is not a solution.

$x=\dfrac{3}{11}$:
$$\left|2 \times \dfrac{3}{11} - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{11},\qquad 9 \times \dfrac{3}{11}=\dfrac{27}{11}$$
These are equal.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{3}{11}$$

solutions.latex:
Rearrange the line to gradient–intercept form:
$$\begin{aligned} 4y &= -x + 1 \\ y &= -\dfrac{1}{4}x + \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $m = -\dfrac{1}{4}$. Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$, so $m_\perp = 4$.

The tangent has gradient $y'$, so set $y'=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2x - 2 \\ 4 &= 2x - 2 \\ 6 &= 2x \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$y = 3^2 - 2 \times 3 - 3 = 0$$
$\therefore$ The point is $(3, 0)$.

questions.stem: A continuous probability distribution is given by $f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2}{279}$, defined in the domain $[4, 7]$.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is the area under $f$ from 4 to $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_4^x \dfrac{3t^2}{279}\,dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^3}{279}\right]_4^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^3}{279} - \dfrac{4^3}{279} \\ &= \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} \end{aligned}$$
for $4\le x\le 7$.

solutions.latex:
The median $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} &= 0.5 \\ x^3 - 64 &= 139.5 \\ x^3 &= 203.5 \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{203.5} \\ &= 5.881951\ldots \\ &\approx 5.9 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median is approximately 5.9.
criteria: Correctly equates to 0.5, allow for 1 error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1+x & v&=e^{-2x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2e^{-2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= e^{-2x} - 2(1 + x)e^{-2x} \\ &= e^{-2x}\left(1 - 2(1 + x)\right) \\ &= e^{-2x}(-1 - 2x) \\ &= -e^{-2x}(1 + 2x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y' = 0$:
$$-e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $1+2x=0$ and $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$ is a stationary point.

Only $1+2x$ decides the sign of $y'$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1140_1}

$\therefore$ Maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$.
criteria: Correct derivative, $x$ and $y$, and tests for a maximum, allowing 1 error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y'=-e^{-2x}(1+2x)$ with the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-e^{-2x} & v&=1+2x\\ u'&=2e^{-2x} & v'&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= 2e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)-2e^{-2x} \\ &= 2e^{-2x}(-1 + 1 + 2x) \\ &= 4xe^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $y'' = 0$:
$$4xe^{-2x}=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $x = 0$.

At $x = 0$, $y = 1$, so $(0, 1)$ is a possible point of inflection.

Only $4x$ decides the sign of $y''$. Testing either side:

Concavity changes, so $(0, 1)$ is a point of inflection.

parts.latex:
A vertical tower of height $h$ metres stands on horizontal ground. From a point $P$ on the ground due east of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $45^\circ$. From a point $Q$ on the ground due south of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the distance $PQ$ is 40 metres, find the exact height of the tower.

\exfigure{1359_q29_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D set-up: two elevation triangles combined via Pythagoras, exact values.

figures.cap: 3D diagram: tower RT of height h, P and Q on the ground, angles of elevation 45 at P and 30 at Q, PQ = 40 m, north arrow

solutions.latex:
Let $R$ be the base of the tower. In right-angled triangles $PRT$ and $QRT$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \qquad \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ PR &= h & QR &= \sqrt{3}h \end{aligned}$$
$P$ is due east and $Q$ due south of $R$, so $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle PRQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} 40^2 &= h^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2 \\ 1600 &= 4h^2 \\ h^2 &= 400 \\ h &= \pm 20 \end{aligned}$$
$h > 0$, so $h = 20$ m.
criteria: Three of: correct $PR$, correct $QR$, correct substitution into Pythagoras' theorem, correct answer, or equivalent merit
Two of the above, or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A population of insects varies according to the formula $P = 3000n^{\frac{t}{10}}$, where $n$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the time in days.

The initial population was 3000. After 20 days the population had grown to 12 000.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of increase is 6000 insects per day.

dif.r: twin of 2021 Q23: find base, differentiate a^{kt}, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Initially $P=3000$; after 20 days $P=12\,000$. Find $n$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 3000n^{\frac{20}{10}} \\ n^2 &= 4 \\ n &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 2$ and $P=3000\times 2^{\frac{t}{10}}$.

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 3000 \times \ln 2 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 6000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{t}{10} &= \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) \\ t &= 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &\approx 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Three of: finds $n$, finds $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, substitutes 6000 into $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, calculates $t$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
Two of the above (or 2 errors), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A light is to be placed over the centre of a circle. The intensity $(I)$ of the light varies as the sine of the angle $(\alpha)$ at which the rays strike the illuminated surface, divided by the square of the distance $(d)$ from the light i.e. $I = \dfrac{k\sin\alpha}{d^2}$ where $k$ is a positive constant.

\exfigure{1359_q33_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that: $I = \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

dif.r: geometry set-up: sine ratio and Pythagoras, substitute

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the optimal height for a light to be placed over the centre of a circle in order to provide maximum illumination to the circumference. Give your final answer as an exact value.

dif.r: quotient rule with 3/2 power, factor, exact optimum height

figures.cap: light at height y above centre O of a circle of radius a; ray of length d to P on the circumference meeting the surface at angle alpha; Radius = a; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the light, the centre and a point on the circumference, using the sine ratio:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{y}{d}$$
Using Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 &= y^2 + a^2 \\ d &= \left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad \text{as } d > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the given formula:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \dfrac{k\sin\alpha}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k \times \frac{y}{d}}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{d^3} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Two of: correct $\sin\alpha$, correct $d$, correctly shows $I$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions copy (images, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=ky & v&=\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\\ u'&=k & v'&=3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dy} &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} - ky \times 3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\left(\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\left(y^2 + a^2\right) - 3y^2\right]}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dI}{dy} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right) &= 0 \\ 2y^2 &= a^2 \\ y^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{2} \\ y &= \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \text{as } y > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Only $a^2-2y^2$ decides the sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dy}$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1158_1}

$\therefore$ The intensity is a maximum when the light is at height $y = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ m.
criteria: Two of: correct derivative, correctly finds $y$, tests for a maximum (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The probability that Young's soccer team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{4}{9}$. The probability that Young's rugby league team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

What is the probability that neither team wins this weekend?

dif.r: product of two complements

solutions.latex:
Let $S$ be "soccer team wins" and $R$ be "rugby team wins". The results are independent, so multiply the complements:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(\overline{S}\cap\overline{R}\right)&=\left(1-\dfrac{4}{9}\right)\times\left(1-\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=\dfrac{5}{36}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are two chance events such that $P(A)=0.45$, $P(B)=0.3$ and $P(A|B)=0.6$.

What is the value of $P(B|A)$?

dif.r: reverse conditional via intersection, formula

solutions.latex:
Using $P(B\cap A)=P(A|B)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B|A)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{P(A|B)\times P(B)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{0.6\times0.3}{0.45}\\&=0.4\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2(1-x)+\log_2(3-x)=3$.

dif.r: log law to quadratic, reject root 5 by domain

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $1-x>0$ and $3-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Using the log law $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2[(1-x)(3-x)]&=3\\(1-x)(3-x)&=2^3\\x^2-4x+3&=8\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x&=5 \text{ or } x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$x=5$ does not satisfy $x<1$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^x+\log_e(2x-1)\\y'&=e^x+\dfrac{2}{2x-1}\end{aligned}$$
Gradient of the tangent when $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m&=y'(1)\\&=e+2\end{aligned}$$
$y$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned}y(1)&=e+\log_e1\\&=e\end{aligned}$$
Equation of the tangent, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=(e+2)(x-1)\\y-e&=(e+2)x-e-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (e+2)x-y-2=0$$
