parts.latex:
A function $f(x)$ is obtained by performing the following operations on $g(x)=\sqrt{x^3+9}$ in the following order:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Reflection in the $y$ axis.
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of 4.
\item Vertical translation of 1 unit up.

\end{enumerate}

Which of the following is the equation of $f(x)$ ?

dif.r: reflect, dilate, shift root of cubic in order

solutions.latex:
Reflection in the $y$-axis (replace $x$ with $-x$):
$$\sqrt{(-x)^3+9}$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of 4 (replace $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{4}$):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\left(-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3+9}&=\sqrt{-\dfrac{x^3}{64}+9}\\&=\sqrt{9-\dfrac{x^3}{64}}\end{aligned}$$
Vertical translation of 1 unit up:
$$f(x)=\sqrt{9-\dfrac{x^3}{64}}+1$$

questions.stem: A frog jumps 180 cm to a lily pad.  It then jumps 135 cm to the next lily pad, 101.25 cm to the next lily pad and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that each successive jump length forms a geometric sequence.

dif.r: check common ratio

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences
Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the length of the $10^{\text{th}}$ jump.  Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: direct GP term

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The first and final lily pad are 8 metres apart.  Following this pattern, can the frog jump from the first lily pad to the last lily pad?  Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.

dif.r: compare S_inf with 8 m

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The jump lengths are $180,\ 135,\ 101.25,\ \ldots$

Testing for a common ratio:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}&=\dfrac{135}{180}\\&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}&=\dfrac{101.25}{135}\\&=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$, the sequence is geometric.

The sequence is geometric with $a=180$, $r=0.75$, $n=10$. Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=180(0.75)^{10-1}\\&=13.51524353\\&\approx 13.52\text{ cm (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes $a$, $r$ and $n$ into $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The frog's first jump lands on the first lily pad, and the last lily pad is 800 cm further, so the frog can reach it only if its total distance reaches $180+800=980$ cm.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=180$, $r=0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{180}{1-0.75}\\&=720\end{aligned}$$
$S_\infty=720<980$

$\therefore$ the frog will not be able to jump from the first to the last lily pad.
criteria: Correctly substitutes $a$ and $r$ into $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The average monthly maximum temperature in Sydney can be modelled using the cosine function, $T=A\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+B,$ where $T$ is the average maximum temperature and $t$ is the time elapsed since the start of the year in months (where $0\leq t\leq 12$).  The lowest average maximum temperature throughout the year is $17^\circ$ and the highest average maximum temperature is $27^\circ$ (in January).  The graph showing the average monthly maximum temperature is shown below.

\exfigure{566_q10_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $A$ and the value of $B$.

dif.r: amplitude and centre from max and min

parts.label: b
parts.latex: State the period of the function.

dif.r: period 2pi/n directly

parts.label: c
parts.latex: An outdoor music festival is being planned.  The event is to be held when the average maximum temperature is at least $24^\circ$.  For what values of $t$ can the event take place?  Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: solve cos=2/5, two intervals in context, 2 dp

figures.cap: graph of T against t for 0 to 12 months: maximum 27 at t = 0 and t = 12, minimum 17 at t = 6

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(27-17)\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $T=27$ (January):
$$\begin{aligned}27&=5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi(0)}{6}\right)+B\\B&=22\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $A$ or $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\&=12\end{aligned}$$

The temperature is $24^\circ$ when
$$\begin{aligned}5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+22&=24\\5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=2\\\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants ($0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\le 2\pi$).

First quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=1.159279481\\t&=2.214060718\end{aligned}$$
Fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-1.159279481\\&=5.123905826\\t&=9.785939282\end{aligned}$$
From the graph, the temperature is at least $24^\circ$ at the start and end of the year:
$$\therefore\ 0\le t\le 2.21\ \text{ or }\ 9.79\le t\le 12$$
criteria: Obtains one correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the question asks for 'at least $24^\circ$', so the intervals include their endpoints: $0\le t\le 2.21$ or $9.79\le t\le 12$ (was $0<t<2.21$ or $9.79<t<12$).

parts.latex: A farmer is monitoring the salinity of a dam on his property.  On the first day of observations, the salinity is measured as 0.15 ppt (parts per thousand).  Each subsequent day, the salinity increases by 2% of the previous day’s measurement.  When the measurement exceeds 10 ppt, the water will no longer be suitable for livestock and the farmer will begin to treat the dam.  On which day will the farmer need to start treating his dam?

dif.r: GP term exceeds 10, logs, day offset

solutions.latex:
The measurements $0.15,\ 0.153,\ 0.15606,\ \ldots$ form a geometric sequence with $a=0.15$, $r=1.02$.

The salinity reaches 10 ppt when $T_n=ar^{n-1}=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}10&=0.15(1.02)^{n-1}\\\dfrac{200}{3}&=(1.02)^{n-1}\\\log_{1.02}\left(\dfrac{200}{3}\right)&=n-1\\n-1&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{200}{3}\right)}{\ln(1.02)} &&(\text{change of base})\\n&=213.078176\end{aligned}$$
$n$ is a whole number, so the salinity first exceeds 10 ppt on day 214.

$\therefore$ the farmer needs to start treating the dam on the $214$th day.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: '$\ln_{1.02}$' is not valid notation; written $\log_{1.02}$ in the working and the criterion.

parts.latex: The first 3 terms of a geometric series are $2x+3,\ x,\ 2x-3$.  Find the value(s) of $x$.

dif.r: GP condition gives x^2=3

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Since the series is geometric, $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{2x+3}&=\dfrac{2x-3}{x}\\x^2&=(2x-3)(2x+3)\\4x^2-9&=x^2\\3x^2&=9\\x&=\pm\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Prove that $f(x)$ is an even function.

dif.r: routine f(-x)=f(x) proof

parts.label: b
parts.latex: State the domain and range of $f(x)$.

dif.r: domain all reals, range from minimum denominator and asymptote

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Hence, or otherwise, graph the function $f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$.

\exfigure{566_q13_1}

dif.r: sketch unfamiliar rational curve without calculus

figures.cap: blank x and y axes for sketching
solution sketch: bell-shaped curve y = 8/(x^2+4), maximum (0,2), horizontal asymptote y = 0

solutions.latex:
A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\dfrac{8}{(-x)^2+4}\\&=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}\\&=f(x)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$ is an even function.

$x^2+4\ge 4>0$ for all $x$, so the denominator is never zero.

$\therefore$ the domain is all real $x$.

The minimum value of $x^2+4$ is 4 (when $x=0$), so the maximum value of $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$ is 2.

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}\to 0$.

$\therefore$ the range is $0<y\le 2$.
criteria: Correct domain or range, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A company starts a page on social media.  Initially, the page has 200 followers $(ie\ T_0=200)$.  Each day the page gains an extra 200 followers but loses 10% of the number of followers on the previous day.

Let $T_n$ be the number of followers on the $n$th day.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write a recurrence relation for $T_n$.

dif.r: model recurrence from verbal description; T_0 offset

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $T_n=2000\left(1-(0.9)^{n+1}\right)$.

dif.r: show closed form from recurrence via GP sum

solutions.latex:
Each day the page keeps $90\%$ of the previous day's followers and gains 200:
$$T_n=200+0.9\times T_{n-1}$$
where $T_0=200$ and $n\ge 1$.

$$\begin{aligned}T_0&=200\\T_1&=200+0.9\times T_0\\&=200+0.9\times 200\\T_2&=200+0.9\times T_1\\&=200+0.9\times(200+0.9\times 200)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2\\T_3&=200+0.9\times T_2\\&=200+0.9\times(200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2+200\times 0.9^3\end{aligned}$$
Each term is the sum of a geometric series with $a=200$, $r=0.9$ and $n+1$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ T_n&=\dfrac{200(1-(0.9)^{n+1})}{1-0.9}\\&=2000(1-(0.9)^{n+1})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression for $T_3$ in terms of powers of $0.9$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The sum of the first ten terms of an arithmetic sequence is $(-50)$.  The next ten terms of this sequence add to $(-450)$.  Find the first term and common difference of the sequence.

dif.r: interpret next ten terms as S_20, two simultaneous sum equations

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $S_{10}=-50$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10}{2}\big(2a+(10-1)d\big)&=-50\\5(2a+9d)&=-50\\2a+9d&=-10 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The first 20 terms add to $(-50)+(-450)=-500$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2a+(20-1)d\big)&=-500\\10(2a+19d)&=-500\\2a+19d&=-50 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
$(2)-(1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}10d&=-40\\d&=-4\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}2a+9(-4)&=-10\\2a&=26\\a&=13\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first term is $13$ and the common difference is $-4$.
criteria: Obtains equations (1) and (2), or equivalent merit
Obtains equation (1) or (2), or $2a+29d=-90$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Consider the sequence $187, 183, 179, \ldots$ What is the $50^{\text{th}}$ term?

dif.r: MCQ: direct T_50

solutions.latex:
The sequence is arithmetic with $a=187$, $d=-4$, $n=50$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{50}&=187+(50-1)(-4)\\&=-9\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} x^3\,dx$?

dif.r: MCQ: odd function integral zero; recognise inverse form

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Since $y=x^3$ is an odd function,
$$\int_{-2}^{2}x^3\,dx=0$$
The area under $y=x^3$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is above the $x$-axis, so
$$\int_0^2x^3\,dx>0$$
Option A adds an absolute value to this positive integral, and option C doubles it, so both are greater than $0$.

Reversing the limits in option D (and using $x^3$ odd):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2x^3\,dx+\int_0^{-2}x^3\,dx&=\int_0^2x^3\,dx-\int_{-2}^{0}x^3\,dx\\&=2\int_0^2x^3\,dx\end{aligned}$$
which is also greater than $0$.

Since $y^{\frac{1}{3}}$ is also an odd function,
$$\int_{-8}^{8}y^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dy=0$$
so option B is equivalent.

parts.latex: The arithmetic sequence $x, 2x+1, 4x-5$, is formed. What is the value of $x$?

dif.r: MCQ: constant difference linear equation

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The terms are in arithmetic sequence, so the common difference is constant:
$$\begin{aligned}(2x+1)-x&=(4x-5)-(2x+1)\\x+1&=2x-6\\x&=7\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the gradient of the normal to the curve $y=\ln(5x+7)$ at the point where $x = 3$?

dif.r: chain on ln, evaluate, negative reciprocal

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(5x+7)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{5}{5x+7}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=\dfrac{5}{5\times3+7}\\&=\dfrac{5}{22}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=\dfrac{-22}{5}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is the graph of $y=\dfrac{x+5}{x+1}$?

dif.r: split rational function into translated 4/x, match graph

figures.cap: option A: option A: hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = 1 and horizontal asymptote y = -1
option B: option B: hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = -1 and horizontal asymptote y = 1
option C: option C: hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = -1 and horizontal asymptote y = -1
option D: option D: hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = 1 and horizontal asymptote y = 1

solutions.latex:
Rewriting the function:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{x+5}{x+1}\\&=\dfrac{x+1+4}{x+1}\\&=\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}+\dfrac{4}{x+1}\\&=1+\dfrac{4}{x+1}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the graph is $y=\dfrac{4}{x}$ translated 1 unit to the left and 1 unit up.

Its asymptotes are $x=-1$ and $y=1$, and since $4>0$ its branches lie above and to the right of, and below and to the left of, the intersection of the asymptotes.

parts.latex: What is the primitive function of $8x\times 4^{x^2+6}$?

dif.r: MCQ: f'a^f form, absorb 4 into exponent

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2+6)=2x$, write $8x=4\times2x$ and use
$$\int f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\,dx=\dfrac{a^{f(x)}}{\ln a}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int 8x\times4^{x^2+6}\,dx&=4\int 2x\times4^{x^2+6}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{4\times4^{x^2+6}}{\ln4}+c\\&=\dfrac{4^{x^2+7}}{\ln4}+c\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The function $f(x)$ has a maximum turning point at $(6, 1)$. The function $g(x)=f\left(\dfrac{-1}{2}x\right)$. Which of the following about $g(x)$ is true?

dif.r: dilation and reflection of turning point, nature unchanged

options.label: A
options.latex: There is a maximum turning point at $(12, 1)$.

options.label: B
options.latex: There is a maximum turning point at $(-12,1)$.

options.label: C
options.latex: There is a minimum turning point at $(12, 1)$.

options.label: D
options.latex: There is a minimum turning point at $(-12,1)$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ has had the following transformations to become $g(x)=f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)$.

Horizontal dilation by a factor of $2$: the turning point moves from $(6,1)$ to $(12,1)$.

Reflection in the $y$-axis: the turning point moves from $(12,1)$ to $(-12,1)$.

Neither transformation changes the $y$-values, so the turning point is still a maximum.

$\therefore$ There will be a maximum turning point at $(-12,1)$.

parts.latex:
It is known that the following geometric series has a limiting sum.

$$2x,4x^2,8x^3,16x^4,\ldots\ldots$$

What could be the value of $x$?

dif.r: MCQ: |2x|<1

solutions.latex:
A limiting sum exists if $|r|<1$.

The common ratio is $r=\dfrac{4x^2}{2x}=2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}|2x|&<1\\|x|&<\dfrac{1}{2}\\-\dfrac{1}{2}&<x<\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $|r|=1$, so it is excluded; of the options only $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ lies in this interval.

The graph of $y=5e^{-x}\ln x$ is shown below. The area is estimated by using the Trapezoidal Rule and 3 function values, from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$ (inclusive). Which of the following statements is true?

\exfigure{572_q10_1}

dif.r: MCQ: trapezoidal values plus concavity for under/over

options.label: A

options.label: B

solution sketch: graph of y = 5e^{-x} ln x with two trapezia from x = 1 to x = 3 shaded, lying under the curve

solutions.latex:
Three function values from $x=1$ to $x=3$ give two strips, so $h=\dfrac{3-1}{2}=1$.

When $x=1$, $y=0$

When $x=2$, $y=5e^{-2}\ln(2)$

When $x=3$, $y=5e^{-3}\ln(3)$

These values can be stored in the memory of your calculator for ease of calculation.

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big(y_0+2y_1+y_2\big)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(0+2\times5e^{-2}\ln2+5e^{-3}\ln3\big)\\&\approx0.606\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
The straight tops of the trapezia lie below the curve, so part of the area is missed:

\exfigure{572_q10_s1}

$\therefore$ It is an underestimate.

dif.r: direct f prime over f
standard a^f(x) derivative, linear index

parts.latex: $y=\ln\sqrt{2x^2-5}$

dif.r: log law for root, then f prime over f

parts.label: e
parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{3x}{\cos 4x}$

dif.r: quotient rule with cos 4x

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(8x+5)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{8}{8x+5}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{f(x)}=\ln a\times f'(x)\times a^{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=6^{2x-1}\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\ln(6)\times2\times6^{2x-1}\\&=2\ln(6)\times6^{2x-1}\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=5x & v&=e^{3x}\\u'&=5 & v'&=3e^{3x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=5x\times3e^{3x}+5e^{3x}\\&=15xe^{3x}+5e^{3x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly differentiates $e^{3x}$ and attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using log laws, then $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\sqrt{2x^2-5}\\&=\ln(2x^2-5)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x^2-5)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4x}{2x^2-5}\\&=\dfrac{2x}{2x^2-5}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses log laws to express $y$ OR correctly differentiates $\sqrt{2x^2-5}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3x & v&=\cos4x\\u'&=3 & v'&=-4\sin4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{3\cos4x-3x\times(-4\sin4x)}{\cos^2 4x}\\&=\dfrac{3\cos4x+12x\sin4x}{\cos^2 4x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly differentiates $\cos 4x$ and attempts to use the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Find:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int 5x^2+8x-3\,dx$

dif.r: term-by-term polynomial primitive

parts.label: b

dif.r: negative power of linear inner, reverse chain

dif.r: direct exponential primitive with linear inner

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \cos x\sin^5 x\,dx$

dif.r: reverse chain f'(x)[f(x)]^5 recognition

solutions.latex:
Integrating term by term:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(5x^2+8x-3)\,dx&=\dfrac{5x^3}{3}+\dfrac{8x^2}{2}-3x+c\\&=\dfrac{5x^3}{3}+4x^2-3x+c\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the function but omits the constant OR incorrectly integrates the function but includes the constant, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Writing with a negative index and using
$$\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{(8x-1)^3}\,dx&=\int(8x-1)^{-3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{(8x-1)^{-2}}{8\times(-2)}+c\\&=\dfrac{1}{-16}(8x-1)^{-2}+c\\&=\dfrac{-1}{16(8x-1)^2}+c\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses index laws on the integral OR incorrectly uses index laws to obtain an integral with a negative index and correctly integrates the ensuing function, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=\sin x$, so $f'(x)=\cos x$ and the integrand is $f'(x)[f(x)]^5$.

Using the reverse chain rule:
$$\int\cos x\sin^5x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin^6x+c$$

questions.stem: Calculate the following definite integrals. Leave your answers in exact form where necessary.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} \dfrac{6}{x+3}\,dx$

dif.r: direct ln primitive, ln1=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sec^2 3x\,dx$

dif.r: sec^2(3x) primitive; tan(3pi/4) sign care

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{x+a}\,dx=\ln|x+a|+c$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{6}{x+3}\,dx&=6\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{1}{x+3}\,dx\\&=\Big[6\ln|x+3|\Big]_{-2}^{0}\\&=6\ln|0+3|-6\ln|(-2)+3|\\&=6\ln3-6\ln1\\&=6\ln3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the function, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sec^2 ax\,dx=\dfrac{1}{a}\tan ax+c$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\sec^2 3x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\tan3x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\tan\left(3\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{3}\tan\left(3\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times0-\dfrac{1}{3}\times(-1)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=x^3-3x^2+4$.

dif.r: solve f'=0, substitute for y-coordinates

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^3-3x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2-6x\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x=0$ or $x=2$

When $x=0$, $y=0^3-3\times0^2+4=4$

When $x=2$, $y=2^3-3\times2^2+4=0$

$\therefore$ Stationary points are $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$
criteria: Correctly differentiates the function and equates to zero, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For which values of $x$ is the curve $y=5x^3-2x^2+6x-1$ concave up?

dif.r: second derivative inequality

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=5x^3-2x^2+6x-1\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=15x^2-4x+6\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=30x-4\end{aligned}$$
Concave up when $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}30x-4&>0\\30x&>4\\x&>\dfrac{4}{30}\\x&>\dfrac{2}{15}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the second derivative and sets it greater than zero, or equivalent merit

dif.r: cubic below axis on [0,2]; take absolute value

figures.cap: cubic y = x^3 - x^2 - 2x with x-intercepts -1, 0, 2; region between x = 0 and x = 2 below the x-axis shaded

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the $x$-axis for $0<x<2$, so take the absolute value of the integral:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left|\int_0^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx\right|\\&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{2x^2}{2}\right]_0^2\right|\\&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right|\\&=\left|\dfrac{2^4}{4}-\dfrac{2^3}{3}-2^2-\left(\dfrac{0^4}{4}-\dfrac{0^3}{3}-0^2\right)\right|\\&=\dfrac{8}{3}\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the function, or equivalent merit

solution sketch: y = 2^x and concave-down parabola y = -2x^2 + 8x - 4 with vertex (2,4), intersecting at (1,2) and (2,4)

solutions.latex:
Test $(2,4)$ in $y=2^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=2^2\\&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(2,4)$ lies on $y=2^x$.

Test $(2,4)$ in $y=-2x^2+8x-4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=-2(2)^2+8\times2-4\\&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(2,4)$ lies on $y=-2x^2+8x-4$.

$\therefore(2,4)$ is a point of intersection of $y=-2x^2+8x-4$ and $y=2^x$.

The vertex lies on the axis of symmetry, $x=\dfrac{-b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-8}{2\times(-2)}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The graph below shows the functions $y=2x^2+x-9$ and $y=3x-5$.

\exfigure{572_q19_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinates of the points of intersection are $x=2$ and $x=-1$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, find the area of the shaded region between the line $y=3x-5$ and the parabola $y=2x^2+x-9$.

dif.r: standard area between line and parabola, bounds known

figures.cap: parabola y = 2x^2 + x - 9 and line y = 3x - 5 meeting at (-1,-8) and (2,1), region between them shaded

solutions.latex:
Equating $y=2x^2+x-9$ and $y=3x-5$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2+x-9&=3x-5\\2x^2-2x-4&=0\\x^2-x-2&=0\\(x-2)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x=2$ or $x=-1$
criteria: Correctly substitutes the equations or eliminates the $y$ variable, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The line is above the parabola for $-1<x<2$, so
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-1}^{2}\big(3x-5-(2x^2+x-9)\big)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{2}(-2x^2+2x+4)\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-2x^3}{3}+\dfrac{2x^2}{2}+4x\right]_{-1}^{2}\\&=\left[\dfrac{-2x^3}{3}+x^2+4x\right]_{-1}^{2}\\&=\left(\dfrac{-2(2)^3}{3}+2^2+4\times2\right)-\left(\dfrac{-2(-1)^3}{3}+(-1)^2+4\times(-1)\right)\\&=9\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\sin x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\cos x+\sin x$$

solutions.latex:
From (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin x)=x\cos x+\sin x$, so integrating both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(x\cos x+\sin x)\,dx&=x\sin x\\\int x\cos x\,dx+\int\sin x\,dx&=x\sin x\\\int x\cos x\,dx-\cos x&=x\sin x+c\\\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x+\cos x+c\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A certain radioactive isotope element decays exponentially according to the model $A=A_0e^{kt}$ where $A$ is the number of grams of the isotope at the end of $t$ days and $A_0$ is the number of grams present initially.

Initially there are 200 grams of this isotope. After 10 days, 16 grams of this substance remain. What is the rate of decay after 5 days? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: find k from data, differentiate, substitute

solutions.latex:
Using the model $A=A_0e^{kt}$.

When $t=0$, $A=200$, so $A_0=200$:
$$A=200e^{kt}$$
When $t=10$, $A=16$:
$$\begin{aligned}16&=200e^{10k}\\\dfrac{16}{200}&=e^{10k}\\\ln\dfrac{16}{200}&=10k\\k&=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{16}{200}\end{aligned}$$
Differentiating,
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=200ke^{kt}$$
When $t=5$, with $k=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{16}{200}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=200ke^{5k}\\&=-14.28767882\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Rate of decay is $14.29\text{ grams/day}$
criteria: Correctly finds the value of the constant $k$ and correctly differentiates to find $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the value of the constant $k$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: hence S_10 = 55 log 3

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\log a^n=n\log a$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\log3,\log9,\log27,\log81,\ldots\\&=\log3,\log3^2,\log3^3,\log3^4,\ldots\\&=\log3,2\log3,3\log3,4\log3,\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Testing for a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_2-T_1&=2\log3-\log3\\&=\log3\\T_3-T_2&=3\log3-2\log3\\&=\log3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ AP where $a=\log3$, $d=\log3$
criteria: Correctly uses a log law OR finds $T_2-T_1$ and $T_3-T_2$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution; 1 (mark value not printed in the guidelines): Correctly uses a log law OR finds $T_2-T_1$ and $T_3-T_2$

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ with $a=\log3$, $d=\log3$, $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{10}{2}\big[2\log3+(10-1)\log3\big]\\&=5(2\log3+9\log3)\\&=5(11\log3)\\&=55\log3\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ in the domain $0\le x\le \pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: chain rule trig, solve within shifted domain, nature

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the points of inflection.

dif.r: solve f''=0 trig within domain, reject out-of-range

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Hence, or otherwise graph the function $f(x)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ on the number plane below in the domain $0\le x\le \pi$.

\exfigure{572_q23_1}

dif.r: sketch shifted sine with endpoints and features

A.note: hence/otherwise sketch of sin(2x+pi/3) on [0,pi]

Curve sketching using calculus.reason: Criteria reward period/amplitude shape only; not_when: features from earlier parts not re-tagged on a hence sketch.

Transformations of trigonometric graphs.evidence: graph f(x)=sin(2x+pi/3); criterion: correct shape with period and amplitude

figures.cap: blank number plane with x and y axes, origin at left
solution sketch: y = sin(2x + pi/3) on [0, pi]: starts (0, sqrt3/2), max (pi/12, 1), x-intercepts pi/3 and 5pi/6, min (7pi/12, -1), ends (pi, sqrt3/2)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies between $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\\2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=1$$
When $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-1$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-4<0 &&\text{maximum}\\x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=4>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12},1\right)$ is a relative maximum turning point and $\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12},-1\right)$ is a relative minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the $y$ values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Solves the trigonometric equation to find the $x$ coordinates of the stationary points, or correctly finds one pair of coordinates, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection can occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=0,\pi,2\pi\end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\ge\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $0$ is rejected:
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ or }2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\2x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{6}\left(=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$\sin\theta$ changes sign at $\theta=\pi$ and $\theta=2\pi$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign at both values: the concavity changes.

When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
When $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
$\therefore$ Points of inflection are $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},0\right)$
criteria: Finds all $x$ values of the points of inflection OR finds the coordinates of one point of inflection, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A sequence is defined by the rule $T_n=5^n-5n$ where $n\ge 1$. Find the sum of the first 20 terms. Leave your answer in simplest index form.

dif.r: split into GP and AP sums, index form

solutions.latex:
Each term is a power of $5$ minus a multiple of $5$, so the sum splits into two series:
$$\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^{20}(5^n-5n)&=5^1-5\times1+5^2-5\times2+5^3-5\times3+\ldots+5^{20}-5\times20\\&=5^1+5^2+5^3+\ldots+5^{20}-(5\times1+5\times2+5\times3+\ldots+5\times20)\end{aligned}$$
Geometric series where $a=5$, $r=5$, $n=20$

Arithmetic series where $a=5$, $d=5$, $n=20$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ and $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}&=\dfrac{5(5^{20}-1)}{5-1}-\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2\times5+(20-1)\times5\big)\\&=\dfrac{5(5^{20}-1)}{4}-1050\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes into the sum of an arithmetic or geometric series formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Feifei ($F$) and Airi ($A$) are on opposing sides of a river bank. Feifei can run at a rate of 7km/hr and row at a rate of 5km/hr. The river bank is 800 metres wide and there would be 2.5 kilometres between Feifei and Airi if they were on the same side of the shore. Feifei wishes to meet Airi. Let $x$ be the distance from directly opposite from Feifei's starting point to her exit point ($E$) from the water and let $t$ be the total time taken for Feifei to meet Airi.

\exfigure{572_q25_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the time ($t$) taken for Feifei to row and then run to Airi can be given by the equation $t=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}$.

dif.r: Pythagoras and time=distance/speed set-up

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find how far Feifei must run along the shore in order to minimise the time taken to reach Airi. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: derivative with surd, solve irrational equation, interpret run distance

figures.cap: river 800 m wide between two shores; F on lower shore, E on upper shore a distance x from the point opposite F, A on upper shore, 2.5 km marked from A to the point opposite F

solutions.latex:
Let $d$ km be Feifei's rowing distance. The river is $800\text{ m}=0.8\text{ km}$ wide, so by Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with legs $0.8$ and $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=0.8^2+x^2\\&=0.64+x^2\\d&=\sqrt{0.64+x^2}\end{aligned}$$
She rows $d$ km at $5$ km/h and runs $(2.5-x)$ km at $7$ km/h. Using time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$t=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}$$

Writing the square root as a power and differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}\\t&=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{1}{5}(0.64+x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\\dfrac{dt}{dx}&=-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times2x(0.64+x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dt}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}&=0\\\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}&=\dfrac{1}{7}\\\dfrac{x}{5}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{7}\\\dfrac{7x}{5}&=\sqrt{0.64+x^2}\\\dfrac{49x^2}{25}&=x^2+0.64\\49x^2&=25x^2+16\\24x^2&=16\\x^2&=\dfrac{16}{24}\\x&=\pm0.8164965809\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Since $x>0$ (a distance),
$$x=0.8164965809\ldots\approx0.82\ (2\text{ d.p.})$$
Testing the nature with the first derivative:

\extable{572_q25_t1}

$\therefore$ When $x=0.816\ldots$ the minimum amount of time is taken for Feifei to reach Airi.

Feifei must run
$$\begin{aligned}2.5-0.816\ldots&=1.683503419\ldots\\&\approx1.68\text{ km (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Tests for maximum/minimum, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.

parts.label: a

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is the particle ever at rest? Give reasons.

dif.r: justify v>0 from positive exponentials

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c

dif.r: integrate exponentials, find constant

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the time when the particle is at $x=4$.(Give your answer in exact form)

dif.r: quadratic in e^t, reject negative root

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2e^0+4e^0\\&=6\end{aligned}$$

Since $2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all values of $t$,
$$2e^t+4e^{-t}>0$$
for all values of $t$.

$\therefore$ The particle will never be at rest.

meta.top_criterion_original: must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ then must show $e^{2t}=-2$
meta.marker_note: Must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ has no solution, must show $e^{2t}=-2$.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(2e^t+4e^{-t})\,dt\\&=2e^t-4e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2e^0-4e^0+C\\C&=-2+4\\\therefore C&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=2e^t-4e^{-t}+2$$

When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^t-4e^{-t}+2&=4\\2(e^t-2e^{-t}-1)&=0\\e^t-\dfrac{2}{e^t}-1&=0\\e^{2t}-e^t-2&=0 &&(\times e^t)\\(e^t-2)(e^t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^t+1>0$, $e^t-2=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=2\\t&=\ln2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
When Fred was born, his parents opened a new savings account and made a deposit of \$300. At the start of each subsequent six-month period, his parents make a deposit of \$300. The account earns an interest rate of 6% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

Let $A_n$ be the amount (in dollars) in the account at the end of $n^{th}$ half-year.

dif.r: unroll to A_2 with start-of-period deposits
annuity-due GP sum with a=1.03, simplify to given form

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the amount available for withdrawal at the end of the 18$^{\text{th}}$ year will be \$19552 to the nearest dollar. (Assume that no withdrawals are made from the fund during this time.)

dif.r: substitute n=36 into given A_n

solutions.latex:
$r=\dfrac{6\%}{2}=3\%$ per half-year.

Each deposit is made at the start of a half-year and earns interest for that half-year:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=300(1.03)\\A_2&=(A_1+300)\times1.03\\&=(300\times1.03+300)\times1.03\\&=300\times1.03^2+300\times1.03\end{aligned}$$

Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a GP with $a=1.03$, $r=1.03$ and $n$ terms, summed with $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=300(1.03)\\A_2&=300\times1.03^2+300\times1.03\\&\;\;\vdots\\A_n&=300\times1.03^n+300\times1.03^{n-1}+\dots+300\times1.03\\&=300(1.03^n+1.03^{n-1}+\dots+1.03)\\&=300\times1.03\times\dfrac{1.03^n-1}{1.03-1}\\&=10300(1.03^n-1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression for $A_n$, or uses the sum of a GP formula without establishing $A_n$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$18$ years $=36$ half-years, so $n=36$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{36}&=10300(1.03^{36}-1)\\&=\$19\,552\text{ (nearest dollar)}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the maximum speed of the object.

dif.r: vertex of quadratic velocity; question loosely posed

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the acceleration when the object is at rest.

dif.r: solve v=0, differentiate, substitute

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the object during the first 15 seconds.

dif.r: distance with direction change at t=12

solutions.latex:
$v=-t^2+10t+24$

The maximum speed is at the turning point of this concave down parabola, $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{10}{2\times(-1)}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}v_{\max}&=24+10\times5-5^2\\&=49\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: marking guideline answers maximum velocity (49 m/s at t = 5); speed |v| is unbounded for t > 12, so 'maximum speed' is only 49 m/s if the domain is limited (e.g. 0 <= t <= 12); guideline line '24 x 10 x 5 - 5^2' transcribed as printed (should be 24 + 10 x 5 - 5^2)
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $v_{\max}=24\times10\times5-5^2$ written as $24+10\times5-5^2$ (the value $49$ is unchanged).

solutions.latex:
The object is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+10t+24&=0\\t^2-10t-24&=0\\(t-12)(t+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge0$, $t=12$.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\&=-2t+10\\&=-2\times12+10\\&=-14\text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int(-t^2+10t+24)\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin: $t=0$, $x=0$ gives $0=0+0+0+C$, so $C=0$.
$$x=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t$$
The object is at rest at $t=12$ (from (b)) and changes direction there, so find the displacement at $t=0$, $12$ and $15$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=0: & x&=0\\t&=12: & x&=-\dfrac{12^3}{3}+5\times12^2+24\times12=432\\t&=15: & x&=-\dfrac{15^3}{3}+5\times15^2+24\times15=360\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled}&=432+(432-360)\\&=504\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct displacement at $t=12$ and at $t=15$, or equivalent merit
Correct displacement at $t=15$ or $t=12$, or equivalent merit

why: Solution note: marking guideline answers maximum velocity (49 m/s at t = 5); speed |v| is unbounded for t > 12, so 'maximum speed' is only 49 m/s if the domain is limited (e.g. 0 <= t <= 12); guideline line '24 x 10

Arjun borrows \$1,000,000 for a period of 10 years at an interest rate of 0.5% per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month, a repayment of \$$M$ is made.

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing after the $n^{th}$ repayment has been made.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence show that the monthly instalment $M$ is given by: $M=\dfrac{5000(1.005)^{120}}{1.005^{120}-1}$.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the amount still owing to the bank after 5 years, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: evaluate M, substitute n=60 into given A_n

solutions.latex:
$r=0.5\%$ per month. Each month interest is added and then $M$ is repaid:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=1000000\times1.005-M\\A_2&=A_1\times1.005-M\\&=(1000000\times1.005-M)\times1.005-M\\&=1000000\times1.005^2-M\times1.005-M\end{aligned}$$

Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms, summed with $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=1000000\times1.005^2-M\times1.005-M\\&\;\;\vdots\\A_n&=1000000\times1.005^n-M\times1.005^{n-1}-M\times1.005^{n-2}-\dots-M\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-M(1.005^{n-1}+1.005^{n-2}+\dots+1)\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-M\times\dfrac{1.005^n-1}{1.005-1}\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-200M(1.005^n-1)\\&=(1000000-200M)\times1.005^n+200M\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially progresses towards the correct solution, or obtains $A_n$ with a GP, or equivalent merit
Obtains the correct $M=11102.05$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression for the object's velocity ($v$) at time $t$.

dif.r: integrate reciprocal square with chain factor, find C

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the limiting speed of the object.

dif.r: limit of velocity as t grows

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the position of the object at the end of the 10$^{\text{th}}$ second. (Answer to the nearest metre)

dif.r: integrate to log, find C, evaluate

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int a\,dt\\&=\int-(5t+1)^{-2}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-(5t+1)^{-2+1}}{(-2+1)\times5}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=\dfrac{1}{5(5\times0+1)}+C\\C&=0.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$$

$v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}\to0$, so
$$v\to0.8$$
$\therefore$ The limiting speed of the object is $0.8$ m/s.

Integrating $v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8\right)dt\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{5}+0.8t+C\\&=\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{25}+0.8t+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3&=\dfrac{\ln(5\times0+1)}{25}+0.8\times0+C\\\therefore C&=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$x=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5t+1)+0.8t-3$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5\times10+1)+0.8\times10-3\\&=5.157\ldots\\&\approx5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The object is about $5$ m to the right of the origin.

The CDF reaches $1$ at the largest value of $X$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(4)&=1\\\therefore\ e&=1\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}P(X=1)&=F(1)\\\therefore\ a&=\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}a+2b+c&=1\\\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{2}+c&=1\\\therefore\ c&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$

Seats in a theatre are arranged in rows. The number of seats in this theatre form the terms of an arithmetic series.

The sixth row has 23 seats, and the fifteenth row has 50 seats. If the theatre has 20 rows, how many seats are in the theatre?

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_6=23$ and $T_{15}=50$:
$$\begin{aligned}a+5d&=23\\a+14d&=50\end{aligned}$$
Solving simultaneously (subtract the first equation from the second):
$$\begin{aligned}9d&=27\\d&=3\\a&=8\end{aligned}$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}\big[2\times 8+19\times 3\big]\\&=730\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ There are a total of 730 seats.
criteria: Correctly finds $a$ and $d$, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{late})&=P(\text{dry, late})+P(\text{rain, late})+P(\text{snow, late})\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{5}+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{9}{10}\\&=\dfrac{9}{20}\end{aligned}$$

Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{rain}\mid\text{late})&=\dfrac{P(\text{rain and late})}{P(\text{late})}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{3}{5}}{\frac{9}{20}}\\&=\dfrac{4}{9}\end{aligned}$$

A random variable is normally distributed with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. The table provided at the back of this exam gives the probability that this random variable lies below $z$ for some positive values of $z$.

Find the probability that in a random week the rep will cover a mileage between 380 and 410.

solutions.latex:
The variance is 600, so $\sigma=\sqrt{600}$. Standardising with $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ and reading the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(380<M<410)&=P(M<410)-P(M<380)\\&=P\left(z<\dfrac{410-365}{\sqrt{600}}\right)-P\left(z<\dfrac{380-365}{\sqrt{600}}\right)\\&=P(z<1.83712\ldots)-P(z<0.61237\ldots)\\&=0.9671-0.7291\\&=0.238\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct probability for both mileages from the provided table, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A water sprinkler covers a circular lawn area of radius 10 metres. The sprinkler $(O)$ is placed 5 metres from a rectangular garden bed. Garden stakes are placed at $A$ and $B$, as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{317_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle AOB=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

dif.r: cos ratio gives pi/3, double by symmetry

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the major arc length of the lawn area covered by the sprinkler is $\dfrac{40\pi}{3}\text{ m}$.

dif.r: major angle then arc length

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the exact area of the lawn that the sprinkler will cover.

dif.r: circle minus minor segment, exact

figures.cap: garden bed with stakes A and B on its edge; lawn is the major segment of a circle centre O radius 10 m, O 5 m from the bed

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $OA=10$ and side 5 (the distance from $O$ to the garden bed), let $\theta$ be the angle at $O$, half of $\angle AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{5}{10}\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
By symmetry:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle AOB&=2\theta\\&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{major }\angle AOB&=2\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Using the arc length $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Arc length}&=10\times\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{40\pi}{3}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds major $\angle AOB$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The lawn covered is the circle minus the minor segment cut off by $AB$. Using segment area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\pi r^2-\left[\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\right]\\&=\pi\times 10^2-\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]\\&=100\pi-\dfrac{100\pi}{3}+50\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{200\pi}{3}+50\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{200\pi}{3}+25\sqrt{3}\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the area of the minor segment, or equivalent merit
Correct substitution into the formula to find the area of the minor segment, or equivalent merit

dif.r: direct quotient rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-\ln x^2}{x^2}\,dx$.

dif.r: log law, factor 2, reverse (a), exact evaluation

solutions.latex:
$$y=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\ln x & v&=x\\u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{x\times\frac{1}{x}-\ln x}{x^2}\\&=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\ln x^2=2\ln x$ and the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-\ln x^2}{x^2}\,dx&=\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-2\ln x}{x^2}\,dx\\&=2\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\,dx\\&=2\left[\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right]_e^{e^2}\\&=2\left[\dfrac{\ln e^2}{e^2}-\dfrac{\ln e}{e}\right]\\&=2\left[\dfrac{2}{e^2}-\dfrac{1}{e}\right]\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly manipulates the integral to obtain the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle $P$ is moving on the $x$ axis and its velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$, $t$ seconds after a given instant, is given by $v=t^2(3-t)$, $t\ge 0$.

When $t=2$, $P$ is observed to be $4\text{ m}$ from the origin $O$, in the positive direction of the $x-$axis.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of $P$ when $t=2$.

dif.r: differentiate polynomial and substitute

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The particle is initially at rest and is also at rest when $t=T$. Determine the distance of $P$ from $O$ when $t=T$.

dif.r: find T, integrate, C from t=2, evaluate

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Expanding, $v=3t^2-t^3$. Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$:
$$a=6t-3t^2$$
When $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=6(2)-3(2)^2\\&=12-12\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}t^2(3-t)&=0\\t&=0\text{ or }3\end{aligned}$$
So $T=3$.

Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int 3t^2-t^3\,dt\\&=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$, $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=2^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 2^4+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4$$
When $t=T=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=3^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 3^4\\&=6.75\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates and finds the constant to find the displacement equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A car dealership has a car for sale for a cash price of \$20 000. It can also be bought on terms over three years. The first six months are interest free. After the first six months, reducible interest is charged at the rate of 1\% per month, calculated at the end of each month.

Repayments are to be made in equal monthly instalments beginning at the end of the first month.

A customer buys the car on these terms and agrees to monthly repayments of $\$M$. Let $\$A_n$ be the amount owing at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ month.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression for $A_6$.

dif.r: interest-free months: simple linear expression 20000-6M
unroll two interest months from A_6 to given A_8

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of $M$.

dif.r: two-phase loan: extend to A_36, GP sum, solve for M

solutions.latex:
No interest is charged in the first six months, so each month the balance falls by $M$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=20\,000-M\\A_2&=20\,000-2M\\&\ \ \vdots\\A_6&=20\,000-6M\end{aligned}$$

From month 7, interest of $1\%$ is added each month before the repayment:
$$\begin{aligned}A_7&=A_6(1.01)-M\\&=(20\,000-6M)(1.01)-M\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_8&=A_7(1.01)-M\\&=\big[(20\,000-6M)(1.01)-M\big](1.01)-M\\&=(20\,000-6M)(1.01)^2-M(1.01)-M\\&=(20\,000-6M)(1.01)^2-M(1+1.01)\end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the guideline wrote A_8 = A_2(1.01) - M; it should be A_7.

criteria: Expresses $A_{36}$ using the sum of a GP, or equivalent merit
Attempts to solve $A_{36}=0$, or equivalent merit

solution sketch: graph of f(x) = e^{2x+1} x^4: maximum (-2, 0.797), inflections (-3, 0.546) and (-1, 0.368), minimum at origin, asymptote y = 0 to the left

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{2x+1} & v&=x^4\\u'&=2e^{2x+1} & v'&=4x^3\end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=2e^{2x+1}x^4+4x^3e^{2x+1}$$
Applying the product rule to each term again:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=4e^{2x+1}x^4+8x^3e^{2x+1}+12x^2e^{2x+1}+8x^3e^{2x+1}\\&=4e^{2x+1}x^4+16x^3e^{2x+1}+12x^2e^{2x+1}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^3e^{2x+1}(x+2)&=0\\x&=0,\ -2\end{aligned}$$
Testing with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-2)&=-0.79\ldots<0 &&\text{maximum}\\f''(0)&=0 &&\text{possible point of inflection, test further}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ maximum point at $(-2,\ 0.79\ldots)$

Test $(0,0)$ with the sign of $f'(x)$ either side:

\extable{317_q28_t1}

$\therefore$ $(0,0)$ is a minimum stationary point.
criteria: Correctly finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes:
$$\begin{aligned}4e^{2x+1}x^4+16x^3e^{2x+1}+12x^2e^{2x+1}&=0\\4x^2e^{2x+1}(x^2+4x+3)&=0\\x&=-3,\ -1,\ 0\end{aligned}$$
\extable{317_q28_t2}

$\therefore$ $(-3,\ 0.545\ldots)$ and $(-1,\ 0.367\ldots)$ are points of inflection.

questions.stem:
The figure below shows the design of coffee jar with a lid sitting directly on top.

\exfigure{317_q30_1}

The jar is in the shape of a right circular cylinder of radius $x\text{ cm}$. It is fitted with a lid of height $2\text{ cm}$, which fits tightly on the top of the jar, so it may be assumed that it has the same radius as the jar. The jar and its lid are made of thin sheet metal and there is no wastage.

The total metal used to make the jar and its lid is $190\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the jar, $V\text{ cm}^3$, is given by $V=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)$.

dif.r: surface area model with lid, eliminate h for volume

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the maximum volume of the jar, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: standard cubic maximisation, reject negative root

figures.cap: cylindrical jar of radius x cm and height h cm with a lid of height 2 cm, shown apart and fitted

solutions.latex:
The metal is the curved surfaces of the jar (height $h$) and the lid (height 2), plus the base and the top of the lid:
$$\begin{aligned}2\pi x(h+2)+2(\pi x^2)&=190\pi\\2x(h+2)+2x^2&=190\\x(h+2)+x^2&=95\\xh+2x+x^2&=95\\xh&=95-2x-x^2\end{aligned}$$
Using the cylinder volume $V=\pi r^2h$ with $r=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi x^2h\\&=\pi x(xh)\\&=\pi x(95-2x-x^2)\\&=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $xh$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)\\\dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\pi(95-4x-3x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\pi(95-4x-3x^2)&=0\\3x^2+4x-95&=0\\(3x+19)(x-5)&=0\\x&=5\text{ or }-\dfrac{19}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The radius is positive, so $x=5$.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=\pi(-4-6x)$$
When $x=5$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-34\pi<0$

$\therefore$ maximum occurs when $x=5$
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi\left(95(5)-2(5)^2-(5)^3\right)\\&=300\pi\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2x-1}$ and $f(g(x))=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}$, find $g(x)$.

dif.r: set up f(g(x)) equation and solve for g, careful algebra

solutions.latex:
Substituting $g(x)$ into $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2x-1}$:
$$f(g(x))=\dfrac{g(x)+1}{2g(x)-1}$$
Equating with $f(g(x))=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{g(x)+1}{2g(x)-1}&=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}\\(g(x)+1)(3x-5)&=(3x+2)(2g(x)-1)\\3xg(x)-5g(x)+3x-5&=6xg(x)-3x+4g(x)-2\\9g(x)+3xg(x)&=6x-3\\g(x)(3x+9)&=6x-3\\g(x)&=\dfrac{6x-3}{3x+9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g(x)=\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}$$
criteria: Rewrites $f(g(x))$ in terms of $g(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{\frac{3}{2}}+5x}}\,dx$.

dif.r: factor x^(1/2) to spot reverse chain on sqrt(sqrt x+5)

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{\frac{3}{2}}+5x}}\,dx&=\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)}}\,dx\\&=\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5}}\,dx\\&=\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\end{aligned}$$
By the reverse chain rule, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=2\int\dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=4\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the reverse chain rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Which of the following is equivalent to

$$\dfrac{\tan^2x-1}{\tan^2x+1}$$

dif.r: MCQ: simplify tan expression to 1-2cos^2x via identities

solutions.latex:
Writing $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, multiplying top and bottom by $\cos^2x$ and using $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\tan^2x-1}{\tan^2x+1}&=\dfrac{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1}{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}+1}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}\\ &=\sin^2x-\cos^2x\\ &=1-\cos^2x-\cos^2x\\ &=1-2\cos^2x\end{aligned}$$

option D: option D: curve through the origin rising from bottom left, plus a branch in the first quadrant

parts.latex: Show that $\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and hence evaluate $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

dif.r: exact values from related angles, then multiply

solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is in the fourth quadrant with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, where $\tan$ is negative:
$$\begin{aligned}\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{-\sqrt{3}}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
With $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (fourth quadrant, related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$):
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{385}&=\dfrac{385}{2}(17+3089)\\ &=597\,905\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=(4x+2)^3$ at the point $(1,216)$.

dif.r: twin of 2023 Q14: chain rule then tangent

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\times4(4x+2)^2\\ &=12(4x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
At $(1,216)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12(4(1)+2)^2\\ &=12(6)^2\\ &=432\end{aligned}$$
$m_{\text{tangent}}=432$

Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-216&=432(x-1)\\ y&=432x-216\\ 432x-y-216&=0\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(2+3x)e^{3x}\,dx$

dif.r: twin of 2020 Q18(b): hence with constant factor

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{3x} & v&=1+3x\\u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(1+3x)\right]&=3e^{3x}+3e^{3x}(1+3x)\\ &=3e^{3x}\big(1+(1+3x)\big)\\ &=3e^{3x}(2+3x)\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $3e^{3x}(2+3x)$ is the derivative of $e^{3x}(1+3x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(2+3x)e^{3x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int 3e^{3x}(2+3x)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}(1+3x)+C\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A farm has a watering system which repeatedly fills a storage tank then empties its’ contents to water different sections of the farm. The volume of water $V$ (in cubic metres) in the tank at a time $t$ is given by the equation

$$V=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos t-2\sin t$$

where $t$ is measured in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$.

dif.r: differentiate trig terms

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine whether the tank is initially filling or emptying, showing all calculations.

dif.r: sign of derivative at t=0

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what time does the tank first become completely full and what is its capacity when it is full?

dif.r: tan equation, choose second root using emptying, evaluate capacity

A.note: full = maximum of periodic model; dV/dt=0 then pick max

B.note: max of periodic volume via dV/dt=0 and tan t=1/sqrt3; primary could be Y12-205 (periodic model) or Y12-303

Related and complementary angles.reason: Evaluating trig ratios of 7π/6 via related angle, beyond solving the equation.

Solving optimisation problems.evidence: The tank is full or empty when dV/dt=0
Solving optimisation problems.reason: Differentiates a contextual function to find its maximum value.

Derivatives of trigonometric functions.reason: dV/dt requires differentiating sin and cos.

Stationary points and their nature.reason: not_when: worded optimisation tags Solving optimisation problems instead (prerequisite applied automatically).

solutions.latex: $$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t$$

The tank is emptying when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0$.

When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dt}&=2\sqrt{3}\sin(0)-2\cos(0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}(0)-2(1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ tank is emptying at this time

The tank is full or empty when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t&=0\\ 2\sqrt{3}\sin t&=2\cos t\\ \dfrac{\sin t}{\cos t}&=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}}\\ \tan t&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \ldots\end{aligned}$$
As the tank is initially emptying, the first value is when it is empty and the second is when it is full.

Tank first full when $t=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ minutes.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-2\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\\ &=6\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation to find $\tan t=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: 25 students sit an exam with a total mark out of 40. For each of the 25 students, the number $x$ of the lessons missed and the number $y$ of the marks lost on the test were recorded. The total number of marks lost was 230 more than the total number of lessons missed. The correlation coefficient between lessons missed and marks lost was $r=0.81$ and the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed has equation $y=1.5x+6$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Describe the nature and strength of the correlation between lessons missed and marks lost.
parts.note: Describing correlation: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

dif.r: Direct recall: interpret r = 0.81 as strong positive linear.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, find the mean number of lessons missed and marks lost.

dif.r: Must build equation from totals and means, solve simultaneously with regression line.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the equation of the least squares regression line of marks gained on lessons missed.
parts.note: Regression line of a transformed response: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

dif.r: Requires seeing marks gained = 40 - y and transforming the line.

solutions.latex: Strong, positive, linear relationship

$y=1.5x+6$

Total marks lost $=25\bar{y}$

Total lessons missed $=25\bar{x}$

The total marks lost is 230 more than the total lessons missed:
$$25\bar{x}+230=25\bar{y}\quad(1)$$
The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\bar{y}=1.5\bar{x}+6\quad(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}25\bar{x}+230&=25(1.5\bar{x}+6)\\ 25\bar{x}+230&=37.5\bar{x}+150\\ 80&=12.5\bar{x}\\ \bar{x}&=6.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y}&=1.5(6.4)+6\\ &=15.6\end{aligned}$$

Since the test is out of 40, marks gained $=40-y$.

$\therefore$ least squares regression line for marks gained on lessons missed:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Marks gained}&=40-(1.5x+6)\\ &=40-6-1.5x\\ &=-1.5x+34\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-3x^2+12\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6x\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3x^2+12&=0\\ 3x^2&=12\\ x^2&=4\\ x&=\pm2\end{aligned}$$
At $x=-2$:

At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-(2)^3+12(2)-7\\ &=-8+24-7\\ &=9\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}(-2,-23)&: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6(-2)=12>0 &&\text{concave up, minimum turning point}\\ (2,9)&: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6(2)=-12<0 &&\text{concave down, maximum turning point}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}y&=-(0)^3+12(0)-7\\ &=-7\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2001_1}

dif.r: quadratic in n from S_n=6020, needs formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
$a=14$, $d=6$

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_5&=14+(5-1)6\\ &=38\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 38 trees in $5^{\text{th}}$ row

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=14$, $d=6$, $S_n=6020$:
$$\begin{aligned}6020&=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(14)+(n-1)6\big)\\ 12\,040&=n(28+6n-6)\\ 12\,040&=28n+6n^2-6n\\ 6n^2+22n-12\,040&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{-22\pm\sqrt{22^2-4(6)(-12\,040)}}{2(6)}\\ &=\dfrac{-22\pm\sqrt{289\,444}}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{-22\pm538}{12}\end{aligned}$$
$n>0$, so $n=43$.

$\therefore$ there are 43 rows.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{320_q27_s1}

$R$ is the area under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=4$ plus the triangle under the normal from $P$ to its $x$-intercept.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\\ &=16x^{-2}+3x-4\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-32x^{-3}+3\end{aligned}$$
At $P(4,9)$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-32(4)^{-3}+3\\ &=2.5\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1m_2=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{normal}}&=-\dfrac{1}{2.5}\\ &=-\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Equation of normal, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-9&=-\dfrac{2}{5}(x-4)\\ 5y-45&=-2x+8\\ 2x+5y-53&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x$-intercept ($y=0$):
$$\begin{aligned}2x+5(0)-53&=0\\ 2x&=53\\ x&=26.5\end{aligned}$$
The triangle has base $26.5-4=22.5$ and height 9:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_1^4\left(\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\right)dx+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times22.5\times9\right)\\ &=\int_1^4\left(16x^{-2}+3x-4\right)dx+101.25\\ &=\left[\dfrac{16x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{16}{x}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{16}{4}+\dfrac{3(4)^2}{2}-4(4)\right)-\left(-\dfrac{16}{1}+\dfrac{3(1)^2}{2}-4(1)\right)+101.25\\ &=22.5+101.25\\ &=123.75\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\int_{3\pi}^{a}\dfrac{1}{4}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_{3\pi}^{a}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\\ \sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $3\pi\le a\le 5\pi$, $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{a}{2}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{2}$, so

The particle starts at the origin, is at rest at $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$ and then turns back.

At $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\ln\left(2\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)+1\right)-3\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)\\ &=5\ln\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)-\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
5 people want to adopt an animal at the local shelter. All 5 people have the same probability of adopting a dog $P(D)$ and the same probability of adopting a cat $P(C)$.

It is given that $P(D)=\dfrac{9}{14}$, $P(D|C)=\dfrac{6}{13}$, and $P(C|D)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Dev is one of the five people looking to adopt a pet.

parts.latex: What is the probability that at least one of the 5 people will NOT adopt a dog. Give your answer correct to two decimal places

dif.r: complement of all five, 1-(9/14)^5

solutions.latex:
Using $P(C|D)=\dfrac{P(C\cap D)}{P(D)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{3}&=\dfrac{P(C\cap D)}{\frac{9}{14}}\\ P(C\cap D)&=\dfrac{3}{14}\end{aligned}$$
Using $P(D|C)=\dfrac{P(D\cap C)}{P(C)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{6}{13}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{14}}{P(C)}\\ P(C)&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{14}}{\frac{6}{13}}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{28}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least 1 not a dog})&=1-P(\text{all dogs})\\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{9}{14}\right)^5\\ &=0.890207\ldots\\ &=0.89\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The monthly interest rate:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=7.1\%\text{ p.a.}\\ &=\dfrac{7.1}{12}\%\text{ per month}\\ &=\dfrac{71}{12\,000}\text{ per month}\end{aligned}$$
Each month interest is added to the amount owing, then the $\$3300$ repayment is subtracted:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=470\,000\left(1+\dfrac{71}{12\,000}\right)^1-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ A_2&=A_1\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=\left[470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\right]\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2-3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2-3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+1\right)\\ A_3&=A_2\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^3-3300\left(\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2+\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+1\right)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_n&=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-3300\left(1+\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{n-1}\right)\end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$ and $r=\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}$, so by $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$A_n=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}$$
After 2 years, $n=24$ months:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{24}&=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{24}-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{24}-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}\\ &=456\,654.2456\\ &=\$456\,654.25\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $\$456\,654.25$ is still owing after 2 years.
criteria: Finds an expression for $A_1$ using exact values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$. Using $A_n$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}&=0\\ 470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n\times\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1\right)&=3300\left(\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)\\ \dfrac{16\,685}{6}\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-3300\\ -\dfrac{3115}{6}\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=-3300\\ \left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=\dfrac{3960}{623}\\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3960}{623}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)}\\ &=313.50738\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The loan is not repaid after 313 months, so round up:
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore n&=314\text{ months}\\ &=26\text{ years }2\text{ months}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Collects terms with power $n$ together, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b

dif.r: 3D diagonal relation to eliminate b in volume

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

figures.cap: hemispherical bowl of depth d with rectangular pyramid apex O, base ABCD on the inner surface, OM = x perpendicular to diagonal DB, OC = r, CB = b, AB = 3b

solutions.latex:
$M$ is the midpoint of $DB$:
$$DB=2MB$$
In right-angled $\triangle OMB$, $OB=r$ (radius) and $OM=x$, so by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned}MB^2&=r^2-x^2\\ MB&=\sqrt{r^2-x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$$

Volume of a pyramid, $V=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah$, with base $3b\times b$ and height $OM=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(3b\times b)x\\ &=b^2x\end{aligned}$$
$DB$ is a diagonal of the rectangular base, so by Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle DAB$:
$$\begin{aligned}DB^2&=b^2+(3b)^2\\ DB&=\sqrt{b^2+9b^2}\\ &=\sqrt{10b^2}\end{aligned}$$
Equating with $DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10b^2}&=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}\\ 10b^2&=4(r^2-x^2)\\ b^2&=\dfrac{4(r^2-x^2)}{10}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $V=b^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-x^2)x\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}x(r^2-x^2)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains an expression for $DB$ in terms of $b$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Expanding and differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}xr^2-\dfrac{2}{5}x^3\\ \dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-3x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-3x^2)\\ 3x^2&=r^2\\ x^2&=\dfrac{r^2}{3}\\ x&=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$.

At $x=\dfrac{r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-3\left(\dfrac{r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-\dfrac{r^2}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{4r^2}{15}>0\end{aligned}$$
At $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-3\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-\dfrac{4}{3}r^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}r^2\right)\\ &=-\dfrac{2r^2}{15}<0\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2020_1}

$\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ changes from positive to negative.

$\therefore$ maximum at $x=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$

meta.concern: source labels this part (b) (its parts are a, b, b, c); mapped to paper part (c)

solutions.latex:
The base of the pyramid must lie inside the bowl. From the diagram, the depth of the bowl plus $OM$ is at least the radius:
$$\begin{aligned}d+x&\ge r\\ \dfrac{r}{3}+x&\ge r\\ x&\ge r-\dfrac{r}{3}\\ x&\ge\dfrac{2r}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}<\dfrac{2r}{3}$, $x\ne\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$, so the maximum from part (c) cannot be achieved.

At $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}<0$ (volume decreasing).

$\therefore$ the maximum under these conditions is at $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)\left(r^2-\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(r^2-\dfrac{4r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(\dfrac{9r^2}{9}-\dfrac{4r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(\dfrac{5r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r^3}{27}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x\ge\dfrac{2r}{3}$ or states why $\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$ would not work, or equivalent merit

dif.r: use oddness to show h=2f, count stationary points

figures.cap: cubics y = f(x) (solid) and y = g(x) (dashed), reflections of each other in the y-axis, both through the origin and the same two other x-intercepts

solutions.latex:
$f$ is odd, so $f(-x)=-f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} h(x)&=f(x)-g(x)\\ &=f(x)-f(-x)\\ &=f(x)+f(x)\\ &=2f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $y=h(x)$ is a vertical dilation of $y=f(x)$, so it has the same number of stationary points as the cubic $y=f(x)$, which has 2.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = xe^{7x}$, expressing your answer in factorised form.

dif.r: product rule with e^{7x}, factorise

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{7x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=7e^{7x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=x(7e^{7x})+e^{7x}(1)\\ &=e^{7x}(7x+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y = e^{2x + 3}$ at the point where $x = 0$.

dif.r: chain on linear exponent, substitute x=0

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{f(x)}=f'(x)e^{f(x)}$:
$$y'=2e^{2x+3}$$
When $x=0$, $y'=2e^{3}$.

$\therefore m_T=2e^3$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{5} - 2 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to the nearest minute.

dif.r: cosec=10 to sin=1/10, two solutions to nearest minute

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{5}-2&=0\\ \operatorname{cosec}x&=10\\ \dfrac{1}{\sin x}&=10\\ \sin x&=\dfrac{1}{10}\end{aligned}$$
$\sin x>0$, so $x$ is in the first or second quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)=5^\circ 44'\\ x&=180^\circ-5^\circ 44'=174^\circ 16'\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=5^\circ 44' \text{ and } 174^\circ 16'$$

parts.latex:
A bag contains six cards that are each printed with one of the following numbers.

$$111,\ 121,\ 122,\ 211,\ 221,\ 222$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first digit of the number on the card is 1, and $N_2$ be the event that the second digit of the number on the card is 1.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.

dif.r: test independence by product of probabilities

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}N_1&=\{111,121,122\}\\ N_2&=\{111,211\}\\ N_1\cap N_2&=\{111\}\end{aligned}$$
Each of the 6 cards is equally likely:
$$P(N_1)=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad P(N_2)=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad P(N_1\cap N_2)=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
If $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events, then $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\\ &=P(N_1\cap N_2)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent.
criteria: Compares $P(N_1\cap N_2)$ with $P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$, or equivalent merit
Finds $P(N_1)$, $P(N_2)$ and $P(N_1\cap N_2)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cos(2x)\,dx$

dif.r: Routine definite integral of cos 2x with exact values.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\cos(2x)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\sin 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin 0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-0)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Darren and Sylvia visit Sydney Harbour on New Year’s Eve to watch the fireworks.

Darren is standing outside the Sydney Opera House and Sylvia is on a yacht in the harbour. They can both see the fireworks at the top of the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

\exfigure{323_q16_1}

From Darren’s position ($D$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge ($B$) is at a bearing of $78^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge ($T$) is $35^\circ$.

From Sylvia’s position ($S$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge is at a bearing of $140^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge is $48^\circ$.

The top of the bridge is 50 m above the base of the bridge.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

\exfigure{323_q16_2}
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

plan view: D, B and S with north arrows at each point
solution sketch: bearing diagram: 140 degrees at S, 78 degrees at D, 40 degrees (co-interior) and theta at B
solution sketch: right triangles TSB (48 deg at S, 42 deg at T, TB = 50) and TDB (35 deg at D, 55 deg at T, TB = 50); triangle SBD with SB = 50 tan 42, BD = 50 tan 55, angle B = 62 deg

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{323_q16_s1}

The north lines at $S$ and $B$ are parallel, so co-interior angles are supplementary:
$$\angle SBN=180^\circ-140^\circ=40^\circ$$
The angle between south at $B$ and $BD$ is $78^\circ$ (alternate angles with the bearing at $D$, parallel north lines).

The north and south lines at $B$ form a straight angle:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle SBD&=180^\circ-40^\circ-78^\circ\\ &=62^\circ\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle SBN=40^\circ$ with a reason, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{323_q16_s2}

In right-angled $\triangle TSB$, $\angle STB=42^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 42^\circ&=\dfrac{SB}{50}\\ SB&=50\tan 42^\circ \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled $\triangle TDB$, $\angle DTB=55^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 55^\circ&=\dfrac{BD}{50}\\ BD&=50\tan 55^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Cosine rule in $\triangle SBD$ with $\angle SBD=62^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} SD^2&=(50\tan 55^\circ)^2+(50\tan 42^\circ)^2-2(50\tan 55^\circ)(50\tan 42^\circ)\cos 62^\circ\\ &=4107.3439\ldots\\ SD&=\sqrt{4107.3439\ldots}\\ \therefore SD&=64.09 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct cosine rule set up, or equivalent merit
Finds both $SB$ and $BD$, or equivalent merit
