parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \dfrac{\ln(x - 1)}{x - 1}$ at the point $(2,0)$.

dif.r: quotient rule with log, normal at point

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln(x-1) & v&=x-1\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x-1} & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{(x-1)\left(\frac{1}{x-1}\right)-\ln(x-1)(1)}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1-\ln(2-1)}{(2-1)^2}\\ &=1-\ln 1\\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore m_T=1$ and $m_N=-1$

Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-1(x-2)\\ y&=-x+2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{323_q18_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function $v_P = 3t^2 - 6t + 4$, where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times where $t = 0$ and $t = 4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the equation for the velocity of car $Q$, $v_Q$, is given by $v_Q = 6t + 4$.

dif.r: line through two velocity points

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.

dif.r: set equal displacements via integral of difference

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: a straight line and a parabola both starting at v = 4 when t = 0 and meeting again later

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$, $v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$

$Q$ accelerates at a constant rate, so $v_Q$ is linear through $(0,4)$ and $(4,28)$:
$$m=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$

Both cars start at the same point, so $P$ passes $Q$ at the time $a>0$ when their displacements are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a \big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a (3t^2-12t)\,dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0\\ a&=0,\ 6 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ car $P$ will pass $Q$ after 6 seconds from the start of the race.
criteria: Correct primitive of the difference in velocities, or equivalent merit
Sets the difference in displacements equal to zero, or equivalent merit

Using $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$, and part (a) for the primitive of $2x\sec^2(x^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx&=\int x\big(\sec^2(x^2)-1\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\big(\sec^2(x^2)-1\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int \big(2x\sec^2(x^2)-2x\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\tan(x^2)-x^2\big)+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \ln x\,dx$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \ln x\,dx&\approx\dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[(\ln 1+\ln 2)+2\ln 1.5\big]\\ &=\dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[(0+\ln 2)+2\ln 1.5\big]\\ &=0.3760\ldots\\ &\approx 0.38 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5 - x^2} & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$.

dif.r: log-form integral equals 1, show k

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ is given by:

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ 1 - \log_5(5 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 1 & x > 2 \end{cases}$$

dif.r: integrate to CDF, change of base to log_5

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, show that the median is $\sqrt{5 - \sqrt{5}}$.

dif.r: F(m)=1/2, solve log equation exactly

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx&=1\\ \int_0^2 \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\int_0^2 \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^2&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln|5-4|-\ln|5-0|\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln 1-\ln 5\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}(0-\ln 5)&=1\\ \dfrac{k\ln 5}{2}&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{2}{\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx=1$ with a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x \dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\left(\dfrac{x}{5-x^2}\right)dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\int_0^x \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\big[\ln|5|-\ln|5-x^2|\big]\\ &=1-\dfrac{\ln|5-x^2|}{\ln 5}\end{aligned}$$
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, and $5-x^2>0$ for $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=1-\log_5|5-x^2|\\ &=1-\log_5(5-x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Outside $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=0 &&\text{for } x<0\\ F(x)&=1 &&\text{for } x>2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral with a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-\log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ \log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ 5-x^2&=5^{0.5}\\ 5-x^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ x^2&=5-\sqrt{5}\\ x&=\pm\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$, since $0\le x\le 2$.

questions.stem:
A factory produces boxes in the shape of an open rectangular prism (without a lid).

\exfigure{323_q23_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k \text{ cm}^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $l = \dfrac{k - 4x^2}{4x}$.

dif.r: surface area of open box, rearrange for l

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of $1200 \text{ cm}^2$.

dif.r: form volume with k=1200, differentiate, test max

figures.cap: open rectangular box with length l, height x and width 2x

solutions.latex:
The open box has a base $l\times 2x$, two sides $l\times x$ and two ends $2x\times x$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+2lx+2(2x^2)\\ k&=4lx+4x^2\\ 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

Volume $=$ length $\times$ width $\times$ height, with $l$ from part (a) and $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}V'&=600-6x^2\\ 600-6x^2&=0\\ 6x^2&=600\\ x^2&=100\\ x&=\pm 10\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $V''=-12x$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10: & V''&=-120<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ x&=-10: & V''&=120>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{max volume}&=2\times 10^2\times\dfrac{1200-4(10)^2}{40}\\ &=4000 \text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x=10$ and shows it gives a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graph $y = \sin x$ is vertically dilated by a scale factor of 2 and horizontally dilated such that it has a period of $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the transformed sine curve and the line $y = \sqrt{2}$ for $x \in [0,2\pi]$.

dif.r: build function from transformations, six solutions over tripled domain

solutions.latex:
Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $n=3$.

A vertical dilation by a factor of 2 gives an amplitude of 2, so $y=2\sin 3x$ for $0\le 3x\le 6\pi$.

Substitute $y=\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 3x&=\sqrt{2}\\ \sin 3x&=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\sin 3x>0$, so $3x$ is in the first or second quadrant:
$$3x=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{4}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Finds $\sin 3x=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and some correct solutions, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Layton has a five-year old brother whose right foot is 13 cm in length.

He extends the line of best fit and notes that it predicts that a five-year old should have a foot length of approximately 17.5 cm.

Give TWO reasons why Layton is incorrect to assume from the bivariate data that his brother has smaller than normal feet for a five-year old.
parts.note: Bivariate data: extrapolation and correlation strength · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

dif.r: Interpret in context: extrapolation and weak correlation as two reasons.

figures.cap: scatterplot "Foot length": age (x years) 0 to 20 against foot length (y centimetres) 0 to 30, fifteen points for ages 12 to 18, dashed regression line

solutions.latex:
Using $(12,22.5)$ and $(19,27.5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{27.5-22.5}{19-12}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}(x-12)\\ y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}x-\dfrac{60}{7}\\ y&=\dfrac{5}{7}x+\dfrac{195}{14} \end{aligned}$$

Layton is extrapolating well outside the data set, as the students measured were aged from 12 to 18; this is always problematic as it assumes a linear relationship which may not be true.

The strength of the relationship between age and foot length is low (the correlation coefficient is close to 0), so even interpolating within the correct age range would be unreliable.
criteria: Gives one correct reason, or equivalent merit

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: y = x^3 and the line y = b meeting at A; region between the curve, the line and the y-axis shaded

solutions.latex:
$A$ is where $y=b$ meets $y=x^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^3&=b\\ x&=\sqrt[3]{b} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A\left(\sqrt[3]{b},b\right)$$

Area between the curve and the $y$-axis: $y=x^3$, so $x=y^{\frac{1}{3}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^b y^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dy\\ \dfrac{4}{27}&=\left[\dfrac{3y^{\frac{4}{3}}}{4}\right]_0^b\\ \dfrac{3b^{\frac{4}{3}}}{4}&=\dfrac{4}{27}\\ 3b^{\frac{4}{3}}&=\dfrac{16}{27}\\ b^{\frac{4}{3}}&=\dfrac{16}{81}\\ b&=\dfrac{8}{27} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle\int_0^b y^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dy$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
An astronomer is attempting to predict the height of a satellite above the ground as it orbits around the Earth. Using precise measurements, the height of the satellite can be modelled with the function:

$$h(t) = 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t - 15)\right) + 8$$

where $h(t)$ is the height of the satellite in thousands of kilometres at time $t$ hours since midnight on any day of the year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the minimum and maximum height reached by the satellite.

dif.r: centre plus/minus amplitude with units

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
On the grid below, sketch the graph of $h(t)$ for $0 \le t \le 24$.

\exfigure{323_q29_1}

dif.r: sketch phase-shifted sine on grid

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The satellite is out of range if it is higher than 11 000 km above the ground.

Use algebraic techniques to find how many hours in the day the satellite is out of range.

dif.r: solve sine equation, length of interval above threshold

figures.cap: grid: t from 0 to 25, h from -15 to 15

solutions.latex:
The sine term ranges from $-6$ to $6$, so $h$ ranges from $8-6$ to $8+6$ thousand km.
$$\begin{aligned} \min&=(8-6)\times 1000=2000 \text{ km}\\ \max&=(8+6)\times 1000=14\,000 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{323_q29_s1}

Out of range when $h(t)>11$; first solve $h(t)=11$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)+8&=11\\ 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)&=3\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\le\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)&=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ t-15&=-11,\ -7,\ 1,\ 5\\ \therefore t&=4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 20 \end{aligned}$$
From the graph, the satellite is above 11 000 km for $4<t<8$ and $16<t<20$.

$\therefore$ the satellite is out of range for 8 hours each day.

$F(A)=1$ (the curve meets the horizontal line $y=1$ at $x=A$):
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=\dfrac{(A-1)^3}{6}\\ (A-1)^3&=6\\ A-1&=\sqrt[3]{6}\\ A&=\sqrt[3]{6}+1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore f(x)=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2}, & 1\le x\le\sqrt[3]{6}+1\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

questions.stem:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation:

$$C = 100(1 - 2^{-kt})$$

The battery is charged at $35\%$ capacity after 50 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $0.01243$, correct to 4 significant figures.

dif.r: show k: rearrange and solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: To prolong the life of the battery, the charger may be set to switch off when the battery reaches $90\%$ capacity. For how long will the battery be on charge until it reaches $90\%$ capacity?

dif.r: rearrange exponential model, solve with logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By considering the first and second derivative, describe the behaviour of $C$ for $t \ge 0$ if the battery is left on charge indefinitely.

dif.r: signs of C prime, C double prime and limit describe behaviour

A.note: describe behaviour via C', C'' and limit

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: C''<0 ... increases from 0 at a decreasing rate
Concavity and points of inflection.reason: Sign of C'' interpreted as concavity.

Increasing and decreasing functions.evidence: C'>0 ... the battery charge capacity increases

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the guideline used $t$ for the unknown constant ($2^{-50t}$, $t=0.01243$); it is $k$.
meta.concern: source solution writes t in place of k throughout (2^{-50t}, t = 0.01243); rewritten with k

solutions.latex:
Initially $C=0$. Since $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$, so $C\to 100$ as $t\to\infty$.
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln 2\times 2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln 2)^2\times 2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Since $k>0$, $C'>0$ and $C''<0$ for all $t\ge 0$.

Hence, the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never reach $100\%$ charge.
criteria: Finds $C'$ and $C''$ with their signs, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned}u&=\sin x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$

For concave down, $f''(x)<0$.

parts.latex: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$

solutions.latex:
Adjust the domain to match the angle:
$$\begin{aligned}-\pi&\le x\le\pi\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\left(\text{add } \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $x^2\tan 3x$

dif.r: product rule with tan 3x

solutions.latex:
Factorise and simplify the fraction first:
$$\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}=\dfrac{(2x+3)(2x-3)}{2x-3}=2x+3$$
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}\right)\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(2x+3)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2x+3}\times 2\\ &=\dfrac{2}{2x+3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies the fraction to $2x+3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(e^{x})&=\cos(e^{x})\times e^{x}\\ &=e^{x}\cos(e^{x})\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^2 & v&=\tan 3x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=3\sec^2 3x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2\tan 3x)&=2x\tan 3x+3x^2\sec^2 3x\\ &=x\left[2\tan 3x+3x\sec^2 3x\right]\end{aligned}$$
criteria: One error (each correct term earns a mark), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\cos x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.

dif.r: derivative of cos, normal gradient, exact line

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\sin x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, $m_{\text{tangent}}\times m_{\text{normal}}=-1$:
$$m_{\text{normal}}=\sqrt{2}$$
Equation of the normal through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&=\sqrt{2}\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ y&=\sqrt{2}x-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ y&=\sqrt{2}x-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3-3x^2\\ 3-3x^2&=0\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(-1)&=1+3\times(-1)-(-1)^3=1-3+1=-1\\ f(1)&=1+3\times1-(1)^3=1+3-1=3\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary points are $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,3)$.

Nature, using $f''(x)=-6x$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-1)&=-6\times(-1)=6>0 &&\text{concave up} &&(-1,-1)\text{ local minimum}\\ f''(1)&=-6\times1=-6<0 &&\text{concave down} &&(1,3)\text{ local maximum}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds a stationary point and determines the nature of one stationary point, or equivalent merit
Finds one stationary point with both $x$ and $y$ coordinates, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: any one point with both x and y coordinates
meta.marker_note: The nature may also be shown using $f'(x)$ for neighbourhood testing around $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection is possible where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6x&=0\\ x&=0\\ y&=1+3\times0-0^3=1\end{aligned}$$
So the possible point is $(0,1)$. Check concavity:

\extable{Ts2090_1}

The concavity changes, so $(0,1)$ is a point of inflection.

Endpoints:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-2)&=1+3\times(-2)-(-2)^3\\ &=1-6+8\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
so the endpoint is $(-2,3)$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(3)&=1+3\times3-3^3\\ &=1+9-27\\ &=-17\end{aligned}$$
so the endpoint is $(3,-17)$.

\exfigure{640_q12_s1}

$\therefore$ the minimum value of $f(x)$ is $-17$ (at the endpoint $x=3$).

questions.stem: The temperature of hot tea poured into a cup can be represented by the equation $T=25+70e^{-0.4t}$ where $T$ is the temperature of the sea in degrees Celsius, $t$ is the time in minutes after it is poured. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.

$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-28e^{-0.4\times4}\approx-5.65\ ^{\circ}\text{C/min}$$
$\therefore$ the temperature is decreasing at the rate of $5.65\ ^{\circ}\text{C/min}$.

The period of $\sin(nx+1.5)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=12\\ n&=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ &\approx0.52\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The lowest temperature occurs when $\sin(nx+1.5)=-1$. With $n=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}x+1.5\right)&=-1\\ \dfrac{\pi}{6}x+1.5&=\dfrac{3}{2}\pi,\ \dfrac{3}{2}\pi+2\pi,\ \dfrac{3}{2}\pi+4\pi,\ \ldots\\ &\approx4.71,\ 10.99557\ldots,\ 17.28\\ \dfrac{\pi}{6}x&\approx3.21,\ 9.49557\\ x&\approx6.13\quad(1\le x\le 12)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $6^{\text{th}}$ month, June, experiences the lowest average monthly temperature.

The diagram below shows a part of the circle described by the equation $x^2+y^2=25$. The point $P(x,y)$ lies on the circle, and with $O$ representing the origin. Point $M$ is located at coordinates $(2,0)$, while point $N$ is at coordinates $(0,4)$ and $\angle MOP$ is measured in radians.

Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.

figures.cap: quarter circle radius 5 with N(0,4), M(2,0), P(x,y) on the arc, angle theta at O between OM and OP; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
Using area $=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in $\triangle OMP$, with $OP=5$ (radius) and $OM=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle OMP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times5\times\sin\theta\\ &=5\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle ONP$, $OP=5$, $ON=4$ and $\angle NOP=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle ONP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\\ &=10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore A&=\text{Area of }\triangle OMP+\text{Area of }\triangle ONP\\ &=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one or both areas of the triangles, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: one or both areas of triangles

solutions.latex:
A maximum may occur where $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta\\ 5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta&=0\\ 10\sin\theta&=5\cos\theta\\ \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
With $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$):
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\quad \cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\\ &=-5\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-10\cos\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=-5\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-10\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}<0\end{aligned}$$
Concave down, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives the maximum area.

For maximum area, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$.

$P$ is on the circle of radius $5$, so $\dfrac{x}{5}=\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\\ &=2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
From $x^2+y^2=25$, with $y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sqrt{25-x^2}\\ &=\sqrt{25-20}\\ &=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore P\left(2\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\right)$

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=(x+1)e^{1-x}$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, points of inflection, intercepts and showing what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.

dif.r: product rule with e^(1-x), inflection, limits both directions

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = (x+1)e^{1-x}: x-intercept -1, maximum (0,e), inflection (1,2), y -> 0 as x -> infinity, y -> -infinity as x -> -infinity

solutions.latex:
$y$-intercept: when $x=0$, $y=e^{1}=e$.

$x$-intercept: $e^{1-x}\ne0$, so $(x+1)e^{1-x}=0$ gives $x+1=0$, that is $x=-1$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x+1 & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{1-x}+(x+1)e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(1-x-1)\\ &=-xe^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=0$, $y=e$.

Product rule again, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=-x & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-1\times e^{1-x}-x\times e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(-1+x)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\times e^{1}<0$, concave down.

$\therefore (0,e)$ is a local maximum turning point.

Points of inflection are possible where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$: $x=1$, $y=2\times e^{0}=2$, that is $(1,2)$.

\extable{Ts2103_1}

The concavity changes, so $(1,2)$ is a point of inflection.

Behaviour as $x\to\pm\infty$:
$$\begin{aligned}&x\to+\infty: && x+1\to+\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to0 && \therefore y\to0\\ &x\to-\infty: && x+1\to-\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to\infty && \therefore y\to-\infty\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{640_q16_s1}

parts.latex: If $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{3-x}$, then the domain for $f(x)\times g(x)$ is:

dif.r: domain of product governed by square root

solutions.latex:
$$f(x)\times g(x)=(x^2+1)\sqrt{3-x}$$

The factor $x^2+1$ is defined for all real $x$; the square root needs $3-x\ge 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3-x &\ge 0 \\ -x &\ge -3 \\ x &\le 3 \end{aligned}$$

So the domain is $(-\infty,3]$.

parts.latex: What is the solution(s) of the equation $\log_2(x-3)+\log_2 x=2$?

dif.r: log law to quadratic, reject invalid root

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need a positive argument, so $x-3>0$ and $x>0$, giving $x>3$.

Using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a mn$:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_2\left[(x-3)x\right] &= 2 \\ x^2-3x &= 2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=4$ or $x=-1$, but $x>3$.

Hence $x=4$ is the only solution.

parts.latex:
Consider the set of scores:

$$\mathbf{9\quad 17\quad 20\quad 23\quad 24\quad 27\quad 27\quad 28\quad 30\quad 31\quad 39\quad 47}$$

Which of the scores could be considered an outlier?
parts.note: Outliers via IQR of a data set · Standard: MST-11-08

dif.r: Find quartiles, IQR and fences, then compare scores; standard multi-step routine.

solutions.latex:
$$Q_1=21.5,\quad Q_2=27,\quad Q_3=30.5$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1 \\ &= 30.5-21.5 \\ &= 9 \end{aligned}$$

A score is an outlier if it is below $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lower bound} &= 21.5-1.5\times 9 = 8 \\ \text{Upper bound} &= 30.5+1.5\times 9 = 44 \end{aligned}$$

Since $9>8$, the score $9$ is not an outlier, and $47>44$, so only $47$ is an outlier.

parts.latex:
Suppose that $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{8} f(x)\,dx=A$ and $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{8} f(x)\,dx=B$.

The value of $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{-3}\left(f(x)+2x\right)dx$ is:

dif.r: MCQ: reversed limits, additivity, plus 2x term

solutions.latex:
Split the interval at $2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{8} f(x)\,dx &= \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx+\int_{2}^{8} f(x)\,dx \\ A &= \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx+B \\ \int_{-3}^{2} f(x)\,dx &= A-B \end{aligned}$$

Reversing the limits,

$$\int_{2}^{-3} f(x)\,dx=-(A-B)=B-A$$

Then

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{2}^{-3}\left(f(x)+2x\right)dx &= \int_{2}^{-3} f(x)\,dx+\int_{2}^{-3} 2x\,dx \\ &= B-A+\left[x^2\right]_{2}^{-3} \\ &= B-A+9-4 \\ &= B-A+5 \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: use sin(x+pi)=-sin x, reflect graph, count intersections incl x=pi

figures.cap: graphs of y = 4 sin x and y = cot(3x/2) with vertical asymptotes, x axis marked in multiples of pi/3

solutions.latex:
Using $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4\sin(x+\pi)-\cot\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right) &= 0 \\ \cot\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right) &= -4\sin x \end{aligned}$$

So the solutions are the intersections of $y=\cot\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)$ with $y=-4\sin x$, the reflection of $y=4\sin x$ in the $x$-axis.

For $0\le x\le 2\pi$ there are three intersections:

$$\begin{aligned} &\text{once between } \dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ and } \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ &\text{at } x=\pi \\ &\text{once between } \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \text{ and } \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

So there are $3$ solutions.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=4}^{n}\ln 3^{2n}$?

dif.r: MCQ: log law, AP from n=4 with odd notation

solutions.latex:
Write each term as a multiple of $\ln 3$:

$$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=4}^{n}\ln 3^{2n} &= \ln 3^8+\ln 3^{10}+\ln 3^{12}+\ldots+\ln 3^{2n} \\ &= 8\ln 3+10\ln 3+12\ln 3+\ldots+2n\ln 3 \\ &= \ln 3\,(8+10+12+\ldots+2n) \end{aligned}$$

The bracket is an arithmetic series with $a=8$, $d=2$ and last term $l=2n$.

Running from $4$ to $n$, it has $n-3$ terms, and the sum is $\dfrac{\text{number of terms}}{2}(a+l)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum} &= \ln 3\left[\dfrac{n-3}{2}(8+2n)\right] \\ &= \ln 3\left[\dfrac{n-3}{2}\cdot 2(4+n)\right] \\ &= (n-3)(n+4)\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: intersection from conditional, then addition rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form $P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)$.

dif.r: complement of union

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram: A only 0.1, A and B 0.2, B only 0.3, neither 0.4

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula:

$$\begin{aligned} P(A\mid B) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} \\ 0.4 &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.5} \\ P(A\cap B) &= 0.2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the addition rule:

$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &= 0.3+0.5-0.2 \\ &= 0.6 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A car leaves a petrol station and drives $N30^\circ W$ at 80 km/h. At the same time, a motor bike leaves the petrol station and travels due east at 60 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that after one hour, the distance between the car and the motor bike is $20\sqrt{37}$ km.

dif.r: angle from directions, cosine rule, surd show-that

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the bearing of the car from the motor bike.

Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

dif.r: sine rule for angle, convert to bearing

figures.cap: solution sketch: bearing diagram: OC = 80 on N30W, OM = 60 due east, angle 30 degrees from north

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{339_q15_s1}

The car's bearing is $N30^\circ W$ and the motor bike travels due east, so

$$\angle COM=30^\circ+90^\circ=120^\circ$$

After one hour, $OC=80$ km and $OM=60$ km.

By the cosine rule in $\triangle COM$:

$$\begin{aligned} CM^2 &= OC^2+OM^2-2\,OC\times OM\cos\angle COM \\ &= 80^2+60^2-2\times 80\times 60\cos 120^\circ \\ &= 80^2+60^2-2\times 80\times 60\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 14800 \end{aligned}$$

Since $CM>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} CM &= \sqrt{14800} \\ &= \sqrt{400\times 37} \\ &= 20\sqrt{37}\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

By the sine rule in $\triangle COM$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\angle CMO}{OC} &= \dfrac{\sin\angle COM}{CM} \\ \dfrac{\sin\angle CMO}{80} &= \dfrac{\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}} \\ \sin\angle CMO &= \dfrac{80\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}} \\ \angle CMO &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{80\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}}\right) \\ &= 34.71500\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 35^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Since $\angle COM=120^\circ$ is obtuse, $\angle CMO$ must be acute.

The motor bike is due east of $O$, so $O$ is due west of $M$ (bearing $270^\circ$), and $C$ lies north of $OM$.

$$\text{Bearing}=270^\circ+35^\circ=305^\circ$$

$$\therefore \text{ the bearing of the car from the motor bike is approximately } 305^\circ\text{T } (N55^\circ W)$$

Alternatively, use the cosine rule to find $\angle CMO$.
criteria: Sets up the sine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.

dif.r: quotient rule, two stationary points, classify nature

figures.cap: solution sketch: first-derivative sign tables at x = 0 (+, 0, -) and x = 4 (-, 0, +) with slope sketches

solutions.latex:
The curve is undefined at $x=2$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^2 & v &= x-2 \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2(1)}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2-4x-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $y'=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} x=0: &\quad y=0 \\ x=4: &\quad y=8 \end{aligned}$$

The denominator $(x-2)^2$ is positive, so the sign of $y'$ is the sign of $x(x-4)$. Testing the nature:

Hence $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.

questions.stem: Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.

dif.r: substitute t=0 into given model

parts.label: b

B.note: P->4000 as t->inf

dif.r: chain rule on reciprocal exponential, substitute t=2

parts.label: d
parts.latex:
How many months will it take for the population of trout to exceed $3\,000$?

Give your answer as a whole number.

dif.r: rearrange logistic model, solve with logs, round up

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$ and $P=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250 &= \dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5(0)}} \\ 250 &= \dfrac{A}{16} \\ A &= 4000 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so $P\to\dfrac{4000}{1+15(0)}=4000$.

Since $1+15e^{-0.5t}>1$, $P$ never reaches $4000$.

Since $t\ge 0$, the smallest value is $P=250$, at $t=0$.

$$\therefore\ 250\le P<4000$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: range given as $250\le P\le 4000$; $P$ never reaches 4000, so $250\le P<4000$.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite $P=4000\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-1}$ and differentiate (chain rule):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 4000(-1)\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-2}(-0.5)(15e^{-0.5t}) \\ &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

When $t=2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5(2)}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5(2)}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{30000}{e\left(1+15e^{-1}\right)^2} \\ &= 259.7601\ldots \\ &\approx 260 \text{ trout per month} \end{aligned}$$

So the population is increasing at approximately $260$ trout per month.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $259.76\ldots$ was given as 259 (truncated); to the nearest trout it is 260.

solutions.latex:
Find when $P=3000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3000 &= \dfrac{4000}{1+15e^{-0.5t}} \\ 1+15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ 15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{45} \\ -0.5t &= \ln\dfrac{1}{45} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 45}{0.5} \\ &= 7.613324\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is increasing, so it exceeds $3000$ after $7.61$ months, which is $8$ months as a whole number.

The area of the bat is the area of the circle minus the area of the minor segment.

discrete conditional probability from table

parts.latex:
The circle $x^2+ax+y^2+by+c=0$ with a radius of 3 units, is shifted to the right by 1 unit.

After the shifting, the circle has the centre at $(3,4)$. Find the value of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: complete squares in general form, reverse the shift

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and $y$:

$$\begin{aligned} x^2+ax+y^2+by+c &= 0 \\ \left(x+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{a^2}{4}+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{b^2}{4}+c &= 0 \\ \left(x+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c \end{aligned}$$

Shifting right by $1$ replaces $x$ with $x-1$:

$$\left(x-1+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c$$

The new centre is $(3,4)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1-\dfrac{a}{2} &= 3 \\ -\dfrac{b}{2} &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

So $a=-4$ and $b=-8$.

The radius is $3$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c &= 3^2 \\ \dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}+\dfrac{(-8)^2}{4}-c &= 9 \\ c &= 4+16-9 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, the original centre is $(2,4)$ (one unit left of $(3,4)$):

$$\begin{aligned} (x-2)^2+(y-4)^2 &= 9 \\ x^2-4x+4+y^2-8y+16-9 &= 0 \\ x^2-4x+y^2-8y+11 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a=-4,\quad b=-8,\quad c=11$$

questions.stem:
A truck travels between two towns. The distance between the towns is $B$ km.

The trucker has the following costs:

The hourly fuel costs are proportional to the square of the speed.

The hourly fuel cost is \$2000 when the speed is 40 km/h.

All other costs are \$4800 per hour. Let $x$ be the speed in km/h and $C$ be the total cost.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $C=B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right)$.

dif.r: proportionality constant, time B/x, build cost model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the most economical speed?

dif.r: C given; differentiate, solve x^2=3840, test minimum

solutions.latex:
The hourly fuel cost is proportional to $x^2$, so it is $kx^2$.

When $x=40$ the hourly fuel cost is $\$2000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= k\times 40^2 \\ k &= \dfrac{2000}{1600} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Hourly cost $=$ fuel cost $+$ other costs:

$$\text{Hourly cost}=\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800$$

Since speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$, the time for the trip is $\dfrac{B}{x}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \left(\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800\right)\times\dfrac{B}{x} \\ &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the hourly cost $\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The most economical speed minimises $C$.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \\ \dfrac{dC}{dx} &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2} &= 0 \\ 5x^2 &= 4800\times 4 \\ x^2 &= 3840 \\ x &= \pm 61.96773\ldots \end{aligned}$$

Speed is positive, so $x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=B\times\dfrac{9600}{x^3}$$

At $x=61.97$, $\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}>0$ since $B>0$ (a distance).

So the cost is a minimum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is } x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97 \text{ km/h}$$

questions.stem:
A moving particle has an acceleration of $a\ \text{m/s}^2$ at time $t$ seconds $(t\ge 0)$.

The acceleration is given by the equation

$$a=15-6t.$$

Initially the particle is at the origin and has a velocity of $v=-12$ m/s.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration, using $x=0$ and $v=-12$ when $t=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= \int(15-6t)\,dt \\ &= 15t-3t^2+c \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} -12 &= 0-0+c \\ c &= -12 \end{aligned}$$

$$v=15t-3t^2-12$$

Integrate again:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(15t-3t^2-12\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t+d \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 0-0-0+d \\ d &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$x=\dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)$ and hence show $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$.

dif.r: product rule then integrate and rearrange

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the area of the logo. Give your answer in exact form.

dif.r: find x=1 crossing, split area, use (a)

figures.cap: shaded regions between y = sin x and y = x sin x from 0 to pi, NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\begin{aligned} \int(\cos x-x\sin x)\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int x\sin x\,dx &= \int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x \\ &= \sin x-x\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

Find the intersection points:

$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= x\sin x \\ \sin x(1-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $\sin x=0$ or $x=1$.

In $0\le x\le\pi$, the curves meet at $x=0,\ 1,\ \pi$.

The intersection at $x=1$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so split the area there.

Using part (a), $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx+\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-(\sin x-x\cos x)\Big]_0^1+\Big[(\sin x-x\cos x)+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi} \\ &= (-\cos 1-\sin 1+\cos 1)-(-\cos 0-\sin 0+0)+\Big[(\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi)-(\sin 1-\cos 1+\cos 1)\Big] \\ &= (1-\sin 1)+(\pi-1-\sin 1) \\ &= \pi-2\sin 1\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=e^{-kx}+3x$, where $k$ is a positive real number.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find, in terms of $k$, the $x$-coordinate of the stationary point of the graph of $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: differentiate exponential with parameter k, solve with logs

B.note: x-coordinate only, no nature

parts.label: b
parts.latex: State the values of $k$ such that the $x$-coordinate of this stationary point is a positive real number.

dif.r: log inequality in parameter k for positive x

can_use: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

A.note: ln inequality on parameter k

req: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions
B.note: ln(3/k)<0 iff k>3; no skill for logarithmic inequalities

Logarithmic equations.evidence: ln 3 - ln k < 0, ln 3 < ln k, k > 3
Logarithmic equations.reason: One of two alternative methods given (log inequality).

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic fu.reason: One of two alternative methods given (sign of ln from its graph).

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -ke^{-kx}+3 = 0 \\ ke^{-kx} &= 3 \\ e^{-kx} &= \dfrac{3}{k} \\ -kx &= \ln\dfrac{3}{k} \\ x &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{3}{k}}{-k} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{k}{3}}{k} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct differentiation and equating to zero, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct differentiation and equating to zero

solutions.latex:
Since $k>0$, $x>0$ when $\ln\dfrac{3}{k}<0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \ln 3-\ln k &< 0 \\ \ln 3 &< \ln k \\ k &> 3 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, $\ln\dfrac{3}{k}$ is defined when $\dfrac{3}{k}>0$ and is negative when $\dfrac{3}{k}<1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 < \dfrac{3}{k} &< 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{3} &> 1 \\ k &> 3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
David is in a life raft, $D$, and Anna is in a cabin cruiser, $A$, searching for him.

They are in contact by mobile telephone. David tells Anna that he can see the top of the mountain Mt Hope, $H$.

From David's position, the mountain has a bearing of $340^\circ$ and the angle of elevation to the top of the mountain is $12^\circ$.

Anna can also see Mt Hope. From her position, the mountain has a bearing of $070^\circ$ and the top of the mountain has an angle of elevation of $19^\circ$. The top of Mt Hope is $1\,244$ m above sea level.

\exfigure{339_q33_1}

Find the distance of the life raft from Anna's position.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: 3D bearings/elevation: two right triangles, then spotting the right angle for Pythagoras.

figures.cap: 3D diagram: mountain HB = 1244 m, A and D at sea level, elevation 19 degrees at A and 12 degrees at D, NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: plan view: A to H bearing 070, D to H bearing 340, angle 70 + 20 degrees at the mountain base
solution sketch: right triangle ABH: HB = 1244, angle 19 degrees at A, 71 degrees at H
solution sketch: right triangle BDH: HB = 1244, angle 12 degrees at D, 78 degrees at H

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{339_q33_s1}

Let $B$ be the point at sea level directly below $H$, so $HB=1244$ m.

In $\triangle ABH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle AHB=90^\circ-19^\circ=71^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s2}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 71^\circ &= \dfrac{AB}{1244} \\ AB &= 1244\tan 71^\circ \end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle BDH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle BHD=90^\circ-12^\circ=78^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s3}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 78^\circ &= \dfrac{BD}{1244} \\ BD &= 1244\tan 78^\circ \end{aligned}$$

The bearings of $B$ from $A$ ($070^\circ$) and from $D$ ($340^\circ$) differ by $70^\circ+20^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\angle ABD=90^\circ$.

By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle ABD$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD^2 &= AB^2+BD^2 \\ &= (1244\tan 71^\circ)^2+(1244\tan 78^\circ)^2 \\ &= 47\,305\,057.68 \end{aligned}$$

Since $AD>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD &= \sqrt{47\,305\,057.68} \\ &= 6877.867\ldots \\ &\approx 6877.87\text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: On a particular day, the depth, $D$ metres, of water in Blue Harbour is given by the function $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 24$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.

parts.latex: Find the amplitude and period of the function.

dif.r: read amplitude, period 2pi/n with fractional n

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the first time when the water depth is 7 metres.

dif.r: solve cos=-1/2 with scaled argument, first solution

figures.cap: solution sketch: angle diagram: cos negative, angles pi/3 either side of the negative x axis

solutions.latex:
For $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$, the amplitude is $2$.

The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{4\pi}{25}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{4\pi}{25} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{25}{4\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{amplitude } 2 \text{ m, period } 12\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ hours}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 2 marks (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
Set the depth equal to $7$:

$$\begin{aligned} 8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= 7 \\ 2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= -1 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{339_q34_s1}

The first positive solution is where the angle is $\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4\pi}{25}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\div\dfrac{4\pi}{25} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{6} \\ &= 4\text{ h }10\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$

So the water depth is first $7$ m at $4{:}10$ am.

Using the log laws, $\log_a x^n=n\log_a x$:

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection of $f$ is where the concavity changes, that is, where $f''$ changes sign.

On the graph of $f'$, this is a turning point of $f'$: the gradient of $f'$ changes sign.

At $x=c$, $f'$ has a maximum turning point, so $f''$ changes sign there.

At $x=a$, $f'$ is stationary but its gradient does not change sign, so $f$ has no change of concavity there.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=81$ and $r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{81}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{243}{4} \end{aligned}$$

$$S=\dfrac{243}{4}=60\dfrac{3}{4}=60.75$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=(2x-1)^3$ at the point where $x=1$.

dif.r: chain rule, perpendicular gradient, normal equation

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= (2x-1)^3 \\ y' &= 2.3(2x-1)^2 \\ &= 6(2x-1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

At $x=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= (2(1)-1)^3 = 1 \\ y' &= 6(2(1)-1)^2 = 6 \end{aligned}$$

The gradient of the normal is

$$m_2=-\dfrac{1}{m_1}=-\dfrac{1}{6}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= -\dfrac{1}{6}(x-1) \\ y &= -\dfrac{1}{6}x+1\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Equivalently, $x+6y-7=0$.
criteria: Correct method to find the gradient of the normal, or the equation, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 70+40+25+15+10 \\ &= 160 \end{aligned}$$

Childcare is $40$ and Overslept is $25$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40+25}{160} &= 0.40625 \\ &= 40.625\% \end{aligned}$$

So approximately $40\%$ of issues were due to Childcare or Overslept.

Alternatively, reading the cumulative percentage line, Traffic is at about $44\%$ and Overslept is at about $84\%$:

$$84\%-44\%=40\%$$

So approximately $40\%$.

solutions.latex:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero:

$$(x+3)(x-2)=0$$

$$\therefore\ x=-3,\ x=2$$

For the horizontal asymptote, divide the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{(3x-3)\div x^2}{(x^2+x-6)\div x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{3}{x}-\frac{3}{x^2}}{1+\frac{1}{x}-\frac{6}{x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $y\to 0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{asymptotes } x=-3,\ x=2 \text{ and } y=0$$

questions.stem:
A probability density function is defined as:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}hx(5-x), & 0\le x\le 5\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $h=\dfrac{6}{125}$.

dif.r: polynomial integral equals 1, show h

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the mode of $f(x)$.

dif.r: f'=0 on quadratic pdf, one linear equation

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The area under a probability density function is $1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5\left(5hx-hx^2\right)dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{5h}{2}x^2-\dfrac{h}{3}x^3\right]_0^5 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{125}{6}h-0 &= 1 \\ h &= \dfrac{6}{125} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the integral from $0$ to $5$ equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: sets the integral from 0 to 5 to equal 1

solutions.latex:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is a maximum, so solve $f'(x)=0$.

$$f(x)=\dfrac{6}{125}\cdot 5x-\dfrac{6}{125}x^2$$

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{6}{25}-\dfrac{12}{125}x$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{125}x &= \dfrac{6}{25} \\ x &= 2.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the mode is } x=2.5$$
criteria: Correctly finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the arithmetic series $124+117.5+111+104.5+\cdots$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$ with $n=15$, $a=124$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left[2(124)+(15-1)(-6.5)\right] \\ &= 1177.5 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find all solutions of $2\sin^2 x+\sin x-1=0$, where $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: quadratic in sin x, three solutions incl. sin=-1

figures.cap: solution sketch: ASTC quadrant diagrams: 30 deg reference angles in quadrants 1 and 2 for sin x = 1/2; 270 deg for sin x = -1

solutions.latex:
Let $u=\sin x$ to factorise the quadratic:

$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2+u-1 &= 0 \\ 2u^2+2u-u-1 &= 0 \\ 2u(u+1)-(u+1) &= 0 \\ (2u-1)(u+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} u=\dfrac{1}{2}: &\quad \sin x=\dfrac{1}{2},\ \ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ u=-1: &\quad \sin x=-1,\ \ x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{347_q26_s1}

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Uses correct angles from the exact value triangles, or equivalent merit

Finds both solutions to $\sin x$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the second criterion referred to $\sin x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin x=1$; the solutions are $\sin x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin x=-1$.

The diagram below is divided into three regions, $I$, $II$ and $III$ by the curves

$$y=\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\text{ and }y=x^2.$$

Find the areas of each of the three regions correct to two decimal places.

figures.cap: unit square from O to (1,1) divided by y=sin(pi x/2) and y=x^2 into region I (above the sine curve), II (between the curves) and III (below the parabola)

solutions.latex:
Region $III$ is under $y=x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} A_{III} &= \int_0^1 x^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &\approx 0.33 \end{aligned}$$

Region $II$ is under $y=\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}$ and above $y=x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} A_{II} &= \int_0^1\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\,dx-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right]_0^1-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= 0-\left(-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= 0.303\ldots \\ &\approx 0.30 \end{aligned}$$

Region $I$ is the rest of the unit square:

$$\begin{aligned} A_I &= 1-\dfrac{2}{\pi} \\ &= 0.363\ldots \\ &\approx 0.36 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds two correct areas, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In a garden, a pond is to be installed with the dimensions shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{347_q30_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Using three applications of the trapezoidal rule, calculate the area of the pond.

dif.r: three-strip trapezoidal from diagram

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The pond is initially empty. During a storm, 20 mm of rain falls into the pond.

Calculate the amount of water in the pond immediately after the storm. Give your answer in cubic metres.

dif.r: area times depth with unit conversion

figures.cap: pond with straight base split into three 3.6 m strips; heights 8 m, 5 m, 2 m, 5 m; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
There are $n=3$ strips across the width $10.8$ m, each of width $\dfrac{10.8-0}{3}=3.6$ m.

Using the trapezoidal rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big(f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right]\Big) \\ &= \dfrac{10.8-0}{2(3)}\Big(8+5+2\left[5+2\right]\Big) \\ &= 48.6\text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress with a correct method, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Convert the rainfall to metres:

$$20\text{ mm}=0.02\text{ m}$$

The volume is the area multiplied by the depth:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 48.6\times 0.02 \\ &= 0.972\text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct change of units, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A game involves flipping a coin, then rolling two six-sided dice. If the coin lands heads, the sum of the dice is recorded. If the coin lands tails, the difference between the dice is recorded instead.

To win the game, the number recorded must be less than 4.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability of winning given the coin landed tails?

dif.r: count dice differences below 4 in 36

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability of winning the game?

dif.r: total probability over coin outcome

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Given the recorded number is 4, what is the probability that the coin landed heads?

dif.r: Bayes: recorded 4 from sum or difference

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

figures.cap: solution sketch: 6 by 6 table of differences of two dice with the 30 outcomes less than 4 enclosed
solution sketch: 6 by 6 table of sums of two dice with the 3 outcomes less than 4 (2, 3, 3) circled

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{347_q31_s2}

When the coin lands heads, a win needs a sum less than $4$, which occurs in $3$ of the $36$ outcomes, so $P(\text{win}\mid H)=\dfrac{3}{36}$.

Heads and tails are equally likely:

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{30}{36}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{11}{24} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Progresses beyond part (a), such as finding $P(\text{win}\mid H)=\dfrac{3}{36}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A recorded $4$ arises from a sum of $4$ ($3$ ways after heads) or a difference of $4$ ($4$ ways after tails).

$$\begin{aligned} P(H\mid 4) &= \dfrac{P(H\cap 4)}{P(4)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{36}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the total number of ways to get $4$, or how many ways to get $4$ after heads, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A homeowner intends to construct a rectangular pool in their backyard with a length of $x$ m and a width of $y$ m.

The depth will steadily increase from 1 m to $\dfrac{2x}{3}$ m, as seen in the diagram below.

The homeowner wishes to put tiles around the edge of the surface of the pool, and has enough to tile a perimeter of 27 m.

\exfigure{347_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the pool is $V(x)=-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x$.

dif.r: volume via average depth, eliminate y using perimeter

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the maximum volume of the pool.

dif.r: V given; quadratic formula for stationary point, evaluate

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Confirm that the volume in part (b) is a maximum.

Include reasoning and calculations in your response.

dif.r: second derivative sign at stationary point, domain note

figures.cap: rectangular pool, length x m, width y m, depth increasing from 1 m at one end to 2x/3 m at the other

solutions.latex:
From the diagram, the volume is the average depth times the length and width:

$$V=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)y \qquad (1)$$

The perimeter is $27$ m:

$$\begin{aligned} 2x+2y &= 27 \\ y &= \dfrac{27}{2}-x \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$

Substitute (2) into (1):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x+9x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}+8x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ V(x) &= -\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes equation (2) into equation (1), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correctly substitutes eq. 2 into eq. 1 or equivalent

solutions.latex:
The maximum occurs where $V'(x)=0$:

$$V'(x)=-x^2+8x+\dfrac{27}{4}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= x^2-8x-\dfrac{27}{4} \\ x &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64-4(1)\left(-\frac{27}{4}\right)}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{91}}{2} \\ &\approx 8.7697 \text{ or } -0.77 \end{aligned}$$

Length is positive, so ignore the negative value.

$$\begin{aligned} V(8.7697) &= -\dfrac{(8.7697)^3}{3}+4(8.7697)^2+\dfrac{27}{4}(8.7697) \\ &= 142\text{ m}^3 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly solves the quadratic, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten substitution omitted the minus sign on the $\frac{x^3}{3}$ term; it should read $-\frac{x^3}{3}$ (final value 142 unchanged).

solutions.latex:
$$V''(x)=-2x+8$$

$$V''(8.7697)\approx -9.5$$

$$\begin{aligned} V'(8.7697) &= 0 &&\text{stationary point} \\ V''(8.7697) &< 0 &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$

So the stationary point is a local maximum.

The domain is $0<x<13.5$ because the perimeter is $27$ m, and $V(0)=V(13.5)=0$.

So the local maximum is the maximum volume.
criteria: Correctly finds the sign of the second derivative at the point, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correctly finds the sign of the second derivative at the point

questions.stem:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that there were 14 hours of daylight 10 days before the start of the year, show that $k=2$.

dif.r: substitute t=-10, solve for k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many days into the year will the number of daylight hours be increasing the fastest? (Answer to the nearest day)

dif.r: fastest increase means max of L', solve L''=0 in context

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the number of daylight hours from that day until the end of the year.

dif.r: definite integral of shifted cosine model, evaluate

solutions.latex:
When $t=-10$, $L=14$:

$$\begin{aligned} 14 &= 12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(-10+10)\right] \\ &= 12+k \\ k &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: substitutes in both values, then shows that $k=2$

solutions.latex:
The daylight hours increase fastest where $L'(t)$ is a maximum, so solve $L''(t)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} L'(t) &= -\dfrac{4\pi}{365}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \\ L''(t) &= -\dfrac{8\pi^2}{365^2}\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] &= 0 \\ \dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ t+10 &= 91.25,\ 273.75 \\ t &= 81.25,\ 263.75 \end{aligned}$$

Test which gives the maximum rate:

$$\begin{aligned} L'(81.25) &\approx -0.03 \\ L'(263.75) &\approx 0.03 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{daylight hours increase fastest } 264 \text{ days into the year}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the first or second derivative, or equivalent merit
Uses a correct method to find the steepest gradient, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct method used to find steepest gradient
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten $L''(t)$ had denominator $365$; it should be $365^2$ (answer unchanged).

solutions.latex:
Daylight hours from day $264$ to the end of the year ($t=365$):

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{264}^{365}\left(12+2\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right)dt &= \left[12t+\dfrac{365}{\pi}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right]_{264}^{365} \\ &= 4399.90137-3051.81796 \\ &= 1348\text{ hours (nearest hour)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct bounds of integral chosen, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For the parabola with equation $y=x^2-4x+6$, which of the following is correct?

dif.r: axis of symmetry formula then substitute

options.label: A
options.latex: has axis of symmetry $x=2$ and vertex is at $(2,-2)$.

options.label: B
options.latex: has axis of symmetry $x=2$ and vertex is at $(2,2)$.

options.label: C
options.latex: has axis of symmetry $x=6$ and vertex is at $(6,-18)$.

options.label: D
options.latex: has axis of symmetry $x=6$ and vertex is at $(6,18)$.

solutions.latex:
The axis of symmetry is $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:

$$x=\dfrac{-(-4)}{2(1)}=2$$

When $x=2$:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2^2-4(2)+6 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

So the vertex is $(2,2)$.

parts.latex:
Consider the simultaneous equations.

$$\begin{aligned}2ax+y-5&=0\\x+3y-2a&=0\end{aligned}$$

If the equations have no real solutions, what is the value of $a$?

dif.r: no solution means parallel lines, equate gradients

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax+y-5 &= 0 && (1) \\ x+3y-2a &= 0 && (2) \end{aligned}$$

Make $y$ the subject:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{From (1)}: \ y &= -2ax+5 \\ \text{From (2)}: \ y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}x+\dfrac{2}{3}a \end{aligned}$$

Both are straight lines. No real solutions means no point of intersection, so the lines are parallel and have equal gradients:

$$\begin{aligned} -2a &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which expression is a term of the geometric series $4x-8x^2+16x^3-\ldots$?

dif.r: MCQ: general term, match power and sign

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=4x$ and $r=\dfrac{-8x^2}{4x}=-2x$.

$$T_n=4x(-2x)^{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}2^{n+1}x^n$$

For the magnitude $2048=2^{11}$, $n+1=11$, so $n=10$.

For $n=10$ the sign is $(-1)^9=-1$, so the term is $-2048x^{10}$.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the elimination by sign (A and D 'wrong sign') was wrong, since A has the correct sign; replaced by the general term $T_n$, which gives $-2048x^{10}$.

parts.latex: Given $f(x)=\tan^2x$, its derivative $f'(x)$ is given by which of the following?

dif.r: chain rule on square of tan

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=\tan^2x=(\tan x)^2$

Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(u^n\big)=nu^{n-1}\,u'$ with $u=\tan x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\sec^2x$:
$$f'(x)=2\tan x\sec^2x$$

$$\begin{aligned}\int x(x^2-1)^2\,dx&=\dfrac{(x^2-1)^3}{6}+c\\\int_{-1}^{1}3^x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln3}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\dfrac{8}{3\ln3}\end{aligned}$$
$y=\sqrt{9-x^2}$ is a semicircle of radius 3, so
$$\int_{-3}^{3}\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(3)^2=\dfrac{9\pi}{2}$$
which is also true.

In the last statement, $-x^3$ is odd so it integrates to $0$ over $[-5,5]$, but $4x^4$ and $\cos x$ are even and positive on average, so
$$\int_{-5}^{5}\left(4x^4-x^3+\cos x\right)dx=2\int_{0}^{5}\left(4x^4+\cos x\right)dx\ne0$$
Hence this is the statement that is not true.

parts.latex:
Which of the following statements is \textbf{true} for the function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{2}{3}x^3-6x^2+20x-5?$$

dif.r: f' discriminant negative; cubic always has inflection

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

req: Discriminant and the nature of roots

can: Discriminant and the nature of roots
B.note: Correct option is the inflection; ruling out max/min needs f' with no real roots (can-use elimination)

Increasing and decreasing functions.evidence: f'(x)>0 for all x. Hence f(x) is increasing for all x

Stationary points and their nature.evidence: For stationary points, f'(x)=0 ... no maximum or minimum

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\dfrac{2}{3}x^3-6x^2+20x-5\\f'(x)&=2x^2-12x+20\\f''(x)&=4x-12\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2-12x+20&=0\\x^2-6x+10&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\Delta=(-6)^2-4(1)(10)=-4<0$$
There are no solutions, and $f'(x)$ is a parabola with $a=2>0$, so $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$.

Hence $f(x)$ is increasing for all $x$ and has no maximum or minimum.

For a point of inflection, $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4x-12&=0\\x&=3\end{aligned}$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(2)&=4(2)-12=-4<0 &&\text{concave down}\\f''(4)&=4(4)-12=4>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=3$, so $f(x)$ has a point of inflection.

parts.latex:
It is given that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x\,.\ (\textbf{DO NOT PROVE THIS})$$

solutions.latex:
Integrate both sides of the given result:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\x\cos x&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\\int x\sin x\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C\quad\text{as required}$$

The curves intersect when
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=x\sin x\\\sin x-x\sin x&=0\\\sin x(1-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $\sin x=0$ or $1-x=0$, giving $x=0,\ \pi$ or $x=1$.

As $\sin x>0$ for $0<x<\pi$, the upper curve changes at $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&>x\sin x &&\text{for } 0<x<1\\x\sin x&>\sin x &&\text{for } 1<x<\pi\end{aligned}$$
Using $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\&=-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1-(-\cos0-\sin0+0)\\&=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=\int_1^\pi(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^\pi\\&=\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi-(\sin1-\cos1+\cos1)\\&=-1+\pi-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total shaded area}&=1-\sin1+(-1+\pi-\sin1)\\&=\pi-2\sin1\\&\approx1.46\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A credit card requires a six-figure personal identification number (PIN) for purchases. The figures are chosen from the digits $0,1,2,3,\ldots,9$.

Repetition is allowed and the PIN can start with any of the 10 digits.

The credit card is lost and the finder tries to guess the PIN by entering six digits.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that the six digits entered are the correct PIN?

dif.r: independent product (1/10)^6

A.note: either count PINs (10^6) or multiply digit probabilities

Multistage events and tree diagrams.evidence: Each of the six digits is correct with probability 1/10: (1/10)^6

Multiplication principle.reason: Counting 10^6 PINs is an alternative to the solution's method.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that the finder will guess at least one digit in its correct position?

dif.r: at least one via complement, (9/10)^6

solutions.latex:
Each of the six digits is correct with probability $\dfrac{1}{10}$:
$$P(\text{all six correct})=\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^6=\dfrac{1}{10^6}$$

'At least one correct' is the complement of 'none correct', and each digit is wrong with probability $\dfrac{9}{10}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one correct})&=1-P(\text{none correct})\\&=1-\left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right)^6\\&=0.468559\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\sqrt{3}\sin2x=-\cos2x$ for the domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

dif.r: reduce to tan2x, doubled domain including negative angles

solutions.latex:
Divide both sides by $\sqrt{3}\cos2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin2x}{\cos2x}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\\tan2x&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$\tan2x$ is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants.

The domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ becomes $-\pi\le2x\le\pi$ for $2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &&\text{2nd quadrant}\\2x&=-\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&\text{4th quadrant } \left(2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ less one revolution}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\ \text{ or }\ x=-\dfrac{\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Has all solutions from the correct quadrants, or equivalent merit
Expresses the equation in terms of $\tan2x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove that

$$\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{1+\sec x}=\sin x$$

dif.r: clear compound fractions, factorise, cancel; routine proof

solutions.latex:
Write in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, then multiply the numerator and denominator by $\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{1+\sec x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}{1+\frac{1}{\cos x}}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x\cos x+\sin x}{\cos x+1}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x(\cos x+1)}{\cos x+1}\\&=\sin x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Multiplies by $\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x}$, or equivalent merit
Expresses the question in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Natalie and her friends have made a post-HSC adventure bucket list. One of their bucket list items is to visit the Figure Eight rock pools and a visit to Figure Eight rock pools requires extreme caution. At all times it is very important to check the depth of water before entering the pools.

The depth of water at Figure Eight rock pools can be modelled by the equation

$$d=2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\,,\ \text{for } 0\le t\le12$$

where $d$ is in metres and $t$ is time after 7 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the depth of the water at high tide?

dif.r: centre plus amplitude

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Figure Eight rock pools is only safe to visit when the depth of the water is below 1.75 m.

Between what times is it safe to visit the pools?

dif.r: solve sine inequality, interpret interval as clock times

solutions.latex:
High tide is when $d$ is greatest, that is when $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}(1)\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The depth of water at high tide is $2.5$ m.

The pools are safe when $d<1.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<1.75\\\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.25\\\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.5\end{aligned}$$
Solve $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=-0.5$. The related angle is $\sin^{-1}(0.5)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=7\\\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=11\end{aligned}$$
By checking the graph or testing values, $d<1.75$ for $7<t<11$.

As $t$ is the number of hours after 7 am, $t=7$ is 2 pm and $t=11$ is 6 pm.

$\therefore$ It is safe to visit the pools between 2 pm and 6 pm.
criteria: Solves for the values of $t$ using trigonometric equation techniques, or equivalent merit
Makes $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t$ the subject, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A wire of length 28 m is to be cut into two pieces. One of the pieces is to be made into a square and the other into a circle.

Let $r$ metres be the radius of the circle and $x$ metres be the length of each side of the square.

The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\ \ (\textbf{DO NOT PROVE THIS})$$

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum? Leave your answer in simplest exact form.

dif.r: A given; solve A'=0, convert x to piece lengths exactly

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the given area to find the stationary point:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\A'&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(14-2x)(-2)+2x\\&=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x\\A''&=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2\end{aligned}$$
Set $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\-\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\-56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\2x(4+\pi)&=56\\x&=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}\end{aligned}$$
$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$ (concave up), so $x=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}$ gives a minimum.

The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has the rest of the wire, so the lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\text{ m}$$
and
$$\begin{aligned}28-4x&=28-\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\\&=\dfrac{28\pi}{4+\pi}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit
Some correct working towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t$, the change in the population from $t=0$ to $t=4$ is
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)-P(0)&=\int_0^4\left(9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\right)dt\\&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\int_0^42t\,dt\end{aligned}$$
With $P(0)=34$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\Big[t^2\Big]_0^4+P(0)\\&=9(22.26)-16+34\\&=218.34\ldots\\&\approx218\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: source dropped the factor 9 before the integral of e^{t^2/5}; restored (P=218 unchanged)

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $P=218$ when $t=4$. Substitute into $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100$:
$$\begin{aligned}218&=A(4)e^{-0.05\times4}-100\\318&=4Ae^{-0.2}\\A&=\dfrac{318}{4e^{-0.2}}\\&=97.10151927\ldots\\&\approx97\end{aligned}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: source bracket enclosed -100: 218=A(4)(e^{-0.2}-100); now 218=4Ae^{-0.2}-100 (A=97 unchanged)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=t & v&=e^{-0.05t}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-0.05e^{-0.05t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97te^{-0.05t}-100\\P'&=97\left(1\times e^{-0.05t}-0.05te^{-0.05t}\right)\\&=97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum, $P'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)&=0\\e^{-0.05t}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-0.05t}\ne0$, $1-\dfrac{t}{20}=0$, so $t=20$.

Since $97e^{-0.05t}>0$, the factor $1-0.05t$ decides the sign of $P'$. Test either side of $t=20$:

\extable{Ts2365_1}

$\therefore\ t=20$ is a maximum.

When $t=20$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97(20)e^{-1}-100\\&=613.6861159\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum population}=613$$

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x)=|x+2|+1$. Which of the following is a true statement?

dif.r: recognise corner of absolute value graph

options.label: A
options.latex: The function is continuous and differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: B
options.latex: The function is not continuous but differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: C
options.latex: The function is not continuous and not differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: D
options.latex: The function is continuous but not differentiable for every value of $x$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=|x+2|+1$ is the graph of $y=|x|$ translated 2 units left and 1 unit up.

It has no breaks, so it is continuous for every $x$.

It has a sharp corner at $x=-2$, so it is not differentiable at $x=-2$.

Hence $f$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable everywhere.

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x)=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$. Which of the following describes $f(x)$?

dif.r: Proving oddness needs a non-obvious rationalisation of f(-x); also monotonicity reasoning.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\ln\left(\sqrt{x^2+1}-x\right)\\&=\ln\dfrac{(x^2+1)-x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1}+x}\\&=\ln\dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}\\&=-\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\\&=-f(x)\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is odd.

$x+\sqrt{x^2+1}$ is increasing, so $f$ is increasing and therefore one-to-one.

Hence $f$ is an odd one-to-one function.

parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does the quadratic equation $x^2+kx-2k=0$ have real roots?

dif.r: discriminant >= 0 gives quadratic inequality in k

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
The equation has real roots when $\Delta\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=k^2-4(1)(-2k)\\&=k^2+8k\\&=k(k+8)\ge0\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}k&\le-8 &&\text{(both factors negative or zero)}\\k&\ge0 &&\text{(both factors positive or zero)}\end{aligned}$$
So $k\in(-\infty,-8]\cup[0,\infty)$, with the end points included because $\Delta=0$ gives a repeated real root.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned}a+b+b+2b+0.2&=1\\a&=0.8-4b\end{aligned}$$
Since $b\ge0$ and $a\ge0$, we have $0\le b\le0.2$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-2a+0\times b+b\times b+2b\times2b+4\times0.2\\&=-2(0.8-4b)+5b^2+0.8\\&=5b^2+8b-0.8\end{aligned}$$
This is increasing for $0\le b\le0.2$ (its derivative $10b+8$ is positive):
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-0.8 &&\text{at } b=0\\E(X)&=1 &&\text{at } b=0.2\end{aligned}$$
Hence $-0.8\le E(X)\le1$.

Katie has deliberately designed a biased six-sided die with the following probability distribution for $X$, the number showing on the uppermost face when the die is rolled.

\extable{355_q11_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What values of $\theta$ allow for $P(X)$ to be a probability distribution function?

dif.r: use 0<=P<=1 on each probability to bound theta

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(1\le X\le 4)$ in terms of $\theta$.

dif.r: add four expressions in theta

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability of rolling an even number in terms of $\theta$.

dif.r: add three expressions in theta

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1 for every $\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sum P(X=x)&=\dfrac{3(1-\theta)}{6}+\dfrac{3(1+\theta)}{6}\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
So this gives no restriction on $\theta$.

Each probability must also satisfy $0\le P(X=x)\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0\le\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -5\le\theta\le1\\0\le\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -1\le\theta\le5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1\le\theta\le1$$
criteria: Solves both inequalities $0\le P(X=x)\le1$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: $-1\le\theta\le 1$. Must show $\sum P(X=x)=1$. Many students wrote $-1<\theta<1$ (incorrect).
meta.marker_note: Must show $\sum P(X=x)=1$. Many students wrote $-1<\theta<1$ (incorrect).

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}P(1\le X\le4)&=\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{4-2\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{2-\theta}{3}\end{aligned}$$

The even outcomes are $2$, $4$ and $6$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\text{ even})&=\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{3+\theta}{6}\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: semicircular sector A1 of radius 4 m (A to B) and sector A2 of radius 3 m (D to C) with angle theta at O

solutions.latex:
Sector area $=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, and $A_1=2A_2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}(4)^2(\pi-\theta)&=2\times\dfrac{1}{2}(3)^2\theta\\8(\pi-\theta)&=9\theta\\17\theta&=8\pi\\\theta&=\dfrac{8\pi}{17}\end{aligned}$$
This is $84^\circ42'$, or $84.71^\circ$.

parts.latex: Prove: $\dfrac{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}{\tan x+\sin x}=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x$

dif.r: compound fractions in cot/cosec, factorise and cancel 1+cos x

solutions.latex:
Method 1: multiply the numerator and denominator by $\sin x\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{1}}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x+1)}{\sin^2x+\sin^2x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)}{\sin^2x(1+\cos x)}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: write the numerator using $\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{\tan x\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct simplification of the compound fraction, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos^2 x-3\cos x=2$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: quadratic in cos x, reject cos=2, two exact solutions

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\cos x$ and factorise:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x-3\cos x-2&=0\\(2\cos x+1)(\cos x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=2$.

$\cos x=2$ has no solution, since $-1\le\cos x\le1$.

For $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Factorises to $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ (rejecting $\cos x=2$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $3\sin x+\sqrt{3}\cos x=0$ over the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: divide by cos to get tan equation, two quadrants

solutions.latex:
Divide both sides by $\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned}3\sin x&=-\sqrt{3}\cos x\\3\tan x&=-\sqrt{3}\\\tan x&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
criteria: One correct solution, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: circle centre O on a vertical wall; A below O at height h, B on the circle with angle AOB = 90 degrees; D on the ground with elevations 30 and 60 degrees and angle ADB = 30 degrees (not to scale)

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle with the angle of elevation $30^\circ$ at $D$ and height $h$ at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{AD}\\AD&=\dfrac{h}{\sin30^\circ}=2h\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is $10$ m above $A$ and $OB$ is horizontal, so $B$ is $h+10$ m above the ground:
$$BD=\dfrac{h+10}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: One correct expression, $AD=2h$ or $BD=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=OB=10$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$, so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$AB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt{2}$$
In $\triangle ABD$, use the cosine rule with $\angle ADB=30^\circ$:
$$\left(10\sqrt{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+(2h)^2-2\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)(2h)\cos30^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}200&=\dfrac{4h^2+80h+400}{3}+4h^2-4h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2+80h+400+12h^2-12h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2-40h+400\\0&=4h^2-40h-200\\&=4\left(h^2-10h-50\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$h=\dfrac{10\pm\sqrt{300}}{2}=5\pm5\sqrt{3}$$
Since $h>0$:
$$\therefore\ h=5+5\sqrt{3}\approx13.66$$
criteria: Correct quadratic equation in $h$, or equivalent merit
