parts.latex: The function $y=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}$ is dilated by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ horizontally and reflected about the $x$-axis. What is the new equation for this function?

dif.r: Apply a dilation then a reflection to a rational function, in order.

solutions.latex:
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$.
$$y=\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}$$
A reflection in the $x$-axis replaces $y$ by $-y$.
$$\begin{aligned}-y&=\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}\\y&=\dfrac{1-2x}{2x+1}\end{aligned}$$
So the new equation is $y=\dfrac{1-2x}{1+2x}$, which is option C.

questions.stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=25n-2n^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the first term.

dif.r: One substitution: T1 equals S1.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the common difference.

dif.r: Use Tn = Sn - S(n-1) to get terms, then the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the general term is given by $T_n=27-4n$.

dif.r: Substitute a and d into the arithmetic general term.

solutions.latex:
The first term is $T_1=S_1$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_1&=25(1)-2(1)^2\\&=23\end{aligned}$$
So the first term is $23$.

Find the first three terms from the sums, using $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=23\\S_2&=25(2)-2(2)^2=42,&T_2&=S_2-S_1=19\\S_3&=25(3)-2(3)^2=57,&T_3&=S_3-S_2=15\end{aligned}$$
The terms are $23,\ 19,\ 15,\ \ldots$
$$d=19-23=-4$$

Use $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=23$ and $d=-4$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=23+(n-1)\times(-4)\\&=23-4n+4\\&=27-4n\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The circle $x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12=0$ is transformed by a vertical translation 3 units down and a horizontal translation 5 units right. What are the coordinates of the new centre of the transformed circle?

dif.r: Complete the square for the centre, then translate it.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12&=0\\(x+2)^2-4+(y-3)^2-9+12&=0\\(x+2)^2+(y-3)^2&=1\end{aligned}$$
The original centre is $(-2,3)$.

Moving $5$ units right and $3$ units down gives the equation
$$(x-3)^2+y^2=1$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the new centre is }(3,0)$$

parts.latex: A factory gets permission to dispose, at the start of every day, 600kg of waste into a stream of water. The running stream removes 40% of any waste present, by the end of the day. Show that the amount of waste present in the stream at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ day is $900(1-0.6^n)$.

dif.r: Build a recurrence from context and recognise the geometric series.

solutions.latex:
The stream removes $40\%$, leaving $60\%$ at the end of each day. Let $W_n$ be the amount at the end of day $n$.
$$\begin{aligned}W_1&=0.6\times 600=360\\W_2&=0.6\left(W_1+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6\\W_3&=0.6\left(W_2+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2\end{aligned}$$
So
$$W_n=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2+\cdots+360\times 0.6^{n-1}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=360$, $r=0.6$ and $n$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned}W_n&=\dfrac{360\left(1-0.6^n\right)}{1-0.6}\\&=\dfrac{360}{0.4}\left(1-0.6^n\right)\\&=900\left(1-0.6^n\right)\end{aligned}$$

Andrew places one grain of rice on the first square, two grains of rice on the second square, four grains on the third, eight on the fourth, and so on, until every square is covered.

The board has $8\times 8=64$ squares, so the last square is the $64^{\text{th}}$ term.

parts.latex: The third and fifth terms of a geometric progression are 6 and $\dfrac{3}{2}$ respectively. Find the common ratio and first term for this progression.

dif.r: Simultaneous geometric term equations with both signs of r, like the anchor.

solutions.latex:
Use $T_n=ar^{n-1}$ for the third and fifth terms.
$$\begin{aligned}T_3&=ar^2=6 & T_5&=ar^4=\dfrac{3}{2}\\a&=\dfrac{6}{r^2} & a&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\end{aligned}$$
Equate the two expressions for $a$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{6}{r^2}&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\\12r^4&=3r^2\\3r^2\left(4r^2-1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $r=0$ or $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$. But $r=0$ gives $ar^2=0\ne 6$, so $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Then $a=\dfrac{6}{r^2}=\dfrac{6}{\frac{1}{4}}=24$.
$$\therefore\ r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ and }a=24$$
criteria: Forms a pair of simultaneous equations

parts.latex: If $4,\ x,\ y$ form a geometric sequence and $x,\ y,\ 12$ form an arithmetic sequence, find the values of $x$ and $y$.

dif.r: Combine geometric and arithmetic conditions into a quadratic system.

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
For the geometric sequence $4,\ x,\ y$ the ratios are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{4}&=\dfrac{y}{x}\\x^2&=4y\\y&=\dfrac{x^2}{4}\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
For the arithmetic sequence $x,\ y,\ 12$ the differences are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}y-x&=12-y\\2y-x&=12\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute (1) into (2).
$$\begin{aligned}2\left(\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-x&=12\\\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x&=12\\x^2-2x-24&=0\\(x-6)(x+4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ or $x=-4$.

When $x=6$, $y=9$. When $x=-4$, $y=4$.
$$\therefore\ (x,y)=(6,9)\text{ or }(-4,4)$$
criteria: Forms a quadratic and solves for $x$
Forms a pair of equations to solve simultaneously

questions.stem:
$A$ and $B$ are two arithmetic series, where all the terms are positive.

In series $A$, the first term is $a$ and common difference is $d$. In series $B$, the first term is $M$ and the common difference is $D$.

Let $P=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $A$ and let $Q=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $B$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$.

dif.r: General show-that, but just cancelling the sum formulas.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Express $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$ in terms of $a,\ d,\ M$ and $D$.

dif.r: Write down the general term formula with n=10.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Given that $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{5n+4}{9n+6}$, evaluate $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$.

dif.r: Insight needed: matching (n-1)/2=9 gives n=19; non-routine link between parts.

solutions.latex:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]\\Q&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{P}{Q}&=\dfrac{\frac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]}{\frac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]}\\&=\dfrac{2a+(n-1)d}{2M+(n-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly shows the sum of both AP's and simplifies to obtain the ratio needed
meta.format_note: Source also listed the nth-term formulas here; moved to part (b), where they are used.

solutions.latex:
The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of each series is $a+(n-1)d$ and $M+(n-1)D$. For $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}&=\dfrac{a+(10-1)d}{M+(10-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$. This matches the ratio of the $10^{\text{th}}$ terms in part (b) when $\dfrac{n-1}{2}=9$, so $n=19$.

Substitute $n=19$ into the given ratio.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}&=\dfrac{5(19)+4}{9(19)+6}\\&=\dfrac{99}{177}\\&=\dfrac{33}{59}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{5x}$

dif.r: Rearrange to standard sin(x)/x limit form

solutions.latex:
Rewrite so the limit takes the standard form $\displaystyle\lim_{\theta\to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{5x}&=\dfrac{4}{5}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4x}\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\times 1\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave the answer 4/5 only; the standard-limit step added.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=x^4+x^3+kx^2-3x-5$, where $k$ is a constant.

Find the values of $k$ for which $f(x)$ is always concave up.

dif.r: Combine second derivative with discriminant condition for positive definite quadratic

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
A function is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4x^3+3x^2+2kx-3\\f''(x)&=12x^2+6x+2k\end{aligned}$$
$f''(x)>0$ for all $x$ requires the quadratic $2\left(6x^2+3x+k\right)$ to have positive leading coefficient ($6>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}3^2-4\times 6\times k&<0\\9-24k&<0\\k&>\dfrac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source wrote 'a>0 or Delta<0'; corrected to 'and' (both conditions are needed for a quadratic to be positive for all x).
meta.format_note: Rubric rows kept from the source. Checked: k=3/8 gives a double root of f'', so f''>=0 with equality at one point; the strict inequality k>3/8 is as in the source.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the curve passing through the point $(2,5)$ with gradient function $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial then find constant from point; two steps

solutions.latex:
Integrate the gradient function, then use the point $(2,5)$ to find the constant.
$$f(x)=\int\left(3x^2-4x+1\right)dx=x^3-2x^2+x+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(2)&=5\\2^3-2\times 2^2+2+c&=5\\2+c&=5\\c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x+3$$

parts.latex: Find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve $y=\dfrac{2}{3x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=2$ and $x=4$.

dif.r: Definite integral of reciprocal giving log, exact simplification

solutions.latex:
The area is the integral of $y$ from $x=2$ to $x=4$ (the curve is above the $x$-axis there).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_2^4\dfrac{2}{3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[\ln x\Big]_2^4\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln 4-\ln 2)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the primitive $\ln 3x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[\ln 3x\Big]_2^4\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln 12-\ln 6)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\text{ units}^2$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^x\sin x$ at the point $(\pi,0)$.

dif.r: Product rule gradient, negative reciprocal, point-gradient line

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent comes from the product rule applied to $y=e^x\sin x$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=e^{\pi}\sin\pi+e^{\pi}\cos\pi\\&=-e^{\pi}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}$$
The normal through $(\pi,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-0&=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}(x-\pi)\\e^{\pi}y&=x-\pi\\e^{\pi}y-x+\pi&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the equation of the tangent or the gradient of the normal
Finds the correct derivative, or finds the equation of the normal with an incorrect derivative

questions.stem: For the following equations, solve for $x$

dif.r: Index manipulation and factorising exponential equation; careful algebra
Apply power and quotient log laws, then equate arguments

solutions.latex:
Rewrite in terms of $2^x$ and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}2^{2x+3}-4\times 2^x&=0\\2^{2x}\times 2^3-4\times 2^x&=0\\4\times 2^x\left(2\times 2^x-1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$2^x=0$ has no solution, so $2\times 2^x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}2^x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Has an equation in terms of $2^x$

meta.format_note: Rubric rows kept from the source. Checked: 2^1 - 4 x 2^-1 = 2 - 2 = 0.

solutions.latex:
Collect the logarithms using the log laws, $n\log_a b=\log_a b^n$ and $\log_a b-\log_a c=\log_a\dfrac{b}{c}$.
$$\begin{aligned}2\log_5 3&=\log_5 x-\log_5 6\\\log_5 3^2&=\log_5\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right)\\3^2&=\dfrac{x}{6}\\x&=54\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses at least one log law correctly

dif.r: Pythagorean identity to sec^2, then routine definite integral.

solutions.latex:
Write $\dfrac{1}{(2x+1)^2}=(2x+1)^{-2}$ and use $\displaystyle\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+c$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(2x+1)^{-2}\,dx&=\dfrac{(2x+1)^{-1}}{-1\times 2}+c\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2(2x+1)}+c\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: The answer must include $+c$ for full marks.
meta.format_note: Only part (a) of this question is in the input.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of the denominator, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(5x^2+3)=10x$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x}{5x^2+3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{10}\int\dfrac{10x}{5x^2+3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln|5x^2+3|+c\end{aligned}$$

Divide each term of the numerator by $x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{3x^2+4}{x}\,dx&=\int\left(3x+\dfrac{4}{x}\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}x^2+4\ln|x|+c\end{aligned}$$

By the index laws, $\dfrac{e^{3x}}{e^{x}}=e^{2x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{e^{3x}}{e^{x}}\,dx&=\int e^{2x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}+c\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The derivative of $4x-3$ is $4$, so the primitive of $\sin(4x-3)$ has a factor $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
$$\int\sin(4x-3)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{4}\cos(4x-3)+c$$

solutions.latex:
Write $5^{x+1}=5\cdot 5^x$ and use $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int 5^{x+1}\,dx&=5\int 5^x\,dx\\&=5\cdot\dfrac{5^x}{\ln 5}+c\\&=\dfrac{5^{x+1}}{\ln 5}+c\end{aligned}$$

Use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}=\sec^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2 x}\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x}\,dx\\&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}2\sec^2 x\,dx\\&=2\Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\&=2\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan 0\right)\\&=2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The parabola $y=-4x^2+16x$ and the line $y=2x$ intersect at the origin and point A.

\exfigure{571_q15_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point A.

dif.r: Equate line and parabola, factorise quadratic.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the area enclosed by the parabola and the line.

dif.r: Standard area between parabola and line with known limits.

figures.cap: parabola y=-4x^2+16x and line y=2x with enclosed region shaded

solutions.latex:
Equate the line and the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=-4x^2+16x\\0&=-4x^2+14x\\0&=2x(7-2x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The root $x=0$ is the origin, so A has
$$x=\dfrac{7}{2}$$

Between the intersection points the parabola is above the line, so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line) from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$ (part (a)).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\left(-4x^2+16x-2x\right)dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3+7x^2\right]_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^3+7\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^2\right)-0\\&=\dfrac{343}{12}\\&\approx 28.583\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\sqrt{3x^2+6}$.

dif.r: Chain rule with fractional power and simplification.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write $y$ as a power and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(3x^2+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(3x^2+6)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 6x\\&=\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\end{aligned}$$

From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{3x^2+6}=\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}$, so $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}$ is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of that derivative.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\sqrt{3x^2+6}\Big]_0^1\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{6}\right)\\&=1-\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\end{aligned}$$

Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ}=\dfrac{\pi}{180}x$ radians.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\log_e\sqrt{e^{x}(2x+1)}$

dif.r: Log laws simplify first, then routine differentiation.

solutions.latex:
Simplify first with the log laws $\ln\sqrt{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln A$ and $\ln(AB)=\ln A+\ln B$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left[e^x(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln e^x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\end{aligned}$$
Now differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{(2x+1)+2}{2(2x+1)}\\&=\dfrac{2x+3}{4x+2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses at least one log law to simplify the question

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows the graph of the function $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

The points $P(0,0)$ and $Q\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ both lie on the curve.

The point $R(t,\sin t)$ is also a point on the curve between $P$ and $Q$, such that $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{571_q21_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\text{ when }t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$$

dif.r: Non-routine set-up: triangle area via trapezia, heavy algebra.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the maximum value of $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$.

Justify your answer, leaving your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Optimise trig expression, inverse cosine, justify maximum numerically.

figures.cap: graph of y=sin x with points P, R, Q and triangle PQR shaded
solution sketch: annotated diagram of triangle PQR with rectangle and trapezoid areas

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{571_q21_s1}

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is the area under $PR$ plus the area under $RQ$, minus the area under $PQ$ (each a trapezium on the $x$-axis).
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\,t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-t\right)\left(\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Expand and simplify.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}-t\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}t\right)-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{6}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}t\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an area that will lead to significant progress to a solution

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary point.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\\\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\cos t-3\sqrt{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0$:
$$\cos t=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\pi}$$
so $t=1.145\ldots$, which lies in $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(-4\pi\sin t\right)$$
When $t=1.145$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=-0.9534<0$, so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin 1.145-3\sqrt{3}\times 1.145\right)\\&\approx 0.46\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum } A\approx 0.46$$
criteria: Satisfies one criteria point. Criteria points: finds $t$; test for concavity; finds maximum $A$

meta.format_note: Checked: t = 1.1445, d2A/dt2 = -0.953, A = 0.458. A = 0 at both ends (t = 0 and t = 2pi/3), so 0.46 is the greatest value; the source does not show the end-point check.

Check by differentiating option D: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\sin x\right)=x+\cos x$. Options A and B differentiate to $\cos x$ and $-\cos x$, and C gives $x-\cos x$.

parts.latex:
The function $y=f(x)$ is transformed to $y=f\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)$.

Which of the following describes the transformations that took place?

dif.r: Identify horizontal dilation and translation from factored form

options.label: A
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of 3, followed by translation left 1 unit.

options.label: B
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of 3, followed by translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

options.label: C
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$, followed by translation left 1 unit.

options.label: D
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$, followed by translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

solutions.latex:
Write $f\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)=f(3x+1)$. In the form $f\big(k(x+h)\big)$, the factor $k=3$ gives a horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{k}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, and $x+h$ with $h=\dfrac{1}{3}$ gives a translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

Dilating first by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ and then translating gives $f\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)$, so the order and sizes match option D.

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_1^a (4-2x)\,dx=-3$ where $a>0$. What is the value of $a$?

dif.r: Evaluate definite integral with unknown limit, solve quadratic

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then substitute the limits.
$$\begin{aligned}\Big[4x-x^2\Big]_1^a&=-3\\(4a-a^2)-(4-1)&=-3\\4a-a^2-3&=-3\\4a-a^2&=0\\a(4-a)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $a>0$, $a\ne 0$, so $a=4$ (option B).

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on the $x$ axis. Its velocity, $v$ metres per second, at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=3-6\cos t$.

Initially the particle is at 4 metres on the right of the origin.

Which expression is the displacement function in terms of $t$ ?

dif.r: Integrate velocity and use initial condition for constant

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(3-6\cos t)\,dt\\&=3t-6\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially $x(0)=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=0-0+C\\C&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x(t)=3t-6\sin t+4$, which is option A.

dif.r: Signed areas of sector, rectangle and triangle combined

figures.cap: sector, rectangle and triangle graph of y=f(x)

solutions.latex:
The integral is the area above the $x$-axis minus the area below it. Here it is the rectangle plus the sector, minus the triangle.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-3}^{5}f(x)\,dx&=(2\times 3)+\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times 2^2\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 1\right)\\&=6+\pi-\dfrac{3}{2}\\&=\pi+\dfrac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^{2x}(x+2)$ at the point $(1,3e^2)$.

Give your answer in general form, with exact values.

dif.r: Product rule, tangent equation in general form

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{2x}&v&=x+2\\u'&=2e^{2x}&v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{2x}\cdot 1+2e^{2x}(x+2)\\&=e^{2x}\left(1+2(x+2)\right)\\&=e^{2x}(2x+5)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=7e^2$, the gradient of the tangent.

The tangent through $(1,3e^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3e^2&=7e^2(x-1)\\y-3e^2&=7e^2x-7e^2\\0&=7e^2x-y-4e^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 7e^2x-y-4e^2=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit
Differentiates using the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is translated $m$ units to the left, dilated vertically by a scale factor of $k$ and then translated 7 units up. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$. Find $m$ and $k$.

dif.r: Same as anchor: equate coefficients or complete square

solutions.latex:
The transformed function is $g(x)=k(x+m)^2+7$ (translate $m$ units left, dilate by $k$, translate 7 up).
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=k\left(x^2+2mx+m^2\right)+7\\&=kx^2+2mkx+m^2k+7\end{aligned}$$
Equate coefficients with $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$.

Coefficient of $x^2$: $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}2mk&=2\\2\times m\times\dfrac{1}{3}&=2\\m&=3\end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: complete the square.
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+30\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+3^2+30-3^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[(x+3)^2+21\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+3)^2+7\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=3,\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

parts.latex:
Ms Iacona notices that the number of emails she receives per week from students is cyclical. Every 12 weeks she receives the highest number of emails.

The number of emails Ms Iacona receives each week, $f(t)$, is modelled by the function

$$f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$$

where $t$ is the number of weeks after 1 January 2023 and $0\le t\le 52$.

The lowest number of emails Ms Iacona receives is 15 per week and the highest number of emails per week is 45.

The number of emails is at a maximum on 1st January 2023 i.e., when $t=0$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: Find amplitude, period and centre from max/min data

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest values.
$$a=\dfrac{45-15}{2}=15$$
The period is $12$ weeks.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=12\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
So $f(t)=15\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+c$. The maximum is at $t=0$, so $f(0)=45$.
$$\begin{aligned}45&=15+c\\c&=30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=15,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ c=30$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds one of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The acceleration of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $a=4t+4$ . Initially the particle has a velocity of $-30$ m/s. When is the particle at rest?

dif.r: Integrate acceleration with initial condition, solve quadratic

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int(4t+4)\,dt\\&=2t^2+4t+c\end{aligned}$$
Initially $v=-30$, so when $t=0$, $c=-30$.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2t^2+4t-30\\&=2(t^2+2t-15)\\&=2(t+5)(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$, so $t=-5$ or $t=3$. Since $t\ge 0$, $t=3$, option C.

parts.latex:
Consider the information about events $A$ and $B$.

\begin{itemize}
\item $P(B)=0.6$
\item $P(A|B)=0.4$
\item $P(A|\overline{B})=0.8$
\end{itemize}

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability needing total probability step

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram with P(A and not B)=8/25 and P(A and B)=6/25

solutions.latex:
Use $P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}$ and find each intersection from the conditional probabilities.
$$P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.6}=0.4\quad\text{so}\quad P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{6}{25}$$
$$P\left(A|\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)}{1-0.6}=\dfrac{P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)}{0.4}=0.8\quad\text{so}\quad P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{8}{25}$$

\exfigure{638_q8_s1}

$$P(A)=P(A\cap B)+P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{6}{25}+\dfrac{8}{25}=\dfrac{14}{25}$$
$$\therefore\ P(B|A)=\dfrac{\frac{6}{25}}{\frac{14}{25}}=\dfrac{3}{7}$$
This is option C.

questions.stem: Consider the geometric series $64-16a+4a^2-\ldots$

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{-16a}{64}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\qquad\left(\text{check: }\dfrac{4a^2}{-16a}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\right)$$
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$, that is $-1<r<1$. One operation per line:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&<-\dfrac{a}{4}<1\\-4&<-a<4&&(\text{multiply by }4)\\4&>a>-4&&(\text{multiply by }-1,\text{ reversing the inequalities})\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Finds the common ratio $r=-\dfrac{a}{4}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A circle is divided into $n$ sectors in such a way that the angles of the sectors are in arithmetic progression. The smallest two angles are $3^\circ$ and $5^\circ$. Find the value of $n$.

The sector angles form an arithmetic series with $a=3^\circ$ and $d=2^\circ$, and they add to a full circle, so $S_n=360$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\times 3+(n-1)\times 2\right]&=360\\n\left(2n+4\right)&=720\\2n^2+4n-720&=0\\n^2+2n-360&=0\\(n+20)(n-18)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=18$.

$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}kx(4-x), & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right\}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx&=1\\k\int_1^4\left(4x-x^2\right)dx&=1\\k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4&=1\\k\left(\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\9k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The curve $y=px^3+qx$ passes through the point $(1, 4)$. The tangent at this point is parallel to the line $y=2x-6$. Find the values of $p$ and $q$.

solutions.latex:
The curve passes through $(1,4)$:
$$p+q=4\qquad(1)$$
Differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3px^2+q$. The gradient of the tangent at $(1,4)$ is $3p+q$. The tangent is parallel to $y=2x-6$, so its gradient is $2$:
$$3p+q=2\qquad(2)$$
From (1), $q=4-p$. Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}3p+4-p&=2\\2p&=-2\\p&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}q&=4-(-1)\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=-1,\ q=5$$
criteria: Forms both equations $p+q=4$ and $3p+q=2$, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=P(1.003)-M\\A_2&=A_1(1.003)-M\\&=\left[P(1.003)-M\right](1.003)-M\\&=P(1.003)^2-M(1.003)-M\end{aligned}$$

The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$. Use the geometric series sum with $a=1$, $r=1.003$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=50\,000(1.003)^n-350\times\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\\&=50\,000(1.003)^n-\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\&=-\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n&=\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\1.003^n&=\dfrac{7}{4}\\n\log 1.003&=\log\dfrac{7}{4}\\n&=\dfrac{\log\frac{7}{4}}{\log 1.003}\\&=186.818\ldots\\&\approx 187\text{ months}\end{aligned}$$
It takes $187$ months, that is $15$ years and $7$ months, to pay off the loan.

parts.latex:
In an arithmetic series, the sum of the first three terms is 21 and the sum of the first four terms is 36.

What is the sum of the first five terms of this series?

dif.r: Two sum equations solved for a and d, then S5

solutions.latex:
In an arithmetic series the sum of three consecutive terms is three times the middle term.
$$3T_2=21\ \text{ so }\ T_2=7$$
The fourth term is the difference of the two sums.
$$T_4=S_4-S_3=36-21=15$$
Since $T_4-T_2=2d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2d &= 15-7 \\ &= 8 \\ d &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
The middle term of the first five terms is $T_3=7+4=11$, and the sum of five terms is five times the middle term.
$$S_5=5\times 11=55$$

For $g(f(x))=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$ we need $x\ge0$ and $\sqrt{x}\ne1$, so the domain is $x\ge0,\ x\ne1$.

The domain on which both composite functions are defined is $x>1$. For $x>1$, $\sqrt{x}-1$ takes every positive value, so $g(f(x))$ also has range $y>0$.
$$\text{Domain } (1,\infty),\quad \text{Range } (0,\infty)$$

parts.latex:
The limiting sum of a geometric series is $\dfrac{10}{9}$ and the sum of its first three terms is $\dfrac{26}{25}$.

What is the common ratio of this series?

dif.r: Combine limiting sum and S3 formulas; ratio gives 1 minus r cubed

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a}{1-r} &= \dfrac{10}{9} \\ a &= \dfrac{10}{9}(1-r) \end{aligned}$$
The sum of the first three terms is $a(1+r+r^2)=\dfrac{26}{25}$. Substituting for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10}{9}(1-r)(1+r+r^2) &= \dfrac{26}{25} \\ (1-r)(1+r+r^2) &= \dfrac{117}{125} \\ 1-r^3 &= \dfrac{117}{125} \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{8}{125} \\ r &= \dfrac{2}{5}=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

In a bag of $n$ coloured discs, exactly 7 are red.

The probability that both discs are red is
$$\dfrac{7}{n}\cdot\dfrac{6}{n-1}=\dfrac{21}{55}$$

parts.latex:
A particle is moving in a straight line such that its displacement $x$ metres at time $t$ seconds from the origin is given by the equation $x=k\cos(at+b)$, where $a$, $b$ and $k$ are constants.

The particle is stationary when $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$.

The initial acceleration of the particle is $6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$.

What could be the values of $a$, $b$ and $k$?

dif.r: Period from stationary times, differentiate twice, test options against initial acceleration

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary at $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12}$. Every second stationary time is one period apart, so
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{17\pi}{12}-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\pi \quad\text{so}\quad a=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$$
Test option D, $x=-3\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 6\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ when $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\pi,\ 2\pi,\ 3\pi,\ldots$ (the first value of $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ for $t\ge0$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$), giving $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$ as required.

At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 12\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= 6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
Options B and C also have $a=2$ and the same stationary times, but their initial acceleration is $-6\sqrt{3}$, so only D fits.

meta.format_note: Source wrote the stationary condition as 0, pi, 2pi... 'taking the positive values'; written here as pi, 2pi, 3pi (t>0). Rejection of A, B, C added by us and checked: B has initial acceleration 12cos(-5pi/6)=-6sqrt3, C has -12cos(pi/6)=-6sqrt3, A has a=4.

parts.latex:
Consider the equation $\left(\sin\theta-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\left(\tan2\theta-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)=0.$

How many solutions are there in the interval $0\le\theta\le\pi$?

dif.r: Solve both factors, then spot the trap where tan 2θ is undefined

solutions.latex:
The product is zero when either factor is zero, provided both factors are defined.
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \quad\text{gives}\quad \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$ we have $0\le2\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\tan2\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \quad\text{gives}\quad 2\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \quad\text{so}\quad \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12}$$
Check each in the original equation. At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, $\tan2\theta$ is $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, which are undefined, so these are rejected.

At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$ both factors are defined and the second is zero, so they are solutions.

There are 2 solutions.

The graph of an even function, $f(x)$, and an odd function, $g(x)$ are shown below.

\exfigure{515_q10_1}

Let $A=\int_{-4}^{-2}f(x)\,dx$, $B=\int_{-2}^{0}g(x)\,dx$ and $C=\int_{2}^{4}\big(g(x)-f(x)\big)\,dx$.

dif.r: Signed areas with odd/even symmetry combined across three given integrals

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: graphs of y=f(x) and y=g(x) with regions A, B and C shaded

solutions.latex:
Let $f$ be even and $g$ be odd. The integrals are signed areas: $A<0$ (region $A$ is below the $x$-axis), $B>0$ (region $B$ is above it), and $C<0$ (on $[2,4]$ the graph of $g$ is below the graph of $f$, so $g(x)-f(x)<0$).

Split the required integral:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx=\int_0^2 g(x)\,dx+\int_2^4 g(x)\,dx$$
Since $g$ is odd, $\displaystyle\int_0^2 g(x)\,dx=-\int_{-2}^0 g(x)\,dx=-B$.

Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_2^4 f(x)\,dx=\int_{-4}^{-2} f(x)\,dx=A$, so
$$\displaystyle\int_2^4 g(x)\,dx=\int_2^4 f(x)\,dx+C=A+C$$
$$\displaystyle\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx=A-B+C$$
This is option B.

The time it takes to complete a task varies inversely with the number of people assigned.

It takes 5 people to complete a task in 4 hours.

Find the amount of time it would take 8 people to complete the same task.

The time varies inversely with the number of people, so $T=\dfrac{k}{n}$ where $n$ is the number of people.

For 5 people, $T=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= \dfrac{k}{5} \\ k &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Prove evenness via trig identity manipulation of shifted sine

parts.label: b

solutions.latex:
Simplify using $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= -\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &= \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \cos\left(\dfrac{-x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \\ &= f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)$ is even.

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row "Correct answer" was written by us.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{515_q17_s1}

From part (a), $f(x)=\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$, which is $\ge0$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ (since $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{x}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$), so the area lies above the $x$-axis.

$f$ is even, so the area is symmetrical about the $y$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\Big[2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\sin0\right) \\ &= 4\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.
questions.review_note: scan path: review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What was the initial temperature of the oven?

dif.r: Substitute t = 0 into the given model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Two substitutions into given model, then average rate formula

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Ben can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ$C per minute.

Given that Ben turned the oven on at 10:30 am, find the earliest time that Ben can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Differentiate a^(kt), solve rate equation with logs, convert to clock time

solutions.latex:
At the start, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 175-150\times(0.9)^{0} \\ &= 175-150 \\ &= 25^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row was written by us.

solutions.latex:
The average rate of change is $\dfrac{T(75)-T(25)}{75-25}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T(25) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times25} \\ &\approx 86.4265 \\ T(75) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times75} \\ &\approx 144.11633 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate} &= \dfrac{144.11633-86.4265}{75-25} \\ &\approx 1.15^\circ\text{C/minute} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $T(25)$ and $T(75)$ and sets up the average rate, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Checked: 57.6898/50=1.1538.

solutions.latex:
The instantaneous rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Differentiating with $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -150\times0.2\times(0.9)^{0.2t}\times\ln0.9 \\ &= -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} \end{aligned}$$
The cut-off is where $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} &= 1 \\ (0.9)^{0.2t} &\approx 0.316374 \\ 0.2t &\approx \log_{0.9}0.316374 \\ t &\approx \dfrac{5\ln0.316374}{\ln0.9} \\ &\approx 54.6\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$
The rate $-30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$ decreases as $t$ increases, so it is $\le1$ for $t\ge54.6$. To the nearest minute this is $55$ minutes after $10{:}30$ am.
$$\text{Time}=10{:}30\ \text{am}+55\ \text{min}=11{:}25\ \text{am}$$

parts.latex:
A factory fills bottles with water. The actual amount of water in each bottle is normally distributed with a mean of 602 mL and a standard deviation of 2.5 mL.

Using the values in the table, determine the percentage of bottles that contain between 599 mL and 604 mL of water.

solution sketch: hand sketch of normal curve with 599, 602, 604 marked and the region between shaded

solutions.latex:
The normal distribution is symmetrical about $0$, so the probability above $-1.2$ equals the probability below $1.2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z>-1.2) &= P(Z<1.2) \\ &= 0.885 \end{aligned}$$
(from the table, row $1$ and column $.2$)

\exfigure{515_q22_s1}

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row was written by us. \exfigure{515_q22_s1} kept. Part (b) of this question is the next solution (3386).

solutions.latex:
Convert 599 mL and 604 mL to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, with $\mu=602$ and $\sigma=2.5$.
$$z=\dfrac{599-602}{2.5}=-1.2 \quad\text{and}\quad z=\dfrac{604-602}{2.5}=0.8$$
From the table, $P(Z<0.8)=0.788$ and $P(Z<1.2)=0.885$, so $P(Z<-1.2)=1-0.885=0.115$ by symmetry.
$$\begin{aligned} P(599<X<604) &= P(-1.2<Z<0.8) \\ &= P(Z<0.8)-P(Z<-1.2) \\ &= 0.788-(1-0.885) \\ &= 0.673 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Percentage}=67.3\%$$
\exfigure{515_q22_s2}

solutions.latex:

solutions.latex:
The volume is $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$, so
$$h=\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}$$
The closed tank has two half-discs (together $\pi r^2$), half of the curved cylinder surface ($\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot2\pi rh$) and a flat rectangular top ($2r\times h$).
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh \\ &= \pi r^2+\pi r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}+2r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{r}+\dfrac{2}{r}\right] \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $A=\pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Face list added by us (the handwriting said 'half cylinder plus rectangles'); checked algebra to the printed result.

solutions.latex:
Write $A$ with negative powers of $r$ so that it can be differentiated.
$$A=\pi r^2+2Vr^{-1}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r-2Vr^{-2}-\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r &= \dfrac{2V}{r^2}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r^2} \\ 2\pi^2r^3 &= 2\pi V+4V \quad(\text{multiplying through by } \pi r^2) \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{2\pi V+4V}{2\pi^2} \\ &= \dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative, for $r>0$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi+4Vr^{-3}+\dfrac{8V}{\pi}r^{-3}>0$$
The graph of $A$ is concave up for all $r>0$, so this stationary point is a minimum. It is the only stationary point for $r>0$, so it is the absolute minimum, and the amount of sheet metal is minimised when $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(2+\pi)}{\pi^2}}$.
criteria: Finds the value of $r$ at the stationary point, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Checked: derivatives and r^3 = V(pi+2)/pi^2.

solutions.latex:
With $V=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \\ &\approx 1.7335\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
From $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{2\times10}{\pi r^2} \\ &\approx 2.118\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{515_q26_s1}

The bearings of $A$ and $B$ from $M$ are $045^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, so
$$\angle AMB=120^\circ-45^\circ=75^\circ$$
Let $MB=x$. Using the area formula $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in triangle $AMB$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,432 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times100\times x\times\sin75^\circ \\ x &= \dfrac{2\times10\,432}{100\sin75^\circ} \\ &\approx 216\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle AMB=75^\circ$ and substitutes into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. \exfigure{515_q26_s1} kept (it was at the end of the source). Checked: x = 215.99999 m, i.e. 216 m.

solutions.latex:
The mast is vertical, so triangles $AMT$ and $BMT$ are right-angled at $M$. Let $MT=h$ and use Pythagoras' theorem with $MA=100$ and $MB=216$:
$$TA=\sqrt{h^2+100^2} \quad\text{and}\quad TB=\sqrt{h^2+216^2}$$
The total length of the wires is $380$ m.
$$\sqrt{h^2+100^2}+\sqrt{h^2+216^2}=380$$
Isolate one root and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} h^2+100^2+2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)}+h^2+216^2 &= 380^2 \\ 2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 380^2-216^2-100^2-2h^2 \\ &= 87\,744-2h^2 \\ \sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 43\,872-h^2 \end{aligned}$$
Square both sides again and let $u=h^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (u+100^2)(u+216^2) &= (43\,872-u)^2 \\ u^2+100^2u+216^2u+100^2\times216^2 &= 43\,872^2-87\,744u+u^2 \\ 100^2u+216^2u+87\,744u &= 43\,872^2-100^2\times216^2 \\ 144\,400u &= 1\,458\,192\,384 \\ u &\approx 10\,098.285 \\ h &= \sqrt{10\,098.285} \\ &\approx 100.49\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms an equation in $h$ alone and reduces it to $u=h^2$ (or equivalent), or equivalent merit
Finds $TA$ and $TB$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the function $f(x)=(x+1)^2$.

The following transformations were applied to the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the order shown below.

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal translation to the right by 4 units
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Vertical translation down by 3 units
\item Reflection in the $x$-axis
\end{itemize}

Find the equation of the transformed function and sketch its graph, showing the location of the vertex and the axis intercepts.

dif.r: Five ordered transformations including dilations, then sketch with intercepts

figures.cap: solution sketch: downward parabola with vertex (4,3) and x-intercepts 0 and 8

solutions.latex:
Apply each transformation to $y=(x+1)^2$ in turn.

Translate right by 4 (replace $x$ with $x-4$):
$$y=(x-4+1)^2=(x-3)^2$$
Horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{4}{3}$ (replace $x$ with $\dfrac{3x}{4}$):
$$y=\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2$$
Vertical dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (multiply $y$ by $\dfrac{1}{3}$):
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2$$
Translate down by 3:
$$y=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2-3$$
Reflect in the $x$-axis (replace $y$ with $-y$):
$$y=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3$$
For the intercepts, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2 &= 3 \\ (x-4)^2 &= 16 \\ x-4 &= \pm4 \\ x &= 0 \text{ or } x=8 \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(0,0)$ and $(8,0)$, so the $y$-intercept (at $x=0$) is also $(0,0)$.

As a check, $y=kx(x-8)$ through the vertex $(4,3)$ gives $3=-16k$, so $k=-\dfrac{3}{16}$ and $y=-\dfrac{3}{16}x(x-8)$.

\exfigure{515_q27_s1}
criteria: Finds the correct equation and its intercepts, or equivalent merit

Applies at least two transformations correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$
questions.review_note: scan path: review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the times when the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Differentiate log for velocity, solve resulting quadratic

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first second.

Leave your answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)-c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.

dif.r: Must check direction before distance, then log-law simplification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

dif.r: Quotient rule for acceleration, solve, justify maximum, evaluate surd

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand diagram of the motion on a line: at rest at t=1 and t=3, particle path between

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of position, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln\left(t^2+3\right)=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}$.
$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}-1=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4t}{t^2+3} &= 1 \\ 4t &= t^2+3 \\ t^2-4t+3 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=1 \text{ or } t=3\ \text{seconds}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the velocity to see whether the particle changes direction in the first second.
$$v=\dfrac{4t-t^2-3}{t^2+3}=-\dfrac{(t-1)(t-3)}{t^2+3}$$
For $0\le t<1$ both $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are negative, so $v<0$. The particle moves in one direction only (it is at rest at $t=1$), so the distance is $x(0)-x(1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 2\ln3 \\ x(1) &= 2\ln4-1=4\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 2\ln3-(4\ln2-1) \\ &= \ln3^2-\ln2^4+1 \\ &= \ln9-\ln16+1 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{9}{16}+1 \\ &\approx 0.42\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The 'v < 0 on [0,1], no change of direction' step was missing in the handwriting and added by us (checked: v = -(t-1)(t-3)/(t^2+3)). The answer ln(9/16) + 1 fits the requested form ln(a/b) - c with a = 9, b = 16, c = -1. Checked: 0.4246.

solutions.latex:
The acceleration is the derivative of velocity, using the quotient rule on $v=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$.
$$a=\dfrac{4(t^2+3)-4t\times2t}{(t^2+3)^2}=\dfrac{12-4t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}$$
Maximum velocity occurs where $a=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12-4t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2 &= 3 \\ t &= \sqrt{3} \quad(t\ge0) \end{aligned}$$
Test: $a>0$ for $0\le t<\sqrt{3}$ and $a<0$ for $t>\sqrt{3}$, so $v$ increases then decreases and has a maximum at $t=\sqrt{3}$ (between the rest times $t=1$ and $t=3$).
$$\begin{aligned} v_{\max} &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3+3}-1 \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1 \\ &\approx 0.1547\ \text{m/s} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{515_q28_s1}
criteria: Finds $t=\sqrt{3}$ and justifies a maximum, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=3x\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3+1$.
questions.review_note: scan path: review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By showing that $f'(x)=3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x)$, find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Product and chain rule with factorising; includes horizontal inflection

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why the graph of $y=f(x)$ must cross the $x$-axis at least once between $x=5$ and $x=6$.

dif.r: Sign change and continuity argument, short justification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the interval $[0,6]$, showing the stationary points, the $y$-intercept and the approximate location of the $x$-intercept.

dif.r: Sketch from earlier stationary points and endpoint values

figures.cap: solution sketch: y=f(x) on [0,6]: (0,1), local max (1,2 17/64), horizontal inflexion (4,1), x-intercept between 5 and 6, end point (6,-1 1/4)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x & v &= \left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3 \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -\dfrac{3}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3-\dfrac{9x}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2\left[\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)-\dfrac{3x}{4}\right] \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $f'(x)=0$, so $x=4$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 3\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3+1 = 2\dfrac{17}{64} \\ f(4) &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The stationary points are $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ and $(4,1)$.

Nature of $x=1$: the factor $(1-x)$ decides the sign of $f'$ near $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(0) &= 3>0 \\ f'(2) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ is a local maximum.

Nature of $x=4$: the squared factor does not change sign.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(3) &= -\dfrac{3}{8}<0 \\ f'(5) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ is negative on both sides of $x=4$, so $(4,1)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
criteria: Shows $f'(x)=3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x)$ and finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Evaluate $f$ at the two ends.
$$\begin{aligned} f(5) &= 15\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3+1=\dfrac{49}{64}>0 \\ f(6) &= 18\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3+1=-\dfrac{5}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f$ is continuous and changes sign between $x=5$ and $x=6$, so there is at least one $x$-intercept in that interval (Intermediate Value Theorem).

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row was written by us. Checked: f(5) = 49/64, f(6) = -5/4.

The end points come from $f(0)$ and $f(6)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= 1 \\ f(6) &= -1\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercept lies between $x=5$ and $x=6$, from part (b).

questions.stem:
Aida has \$500 000 in an investment account earning interest at a rate of 3% per annum compounded annually.

At the end of the first year, Aida withdraws \$25 000 for expenses.

Each subsequent year, the amount that Aida withdraws increases by 5% due to rising expenses.

Let $A_n$ be the balance of Aida’s investment account at the end of the $n$th year.
questions.review_note: scan path: review

dif.r: Recurrence with growing withdrawals expanded over three years

parts.label: b
parts.latex: For how many complete years will Aida be able to withdraw money from this account in order to meet her expenses?

dif.r: Generalise, see geometric series with ratio 1.05/1.03, solve and interpret

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern of part (a), after $n$ years
$$A_n=500\,000(1.03)^n-25\,000\left[(1.05)^{n-1}+(1.05)^{n-2}(1.03)+\cdots+(1.03)^{n-1}\right]$$
The money runs out when $A_n=0$.
$$25\,000\left[(1.05)^{n-1}+(1.05)^{n-2}(1.03)+\cdots+(1.03)^{n-1}\right]=500\,000(1.03)^n$$
Divide both sides by $25\,000(1.03)^{n-1}$:
$$\left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^{n-1}+\cdots+\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}+1=20(1.03)=20.6$$
The left side is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}$ and $n$ terms, so
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1}{\frac{1.05}{1.03}-1} &= 20.6 \\ \left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1 &= 0.4 \\ \left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n &= 1.4 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln1.4}{\ln\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)} \\ &\approx 17.496 \end{aligned}$$
The balance is still positive after 17 withdrawals and cannot cover the 18th, so Aida can withdraw money for 17 complete years.
criteria: Forms the geometric series equation and solves for $n$, or equivalent merit
Writes $A_n=0$ with the general expression for $A_n$, or equivalent merit

The conclusion sentence was added by us; checked: A_n > 0 exactly when (1.05/1.03)^n < 1.4, true for n = 17 and false for n = 18. Source wrote 'withdraw money 17 times'.

questions.stem:
The time taken, $t$ minutes, for a machine to produce car parts can be modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function given by

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}k(t-1)^2, & 1\le t\le2\\[6pt] k\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right), & 2<t\le4\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
questions.review_note: scan path: review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

dif.r: Integrate a piecewise pdf, set total area equal to one

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Let $F(t)$ be the cumulative distribution function of $f(t)$, where $F(2.16)=0.3652$.

Find the least amount of time taken to produce 88% of the parts.

dif.r: Locate percentile's piece, solve quadratic, reject root; ignore distractor

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total area under the density function is 1.
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^2(t-1)^2\,dt+k\int_2^4\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(t-1)^3}{3}\right]_1^2+k\left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{1}{3}-0\right]+k\left[(8-4)-(4-1)\right] &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{3}k+k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4}{3}k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes and integrates both pieces of $f(t)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style.

solutions.latex:
The first piece gives the probability up to $t=2$.
$$F(2)=\dfrac{1}{3}k=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25$$
Since $0.25<0.88$, the required time lies in the second piece, and we still need $0.88-0.25=0.63$. Call the time $x$.
$$\dfrac{3}{4}\displaystyle\int_2^x\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=0.63$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^x &= 0.84 \\ \left(2x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-(4-1) &= 0.84 \\ 0 &= \dfrac{1}{4}x^2-2x+3.84 \\ x^2-8x &= -15.36 \\ (x-4)^2 &= 0.64 \\ x-4 &= \pm0.8 \\ x &= 3.2 \text{ or } 4.8 \end{aligned}$$
$x=4.8$ is outside the domain $2<t\le4$, so $x=3.2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Time}=3.2\ \text{minutes}\ (3\text{ min }12\text{ s})$$
criteria: Sets up and solves the equation for $x$ using the second piece, or equivalent merit
Finds $F(2)=0.25$ or sets up $\dfrac{3}{4}\displaystyle\int_2^x\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=0.63$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The given F(2.16) = 0.3652 is not needed in this method (checked: 0.25 + 0.75 x 0.1536 = 0.3652). Checked: F(3.2) = 0.25 + 0.75(0.84) = 0.88.

parts.latex:
A heater converts electrical power, measured in watts, into heat in such a way that the heat produced is given by the function $h(x)=\left(f(x)\right)^2$.

The heater is plugged into a faulty socket which outputs $x=g(t)$ watts at time $t$ seconds.

The power output at time $t=1$ is 3 watts and is increasing at a rate of 4 watts per second.

By considering $h'(x)$ and using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dt}f\left(g(t)\right)=f'\left(g(t)\right)\times g'(t)$, find the rate of change of the heat produced at time $t=1$, given that $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

dif.r: Chain rule through squared composite, values read from context

solutions.latex:
Given $h(x)=\left[f(x)\right]^2$, differentiate with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dh}{dx}=2f(x)f'(x)$$
The power output is $x=g(t)$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=g'(t)$.

Given: $g(1)=3$ (so $x=3$ when $t=1$), $g'(1)=4$, $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dh}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(x)f'(x)\,g'(t) \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$, $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(3)f'(3)g'(1) \\ &= 2\times5\times2\times4 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The answer is left as the bare number 80 because the question gives no units for h. The question's hint 'f'(x) = f'(g(t)) x g'(t)' is the derivative of f(g(t)), not f'(x); left as printed (question not changed).

dif.r: Single step: square root of variance gives standard deviation.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \\ &= \sqrt{0.42} \\ &= 0.6480\dots \\ &\approx 0.65 \text{ (2 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Find an expression for the $n$th term of the arithmetic sequence $100, 92, 84, \dots$?

dif.r: Direct substitution into arithmetic nth term formula.

solutions.latex:
The sequence is arithmetic with first term and common difference
$$a=100,\quad d=-8$$
Using the formula for the $n$th term:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 100+(n-1)(-8) \\ &= 108-8n \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_n = 108-8n$$

parts.latex: Find the limiting sum of the geometric series $1-\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{27}+\dots$.

dif.r: Identify a and r, substitute into limiting sum formula.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with
$$a=1,\quad r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty = \dfrac{3}{4}$$

parts.latex:
Two identical coins with the same bias are tossed together, and the outcome is recorded. After a large number of trials, it is observed that the probability that both coins land showing tails is $0.49$.

What is the probability that both coins land showing heads?

dif.r: Product rule used in reverse via square root, then complement.

solutions.latex:
Both coins have the same bias, so
$$P(T)\times P(T)=0.49$$
$$P(T)=\sqrt{0.49}=0.7$$
Hence
$$P(H)=1-0.7=0.3$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(HH) &= 0.3\times 0.3 \\ &= 0.09 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(HH)=0.09$$

dif.r: Routine: sum probabilities to 1, then standard E(X) and Var(X).

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$0.1+0.3+n+0.2=1$$
so $n=0.4$.

The expected value is
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 4(0.1)+5(0.3)+6(0.4)+7(0.2) \\ &= 5.7 \end{aligned}$$
The variance is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 4^2(0.1)+5^2(0.3)+6^2(0.4)+7^2(0.2)-5.7^2 \\ &= 33.3-32.49 \\ &= 0.81 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E(X)=5.7,\quad \text{Var}(X)=0.81$$
criteria: Calculates the expected value and finds $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Louisa is training for the London marathon. She runs 10 km on the first day and on each day after that she runs $10\%$ further than the previous day.

On what day of training will she run further than 25 km for the first time?

dif.r: Recognise geometric growth, test terms or solve exponential inequality.

solutions.latex:
The distances form a geometric sequence with
$$a=10,\quad r=1.1,\quad T_n=ar^{n-1}$$
Test the 10th and 11th days:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= 10(1.1)^9 = 23.57\dots < 25 \\ T_{11} &= 10(1.1)^{10} = 25.93\dots > 25 \end{aligned}$$
So she first runs further than 25 km on day 11, which is option C.

Alternatively, solve $10(1.1)^{n-1}>25$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1.1^{n-1} &> 2.5 \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{\log 2.5}{\log 1.1} = 9.61\dots \\ n &> 10.61\dots \end{aligned}$$
so the 11th day.

questions.stem: A standard six-sided die is marked with the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 6$. A game is played by rolling the die until a 6 appears on the uppermost face. At this point the game ends.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Using a tree diagram, or otherwise, explain why the probability of the game ending before the fourth roll is:

$$\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2\times\dfrac{1}{6}$$

dif.r: Explain tree-diagram paths for ending on rolls one to three.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability of the game ending before the $n$th roll is more than $90\%$?

dif.r: Sum geometric series with n-1 terms, log inequality, round up.

solutions.latex:
On each roll, $P(6)=\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $P(\text{not } 6)=\dfrac{5}{6}$.

In the tree diagram, at each roll the game ends with probability $\dfrac{1}{6}$ or continues with probability $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

The game ends before the 4th roll if it ends on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd roll:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{ends before 4th roll}) &= \dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2\times\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Draws tree diagram or sets up correct reasoning, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Alternate solution (add the probabilities of winning on rolls 1, 2, 3) folded into the working. A tree diagram is not drawn.

solutions.latex:
The game ends before the $n$th roll if it ends on one of rolls $1$ to $n-1$:
$$P(\text{ends before } n\text{th roll})=\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^0\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^1\dfrac{1}{6}+\dots+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-2}\dfrac{1}{6}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{6}$, $r=\dfrac{5}{6}$ and $n-1$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{n-1} &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{6}\left(1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1}\right)}{1-\frac{5}{6}} \\ &= 1-\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} \end{aligned}$$
We need this to exceed $0.9$. Solve the equality first:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.9 &= 1-\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} \\ \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} &= 0.1 \\ (n-1)\log\dfrac{5}{6} &= \log 0.1 \\ n-1 &= \dfrac{\log 0.1}{\log\frac{5}{6}} = 12.629\dots \\ n &= 13.629\dots \end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number, so we round up.
$$\therefore\ \text{the smallest value of } n \text{ is } 14$$
criteria: Correct simplified equation to solve, or equivalent merit
Establishes the series for the probability of ending before the $n$th roll

There are 8 chocolates in a box. Three have peppermint centres (P) and five have caramel centres (C).

Seiko randomly chooses a chocolate from the box and eats it. Mark then randomly chooses and eats one of the remaining chocolates.

A partially completed probability tree is shown.

What is the probability that \textbf{at least one} chocolate with a caramel centre was eaten?

figures.cap: partially completed probability tree: first pick P (3/8) or C (5/8), second pick P or C

$$\begin{aligned} 1-P(PP) &= 1-\dfrac{3}{8}\times\dfrac{2}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{28} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Elizabeth is a teacher. At the school where she works, $80\%$ of the teachers own a car, $15\%$ of the teachers own a motorbike and $8\%$ of the teachers do not own a car or a motorbike. What is the probability that Elizabeth owns a car given that she owns a motorbike?

dif.r: Find intersection via addition rule, then conditional probability.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Let $C$ = owns a car and $M$ = owns a motorbike. The proportion owning neither is $0.08$, so
$$P(C\cup M)=1-0.08=0.92$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} P(C\cap M) &= P(C)+P(M)-P(C\cup M) \\ &= 0.80+0.15-0.92 \\ &= 0.03 \end{aligned}$$
The two-way table of proportions is

\extable{Ts3417_1}

$$\begin{aligned} P(C\mid M) &= \dfrac{P(C\cap M)}{P(M)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.03}{0.15} \\ &= 0.2 = 20\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(C\mid M)=20\%$$
criteria: Sets up two-way table or Venn diagram with the information, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In a reducing balance loan, an amount $\$P$ is borrowed for a period of $n$ months at an interest rate of $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month a repayment of $\$M$ is made. After the $n$th repayment has been made the amount owing, $\$A_n$ is given by:

$$A_n = P(1.004)^n - M\left(1+(1.004)^1+(1.004)^2+\dots+(1.004)^{n-1}\right)$$

(Do NOT prove this.)

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Celeste borrows \$500 000 in a reducing balance loan as described. The loan is to be repaid in 240 monthly repayments.

Show that $M = \$3244.79$, when rounded to the nearest cent.

dif.r: Set A_n=0, sum geometric series, rearrange for M.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
After 150 repayments of \$3244.79 have been made, the interest rate changes to $0.5\%$ per month.

At this stage the amount owing to the nearest dollar is \$244 837. (Do NOT prove this.)

Celeste increases her monthly repayments to \$3500.

For how many months will Celeste need to make full monthly repayments of \$3500?

dif.r: Rebuild loan formula with new rate, solve with logs, interpret full payments.

criteria: Sums the geometric series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The new rate is $0.5\%$ per month, so the monthly factor is $1.005$. Starting from $\$244\,837$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 244\,837\times 1.005-3500 \\ A_2 &= 244\,837\times 1.005^2-3500\times 1.005-3500 \end{aligned}$$
Continuing, and summing the geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n-3500\left(1+1.005+\dots+1.005^{n-1}\right) \\ &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n-\dfrac{3500(1.005^n-1)}{0.005} \end{aligned}$$
Set $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3500(1.005^n-1) &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n\times 0.005 \\ 3500\times 1.005^n-3500 &= 1224.185\times 1.005^n \\ 2275.815\times 1.005^n &= 3500 \\ 1.005^n &= \dfrac{3500}{2275.815} \\ n &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{3500}{2275.815}\right)}{\log 1.005} = 86.299\dots \end{aligned}$$
The loan is not cleared after 86 repayments, so the last payment is smaller.
$$\therefore\ \text{86 full payments of } \$3500 \text{ are made}$$
criteria: Sets up correct equation to solve for $n$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Translate independence into equation from Venn counts and solve.

figures.cap: Venn diagram: A only 4, intersection x, B only 9, outside 3

solutions.latex:
Since $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A)=P(A\mid B)$.

From the Venn diagram: $|A\cap B|=x$, $|B|=x+9$, $|A|=x+4$, $|S|=x+16$.
$$\dfrac{x+4}{x+16}=\dfrac{x}{x+9}$$
$$\begin{aligned} (x+4)(x+9) &= x(x+16) \\ x^2+13x+36 &= x^2+16x \\ 36 &= 3x \\ x &= 12 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: If $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{5}{6}$, find $P(A\cap B)$

dif.r: Direct use of addition rule with fractions.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Using the addition rule:
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{5}-\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{4}{15}$$

parts.latex:
A table of future value interest factors for an annuity of \$1 is shown.

\exfigure{1585_q4c_1}

Adelaide deposits \$2000 into a savings account at the end of each quarter for 5 years. The interest rate for these 5 years is $8\%$ per annum compounded quarterly. After the final deposit in the 5th year, Adelaide stops making deposits but leaves the money in the savings account. The money in her savings account then earns interest at $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually for a further 3 years.

Find the amount of money in Adelaide's savings account at the end of the 8 years.
parts.note: Annuity future value found from an interest-factor table (removed from 2024 Advanced; now Standard).

dif.r: Table lookup for annuity factor then compound interest; two stages.

figures.cap: table of future value interest factors for an annuity of $1 (N = 10, 20, 30, 40; r = 0.002 to 0.240)

solutions.latex:
First stage: $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly is $2\%$ per quarter, so $r=0.02$, and 5 years is $N=20$ quarters.

From the table ($N=20$, $r=0.02$) the factor is $24.29737$:
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 2000\times 24.29737 \\ &= \$48\,594.74 \end{aligned}$$
Second stage: this amount earns $5\%$ p.a. compounded annually for 3 years.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= PV(1+r)^n \\ &= 48\,594.74(1+0.05)^3 \\ &= 56\,254.485\dots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the savings account holds } \$56\,254.49$$
criteria: Calculates the value of the annuity, or equivalent merit
Correctly identifies the value from the table to use

questions.std: Standard, Year 12: Investment, loans and annuities (annuity table lookup) (MST-12-S2-03)

dif.r: Identical to HSC anchor: geometric sum condition plus clever E(X) pairing.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$r+r^2+r^3+\dots+r^{n-1}+r^n=1$$
This is a geometric series with $a=r$, ratio $r$ and $n$ terms:
$$S_n=\dfrac{r(r^n-1)}{r-1}=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} r^{n+1}-r &= r-1 \\ r^{n+1} &= 2r-1 \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
The expected value pairs each value with its probability:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum xP(X=x) \\ &= r\cdot r^n+r^2\cdot r^{n-1}+r^3\cdot r^{n-2}+\dots+r^n\cdot r \\ &= r^{n+1}+r^{n+1}+\dots+r^{n+1} \\ &= nr^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
Using (1):
$$E(X)=n(2r-1)$$
as required.
criteria: Uses the sum of a geometric series to establish $r^{n+1}=2r-1$, or determines $E(X)=nr^{n+1}$, or equivalent merit
Sets up the series equal to 1

parts.latex: Select which graph best represents $y=\sqrt{4-x}$. Circle your correct alternative.

dif.r: Recognise reflected and translated square-root graph from domain and endpoint

figures.cap: option A: graph of square-root curve starting at x=4 going right
option B: graph of square-root curve ending at x=4 going left
option C: graph of square-root curve starting at x=-4 going right
option D: graph of square-root curve ending at x=-4 going left

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=\sqrt{4-x}$ exists only for $x\le 4$, since $4-x\ge 0$.

Its endpoint is $(4,0)$ and $y\ge 0$.

Therefore the graph is the one in option B.

parts.latex: Calculate the area under $y=|2x-4|$ bounded by the $x$–axis over the domain $[0,6]$.

dif.r: Split absolute value at vertex; two triangle areas or integrals

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=|2x-4|$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=2$, so split the area at $x=2$.

For $0\le x\le 2$, $|2x-4|=4-2x$. For $2\le x\le 6$, $|2x-4|=2x-4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^2 (4-2x)\,dx+\int_2^6 (2x-4)\,dx \\ &= \Big[4x-x^2\Big]_0^2+\Big[x^2-4x\Big]_2^6 \\ &= 4+12-(-4) \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, from the graph the area is two triangles:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 8 \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Split the integral at $x=0$ and $x=1$.

$$\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx=\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx$$

Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The graph of the function $f(x)=8x^2$ is translated $b$ units to the left, then dilated horizontally by a scale factor of $a$ with $a>0$ and then translated $c$ units up. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=2x^2+4x+21$.

Find possible values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: Compose three transformations, expand, equate coefficients for three unknowns

solutions.latex:
Translating $b$ units left gives $8(x+b)^2$.

Dilating horizontally by factor $a$ replaces $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{a}$, giving $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2$.

Translating $c$ units up gives $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c$.

Equate to $g(x)$ and expand:

$$8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c\equiv 2x^2+4x+21$$

$$\dfrac{8}{a^2}x^2+\dfrac{16b}{a}x+(8b^2+c)\equiv 2x^2+4x+21$$

Equating coefficients of $x^2$:

$$\dfrac{8}{a^2}=2$$

so $a=2$, since $a>0$.

Equating coefficients of $x$:

$$\dfrac{16b}{a}=4$$

so $b=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Equating constants: $8b^2+c=21$, so $c=19$.

$$\therefore\ a=2,\ b=\dfrac{1}{2},\ c=19$$

The alternative working with a translation $b$ to the right gives $a=2$, $b=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, $c=19$.
criteria: Makes progress towards the transformed equation or equates coefficients, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^5 \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx$.

dif.r: Standard reverse chain rule definite integral of linear power

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5 (3x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{(3x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{3\cdot\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^5 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{3x+1}\right]_0^5 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\sqrt{16}-\sqrt{1}\right) \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule with $y=(4-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$:

From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{4-x^2}=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx &= -2\int\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx \\ &= -2\sqrt{4-x^2}+C \end{aligned}$$

For $y=4-2\cos 2x$ the amplitude is $2$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

parts.latex: Consider the curve $y=2x^3-6x^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with second derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any points of inflection. Make sure you justify your answer(s).

dif.r: Solve second derivative zero and check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve showing the stationary points and the point of inflection.

dif.r: Sketch cubic from found features plus easy intercepts

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=2x^3-6x^2 with stationary points and inflection

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-12x=6x(x-2)=0$$

So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=2$, $y=2(8)-6(4)=-8$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(2,-8)$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-12$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=0:\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= -12<0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ \text{At } x=2:\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum turning point} \end{aligned}$$

A table of values of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of each point is an equivalent justification.

$$\therefore\ (0,0)\text{ is a maximum and }(2,-8)\text{ is a minimum}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points and the second derivative, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and a change in concavity.

$$12x-12=0$$

So $x=1$, and $y=2-6=-4$.

Test the concavity either side of $x=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x<1 &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>1 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at $x=1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,-4)\text{ is a point of inflection}$$
criteria: Finds the point of inflection without justification, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with five subintervals to find the approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_1^6 \dfrac{2}{x}\,dx$.

dif.r: Direct trapezoidal rule application with simple function values

solutions.latex:
With five subintervals on $[1,6]$, the width is $h=\dfrac{6-1}{5}=1$, so the $x$ values are $1,2,3,4,5,6$.

For $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x}$ the function values are $2,\ 1,\ \dfrac{2}{3},\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{2}{5},\ \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left[f_0+f_n+2(f_1+\dots+f_{n-1})\right]$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^6\dfrac{2}{x}\,dx &\approx \dfrac{6-1}{2\times 5}\left[\left(2+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+2\left(1+\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{7}{3}+\dfrac{77}{15}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{56}{15} \\ &\approx 3.73 \end{aligned}$$

Any valid rounding is accepted.
criteria: Correct trapezoidal set-up, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A pipe costs \$4000/km when laid on land and \$5000/km when laid under the ocean.

In the diagram below a pipeline needs to be laid from $A$ along a coast to $B$ on an island. The pipe is to be laid in straight lines from $A$ on land along the coast until $C$ and then under the ocean to $B$.

Let $x=CD$.

\exfigure{1597_q5b_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write an expression for the total price (\$$P$) of laying the cable from $A$ to $B$ via $C$ in terms of $x$.

dif.r: Build cost model from diagram using Pythagoras

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the length for $x$ that will minimise the total price (\$$P$) of laying the whole pipe from $A$ to $B$ via $C$.

dif.r: Optimise surd cost function; solve radical equation, justify minimum and endpoints

figures.cap: coast line D to A of 10 km, island point B 6 km from D, point C on coast with CD = x

solutions.latex:
The land section is $AC=10-x$ km at \$4000/km, and the ocean section $CB$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides $6$ and $x$, so $CB=\sqrt{36+x^2}$ km at \$5000/km (Pythagoras' theorem).

$$P=4000(10-x)+5000\sqrt{36+x^2}$$

meta.format_note: Lengths 10 and 6 read from the source expression (figure not visible here).

solutions.latex:
$P$ is minimised where $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dx} &= -4000+5000\times\dfrac{1}{2}(36+x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x \\ &= \dfrac{5000x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}}-4000 \end{aligned}$$

Set this to zero:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}} &= 4 \\ 25x^2 &= 16(36+x^2) \\ 9x^2 &= 576 \\ x^2 &= 64 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=\pm 8$. Since $0\le x\le 10$, $x=8$ only.

First derivative test:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=7:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx -204<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \text{At } x=9:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx 160>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$

So a relative minimum occurs at $x=8$.

Check against the end points:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0) &= \$70\,000 \\ P(10) &\approx \$58\,310 \\ P(8) &= \$58\,000 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=8$ gives the absolute minimum on $[0,10]$.

Alternatively, by the second derivative test:

$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\dfrac{180\,000}{(36+x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$$

which equals $180>0$ at $x=8$.

$$\therefore\ CD=8 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$ to find $x=8$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates $P$ and sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit
