questions.stem:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution to this equation.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential and substitute back to verify the given equation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If $68$g remains after a period of $2$ years, find $k$ correct to two significant figures.

dif.r: Substitute data and solve exponential equation using logarithms for k.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Find the mass of the substance that remains after $6$ years.

Give your answer to one decimal place.

dif.r: Single substitution into the exponential model.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: At what rate is the substance decaying after $6$ years ?

dif.r: Substitute into given rate equation dM/dt = -kM.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $M = 75e^{-kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -k\cdot 75e^{-kt}$$
But $75e^{-kt} = M$, so
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$$
Hence $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution.

Substitute $M=68$ and $t=2$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 68 &= 75e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{68}{75} &= e^{-2k} \\ -2k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ &\approx 0.049 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.049$$

Substitute $t=6$ and $k \approx 0.049$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 75e^{-6k} \\ &\approx 55.9 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx 55.9 \text{ g}$$

meta.format_note: 55.9 g follows from using the rounded $k=0.049$ from part (b).

solutions.latex:
The rate of decay is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, with $k \approx 0.049$ and $M \approx 55.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= -kM \\ &\approx -2.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the substance is decaying at approximately } 2.7 \text{ g/year}$$

questions.stem: The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.

dif.r: Substitute t = 0 into velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an expression for the displacement of the particle, $x$, in terms of $t$.

dif.r: Integrate trig velocity and use initial condition for constant.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find when the particle first comes to rest.

dif.r: Set velocity zero and solve simple trig equation for first positive root.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $7$ seconds.

dif.r: Must recognise direction change and split distance into two stages.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=0$ into the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cdot 0\right) \\ &= \cos 0 \\ &= 1 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$, so $C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x} = 0$.
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) = 0$$
The first positive solution of $\cos\theta=0$ is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 3 \text{ seconds}$$

The particle is at rest at $t=3$ and then reverses, so find the distance in two stages.
$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x(7) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance travelled} &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} + \left(\dfrac{6}{\pi} + \dfrac{3}{\pi}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{15}{\pi} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the $x$ coordinate(s) of any stationary point(s) on the graph of $y = e^{2x}(1 - x)$. You do not need to determine the nature.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential, factorise and solve derivative equals zero.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=1-x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= -e^{2x} + 2e^{2x}(1-x) \\ &= -e^{2x} + 2e^{2x} - 2xe^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(1-2x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$. Since $e^{2x} \neq 0$, we need $1-2x=0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

dif.r: Rearrange and solve exponential equation using logarithms.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What will be the eventual temperature of the iron ?

dif.r: Recognise exponential term tends to zero; read off limiting value.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4(8)} \\ &\approx 106^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt} = k a^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -0.4\left(155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\right)\ln(1.2) \\ &= -62(1.2)^{-0.4t}\ln(1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -62(1.2)^{-3.2}\ln(1.2) \\ &\approx -6.3^\circ\text{C/min} \end{aligned}$$

Set $T=36$ and solve for $t$, taking logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned}36 &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ 16 &= 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ \dfrac{16}{155} &= 1.2^{-0.4t}\\ \ln\left(\dfrac{16}{155}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.2)\\ t &= \dfrac{-\ln\left(\frac{16}{155}\right)}{0.4\ln 1.2} \\ &\approx 31\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 31 \text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Obtains $\dfrac{16}{155} = 1.2^{-0.4t}$ or an expression for $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t \to \infty$, $(1.2)^{-0.4t} \to 0$, so $T \to 20$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the eventual temperature is } 20^\circ\text{C}$$

parts.latex: It is given that $\ln x = 2\ln y + 1$, where $x$ and $y > 0$. The correct expression for $x$ in terms of $y$ is,

dif.r: Combine log laws, writing 1 as ln e, to make x the subject.

solutions.latex:
Write $1$ as $\ln e$ and use the power and addition laws of logarithms.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x &= 2\ln y + 1 \\ &= \ln y^2 + \ln e \\ &= \ln(ey^2) \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x = ey^2$, which is option D.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos 2x\right) = \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x$.

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on cos 2x; given result to show.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx$.

dif.r: Reverse the derivative result, rearrange integrals, evaluate exact trig values.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x) &= x(-2\sin 2x) + \cos 2x(1)\\ &= -2x\sin 2x + \cos 2x\\ &= \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the result of part (a) over the interval, since integration reverses differentiation.
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(\cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x)\,dx = \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$
Rearranging,
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos 2x\,dx - \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} - \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} - 0\right)\\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{12}\\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3} - \pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses in the form $\displaystyle\int 2x\sin 2x\,dx = \int\cos 2x\,dx - [x\cos 2x]$, or equivalent merit
Integrates the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The height of the tide in a harbour can be modelled using the sine function.

The time, $t$ in hours, between high tide and low tide is 6 hours.

Which one of the following could be the function representing the height of the tide?

dif.r: Recognise high-to-low is half period, then n=2π/T

solutions.latex:
High tide to low tide is half a period, so the period is $T=12$.

Using $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\dfrac{2\pi}{T} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
So the function is $h=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)$.

dif.r: Signed area from geometric shapes including quarter circle

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): line, constant, quarter-circle-like decay; drawn to scale

solutions.latex:
The integral is the signed area: a triangle, a rectangle, a square, less a quarter circle of radius 2.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^8 f(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2+(2\times4)+2\times2-\dfrac{1}{4}\pi(2)^2 \\ &=2+8+4-\pi \\ &=14-\pi \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The product of the $1^{\text{st}}$ term and $2^{\text{nd}}$ term of a geometric sequence is 48 while the product of the $3^{\text{rd}}$ term and the $4^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence is 3888.

What is the product of the $4^{\text{th}}$ term and the $5^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence?

dif.r: Set up term products, divide equations, choose sign of r

solutions.latex:
Let the first term be $a$ and the common ratio $r$. The products give
$$\begin{aligned} a^2r&=48 &&(1)\\ a^2r^5&=3888 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$r^4=\dfrac{3888}{48}=81$$
So $r=3$, since $r>0$ as the products are positive.

Then $a^2=\dfrac{48}{3}=16$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_4\times T_5&=a^2r^7 \\ &=16\times3^7 \\ &=34\,992 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle moving along the $x$ axis at time $t$ is given by:

$$x=t^3+\ln\left(2t^3+1\right)\ \text{ for } t\ge 0$$

How many times is the particle stationary?

dif.r: Log chain rule, combine fractions, factorise, apply domain restriction

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3t^2+\dfrac{6t^2}{2t^3+1}$$
The particle is stationary when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2(2t^3+1)+6t^2&=0 \\ 3t^2(2t^3+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Then $t=0$ or $t=-\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{2}}$, and only $t=0$ is valid for $t\ge0$.

Hence there is one solution.

parts.latex:
$\triangle ABC$ is an isosceles triangle such that $AB=AC=8$ cm.

Given that the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $16$ cm$^2$, which one of the following gives the possible values of $\angle ABC$?

dif.r: Ambiguous sine case, then convert apex angle to base angles

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned} 16&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times8\times8\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So $\theta=30^\circ$ or $150^\circ$.

The triangle is isosceles, so $\angle ABC=\dfrac{180^\circ-\theta}{2}$:
$$\angle ABC=75^\circ \text{ or } 15^\circ$$

meta.format_note: Corrected the base-angle step; the answer is unchanged.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Source computed ∠ABC as θ/2 (giving 15° and 75°), which is not the base-angle formula; the base angles are (180°−θ)/2, giving 75° and 15°. The same pair of values results, so the answer is unchanged.

parts.latex:
It is given that $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{3}{5}$

What is the value of $P(\overline{B}\mid\overline{A})$?

dif.r: Needs complement of union for both complements, then conditional probability

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(\overline{B}\mid\overline{A})&=\dfrac{P(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B})}{P(\overline{A})} \\ &=\dfrac{1-P(A\cup B)}{1-P(A)} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\frac{3}{5}}{1-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{2}{5}}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\left(\tan^2 x+1\right)^2$?

dif.r: Chain rule on tan with Pythagorean identity simplification

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule and $\tan^2x+1=\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^2x+1\right)^2&=2\left(\tan^2x+1\right)\times2\tan x\sec^2x \\ &=2\sec^2x\times2\tan x\sec^2x \\ &=4\sec^4x\tan x \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Factorise difference of squares, analyse both cases, avoid double counting

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: graphs of y=ln x and y=x^2-1

solutions.latex:
Factorising the difference of squares:
$$[f(x)]^2-[g(x)]^2=[f(x)+g(x)][f(x)-g(x)]=0$$
$f(x)+g(x)=0$ only when $f(x)=g(x)=0$, which occurs at $x=1$.

$f(x)-g(x)=0$ means $f(x)=g(x)$, at the points of intersection. One of these is $x=1$, already counted, and there is one other point of intersection.

So there are 2 solutions.

dif.r: Standard log primitive of linear denominator with 1/2 factor

parts.latex: Calculate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{2\ln 2} e^{2x}\,dx$

dif.r: Routine exponential integral with log-limit simplification

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\ln2}^{2\ln2}e^{2x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{2x}\right]_{\ln2}^{2\ln2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{4\ln2}-e^{2\ln2}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{\ln16}-e^{\ln4}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}[16-4] \\ &=6 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
It is given that $f''(x)=6x$ and that $f(x)$ has a stationary point at $(-1,2)$.

Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate twice using stationary point for both constants

solutions.latex:
Integrating $f''(x)$:
$$f'(x)=\displaystyle\int6x\,dx=3x^2+C$$
The stationary point at $x=-1$ gives $f'(-1)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(-1)^2+C&=0 \\ C&=-3 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=3x^2-3$.

Integrating again:
$$f(x)=\displaystyle\int(3x^2-3)\,dx=x^3-3x+D$$
Using $f(-1)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=(-1)^3-3(-1)+D \\ D&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-3x$$
criteria: Correct $f'(x)$ and integrates it, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
It is given that $1+2x-3x^2\ge 0$ in the domain $[0,1]$.

Prove that $f(x)=1+2x-3x^2$ is a probability density function for $[0,1]$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial to show total probability is one

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, $f(x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$ (given) and $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1(1+2x-3x^2)\,dx&=\left[x+x^2-x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &=(1+1-1)-0 \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$ and the integral equals 1, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Integral evaluated to 1, or equivalent merit
Correct primitive, or states both conditions

parts.latex: A normally distributed variable, $X$, has a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 0.5. Use the empirical rule to find $P(0.5\le X\le 3)$.

dif.r: Z-scores then combine empirical rule halves

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Convert to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} X=0.5:\ z&=\dfrac{0.5-2}{0.5}=-3 \\ X=3:\ z&=\dfrac{3-2}{0.5}=2 \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0.5\le X\le3)&=P(-3\le Z\le2) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(0.95+0.997) \\ &=0.9735 \end{aligned}$$
That is, $97.35\%$.

parts.latex: Find the second derivative of $y=x\left(x+1\right)^3$, leaving your answer in fully factorised form.

dif.r: Product rule twice with factorisation

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(x+1)^3\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3(x+1)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=(x+1)^3\times1+3(x+1)^2\times x \\ &=(x+1)^2\left[(x+1)+3x\right] \\ &=(x+1)^2(4x+1) \end{aligned}$$
Applying the product rule again, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+1)^2 & v&=4x+1\\ u'&=2(x+1) & v'&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y''&=(4x+1)\times2(x+1)+(x+1)^2\times4 \\ &=2(x+1)\left[4x+1+2(x+1)\right] \\ &=2(x+1)(6x+3) \\ &=6(x+1)(2x+1) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $y''$, unfactorised or equivalent, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The circle $x^2+y^2-6x+8y-11=0$ is transformed by a horizontal translation to the left by 4 units and a vertical translation up 3 units.

What is the centre and radius of the new circle?

dif.r: Complete the square, then translate centre

solutions.latex:
Complete the square:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+9+y^2+8y+16&=11+9+16 \\ (x-3)^2+(y+4)^2&=36 \end{aligned}$$
So the centre is $(3,-4)$ and the radius is $6$.

After translating 4 units left and 3 units up, the centre is $(-1,-1)$ and the radius is unchanged.

$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (-1,-1),\ \text{radius } 6 \text{ units}$$
criteria: Correct original centre and radius, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_e x-x\right)=\log_e x$

dif.r: Single product rule derivative show-that

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int_1^e \log_e x\,dx$ as an exact value.

dif.r: Use given primitive, evaluate with log values

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $x\log_ex$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_ex-x\right)&=\log_ex\times1+x\times\dfrac{1}{x}-1 \\ &=\log_ex+1-1 \\ &=\log_ex \end{aligned}$$

By part (a), a primitive of $\log_ex$ is $x\log_ex-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^e\log_ex\,dx&=\left[x\log_ex-x\right]_1^e \\ &=(e\log_ee-e)-(1\log_e1-1) \\ &=(e-e)-(0-1) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A rainwater tank manufacturer wants to make a new storage tank that has a standard height, to reduce the obstruction of views. The manufacturer decides that it will be a 2 metre high rectangular prism with all faces made from sheet metal, including the top and bottom, and needs to hold 6000 litres of water,

Let the other dimensions be $x$ metres and $y$ metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1614_q13_1}

For cost reasons, the manufacturer wants to use the least amount of area of sheet metal possible.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that for the given capacity of the tank, $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$

dif.r: Volume equation with litres to cubic metres conversion

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, calculate the exact dimensions of the tank that uses the least amount of area of sheet metal as possible. Show all reasoning.

dif.r: Build surface area function, optimise, justify minimum

figures.cap: rectangular prism tank, 6000 L, height 2 m, sides x m and y m

solutions.latex:
Convert the capacity: $6000\text{ L}=6\text{ m}^3$.

The volume of the prism is length $\times$ width $\times$ height:
$$\begin{aligned} x\times y\times2&=6 \\ 2xy&=6 \\ y&=\dfrac{6}{2x} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{x} \end{aligned}$$

The surface area is the top and bottom plus four sides:
$$A=2(xy+2x+2y)=2xy+4x+4y$$
Substituting $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$:
$$A=4x+\dfrac{12}{x}+6$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=4-\dfrac{12}{x^2}$$
For a minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2&=12 \\ x^2&=3 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\sqrt{3}$, since $x>0$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{24}{x^3}>0 \text{ for all } x>0$$
So the curve is concave up and the area is a minimum at $x=\sqrt{3}$.

Then $y=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{dimensions } \sqrt{3}\text{ m}\times\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\times2\text{ m}$$

meta.marker_note: No penalty for not writing a dimension statement.

questions.stem:
There are three towns in a rural area. Town $B$ is 37 km from Town $A$ at a bearing of $040^\circ$T. Town $C$ is 45 km from Town $B$ at a bearing of $160^\circ$T.

\exfigure{1614_q13_2}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the size of $\angle ABC$.

dif.r: Angle from bearings using parallel north lines

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the distance from Town $A$ to Town $C$, correct to 1 decimal place.

dif.r: Find included angle from bearings, then routine cosine rule

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the bearing of Town $A$ from Town $C$.

dif.r: Find angle by cosine rule, then convert to reverse bearing

figures.cap: bearings diagram of towns A, B, C

solutions.latex: $$\angle ABC=40^\circ+20^\circ=60^\circ$$

meta.format_note: Working in source is brief; diagram not checked. Source check: Source gives 40°+20°=60°. With bearings 040° at B (from A) and 160° from B, the angle at B would be 180°−40°−(180°−160°)... check: ∠ABC = 40°+(180°−160°)=60° gives same answer, so source working is consistent but unexplained.

solutions.latex:
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $AB=37$, $BC=45$ and $\angle ABC=60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 37^2+45^2-2\times37\times45\times\cos60^\circ \\ &= 1729 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC &= \sqrt{1729} \\ &= 41.5812\ldots \\ &\approx 41.6 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The distance from $A$ to $C$ is $41.6$ km (no penalty for incorrect rounding).
criteria: Correct cosine rule substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram of the triangle not added.

solutions.latex:
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, find $\angle BAC$:
$$\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{37^2+1729-45^2}{2\times37\times\sqrt{1729}}$$
so $\angle BAC=70^\circ$ (nearest degree; no penalty for using $41.6$ km).

The bearing of $C$ from $A$ is $110^\circ$T.

The bearing of $A$ from $C$ is the reverse bearing:
$$110^\circ+180^\circ=290^\circ\text{T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } A \text{ from } C \text{ is } 290^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Correct $\angle BAC$ (or bearing of $A$ to $C$ identified), or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)=x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}$ is an odd function.

dif.r: Routine substitution of -x to verify odd function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{5}\left(x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}\right)dx$.

dif.r: Odd function over symmetric interval integrates to zero

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Replace $x$ by $-a$ in $f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-a) &= (-a)^3-5(-a)+\dfrac{-ae^{-(-a)^2}}{1+(-a)^4} \\ &= -a^3+5a-\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4} \\ &= -\left(a^3-5a+\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4}\right) \\ &= -f(a) \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f$ is an odd function.

Since $f$ is odd, the areas either side of the origin cancel.
$$\int_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,dx=0$$

questions.stem:
A quantity $Q$ of the radioactive isotope Carbon-14 decays according the equation of natural decay $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$ where $Q_0$ is the initial mass of Carbon-14, $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the time in years.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes to reduce to half its original mass. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $k$.

dif.r: Standard half-life substitution and logarithm to find k

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A fossilised leaf contains $9\%$ of its original amount of Carbon-14.

How old is the fossilised leaf? Give your answer correct to the nearest year.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for t using logarithms

solutions.latex:
After one half-life, $Q=\dfrac{Q_0}{2}$ when $t=5730$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Q_0}{2} &= Q_0e^{-5730k} \\ 0.5 &= e^{-5730k} \\ \ln0.5 &= -5730k \\ k &= -\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2}{5730} \end{aligned}$$
No penalty for writing $k=0.0001$ to 4 d.p.

The leaf has $9\%$ of its original amount, so $Q=0.09Q_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.09Q_0 &= Q_0e^{-kt} \\ 0.09 &= e^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Using $k=-\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}$, this is
$$0.09=e^{\frac{\ln0.5}{5730}t}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln0.09 &= \dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{5730\ln0.09}{\ln0.5} \\ &\approx 19\,906 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\ln\left(2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta\right)=0$ for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\ln X=0$ when $X=1$:
$$2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta=1$$
Using $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-\cos^2\theta)-\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ 2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ (2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature, and any points of inflection for $y=x^4-2x^3+1$, showing all reasoning.

dif.r: Quartic stationary points, horizontal inflexion, concavity testing

parts.label: b

dif.r: Sketch quartic using points already found

figures.cap: blank axes grid -5 to 5 for sketching
solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y = x^4 - 2x^3 + 1 with turning and inflexion points

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$y'=4x^3-6x^2,\qquad y''=12x^2-12x$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^3-6x^2 &= 0 \\ 2x^2(2x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

At $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$, $y''=9>0$, so the curve is concave up: a minimum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$.

At $x=0$, $y''=0$, so the test is inconclusive and this is a possible horizontal point of inflexion.

Possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:
$$12x(x-1)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''&=24>0 &&\text{at } x=-1 &&\text{concave up}\\ y''&=0 &&\text{at } x=0 &&\\ y''&=-3<0 &&\text{at } x=0.5 &&\text{concave down}\\ y''&=0 &&\text{at } x=1 &&\\ y''&=24>0 &&\text{at } x=2 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both $x=0$ and $x=1$.

Since $y'=0$ at $x=0$, there is a horizontal point of inflexion at $(0,1)$. There is also a point of inflexion at $(1,0)$.
criteria: Correct stationary points and nature, and possible inflexion $x$-values, or equivalent merit
Correct stationary $x$-values and correct test for the minimum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

The Moon has a lower gravity than Earth, and there is no atmosphere to cause air resistance, so a ball would bounce higher and for much longer on the Moon than on Earth.

solutions.latex:
Each ball falls 2 m, then each bounce goes up and down, so the distance is a limiting sum of a G.P. with the initial 2 m subtracted.

Moon: $a=2$, $r=0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Moon}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.95}-2 \\ &= 78 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Earth: $a=2$, $r=0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Earth}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.5}-2 \\ &= 6 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Difference} &= 78-6 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, a student who neglects the initial drop and finds $80-8=72$ m is awarded full marks (with correct working).
criteria: Correct Moon and Earth distances, or equivalent merit

The graph $y=\sin x$ only has one tangent in the domain $[\pi,2\pi]$ that passes through the origin as shown in the diagram below.

Let the point of contact of this tangent be $P(h,\sin h)$.

dif.r: General tangent through origin, rearrange to h = tan h

figures.cap: y=sin x with tangent through origin touching at P(h, sin h)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y=\sin x$:
$$y'=\cos x$$
At $x=h$ the gradient is $\cos h$.

The tangent at $P(h,\sin h)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\sin h &= \cos h\,(x-h) \\ y &= (\cos h)x-h\cos h+\sin h \end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through the origin $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -h\cos h+\sin h \\ h\cos h &= \sin h \\ h &= \dfrac{\sin h}{\cos h} \\ &= \tan h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=\tan h$$
criteria: Substitutes the origin into the tangent, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

Show that after seven months, the total amount Sergio owes is:

$$A_7=12500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1)$$

dif.r: Non-standard interest-free period before compounding recurrence begins

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the monthly repayment \$$R$ required to pay back the loan, correct to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: Generalise unusual recurrence, sum GP of 54 terms, solve for R

solutions.latex:
In the first six months no interest is charged, so each repayment reduces the balance by $R$:
$$A_1=12\,500-R,\quad A_2=12\,500-2R,\quad A_3=12\,500-3R$$
so $A_6=12\,500-6R$.

The monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{0.09}{12}=0.0075$.

In month 7, interest is added and then $R$ is paid:
$$\begin{aligned} A_7 &= A_6\times1.0075-R \\ &= (12\,500-6R)\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-6R\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source rubric was one-mark-per-step; rewritten top-down by us.

solutions.latex:
Continue the pattern, interest then repayment each month:
$$A_8=A_7\times1.0075-R=12\,500\times1.0075^2-R(6\times1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
$$A_9=12\,500\times1.0075^3-R(6\times1.0075^3+1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
Hence
$$A_n=12\,500\times1.0075^{n-6}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{n-6}+1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{n-7}\right)$$
The loan lasts $n=5\times12=60$ months:
$$A_{60}=12\,500\times1.0075^{54}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\left(1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{53}\right)\right)$$
The bracketed sum is a G.P. with $a=1$, $r=1.0075$ and $54$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{1.0075-1}$.

The loan is repaid, so $A_{60}=0$:
$$12\,500\times1.0075^{54}=R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{0.0075}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= \dfrac{12\,500\times1.0075^{54}}{6\times1.0075^{54}+\frac{1.0075^{54}-1}{0.0075}} \\ &\approx \$248.66 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R\approx\$249$$
criteria: Correct equation for $R$, or equivalent merit
Develops the series, or equivalent merit

The heights are $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=1.5$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{4}$ at $x=2$.

Lower rectangles:

Upper rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{5}{12}$$
The exact area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{dx}{2x} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln x\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(\ln2-\ln1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln2 \\ &= \ln\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt2<\dfrac{5}{12}$$

dif.r: Common denominator then two Pythagorean identities.

solutions.latex:
Use a common denominator, then $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta + 1 - \sin\theta}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= 2\sec^2\theta \\ &= 2\left(1 + \tan^2\theta\right) \\ &= 2 + 2\tan^2\theta\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which if the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,(2x+1)}{3-4x^2}\right)$?

dif.r: Log laws to expand, then three chain-rule log derivatives; sign care.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, expand the logarithm first.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,(2x+1)}{3-4x^2}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\ln x + \ln(2x+1) - \ln\left(3-4x^2\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2x} + \dfrac{2}{2x+1} + \dfrac{8x}{3-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: Which transformations listed are required to obtain the graph of $y = x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3$ from the graph of $y = 4x^2 + x$?

dif.r: Must recognise target as f(x/2)+3; horizontal dilation easily misread.

options.label: A
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of 2; vertical translation of 3 units upwards

options.label: B
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$; vertical translation of 3 units to downwards

options.label: C
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of 2; horizontal translation of 3 units in to the right

options.label: D
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$; horizontal translation of 3 units to the left

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x) = 4x^2 + x$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) + 3 &= 4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3 \\ &= x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3 \end{aligned}$$
The graph of $y = f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) + 3$ is obtained from $y = f(x)$ by a horizontal dilation of factor 2 and a vertical translation of 3 units upwards.

This is option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is equal to $\displaystyle\int_0^3 2\left|x-1\right|\,dx$?

dif.r: Integral of absolute value evaluated as two triangle areas.

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=2|x-1| with areas A1, A2

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=2|x-1|$ forms two triangles, $A_1$ for $0\le x\le1$ and $A_2$ for $1\le x\le3$.

\exfigure{833_q9_s1}
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^3 2|x-1|\,dx &= A_1 + A_2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 4 \\ &= 5\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by

$$P\left(X = 2^{-n}\right) = 0.1 \times 0.9^{n-1}, \text{ where } n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$$

What is the expected value of $X$?

dif.r: Infinite distribution; recognise expected value as geometric limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
$X$ takes the values $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, 2^{-3}, \ldots$ with probabilities $0.1,\ 0.1 \times 0.9,\ 0.1 \times 0.9^2, \ldots$

The expected value is a geometric series with first term $2^{-1}\times 0.1$ and common ratio $2^{-1}\times 0.9$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X) &= \left(2^{-1} \times 0.1\right) + \left(2^{-2} \times 0.1 \times 0.9\right) + \left(2^{-3} \times 0.1 \times 0.9^2\right) + \ldots \\ &= \dfrac{2^{-1} \times 0.1}{1 - 2^{-1} \times 0.9} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{11}\end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

questions.stem: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $f'(x)$.

dif.r: Routine quotient rule with simplification.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the equation of the normal to the graph of $y = f(x)$ at the point where $x = 2$, in general form.

dif.r: Normal gradient, point-gradient form with fractions, general form.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x^2-1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{x^2 - 1 - 2x^2}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f'(x) = \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the point and the gradient at $x=2$.
$$f(2) = \dfrac{2}{2^2 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$f'(2) = \dfrac{-(2)^2 - 1}{\left(2^2 - 1\right)^2} = -\dfrac{5}{9}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_{\text{normal}} = \dfrac{9}{5}$$
The equation of the normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y - \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{9}{5}(x - 2) \\ 15y - 10 &= 27x - 54 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore 27x - 15y - 44 = 0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let there be two events, $A$ and $B$, such that $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.55$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $P\left(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}\right)$.

dif.r: One step complement of union.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $P\left(A \mid \bar{B}\right)$.

dif.r: Fill Venn regions then apply conditional probability formula.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram

solutions.latex:
Neither $A$ nor $B$ occurs exactly when $A \cup B$ does not occur.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}\right) &= 1 - P(A \cup B) \\ &= 1 - 0.8 \\ &= 0.2 \end{aligned}$$

Draw a Venn diagram using the probabilities found.

\exfigure{833_q13_s1}

Using conditional probability,
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(A \mid \bar{B}\right) &= \dfrac{P\left(A \cap \bar{B}\right)}{P\left(\bar{B}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 + 0.2} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{9} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Existing figure kept

questions.stem:
The sum of the first $n$ terms in an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$$S_n = 3n^2 - 17n$$

where $n > 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the common difference is 6.

dif.r: Must use S1 and S2 to recover terms; unfamiliar to many.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the tenth term in the series.

dif.r: Direct substitution into arithmetic term formula.

solutions.latex:
The series is arithmetic, so $a = S_1$ and $T_2 = S_2 - S_1$.
$$S_1 = 3(1)^2 - 17(1) = -14$$
so $a=-14$.
$$S_2 = 3(2)^2 - 17(2) = -22$$
$$T_2 = -22 - (-14) = -8$$
The common difference is
$$\begin{aligned} d &= T_2 - T_1 \\ &= -8 - (-14) \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the first term of the arithmetic series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$ with $a=-14$ and $d=6$,
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= -14 + (10 - 1) \times 6 \\ &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the correct formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \sin x\,(1 - \cos^2 x)\,dx$.

dif.r: Expand, then reverse chain rule for sin x cos^2 x unprompted.

solutions.latex:
Expand the integrand, then integrate each term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int \sin x\left(1 - \cos^2 x\right)dx &= \int \left(\sin x - \sin x\cos^2 x\right)dx \\ &= -\cos x + \dfrac{1}{3}\cos^3 x + c\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Since the introduction of the internet, the number of emails sent has been modelled using the exponential equation

$$M = M_0 e^{kt}$$

where $M$ is the number of emails sent worldwide, in millions, and $t$ is the number of years after the year 1980.

Records show that $45\,000$ emails were sent in 1980 and 306 billion emails were sent in the year 2020.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $M_0$ and $k$, correct to three decimal places.

dif.r: Unit conversion to millions, then solve exponential for k with logs.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many emails, to the nearest million, are expected to be sent in the year 2025?

dif.r: Substitute t=45 into found model.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the rate at which the number of emails sent increased in the year 2000, correct to the nearest million per year.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model, substitute t=20, interpret units.

criteria: Finds the value of $M_0$ or $k$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added final decimal line $k\approx0.393$ (computed: ln 6,800,000 ≈ 15.73, /40 ≈ 0.393), since question asks three decimal places; source stopped at exact form

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t = 45$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 0.045e^{45 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln 6\,800\,000} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679.032 \text{ million} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679 \text{ million (to the nearest million)} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating $M = M_0e^{kt}$ gives
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = kM_0e^{kt}$$
In 2000, $t = 20$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= \dfrac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000) \times 0.045e^{20 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000)} \\ &\approx 46.153 \text{ million per year} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \text{rate} \approx 46 \text{ million/year (to the nearest million/year)}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of $M$ with respect to time, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At a local fast food restaurant, the probability, $W$, of the ice cream machine working on any given day is $40\%$. Ronald visits the restaurant on three consecutive days attempting to order an ice cream.

parts.label: a

dif.r: Complete tree, complement of all three working.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many days must Ronald visit in order to be $95\%$ confident that he will eventually visit the restaurant when the ice cream machine is working?

dif.r: Set up 1-0.6^n inequality, solve with logs, round up.

figures.cap: partially completed tree diagram
solution sketch: completed tree diagram

criteria: Finds the probability of the ice cream machine working on all three days, or equivalent merit
Completes the tree diagram, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Existing figure kept

solutions.latex:
The machine works on at least one of $n$ days unless it fails on every day.
$$P(W \text{ eventually}) = 1 - (0.6)^n$$
Set this equal to $0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.95 &= 1 - (0.6)^n \\ (0.6)^n &= 0.05 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.6} \\ &= 5.864\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number, Ronald must visit for $6$ days.
criteria: Establishes an equation in terms of the number of days required, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points on the graph of $y = f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of a cubic, factorise and second-derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, sketch the graph of $y = f(2x)$.

dif.r: Horizontal dilation of known cubic sketch, halving x-coordinates of key points

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the possible values of $a$ such that the graph of $y = f(2x) + a$ has only one $x$-intercept.

dif.r: Must reason vertical shift against turning values; dilation leaves y-values unchanged

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=f(2x)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating,
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2 + 2x - 1 \\ f''(x) &= 6x + 2 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 + 2x - 1 &= 0 \\ (3x - 1)(x + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ or } x = -1$$
Test the nature using the sign of $f''(x)$.

When $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$: $f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{5}{27}$ and $f''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) > 0$.

So $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, -\dfrac{5}{27}\right)$ is a minimum turning point.

When $x = -1$: $f(-1) = 1$ and $f''(-1) < 0$.

So $(-1, 1)$ is a maximum turning point.
criteria: Makes some progress towards solution, e.g. finds the turning points, or equivalent merit
Makes limited progress towards solution, e.g. writes the first two derivatives, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{833_q18_s1}
criteria: Draws a graph with some correct features, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\therefore\ a < -1 \text{ or } a > \dfrac{5}{27}$$
criteria: Finds some possible value(s) of $a$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The correlation coefficient is 0.8721. Describe the association between weekly income and life expectancy.
parts.note: Bivariate data, correlation and regression are Mathematics Standard content, not in 2024 Advanced.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $b$, correct to three decimal places.

parts.label: c

parts.note: Prediction and reliability from a line of best fit (bivariate data) are Mathematics Standard content, not in 2024 Advanced.

figures.cap: scatterplot of life expectancy against weekly income with line of best fit

solutions.latex: There is a strong positive linear correlation between weekly income and life expectancy.

The line passes through the point $x = 660$, $y = 76$, so
$$76 = 0.1072 \times 660 + b$$
$$\therefore b = 5.248$$

Substituting $x = 1000$ into the line of best fit,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 0.1072 \times 1000 + 5.248 \\ &= 112.448 \\ &\approx 112.45 \text{ years (to 2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
This prediction is unreliable because it is an extrapolation of the data (the independent variable only goes up to $\$760$).
criteria: Makes a valid prediction, or comments on the reliability of the prediction, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve $2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x = 0$, for $x \in [0, 2\pi]$.

Leave your answer in exact form

dif.r: Factorise homogeneous quadratic in sin, cos; two tan cases over domain

solutions.latex:
Factorise the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x &= 0 \\ (2\sin x - 3\cos x)(\sin x - \cos x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Case 1: $2\sin x = 3\cos x$, so $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \text{ or } x = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$
Case 2: $\sin x = \cos x$, so $\tan x = 1$.
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Expresses the equation as a product of its factors, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f'(x) = x^2 + kx$.

The line $y = 2x + 1$ is a tangent to the graph of $y = f(x)$ at the point where $x = -1$.

Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Combine tangent gradient and point conditions with integration constant

solutions.latex:
Integrating $f'(x)$,
$$f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + c$$
The tangent $y = 2x + 1$ touches the curve at $x = -1$, so $f'(-1) = 2$ and $f(-1) = 2(-1) + 1 = -1$.

From $f'(-1) = 2$:
$$(-1)^2 + k(-1) = 2$$
$$\therefore k = -1$$
From $f(-1) = -1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}(-1)^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}k(-1)^2 + c &= -1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2}k + c &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}\times(-1) + c &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \\ c &= -\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 - \dfrac{1}{6}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Finds a valid primitive function, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What are the values of $X$ and $Y$?

dif.r: Fill table entries by one-step interest and addition

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The account balance, $\$A_n$, at the end of $n$ months is given by the recurrence relation

$$A_n = \left(A_{n-1} + 500\right) \times q$$

What is the value of $q$?

dif.r: Direct recall of monthly growth factor

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the time, to the nearest whole month, that it takes for Sienna to reach her savings goal.

dif.r: Build annuity pattern with start-of-month deposits, GP sum, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Interest for the first month is the monthly rate times the balance of $\$500$.
$$X = \dfrac{4.2\%}{12}\times 500 = \$1.75$$
The balance is the previous balance, plus the deposit, plus the interest.
$$Y = 1005.26 + 500 + 5.27 = \$1510.53$$
criteria: Finds the value of $X$ or $Y$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The monthly growth factor is
$$q = 1 + \dfrac{4.2\%}{12} = 1.0035$$

Build up the balance month by month.
$$A_1 = 500\times 1.0035$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \left(500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= \left(500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^3 + 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \\ &= 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.0035$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2 + \cdots + 1.0035^{n-1}\right)$$
Set $A_n = 50\,000$ and use the sum of a GP.
$$\begin{aligned} 50\,000 &= 500(1.0035)\times\dfrac{1.0035^n - 1}{0.0035} \\ \dfrac{2707}{2007} &= 1.0035^n \\ n &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{2707}{2007}\right)}{\log 1.0035} \\ &\approx 85.64 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore it will take 86 months for Sienna to reach her savings goal.
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Expresses $A_n$ in terms of a geometric progression, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
At a local bay, the tide height is measured by a buoy. Based on the data, the average tide height of the bay is modelled using the function

$$H(t) = 0.7\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right) + 0.8$$

where $H$ is the average tide height, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, since 12.00 am midnight.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time when the maximum tide height occurs.

dif.r: Set sine term to 1 and solve for t, convert to clock time

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $H$ against $t$ for $0 \leq t \leq 24$.

dif.r: Sketch shifted sine with phase, amplitude, centre over two periods

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the vertical distance travelled by the buoy between 10.00 am and 6.00 pm.

dif.r: Must account for turning point at 4 pm when totalling distance

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of H against t

solutions.latex:
The maximum occurs when the sine term equals 1.
$$\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right) = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t - 1 &= 3 \\ t &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the maximum tide height occurs at 4.00 am.
criteria: Recognises that the maximum average tide height occurs when the sine term equals 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{833_q23_s1}
criteria: Draws a graph with some correct features, e.g. maximum and minimum values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the height at 10 am, 4 pm (the maximum at $t = 16$) and 6 pm.
$$\begin{aligned} H(10) &= 0.1 \\ H(16) &= 1.5 \\ H(18) &= 1.15 \end{aligned}$$
The buoy rises from $0.1$ to $1.5$, then falls to $1.15$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 1.4 + 0.35 \\ &= 1.75 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds part of the distance travelled by the buoy, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Two groups, Group $X$ and Group $Y$, compare the number of pushups their members can perform. Data from Group $X$ is normally distributed with a mean of 12 pushups. Data from Group $Y$ is normally distributed with a mean of 22 pushups. Both groups have the same standard deviation.

\exfigure{833_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that, if that $P\left(X > a\right) = P\left(Y < a\right)$, then $a = 17$.

dif.r: Symmetry argument: equal spreads so a is midway between means

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b

dif.r: Translate Y to X then use symmetry to reach tabled values

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: normal curves for Group X (mean 12) and Group Y (mean 22)
Group X normal curve shaded up to n

solutions.latex:
The distributions have the same shape, so $P(X>a)=P(Y<a)$ when $a$ is midway between the means.
$$a = \dfrac{12 + 22}{2} = 17$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(17 \le Y \le 29) &= P(Y \le 29) - P(Y \le 17) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - P(X \le 7) &&(\text{the distribution of } Y \text{ is } X \text{ shifted up by } 10) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - P(X \ge 17) &&(\text{symmetry about } 12) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - \left(1 - P(X \le 17)\right) \\ &= 0.8275 - (1 - 0.7500) \\ &= 0.5775 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the equivalent probabilities in the distribution of $X$, or equivalent merit
Expresses the desired probability as a sum, or difference, of other probabilities in the distribution of $Y$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$$

where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.

dif.r: Maximum of quadratic velocity via derivative or vertex

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0, integrate velocity with initial position

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

dif.r: Split integral at direction change and add magnitudes

solutions.latex:
Method 1: maximum velocity occurs when $a(t) = 0$.

Differentiating $v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$,
$$a(t) = -4t + 2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -4t + 2 &= 0 \\ t &= 0.5 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: since velocity is a quadratic function, the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{2}{2(-2)} = 0.5 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Attempts to solve $a(t) = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t) = 0$.
$$v(t) = 0 \text{ gives } t = -1 \text{ or } t = 2$$
Since $t \ge 0$, it first comes to rest at $t = 2$.

Since $x(0) = 4$, the position at $t = 2$ is
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 4 + \displaystyle\int_0^2 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 4 + \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_0^2 \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is $10\dfrac{2}{3}$ metres to the right of the origin.
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in the first two seconds, or equivalent merit
Finds the time the particle comes to rest, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = 2$, so the distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the displacements on $[0,2]$ and $[2,3]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled} &= \int_0^2 v(t)\,dt + \left|\int_2^3 v(t)\,dt\right| \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \int_2^3 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_2^3 \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(3)^3 + (3)^2 + 4(3)\right) - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(2)^3 + (2)^2 + 4(2)\right)\right] \\ &= 10\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled by the particle in the third second, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Non-routine composite solid set-up, exposed area insight, then optimise

figures.cap: cylinder of radius r on a cube

solutions.latex:
The volume is the cylinder plus the cube of side $2r$.
$$\pi r^2 h + (2r)^3 = 1.5$$
$$h = \dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}$$
The coated surface is the 6 faces of the cube plus the curved surface of the cylinder. Let $S$ be this area.
$$S = 6\times(2r)^2 + 2\pi rh$$
Substituting $h$,
$$\begin{aligned} S(r) &= 24r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 24r^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16r^3}{r} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating,
$$S'(r) = 48r - \dfrac{3}{r^2} - 32r$$
For a stationary point, $S'(r) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16r &= \dfrac{3}{r^2} \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{3}{16} \end{aligned}$$
$$r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} \text{ since } r > 0$$
Test the nature using the sign of $S'(r)$.
$$\begin{aligned} S'(r) &< 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just below } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{decreasing}\\ S'(r) &= 0 &&\text{at } r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{stationary}\\ S'(r) &> 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just above } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So this is a minimum.
$$S_{\min} = 24\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}}\right)^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16\times\frac{3}{16}}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{16}}} \approx 7.86 \text{ m}^2$$
The minimum surface area is $7.86 \text{ m}^2$ (to 2 d.p.).
criteria: Finds the value of $r$ that minimises the surface area, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative of their equation for surface area, or equivalent merit
Finds an equation for the surface area in terms of one variable, or equivalent merit
Formulates equations to describe the information provided, or equivalent merit

why: Checker got a different answer — The stationary point r^3=3/16 gives h=(1.5-8r^3)/(πr^2)=0, so the 'minimum' is a bare cube with no pillar. The feasible domain is 0<r≤(3/16)^(1/3), and the stored test 'S'(r)>0 just above' uses infeasible r (h<0). 7.86 is only the endpoint

The answer 7.86 m² is the value at that end point. Keep the question as is, keep it with the working corrected to "S is decreasing on the whole domain, least at the end point $h=0$", or drop it?

questions.stem:
The graphs of $y = \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2}$ and $y = e^x - 2$ are shown in the diagram below. The two curves intersect at point $A$.

\exfigure{833_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\ln 4$.

dif.r: Equate curves, quadratic in e^x, reject negative root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $y$-axis. Express your answer in the form $\ln a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

dif.r: Area between curves needing f'/f integral and log simplification

figures.cap: graphs of y=3e^x/(e^x+2) and y=e^x-2 meeting at A

solutions.latex:
At the intersection the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} &= e^x - 2 \\ 3e^x &= (e^x - 2)(e^x + 2) \\ 3e^x &= e^{2x} - 4 \\ e^{2x} - 3e^x - 4 &= 0 \\ (e^x + 1)(e^x - 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x > 0$, $e^x \ne -1$, so $e^x = 4$.
$$\therefore x = \ln 4$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve $y = \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x+2}$ is above $y = e^x - 2$ on $[0, \ln 4]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \int_0^{\ln 4} \left(\dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} - \left(e^x - 2\right)\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{\ln 4} \left(\dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} - e^x + 2\right)dx \\ &= \left[3\ln\left(e^x + 2\right) - e^x + 2x\right]_0^{\ln 4} \\ &= \left(3\ln 6 - 4 + 2\ln 4\right) - \left(3\ln 3 - 1 + 0\right) \\ &= \ln 128 - 3 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Describes the area using a definite integral, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{6}{55}$.

dif.r: Total probability equals 1 across two pieces

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function of $X$.

dif.r: Piecewise CDF, carrying accumulated probability into second piece

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of $m$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Choose correct piece, solve F(m)=0.5 cube root

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1.
$$\displaystyle\int_0^1 kx\,dx + \int_1^3 kx^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 + \left[\dfrac{k}{3}x^3\right]_1^3 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2} + \left(9k - \dfrac{k}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{55}{6}k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k = \dfrac{6}{55}$$
criteria: Writes a valid equation involving the sum of all probabilities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0 \le x < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_0^x t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}t^2\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 \end{aligned}$$
For $1 \le x \le 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_1^x t^2\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}t^3\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 - \dfrac{2}{55} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 & \text{if } 0 \le x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 & \text{if } 1 \le x \le 3 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Describes the cumulative distribution function using an integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Changed dummy variable in integrals from x to t (same mathematics).

solutions.latex:
Since $F(1) = \dfrac{3}{55} < 0.5$, the median satisfies $1 \le m < 3$, so use the second piece with $F(m) = 0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}m^3 &= 0.5 \\ 2 + 4m^3 &= 55 \\ m &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{53}{4}} \\ &\approx 2.37 \end{aligned}$$
The median is $m \approx 2.37$ (to 2 d.p.).
criteria: Recognises that $1 \le m < 3$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source solved for x; written with m (same value).

parts.latex:
Two surveyors, $A$ and $B$, stand on level ground to observe a large tree. The tree is directly north of surveyor $A$ who sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $52^\circ$.

Surveyor $B$ is 27 metres away from Surveyor $A$ on a bearing of $043^\circ$ and sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $46^\circ$.

Find the height, $h$, of the tree correct to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tree seen from two points on level ground, elevation and bearings) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: 3D elevations combined with cosine rule giving quadratic in h

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of surveyors and tree

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{833_q29_s1}

Let $C$ be the point at the base of the tree. Using the tangent ratio in the two right-angled triangles,
$$AC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}, \qquad BC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 27$ and $\angle CAB = 43^\circ$ (the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $043^\circ$ and $C$ is due north of $A$). Apply the cosine rule.
$$\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\right)^2 + 27^2 - 2\times\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\times 27\times\cos 43^\circ$$
Rearranging,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 52^\circ} - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 46^\circ}\right)h^2 - \dfrac{54\cos 43^\circ}{\tan 52^\circ}h + 27^2 \\ 0 &\approx -0.32215h^2 - 30.85539h + 729 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $h > 0$,
$$h = \dfrac{30.855\ldots - \sqrt{30.855\ldots^2 - 4\times(-0.322\ldots)\times 729}}{2\times(-0.322\ldots)} \approx 19.6$$
$$\therefore h \approx 20 \text{ metres (to the nearest metre)}$$
criteria: Makes progress in solving for $h$, or equivalent merit
Forms a relationship, in terms of $h$, between the edges in the base triangle, or equivalent merit
Expresses the edge $AC$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Quadratic formula root choice: the negative-denominator form gives the positive root.

The circle $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 9$ is translated 3 units up and 2 units left.

What is the equation of the circle after these translations?

dif.r: Direct translation of circle equation, one routine step

solutions.latex:
Translating 2 units left replaces $x$ by $x+2$; translating 3 units up replaces $y$ by $y-3$.

$$(x-1+2)^2+(y-3)^2=9$$
so
$$(x+1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: The graph of $f(x)$ is obtained from $g(x) = \sqrt{x-6}$ by a dilation with a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ from the $y$-axis. Which of the following is $f(x)$?

dif.r: Horizontal dilation: must know scale 1/3 replaces x by 3x

solutions.latex:
A dilation by scale factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ from the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $3x$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= g(3x) \\ &= \sqrt{3x-6} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

solutions.latex:
The graph is flipped (reflected in the horizontal axis), so $k<0$, and $|k|=3$, hence $k=-3$.

The period is $4\pi$, and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{a}$, so
$$a=\dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The centre line is the mean of the maximum and minimum values:
$$c=\dfrac{4+(-2)}{2}=1$$
This matches option C.

dif.r: Bound semicircle expression then scale and shift to get range

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $9-x^2\ge 0$, so $x\in[-3,3]$.

Then $0\le\sqrt{9-x^2}\le 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le 2\sqrt{9-x^2}\le 6 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ 1&\le 2\sqrt{9-x^2}+1\le 7 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$
So the range is $[1,7]$, option A.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\sqrt{3}\tan 2x = 1$ for the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$.

dif.r: Doubled-angle domain, four solutions including negative angles

solutions.latex:
Since $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$, we have $2x\in[-2\pi,2\pi]$, which is 2 revolutions.
$$\tan 2x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$$
Tangent is positive in quadrants 1 and 3.

Positive revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q1})\\ 2x&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q3})\end{aligned}$$
Negative revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}-2\pi=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q1})\\ 2x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}-2\pi=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q3})\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by 2:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Finds the values of $2x$ in the whole domain, or equivalent merit
Finds $\tan 2x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and the related angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Explain why the graph of $y = \tan x$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ .

dif.r: Short explanation: cos zero makes tan undefined

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, and at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ we have $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0$ while $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$.

So $\tan x$ would be $\dfrac{1}{0}$, which is undefined.

Hence $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a vertical asymptote.

questions.stem:
The velocity of a particle is given by

$$v = 2 - 4\cos t \quad \text{for } 0 \le t \le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.label: a

The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-4\cos t&=0 \\ \cos t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3} &&(\text{Q1})\\ t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{3} &&(\text{Q4})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ s or } t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\text{ s}$$

$v=2-4\cos t$ is greatest when $\cos t=-1$, that is, at $t=\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=2-4(-1) \\ &=6 \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
The particle reaches a maximum velocity of $6$ m/s at $t=\pi$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: write the fraction in the form $\dfrac{a}{x-3}+b$.
$$\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}=\dfrac{a+b(x-3)}{x-3}$$
Equating numerators, $bx+(a-3b)=2x-5$, so $b=2$ and $a-3b=-5$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-5+6 \\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}=\dfrac{1}{x-3}+2$$
Method 2: start from the right-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{x-3}+2&=\dfrac{1+2(x-3)}{x-3} \\ &=\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}\end{aligned}$$
So LHS $=$ RHS.

The $x$-intercept (put $y=0$):

questions.stem:
Given: $f(x) = x^2 - 1$

The function $g(x)$ is produced by making the following transformations to $f(x)$:

\begin{itemize}
\item reflecting on the $x$-axis
\item translating 3 units to the left
\item translating 2 units upwards
\end{itemize}

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The point $A(3,8)$ lies on $f(x)$. Determine coordinates of this point after the above transformations have occurred.

solutions.latex:
The transformations are applied in order.
$$\begin{aligned} h(x)&=-f(x)=-x^2+1 &&(\text{reflect in the } x\text{-axis})\\ k(x)&=h(x+3)=-(x+3)^2+1 &&(\text{3 units left})\\ g(x)&=k(x)+2=-(x+3)^2+3 &&(\text{2 units up})\end{aligned}$$
Expanded:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)&=-(x^2+6x+9)+3 \\ &=-x^2-6x-6\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies some of the transformations correctly, or equivalent merit

Vertical: reflecting then moving up 2 changes $y=8$ to
$$8\times(-1)+2=-6$$
$$\therefore\ (3,8)\text{ becomes }(0,-6)$$
Check: $g(0)=-6$.

Consider the following data set.

$4\quad 7\quad 7\quad 9\quad 12\quad 15$

Which row of the table shows how the median and mean are affected when a score of 9 is added to the data set?

dif.r: Direct median and mean recalculation after adding one score

options.label: B
options.latex: Median: stays the same; mean: stays the same

options.label: C
options.latex: Median: changes; mean: stays the same

options.label: D
options.latex: Median: stays the same; mean: changes

solutions.latex:
Original data set (6 scores): the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th scores.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{median} &= \dfrac{7+9}{2} = 8 \\ \text{mean} &= \dfrac{4+7+7+9+12+15}{6} = \dfrac{54}{6} = 9 \end{aligned}$$
Add a score of 9: the data set is $4,\ 7,\ 7,\ 9,\ 9,\ 12,\ 15$ (7 scores), so the median is the 4th score.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{median} &= 9 \\ \text{mean} &= \dfrac{54+9}{7} = \dfrac{63}{7} = 9 \end{aligned}$$
The median changes from $8$ to $9$, and the mean stays at $9$ (adding a score equal to the mean does not change the mean).

Therefore the row is: median changes, mean stays the same.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\dfrac{x}{\sin x}$ ?

dif.r: Standard quotient rule with trig function, MCQ

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{\sin x}\right) &= \dfrac{1\cdot\sin x - x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{-x\cos x+\sin x}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating, we have the first and second derivatives.
$$f'(x) = 2x^3 - 18x^2 + 40x,\qquad f''(x) = 6x^2 - 36x + 40$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^3 - 18x^2 + 40x &= 0 \\ 2x(x^2 - 9x + 20) &= 0 \\ 2x(x-4)(x-5) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0, 4, 5$.
$$f(0)=0,\qquad f(4)=64,\qquad f(5)=\dfrac{125}{2}=62.5$$
The sign of $f''(x)$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=40>0 &&\text{minimum at } (0,0)\\ f''(4)&=-8<0 &&\text{maximum at } (4,64)\\ f''(5)&=10>0 &&\text{minimum at } (5,62.5) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 40 500, varies according to the formula $P = 40500\,b^{\frac{-t}{5}}$ where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t \ge 0$

The population is 1500 after 15 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 25 people per year.

dif.r: Find b, differentiate exponential base b, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Substitute $P = 1500$, $t = 15$ to find $b$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= 40500\,b^{-\frac{15}{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{27} &= b^{-3} \\ 27 &= b^3 \\ b &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
We want $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -25$.

Using $y = a^x$, $y' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ on $P = 40500 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 40500 \times \dfrac{-1}{5}\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \\ &= -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $-25$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= -25 \\ 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{324\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{t}{5} &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ t &= \dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ &= 26.737\ldots \\ &\approx 26.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 26.7 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $b$, sets $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-25$ and finds a correct derivative, or equivalent merit
Finds $b = 3$ and sets $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -25$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$, show that $A = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760}{r}$

dif.r: Substitute h from volume formula into given area expression

parts.latex: Show that $A$ has a minimum value and find the value of $r$ for which the minimum occurs.

dif.r: Standard optimisation: differentiate, solve, second derivative test

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r and height h

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$, and $V = 380$, so we make $h$ the subject.
$$380 = \pi r^2 h,\qquad h = \dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}$$
Substitute into $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760\pi r}{\pi r^2} \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760}{r} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria rewritten top-down from source rows.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $A$ twice.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{1520}{r^3}$$
Since $r > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} > 0$, therefore $A$ has a minimum value.

The minimum occurs when $\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3 &= 760 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{760}{4\pi} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{760}{4\pi}} \\ &\approx 3.925 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r \approx 3.925 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct first derivative and shows minimum using the second derivative, or equivalent merit

The $x$-intercept occurs when $f(x) = 0$; since $x > 0$, we need $\ln x = 0$.

criteria: Correct domain or correct $x$-intercept, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria rewritten top-down; one line of reasoning added for the intercept.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \ln x + \dfrac{x}{x} \\ &= \ln x + 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$$
criteria: Correct first derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria rewritten top-down from source rows.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x + 1 &= 0 \\ \ln x &= -1 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{e} \end{aligned}$$
This is the only solution, so there is one stationary point.
$$f(e^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{e}\ln e^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{e}$$
The sign of $f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ decides the nature. The domain is $x > 0$, so $f''(x) > 0$.
$$\therefore\ \left(e^{-1}, -e^{-1}\right) \text{ is a minimum.}$$
criteria: Shows one stationary point, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be an odd function and $g(x)$ be an even function.

Given that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are continuous and $k$ is a positive constant,

which of the following is NOT always true?

dif.r: Abstract odd/even composition and integral reasoning across four options.

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Option A: $g(f(-x))=g(-f(x))=g(f(x))$, which is even, so A is true.

Option B: $f(-2x)+2(-x)=-\big[f(2x)+2x\big]$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and B is true.

Option C: $g(-2x)f(-2x)=-g(2x)f(2x)$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and C is true.

Option D: $f(g(-x))=f(g(x))$ is even, and the integral of an even function can be zero, so D is not always true.

solutions.latex:
Make $x$ the subject: $y=\ln x$ gives $x=e^y$.

When $x=e$, $y=1$; when $x=e^2$, $y=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_1^2 x\,dy \\ &= \int_1^2 e^y\,dy \\ &= \Big[e^y\Big]_1^2 \\ &= e^2-e \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Find the first derivative of the following functions:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $y = \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{x^2+1}\right)$

dif.r: Log laws to expand, then routine differentiation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $f(x) = \tan^3 2x$

dif.r: Chain rule applied twice to tan cubed.
Exponential with base 8; recognise 8^e is a constant.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $y = e^{\cos 2x}\cos 2x$

dif.r: Product rule with chain-rule exponential factor.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ and $\ln a^n=n\ln a$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln x-\ln(x^2+1)$$
Differentiating,
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{2x}-\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
criteria: Applies the log laws correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $u=\tan 2x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan 2x)=2\sec^2 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3\tan^2 2x\cdot\sec^2 2x\cdot 2 \\ &= 6\tan^2 2x\sec^2 2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6\tan^2 2x\sec^2 2x$$
criteria: Sets up the chain rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{kx}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kx}$, and since $8^e$ is a constant:
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=e\ln 8\cdot 8^{ex}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{\cos 2x} & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=-2\sin 2x\, e^{\cos 2x} & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -2\sin 2x\, e^{\cos 2x}\cos 2x+e^{\cos 2x}(-2\sin 2x) \\ &= -2e^{\cos 2x}\sin 2x\,(1+\cos 2x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2e^{\cos 2x}\sin 2x\,(1+\cos 2x)$$
criteria: Applies the product rule correctly in part, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line had the product-rule terms in a different order and with $u'$ written as $-2\sin 2x\,e^{\cos 2x}$ split; the result is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Expanding the square and using $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2dx &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}+\tan^2\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}-2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx \\ &= \left[2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}+4\ln\left|\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\right|\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 2+4\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ &= 2+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2dx=2+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Expands and uses the identity, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\right)=2x$, write the integrand as $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2x\sin x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^2 2x\sin x^2\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos x^2\right]_0^2 \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 4-1) \\ &\approx 0.83 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx\approx 0.83$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{-2e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C$$
