questions.stem: For the function $y = 4xe^{-x}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary point and determine its nature.

dif.r: Standard stationary point and nature for xe^{-x}.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any point of inflection.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and test concavity change.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the function showing all important features.

dif.r: Sketch with asymptotic behaviour; mirrors anchor curve sketch.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find an estimation to the area under the graph in the domain $[0, 2]$ using the Trapezoidal rule with three function values.

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule, two strips, direct substitution.

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Explain whether the Trapezoidal rule over estimated or under estimated the exact area in part (d).

dif.r: Justify underestimate via concavity on interval.

figures.cap: solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 4e^{-x}-4xe^{-x} \\ &= 4e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=4e^{-1}$.

To find the nature, use the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-x}(2-x)$$
At $x=1$,
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-1}<0$$
$$\therefore\ (1,4e^{-1})\text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary point and tests its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$-4e^{-x}(2-x)=0$$
Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=2$. Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=1.9:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=2.1:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, and $y=8e^{-2}$ when $x=2$.
$$\therefore\ (2,8e^{-2})\text{ is a point of inflection}$$

The curve passes through the origin, has a maximum at $(1,4e^{-1})$ and an inflection at $(2,8e^{-2})$, and approaches the $x$-axis as $x\to\infty$.

\exfigure{1037_q21_s1}
criteria: Correct shape, or correct coordinates of the points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw (key 1037_q21_s1): origin, maximum $(1,4e^{-1})$, inflection $(2,8e^{-2})$, asymptote $y=0$.

solutions.latex:
Three function values on $[0,2]$ give two strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$$
The values are at $x=0,1,2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y(0)&=0\\ y(1)&=4e^{-1}\\ y(2)&=8e^{-2}\end{aligned}$$
By the trapezoidal rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left(0+4e^{-1}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(4e^{-1}+8e^{-2}\right) \\ &= 4\left(e^{-1}+e^{-2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}\approx 4\left(e^{-1}+e^{-2}\right)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
On $[0,2]$ the curve has a maximum at $x=1$ and the inflection is at $x=2$, so the curve is concave down throughout $0<x<2$.

The trapezium chords lie below a concave down curve.
$$\therefore\ \text{the trapezoidal rule underestimated the area}$$

meta.format_note: Added reason that the curve is concave down on $[0,2]$ (from $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ for $x<2$) and chords lie below it.

questions.stem: The water level, measured in meters, at a dam has been changing at a rate of $R = t^3 - 11t^2 + 35t - 29$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When is the water level decreasing most rapidly?

dif.r: Minimise the rate itself; endpoint check overturns the stationary-point answer.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the change in water level of the dam for the 6 years?

dif.r: Integrate a rate over the interval to get net change.

solutions.latex:
The water level decreases most rapidly where $R$ is least, so find the stationary points of $R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= 3t^2-22t+35 \\ &= (3t-7)(t-5) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dR}{dt}=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $t=5$.

Nature, using the second derivative $\dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=6t-22$:
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{7}{3}:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ t=5:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=8>0 &&\text{minimum, } R=-4\end{aligned}$$
Check the endpoints of the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ & R=-29\\ t=6:\ & R=1\end{aligned}$$
The least value of $R$ is $-29$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreases most rapidly at } t=0$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The change in level is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\left(t^3-11t^2+35t-29\right)dt &= \left[\dfrac{t^4}{4}-\dfrac{11t^3}{3}+\dfrac{35t^2}{2}-29t\right]_0^6 \\ &= -12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreased by } 12 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule, find an estimate for the area of the irregular shape shown below. (Each square on the grid is one square unit.)

solutions.latex:
Each trapezium has width $h=2$ units. The parallel sides $d_f$ and $d_l$ are the first and last vertical sides of each trapezium.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{h}{2}(d_f+d_l)$ for each trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}(2+4)+\dfrac{2}{2}(4+3) \\ &=1(6)+1(7) \\ &=13 \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex:
The curve $y=\ln x$ is translated to the left by $\pi$ units and then dilated horizontally by a scale factor of 3.

What is the equation which describes this new curve?

dif.r: Order of translation then horizontal dilation is a common trap

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

solutions.latex:
To translate left by $a$ units, replace $x$ by $x+a$. So $x$ becomes $x+\pi$.

To dilate horizontally by a factor of $k$, replace $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{k}$. Then $x$ is replaced by $\dfrac{x}{3}$ in $\ln(x+\pi)$, so $x+\pi$ becomes $\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi$.

Hence $y=\ln x$ becomes
$$y=\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi\right)$$
This is option A. (Option D, $\ln\left(\dfrac{x+\pi}{3}\right)$, is the result of dilating first and then translating.)

parts.latex: Find the range of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

dif.r: Range from centre line and amplitude, routine

solutions.latex:
The curve oscillates about $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ with amplitude $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

The minimum and maximum values are
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}&=-1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Range}=[-1,2]$$

parts.latex: $$\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}dx$$

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}dx&=\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^x}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{\ln 1-\ln 5}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{-\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{5^x}\times\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5\cdot 5^x}+C \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Assume the weights of newborn babies are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma$. A particular baby has a weight below the lower quartile of the distribution but not in the bottom 10% of the distribution. Which of the following best represents the region in which this baby's weight lies?

option B: normal curve, shaded from far left up to about mu-0.7 sigma
option C: normal curve, shaded between about mu-1.7 sigma and mu-0.7 sigma
option D: normal curve, narrow shaded band between mu-2 sigma and mu-1.2 sigma

solutions.latex:
The baby is below the lower quartile (bottom $25\%$) but not in the bottom $10\%$, so its weight is between the 10th and 25th percentiles.

The lower quartile lies between $0$ and $-1$ standard deviations from the mean.

parts.latex: Differentiate $x\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on sin(1/x)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\right]&=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)-\dfrac{x}{x^2}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \\ &=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)-\dfrac{1}{x}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $[-\pi\le x\le\pi]$

dif.r: Shifted tan equation, adjusting domain to select solutions

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta=x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$. Then $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ gives $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$, and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ has solutions $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+n\pi$.

Listing solutions of $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$:
$$\theta=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6},-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{13\pi}{6}$$
Subtract $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ from each:
$$x=-\dfrac{16\pi}{6},-\dfrac{10\pi}{6},-\dfrac{4\pi}{6},\dfrac{2\pi}{6},\dfrac{8\pi}{6}$$
$$x=-\dfrac{8\pi}{3},-\dfrac{5\pi}{3},-\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Only $-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lie in $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.

This is option C.

parts.latex:
The probability density function of a random variable is given by:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{50}e^{-\frac{x}{50}} & x\ge 0\\[6pt] 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$

What is the median to 1 decimal place?

dif.r: Integrate exponential pdf, set to 0.5, solve with logs

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies
$$\int_0^m\dfrac{1}{50}e^{-\frac{x}{50}}\,dx=0.5$$
Evaluating the integral:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\left[-e^{-\frac{x}{50}}\right]_0^m \\ &=-e^{-\frac{m}{50}}+1 \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-\frac{m}{50}}&=0.5 \\ -\dfrac{m}{50}&=\ln 0.5 \\ m&\approx 34.7 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be leader with Miao as mascot?

dif.r: Multiply two branch probabilities on a tree

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be the leader or Miao will be the mascot, but not both?

dif.r: Identify three exactly-one outcomes and sum products

can_use: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

figures.cap: probability tree: leader A, B, C then mascot M, W

solutions.latex:
The leader and mascot choices are independent, so multiply the branch probabilities from the tree:
$$\begin{aligned} P(AM)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

Exactly one of the two events happens in three outcomes: Andie with Woof, Bec with Miao, or Cat with Miao.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one})&=P(AW)+P(BM)+P(CM) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{9}+\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{18} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates at least one of the relevant product probabilities correctly from the tree, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Chloe plans to build a rectangular enclosure for her new chickens against an existing wall, using 16 metres of wire fencing as shown below. She calls the dimensions of the enclosure $x$ and $y$.

\exfigure{1544_q12_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: She reasons that $2x+y=16$. Write $y$ in terms of $x$ and hence, show that the area of the enclosure can be written as $A=16x-2x^2$.

dif.r: Rearrange given constraint and substitute into area

parts.label: b

dif.r: Read two x-values from graph, compute y each

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the dimensions (both $x$ and $y$) that will achieve the maximum possible area for the enclosure.

dif.r: Read vertex from graph and find y

figures.cap: rectangular enclosure against existing wall
graph of A=16x-2x^2

solutions.latex:
The fencing covers two sides of length $x$ and one of length $y$, so $2x+y=16$.

Making $y$ the subject:
$$y=16-2x$$
The area is length times width:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=xy \\ &=x(16-2x) \\ &=16x-2x^2 \end{aligned}$$

Draw the line $A=24$ on the graph. It meets the curve where $x=2$ and $x=6$.

These can be checked by solving $16x-2x^2-24=0$.

For each $x$, $y=16-2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=2&:\ y=12 \\ x=6&:\ y=4 \end{aligned}$$
The dimensions are $2$ m by $12$ m, or $6$ m by $4$ m.
criteria: Correct values of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum area on the graph is $32 \text{ m}^2$, at $x=4$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} y&=16-2\times 4 \\ &=8 \end{aligned}$$
The dimensions are $4$ m by $8$ m.

questions.stem: Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:

dif.r: Power rule on negative index with constant e

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\dfrac{\log_e x}{x^2}$

dif.r: Quotient rule with ln x and simplification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $\sqrt{\sin x}$

dif.r: Chain rule with fractional power of sin x

solutions.latex:
Rewrite as a power of $x$ and use the power rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{3e}{2}x^{-2}\right]&=-2\times\dfrac{3e}{2}x^{-3} \\ &=-\dfrac{3e}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}\right]&=\dfrac{\frac{x^2}{x}-2x\ln x}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x-2x\ln x}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x(1-2\ln x)}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write $\sqrt{\sin x}=(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and use the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cos x\,(\sin x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos x}{2\sqrt{\sin x}} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vanna Beach.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Weston.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1544_q14_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
It then plans to fly directly back to Underwood.

Calculate, to the nearest km, the distance that it will fly.

dif.r: Derive 85 degree angle from bearings, then cosine rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Determine the bearing (from Weston) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

Give your answer to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Sine rule plus parallel-line angle reasoning to get bearing

figures.cap: journey U to V to W with bearings
solution sketch: journey diagram with north lines and angles, including start of working

solutions.latex:
Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be points due north of $U$, $V$ and $W$ respectively.

\exfigure{1544_q14_s1}

The angle at $V$ is
$$\angle UVW=55^\circ+30^\circ=85^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $UVW$:
$$\begin{aligned} UW^2&=70^2+82^2-2\times70\times82\times\cos 85^\circ \\ &\approx 10\,623.452 \end{aligned}$$
$$UW\approx 103.07$$
The helicopter flies $103$ km (nearest km).
criteria: Finds $\angle UVW$ and applies trigonometry to find $UW$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram 1544_q14_s1 already referenced in source; needs to show the bearings, north lines at U, V, W, angles 55 and 30 degrees, and sides 70 and 82 km. Source solution sketch_id is 1544_q14_s2 but figure key 1544_q14_s1 kept as written.

solutions.latex:
Applying the sine rule in triangle $UVW$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle VWU}{70}=\dfrac{\sin 85^\circ}{103.07}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\angle VWU&=\dfrac{70\times\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ &\approx 0.67656 \end{aligned}$$
$$\angle VWU\approx 42.575^\circ$$
Since $WZ$ and $VY$ are parallel north lines, $\angle ZWV=30^\circ$ (alternate angles). So
$$\angle UWZ\approx 30^\circ+43^\circ=73^\circ$$
The bearing of $U$ from $W$ is
$$360^\circ-73^\circ=287^\circ$$
Alternatively, find $\angle VUW\approx 52.4^\circ$ by the sine rule, then $\angle XUW\approx 55^\circ+52^\circ=107^\circ$ and $\angle UWZ=180^\circ-107^\circ=73^\circ$.

Or use the cosine rule:
$$\cos\angle VWU=\dfrac{82^2+103.07^2-70^2}{2\times82\times103.07}\approx 0.73638$$
This gives $\angle VWU\approx 42.576^\circ$ and the same bearing, $287^\circ$.
criteria: Finds a correct acute angle by any method but does not find the bearing, or finds an acute angle incorrectly and applies it correctly to find the bearing

meta.format_note: Source's cosine-rule value was quoted to more decimals; shortened to 5 places. Could reference the part (a) diagram.

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle at time $(t)$ seconds is given by:

$$x=3e^{-2t}+4e^{-t}+2t.$$

Find the exact time at which the particle comes to rest.

dif.r: Velocity zero gives hidden quadratic in e^{-t}, reject negative root

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2$$
Setting this to zero:
$$-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2=0$$
Let $u=e^{-t}$, so $e^{-2t}=u^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6u^2+4u-2&=0 \\ 3u^2+2u-1&=0 \\ (u+1)(3u-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-t}>0$, $e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution. So $e^{-t}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} -t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ t&=-(\ln 1-\ln 3) \\ &=\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\ln 3 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Correct differentiation and progress towards solving $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$

meta.format_note: Source substituted x=e^{-t}, clashing with displacement x; renamed to u.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show $\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}=3\sec 3x\,\operatorname{cosec}3x$

dif.r: Short identity proof via sin and cos

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise find $\displaystyle\int 3\sec 3x\,\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx$

dif.r: Hence recognise f'/f form, giving ln|tan 3x|

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec$ and $\tan$ in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{\cos^2 3x}}{\frac{\sin 3x}{\cos 3x}} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{\cos^2 3x}\times\dfrac{\cos 3x}{\sin 3x} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{\cos 3x\sin 3x} \\ &=3\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes correct equivalent fractions in terms of sine and cosine

solutions.latex:
By part (a), the integrand equals $\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}$, which has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=\tan 3x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int 3\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}\,dx \\ &=\ln|\tan 3x|+C \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave ln(tan 3x)+C; modulus signs added since the integral of f'/f is ln|f|.

dif.r: Read amplitude, period and phase from graph

figures.cap: cosine curve, amplitude 2, from -3pi to 3pi, y(0)=-2

solutions.latex:
The curve has the form $y=k\cos(ax+b)$.

The amplitude is $2$ and $k>0$, so $k=2$.

The graph completes $3$ cycles for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, so $a=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&=2\cos b \\ \cos b&=-1 \\ b&=\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is the value with $0\le b\le\pi$.
$$\therefore\ y=2\cos(3x+\pi)$$
Equivalently, from the graph, there is a phase shift of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left, giving $y=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

As a transformation of $y=\cos x$: dilate in the $y$ direction by a factor of $2$ (replace $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{2}$), dilate in the $x$ direction by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (replace $x$ by $3x$), and translate $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left (replace $x$ by $x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y}{2}&=\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ y&=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Any two of $k$, $a$, $b$ correct, or equivalent merit
Any one of $k$, $a$, $b$ correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The gradient of a curve is given by $y'=1-6\sin 3x$.

The curve passes through the point $(0,7)$.

What is the equation of the curve?

dif.r: Integrate trig gradient and find constant from point

solutions.latex:
Integrate the gradient:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\int(1-6\sin 3x)\,dx \\ &=x+2\cos 3x+C \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,7)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=0+2\cos 0+C \\ 7&=2+C \\ C&=5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=x+2\cos 3x+5$$
criteria: Correct integration but does not find $C$, or small error in solution, or equivalent merit
Some attempt to integrate, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: For an arithmetic series the third term ($T_3$) is 32 and the sixth term ($T_6$) is 17.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the common difference.

dif.r: Two term equations, subtract to find d

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ inclusive.

dif.r: Find a, then S20 minus S9 with negative d; careful arithmetic

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series, $T_n=a+(n-1)d$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=a+2d=32 &&(1)\\ T_6&=a+5d=17 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract $(1)$ from $(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3d&=-15 \\ d&=-5 \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $d=-5$.
criteria: Sets up the two equations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=-5$ into equation (1): $a-10=32$, so $a=42$.

The sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ is $S_{20}-S_9$, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}[2\times42+(20-1)(-5)]=-110 \\ S_9&=\dfrac{9}{2}[2\times42+(9-1)(-5)]=198 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum}&=S_{20}-S_9 \\ &=-110-198 \\ &=-308 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Sum}=-308$$
criteria: Finds either $S_{20}$ or $S_9$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source refers to $d=-5$ from part (a), made explicit. Sketch id in the item is unused.

questions.stem: At 7 pm on a Wednesday evening after a storm, Jack's water tank was full. The capacity of the tank was 3 000 litres. The tap on the tank, however, was leaking such that the change in volume at any time ($t$) hours was proportional to the volume ($V$) of the tank and can be modelled by the equation $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $V_0$, the initial volume of the tank.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into exponential model; one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the volume of the tank after 3 hours is 1 900 litres, find the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for k using logarithms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By the time Jack discovered that the tank was leaking, there were only 250 litres of water remaining. At what time and on which day did Jack discover the leak (correct to the nearest minute)?

dif.r: Solve for t with logs, convert hours to clock time and day

solutions.latex:
The model is $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

When $t=0$, $V=3\,000$:

$$3\,000=V_0e^0$$

$$\therefore\ V_0=3\,000 \text{ litres}$$

The model is $V=3\,000e^{-kt}$. When $t=3$, $V=1\,900$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1\,900&=3\,000e^{-3k} \\ \dfrac{19}{30}&=e^{-3k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right)&=-3k \\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right) \\ &\approx 0.1522528008 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k\approx 0.1523 \text{ (4 decimal places)}$$
criteria: Correct progress towards finding $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $V=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250&=3\,000e^{-kt} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{25}{300}\right)&=-kt \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{25}{300}\right)}{-0.1522528008} \end{aligned}$$

So $t=16$ hours $19$ minutes.

Adding this to 7 pm Wednesday gives 11:19 am Thursday.

$$\therefore\ \text{The leak was discovered at 11:19 am on Thursday.}$$

The table below gives the future value of an annuity of \$1 per period for various periods and interest rates.

\extable{1544_q21_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Julia invests \$250 per month in an annuity which pays 5.4\% p.a. compounding monthly. What will be the value of the annuity after 5 years?
parts.note: Annuity future value read from an interest-factor table (moved to Standard).

dif.r: Convert rate and periods, read table factor, multiply

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Carrington finds that he can only get an interest rate of 3.6\% p.a. compounding monthly.

If he wants to achieve the same total amount as Julia after the same period, what amount should he invest each month?
parts.note: Annuity contribution found with an interest-factor table (moved to Standard).

dif.r: Table factor used in reverse to find monthly contribution

solutions.latex:
The rate is $5.4\%\div12=0.45\%$ per month.

$5$ years is $5\times12=60$ months.

From the table, the factor for $0.45\%$ and $60$ months is $68.7047$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value}&=250\times68.7047 \\ &=\$17\,176.18 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The annuity is worth } \$17\,176.18$$
criteria: Finds the correct interest factor, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The rate is $3.6\%\div12=0.30\%$ per month.

From the table, the factor for $0.30\%$ and $60$ months is $65.6316$.

The monthly amount $M$ must satisfy $65.6316M=17\,176.18$.

$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{17\,176.18}{65.6316} \\ &\approx 261.70595 \\ &\approx \$261.71 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{He should invest } \$261.71 \text{ per month.}$$
criteria: Finds the correct interest factor, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2e^{4x} \\ \dfrac{y}{2}&=e^{4x} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right)&=4x \\ x&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $y=2e^{4x}$:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=8e^{4x}$$

From part (a), $x=\dfrac{\ln y}{4}-\dfrac{\ln 2}{4}$, so

$$\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac{1}{4y}$$

$$\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac{1}{8e^{4x}}$$

Hence

parts.latex:
Consider the geometric series below:

$$\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)+\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)^3+\cdots$$

Show that the series will have a sum to infinity when $x=4$, but not when $x=-4$.

dif.r: Identify ratio, test |r|<1 for two values

solutions.latex:
The ratio is $r=\dfrac{4}{x+1}$. A sum to infinity exists if $|r|<1$.

When $x=4$:

$$r=\dfrac{4}{4+1}=\dfrac{4}{5},\qquad \left|\dfrac{4}{5}\right|<1$$

So there is a limiting sum.

When $x=-4$:

$$r=\dfrac{4}{-4+1}=-\dfrac{4}{3},\qquad \left|-\dfrac{4}{3}\right|=\dfrac{4}{3}>1$$

So there is no limiting sum.
criteria: Sets up and evaluates $r$ for either value, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A company manufactures light bulbs. The expected life of the light bulb $t$ in days is given by the probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}} & t\ge 0\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

dif.r: Total probability 1 with improper exponential integral

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A light bulb is considered faulty if its lifespan is less than 100 days.

Determine the percentage of light bulbs that are considered faulty and the $z$-score that 100 days would represent on a normal distribution curve.

dif.r: Integrate pdf, then link 2.5% tail to z=-2 via empirical rule

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the median number of days a light bulb lasts if it is produced by this company.

dif.r: Set CDF to 0.5 and solve with logarithms

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt&=1 \\ \left[-\dfrac{4\,000}{k}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^\infty&=1 \\ -\dfrac{4\,000}{k}[0-1]&=1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k=4\,000$$

A bulb is faulty if its life is under $100$ days, using $k=4\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(0\le T\le100)&=\int_0^{100}\dfrac{1}{4\,000}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt \\ &=\left[-e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^{100} \\ &=1-e^{-\frac{1}{40}} \\ &\approx 0.0246 \\ &\approx 2.5\% \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ $2.5\%$ of bulbs last less than $100$ days and are considered faulty.

In a normal distribution, $95\%$ of scores lie within $2$ standard deviations of the mean. This leaves $5\%$ outside, so $2.5\%$ at each end.

$$\therefore\ 100 \text{ days is approximately a } z\text{-score of } -2$$
criteria: Finds either the probability or the $z$-score, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let the median be $x$, so the area from $0$ to $x$ is $0.5$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{4\,000}e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\,dt \\ &=\left[-e^{-\frac{t}{4\,000}}\right]_0^x \\ &=1-e^{-\frac{x}{4\,000}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} e^{-\frac{x}{4\,000}}&=0.5 \\ -\dfrac{x}{4\,000}&=\ln 0.5 \\ x&=-4\,000\ln 0.5 \\ &\approx 2\,772.55 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The median is } 2\,773 \text{ days}$$
criteria: Sets the integral equal to $0.5$ and makes some progress towards finding $x$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Reverse z-score for raw mark, then compare z-scores

solutions.latex:
For each student, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lachie: } z&=\dfrac{68-68}{8}=0 \\ \text{Emily: } z&=\dfrac{68-74}{6}=-1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Lachie performed best compared to his cohort.}$$

meta.format_note: Table values for English come from the question tables; not rechecked.

solutions.latex:
Lachie's $z$-score is $2$, so

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-62}{9}&=2 \\ x-62&=2\times9=18 \\ x&=80 \end{aligned}$$

Lachie's raw score was $80$.

Emily's $z$-score is

$$z=\dfrac{79-64}{5}=3$$

Emily has the higher $z$-score.

$$\therefore\ \text{Emily performed better on the Maths exam compared to her cohort.}$$
criteria: Finds the correct raw score for Lachie, or the correct $z$-score for Emily

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a shaded sector in a circle with radius $r$ and centre O.

The sector subtends an angle of $\theta$ at the centre of the circle. The area of the sector is 49 cm$^2$.

\exfigure{1544_q28_1}

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$ and hence show that the minimum perimeter of the sector will occur when the arc length of the sector is equal to the diameter of the circle.

dif.r: Build perimeter function from sector area, optimise, interpret arc length

figures.cap: shaded sector of circle, centre O, radius r, angle theta

solutions.latex:
The area of a sector is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, and $A=49$ cm$^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} 49&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \\ 98&=r^2\theta \\ \theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2} \end{aligned}$$

The arc length is

$$l=r\theta=r\times\dfrac{98}{r^2}=\dfrac{98}{r}$$

The perimeter is two radii plus the arc:

$$P=2r+\dfrac{98}{r}=2r+98r^{-1}$$

Differentiating:

$$\dfrac{dP}{dr}=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{r^3}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}&=0 \\ r^2&=49 \\ r&=7 \quad (r>0) \end{aligned}$$

Nature: when $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{7^3}>0$, so this is a minimum.

The minimum perimeter occurs when $r=7$ cm, so the diameter is $14$ cm.

Then $\theta=\dfrac{98}{7^2}=2$, so

$$l=r\theta=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14 \text{ cm}$$

This equals $2r$, the diameter.

$$\therefore\ \text{The perimeter is a minimum when the arc length equals the diameter.}$$
criteria: Shows $\theta$, forms an expression for $P$ and differentiates to find the minimum at $r=7$, or equivalent merit
Shows $\theta$, finds an equation for the perimeter and differentiates, or equivalent merit
Shows the equation for $\theta$, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ \text{The graph has a maximum turning point at } t=1.$$

questions.stem:
The function below models the general normal distribution.

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f'(x)$ can be written as $f'(x)=\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2}f(x)$.

dif.r: Chain rule on parametric exponent, rearrange to general form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $f''(x)$ in terms of $f(x)$

dif.r: Product rule using f' in terms of f; symbolic algebra

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the points of inflection for this function occur when $x$ is exactly one standard deviation from the mean $\mu$. You do not need to test or show the change in concavity at these points.

dif.r: General show-that: solve f''=0, argue f nonzero, get μ±σ

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on the exponent $-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\times\dfrac{1}{\sigma}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left(-\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \\ &=-\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2}f(x) \end{aligned}$$

as required.
criteria: Shows some progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2} & v&=f(x) \\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2} & v'&=\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2}f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=u'v+uv' \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}f(x)+\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2}\times\dfrac{\mu-x}{\sigma^2}f(x) \\ &=\dfrac{(\mu-x)^2}{\sigma^4}f(x)-\dfrac{f(x)}{\sigma^2} \\ &=\dfrac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\dfrac{(\mu-x)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right] \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule and makes some progress towards $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$:

$$\dfrac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\dfrac{(\mu-x)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right]=0$$

Since $f(x)\ne0$, the first factor is never zero, so

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{(\mu-x)^2}{\sigma^2}-1&=0 \\ (\mu-x)^2&=\sigma^2 \\ \mu-x&=\pm\sigma \\ x&=\mu\pm\sigma \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The inflections are one standard deviation either side of the mean.}$$
criteria: Sets $f''(x)=0$ and makes progress towards finding the inflection points, or equivalent merit (change in concavity not required)

questions.stem: Rylie deposits \$2000 at the beginning of every month for 35 years into a superannuation account, which pays an interest rate of 3.6\% per annum, compounding monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that when Rylie retires, at the end of the final month, he has $A=\$1\,684\,222.89$ in his account.

dif.r: Construct annuity-due geometric series with start-of-month deposits

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
After Rylie retires, he stops all deposits and now withdraws \$9000 at the end of each month from this account. If the account continues to gain interest at the same amount 3.6\% pa compounded monthly, show that after $n$ withdrawals, the account has

$$M_n=3000000-(3000000-A)r^n$$

Where $r=1.003$

dif.r: Derive general withdrawal formula from recurrence and geometric sum

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If Rylie turns 67 the day after the final interest is paid, at what age will Rylie no longer be able to withdraw his full \$9000.

dif.r: Solve M_n=0 with logs, interpret months as age

solutions.latex:
Here $P=\$2\,000$, the monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{3.6}{100\times12}=0.003$, and $n=35\times12=420$ months.

Each deposit grows for a different number of months:

$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=2\,000(1.003)^{420} \\ A_2&=2\,000(1.003)^{419} \\ A_3&=2\,000(1.003)^{418} \\ &\ \ \vdots \\ A_{420}&=2\,000(1.003) \end{aligned}$$

The total is

$$A_T=2\,000\left[1.003+1.003^2+\cdots+1.003^{420}\right]$$

This is a geometric series with $a=1.003$, ratio $1.003$ and $420$ terms, so using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:

$$\begin{aligned} A_T&=2\,000\times\dfrac{1.003\,(1.003^{420}-1)}{0.003} \\ &=\$1\,684\,222.89 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up an expression for the total amount invested, or equivalent merit
Writes $M_1=A(1.003)-9\,000$ and $M_2$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The money runs out when $M_n=0$:

$$0=3\,000\,000-(3\,000\,000-1\,684\,222.89)(1.003)^n$$

$$\begin{aligned} 1\,315\,777.11\,(1.003)^n&=3\,000\,000 \\ (1.003)^n&=\dfrac{3\,000\,000}{1\,315\,777.11} \\ n\ln(1.003)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{3\,000\,000}{1\,315\,777.11}\right) \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3\,000\,000}{1\,315\,777.11}\right)}{\ln(1.003)} \\ &\approx 275.14 \text{ months} \end{aligned}$$

This is one month short of $23$ years ($276$ months), and $67+23=90$.

$$\therefore\ \text{Rylie can no longer withdraw the full } \$9\,000 \text{ one month before his 90th birthday.}$$
criteria: Correct substitution and some progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=x^2e^x$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, inflections, intercepts and show what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.

dif.r: Full curve sketch: product rule, surd inflections, limits; long but standard

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x^2 e^x with labelled features

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^x \\ u'&=2x & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$

$$y'=2xe^x+x^2e^x=xe^x(2+x)$$

Differentiating again (product rule on each term):

$$y''=e^x(2+4x+x^2)$$

Stationary points: $y'=0$. Since $e^x\ne0$, either $x=0$ or $2+x=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=-2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=-2$, $y=\dfrac{4}{e^2}$.

Nature, using the sign of $y''$:

$$\begin{aligned} x=0:\ y''&=1(2)>0 &&\text{minimum at }(0,0) \\ x=-2:\ y''&=e^{-2}(2-8+4)<0 &&\text{maximum at }\left(-2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Inflections: $y''=0$. Since $e^x\ne0$,

$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+2&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-8}}{2} \\ &=-2\pm\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

Test the concavity either side of each root, using the sign of $x^2+4x+2$:

$$\begin{aligned} x=-4,\ -3.4,\ -1 &&&\text{signs of }y''\text{: }>0,\ 0,\ <0 \\ x=-1,\ -0.6,\ 0 &&&\text{signs of }y''\text{: }<0,\ 0,\ >0 \end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at both roots, so both are points of inflection.

As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to0^+$ (the exponential dominates), and as $x\to\infty$, $y\to\infty$.

\exfigure{1544_q32_s1}
criteria: Correct answer (stationary points, their nature, inflections, intercepts, behaviour as $x\to\pm\infty$, clear sketch showing all points)
Shows only three key features, or equivalent merit
Shows only two key features, or equivalent merit
Finds stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The bearing $070^\circ$ gives
$$\angle RPQ=90^\circ-70^\circ=20^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:
$$\begin{aligned} RQ^{2}&=16^{2}+35^{2}-2\times16\times35\times\cos 20^\circ \\ &=428.54\ldots \end{aligned}$$

Let $\angle RQP=\theta$. By the sine rule:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{16}=\dfrac{\sin 20^\circ}{20.7}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta&=\dfrac{16\sin 20^\circ}{20.7} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}(0.264) \\ &=15.3^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The obtuse value $180^\circ-15.3^\circ=164.7^\circ$ would make the angle sum of $\triangle PQR$ exceed $180^\circ$, so $\theta$ is acute.

Alternatively, by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{20.7^{2}+35^{2}-16^{2}}{2\times20.7\times35} \\ &=0.9645 \end{aligned}$$
So $\theta=15.30^\circ$.

The bearing is
$$270^\circ+15^\circ=285^\circ$$ to the nearest degree.
criteria: Uses the sine or cosine rule correctly to find $\theta$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Interpret horizontal line intersections using turning point heights

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: cubic with turning points A and B and y-intercept (0,3)

solutions.latex:
Turning points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-3x^{2}+2x+1$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^{2}-2x-1&=0 \\ (3x+1)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$.

When $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=-\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{3}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+3 \\ &=2\dfrac{22}{27} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=-1+1+1+3 \\ &=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},2\dfrac{22}{27}\right),\ B(1,4)$$
criteria: Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve is concave down when $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}<0$.
$$\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-6x+2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -6x+2&<0 \\ 6x&>2 \\ x&>\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is concave down for } x>\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Finds the second derivative $-6x+2$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
One real solution means the line $y=k$ meets the curve only once.

This happens when $y=k$ lies above the maximum turning point $y=4$ or below the minimum turning point $y=2\dfrac{22}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ k>4 \text{ or } k<2\dfrac{22}{27}$$

questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$ from a sample space, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{5}{8}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{5}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate $P(A\cap B)$.

dif.r: Rearrange conditional probability formula, one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate $P(A'\cap B)$.

dif.r: Uses P(B) minus P(A∩B), with the intersection from part (a)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If events $A$ and $B$ are independent, calculate $P(A\cup B)$.

dif.r: Independence gives P(A)=P(A|B), then the standard union formula

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A\mid B)\times P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{1}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$

Using $P(A'\cap B)=P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ with $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{1}{8}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P(A'\cap B)&=\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{40} \end{aligned}$$

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $P(A)=P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{5}{8}$.

Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=\dfrac{5}{8}+\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{10} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x}=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x.$

dif.r: Trig proof needing two Pythagorean identities and fraction splitting

solutions.latex:
Method 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sin^{2}x}-\dfrac{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x-\cos^{2}x \\ &=1+\cot^{2}x-\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right) \\ &=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right)}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x+\sin^{4}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x}+\dfrac{\sin^{4}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct first step (or progress on another method), or equivalent merit

dif.r: Complement over two turns; must identify the qualifying score pairs

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Table of scores:

\extable{Ts3733_1}

There are $36$ equally likely outcomes, and $11$ of them give a score of zero.
$$P(\text{zero})=\dfrac{11}{36}$$
criteria: Table of outcomes (or similar), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From the table, $4$ of the $36$ outcomes give a score of $64$ or more.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\ge 64)&=\dfrac{4}{36} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: the sum is $180$ or more only for the score pairs $(100,100)$, $(100,80)$ and $(80,100)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(<180)&=1-P(\ge180) \\ &=1-\left[P(100,100)+P(100,80)+P(80,100)\right] \\ &=1-\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{1}{36}\times\dfrac{2}{36}+\dfrac{2}{36}\times\dfrac{1}{36}\right] \\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{36^{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1291}{1296} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the cases with sum $\ge180$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find all possible solutions to $\left(\tan^{2}x-1\right)\left(\sin^{2}x-3\cos^{2}x\right)=0$, for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.

dif.r: Two trig equations from factors, many solutions in a negative domain

solutions.latex:
A product is zero when one factor is zero, so
$$\tan^{2}x-1=0 \quad \text{or} \quad \sin^{2}x-3\cos^{2}x=0$$
First factor: $\tan x=\pm1$, with acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
Second factor: $\sin^{2}x=3\cos^{2}x$. Here $\cos x=0$ is not a solution, so divide by $\cos^{2}x$:
$$\tan^{2}x=3$$
So $\tan x=\pm\sqrt{3}$, with acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
Alternatively, using $\cos^{2}x=1-\sin^{2}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin^{2}x-3\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right)&=0 \\ 4\sin^{2}x&=3 \\ \sin x&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This gives the same solutions.
$$\therefore\ x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Solutions from one factor and progress on the other, or equivalent merit
Separates into two factors, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the exact value of the limiting sum.

Write your answer with a rational denominator.

dif.r: Limiting sum with a compound surd fraction and rationalising

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-1}\approx0.809$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.

Here $a=r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-1}$, and $S_{\infty}=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{\infty}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}-1}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}-1}} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}-1}}{\frac{\sqrt{5}-1-1}{\sqrt{5}-1}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+2}{\sqrt{5}+2} \\ &=\sqrt{5}+2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A water cooler, which is initially full, is drained so that at time $t$ seconds the volume of water $V$, in litres, is given by

$$V=32\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2}\ \text{ for } 0\le t\le 90.$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How much water was initially in the cooler?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into the model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how many seconds was the cooler one-quarter full?

dif.r: Interpret one-quarter full, then solve a squared equation

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what rate was the water draining out when the cooler was one-quarter full?

dif.r: Chain rule derivative evaluated, interpreting the negative rate

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=32(1-0)^{2} \\ &=32 \text{ litres} \end{aligned}$$

One-quarter full means $V=\dfrac{32}{4}=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8&=32\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{4}&=\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=1-\dfrac{t}{90} \\ \dfrac{t}{90}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ t&=45 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=32\times2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right)=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)$$
When $t=45$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt}&=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{45}{90}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{64}{90}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=-\dfrac{32}{90} \\ &=-\dfrac{16}{45} \end{aligned}$$
The water is draining at $\dfrac{16}{45}$ litres/sec when the cooler is one-quarter full.
criteria: Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

criteria: Sum of probabilities equals 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ the probabilities are $0.3,\ 0.15,\ 0.5,\ 0.05$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\sum xp(x) \\ &=0.15+2(0.5)+3(0.05) \\ &=1.30 \end{aligned}$$

Since $E(X)=1.3$, the values of $X$ below $1.3$ are $0$ and $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<1.3)&=P(X\le1) \\ &=0.3+0.15 \\ &=0.45 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:

$$x^{2}+y^{2}=\left(\sqrt{5}\right)^{2}$$

$$\dfrac{dL}{dx}=4+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(5-x^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-2x)=4-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{5-x^{2}}}$$

Squaring:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^{2}&=16\left(5-x^{2}\right) \\ x^{2}&=20-4x^{2} \\ 5x^{2}&=20 \\ x^{2}&=4 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x$ is a length, $x=2$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dL}{dx}$ either side of $x=2$:

\extable{Ts3752_1}

$$\therefore\ x=2$$

questions.stem:
Benjamin borrows \$135 000 to be paid over a period of 30 years at 5% per annum reducible interest. Each year there are $k$ regular repayments of \$$M$.

Interest is calculated and charged just before each repayment.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write an expression for the amount owing after two repayments.

dif.r: Recurrence for two repayments with a general rate 0.05/k

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the amount owing after $n$ repayments is

$$A_{n}=135\,000\,\beta^{n}-\dfrac{kM\left(\beta^{n}-1\right)}{0.05},\qquad \text{where } \beta=1+\dfrac{0.05}{k}.$$

dif.r: General show-that: geometric series in β with a parameter k

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Calculate the amount of each repayment if the repayments are made quarterly (ie. $k=4$).

dif.r: Set A_n=0 in a given formula and solve for M

parts.label: d
parts.latex: How much would Benjamin have saved over the term of the loan if he had chosen to make monthly rather than quarterly repayments?

dif.r: Find the monthly repayment, then compare total costs of both schemes

solutions.latex:
The rate per repayment period is $\dfrac{5\%}{k}=\dfrac{0.05}{k}$.
$$A_{1}=135\,000\left(1+\dfrac{0.05}{k}\right)-M$$
After the second repayment:
$$A_{2}=135\,000\left(1+\dfrac{0.05}{k}\right)^{2}-M\left(1+\dfrac{0.05}{k}\right)-M$$

From part (a), with $\beta=1+\dfrac{0.05}{k}$:
$$A_{2}=135\,000\beta^{2}-M\beta-M$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} A_{n}&=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\beta^{n-1}-M\beta^{n-2}-\cdots-M \\ &=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\left(1+\beta+\beta^{2}+\cdots+\beta^{n-1}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=\beta$ and $n$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{n}&=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\dfrac{\beta^{n}-1}{\beta-1} \\ &=135\,000\beta^{n}-M\dfrac{\beta^{n}-1}{\frac{0.05}{k}} \\ &=135\,000\beta^{n}-\dfrac{kM\left(\beta^{n}-1\right)}{0.05} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Expresses $A_n$ using the geometric series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $k=4$: $n=30\times4=120$ and $\beta=1+\dfrac{0.05}{4}=1.0125$.

The loan is repaid when $A_{120}=0$:
$$135\,000\beta^{120}-\dfrac{4M\left(\beta^{120}-1\right)}{0.05}=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{135\,000\beta^{120}\times0.05}{4\left(\beta^{120}-1\right)} \\ &=\$2178.02 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the sequence:

$2, 6, 18, 54, \ldots$

How many terms of the sequence are less than 300?

dif.r: List geometric terms and count those below 300

solutions.latex:
The sequence is geometric with $a = 2$ and $r = 3$, so $T_n = 2\times 3^{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_4 &= ar^3 = 54 \\ T_5 &= ar^4 = 162 < 300 \\ T_6 &= 2\times 3^5 = 486 > 300 \end{aligned}$$
Hence exactly 5 terms are less than 300, which is option B.

parts.latex: Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the series: $2 + 6 + 18 + 54 + \ldots$

dif.r: Direct substitution into geometric sum formula

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a = 2$, $r = 3$, $n = 15$, so $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{2(3^{15}-1)}{3-1} \\ &= 3^{15}-1 \\ &= 14348906 \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

dif.r: Probabilities sum to one; single linear equation

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} k+2k+k+3k+k+2k &= 1 \\ 10k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Find the sum of the first 6 terms of the series $\log 3 + \log 9 + \log 81 + \ldots$

solutions.latex:
Writing each term as a multiple of $\log 3$:

parts.latex: How many weeks will it take for the total membership to pass $10^8$ members? (1 dp)

dif.r: Solve exponential inequality with logs, convert days to weeks

solutions.latex:
The sequence is geometric with $a = 13$ and $r = 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= ar^{n-1} \\ &= 13\times 3^{n-1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T_{15} &= 13\times 3^{14} \\ &= 62178597 \end{aligned}$$

The membership on day $n$ must exceed $10^8$.
$$\begin{aligned} 13\times 3^{n-1} &> 10^8 \\ 3^{n-1} &> \dfrac{10^8}{13} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} (n-1)\log_{10} 3 &= \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{10^8}{13}\right) \\ n &= \dfrac{\log_{10}\left(\frac{10^8}{13}\right)}{\log_{10} 3} + 1 \\ &= 15.4325\ldots \text{ days} \\ &\approx 2.2 \text{ weeks} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
At which point on this curve are the first and second derivatives both negative?

\exfigure{175_q3_1}

dif.r: Read the signs of the first and second derivatives from a curve's shape

figures.cap: cubic curve through O with points A, B, C, D

solutions.latex:
The first derivative is negative where the curve is decreasing. The second derivative is negative where the curve is concave down.

The curve is decreasing only between the maximum at $O$ and the minimum, so only $B$ and $C$ can have $f'(x)<0$ ($A$ and $D$ are on rising parts).

The curve is concave down from the left up to the point of inflection, which lies between $B$ and $C$. After that it is concave up.

So $B$ is decreasing and concave down, while $C$ is decreasing and concave up.
$$\begin{aligned} B&: f'(x)<0,\ f''(x)<0\\ C&: f'(x)<0,\ f''(x)>0\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is $B$.

The function $y = \sqrt{x}$ is transformed by the following transformations in order:

\begin{itemize}
\item Translation 3 units right
\item Dilation horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Translation 1 unit down
\item Dilation vertically by a factor of 4
\end{itemize}

Apply the transformations in order.

Translation 3 units right replaces $x$ by $x-3$:

Dilation horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$:
$$y=\sqrt{2x-3}$$
Translation 1 unit down subtracts 1:
$$y=\sqrt{2x-3}-1$$
Dilation vertically by a factor of 4 multiplies by 4:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 4\left(\sqrt{2x-3}-1\right) \\ &= 4\sqrt{2x-3}-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4\sqrt{2x-3}-4$$

solutions.latex:

Cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants.

The related acute angle is $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

In the 2nd quadrant, $x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

In the 3rd quadrant, $x=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$

questions.stem:
The surface area of a box in the shape of a rectangular prism is $294\text{cm}^2$. The box has a square base $x\text{cm}$ long and is $h\text{cm}$ high.

\exfigure{175_q12_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the box is $V = \dfrac{147x - x^3}{2}$

dif.r: Model surface area, eliminate h, derive the volume expression

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $x$ for which this volume is a maximum.

dif.r: Standard stationary point with a second-derivative test on a given function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find this maximum volume.

dif.r: Substitute the found x into the given formula

figures.cap: rectangular prism with square base x and height h

solutions.latex:
The surface area is two square ends plus four rectangular sides:
$$\begin{aligned} 294 &= 2x^2+4xh \\ 4xh &= 294-2x^2 \\ h &= \dfrac{294-2x^2}{4x} \\ &= \dfrac{2\left(147-x^2\right)}{4x} \\ &= \dfrac{147-x^2}{2x} \end{aligned}$$
The volume is base area times height:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= x^2h \\ &= x^2\left(\dfrac{147-x^2}{2x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{147x-x^3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $h$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit
Writes the surface area equation, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write the volume as
$$V=\dfrac{147x}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{2}$$
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=\dfrac{147}{2}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-3x$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{147}{2}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2} &= 0 \\ 147-3x^2 &= 0 \\ 3\left(49-x^2\right) &= 0 \\ 3(7+x)(7-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x>0$, $x=7$.

When $x=7$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-3\times 7=-21<0$$
so the volume is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ x=7$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{147x-x^3}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{147(7)-7^3}{2} \\ &= 343 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum volume}=343 \text{ cm}^3$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is true for the function $y=2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+4$

dif.r: Standard period and range of transformed cosine.

solutions.latex:
The period is
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{3}}=6\pi$$
The cosine term lies between $-2$ and $2$, so $y$ lies between $4-2=2$ and $4+2=6$.

The range is $[2,6]$.

Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: Which of the following could be the graph of the function $y=2\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+1$

dif.r: Log law simplification then identify transformed log graph.

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

option B: log graph option B
option C: log graph option C
option D: log graph option D

solutions.latex:
Using $\ln x^{-1}=-\ln x$:
$$y=2\ln x^{-1}+1=-2\ln x+1$$
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-2\ln x+1 \\ \ln x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ x&=e^{\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{e} \end{aligned}$$
The graph is decreasing, so the answer is (D).

dif.r: Read asymptotes, substitute intercept to find k, compare.

figures.cap: hyperbola with asymptotes x=3, y=2 and y-intercept 10/3

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2$, so $c=2$, and the vertical asymptote is $x=3$, so $b=-3$.

Hence $y=\dfrac{k}{x-3}+2$.

Substitute the $y$-intercept $\left(0,\dfrac{10}{3}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10}{3}&=\dfrac{k}{-3}+2 \\ -10&=k-6 \\ k&=-4 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $k<b<c$, since $-4<-3<2$.

The answer is (A).

dif.r: Two equations: probabilities sum to one and expected value.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$m+n+0.5=1$$
so $m+n=0.5$ and $n=0.5-m$.

Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)=1.8$:
$$\begin{aligned} m+0.6+3n&=1.8 \\ m+0.6+3(0.5-m)&=1.8 \\ m+0.6+1.5-3m&=1.8 \\ 0.3&=2m \\ m&=0.15 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $n=0.35$.

The answer is (A).

parts.latex:
Consider the cumulative probability density function

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\[6pt] \cos^2 x, & \dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\pi\\[6pt] 1, & x>\pi\end{cases}$$

What is the 3rd quartile of the distribution?

dif.r: Solve F(x)=3/4 with trig, choosing correct quadrant.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The third quartile satisfies $F(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2 x&=\dfrac{3}{4} \\ \cos x&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. For $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\pi$, $\cos x$ is negative, so $x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

The answer is (D).

parts.latex: Factorise: $4x^2-(w+y)^2$

dif.r: Difference of two squares with a binomial term.

solutions.latex:
Using the difference of two squares, $a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2-(w+y)^2&=(2x)^2-(w+y)^2 \\ &=(2x-(w+y))(2x+(w+y)) \\ &=(2x-w-y)(2x+w+y) \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Given that $f(x)=3x-1$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2x}$ find:

dif.r: Single substitution to form a composite function.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: The domain of $g(f(x))$.

dif.r: Domain excludes zero denominator; one routine step.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $f(x)$ into $g$:
$$\begin{aligned} g(f(x))&=\dfrac{1}{2(3x-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6x-2} \end{aligned}$$

The denominator cannot be zero:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-2&\ne 0 \\ x&\ne\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Domain: } x\in\left(-\infty,\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\cup\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\infty\right)$$

parts.latex: Differentiate with respect to $x$: $f(x)=\dfrac{3\sin x^2}{x}$

dif.r: Quotient rule combined with chain rule on sin x^2.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3\sin x^2 & v&=x \\ u'&=6x\cos x^2 & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{(6x\cos x^2)(x)-(1)(3\sin x^2)}{x^2} \\ &=\dfrac{6x^2\cos x^2-3\sin x^2}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule with a correct $u'$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Oliver buys a car for \$19000 and repays it over 4 years through equal monthly instalments. He pays a 20\% deposit and interest is charged at 9\% p.a. on the balance of the loan.

[Below is a table of present value interest factors for an annuity of \$1]

\exfigure{1320_q15_1}

What is the total amount that Oliver pays for the car?
parts.note: Annuity present-value interest-factor table look-up (2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only).

dif.r: Several steps: loan, rate, table factor, repayment, add deposit.

figures.cap: Table of Present Value Interest Factors (N = 45 to 50, r = 0.0060 to 0.0085)

solutions.latex:
The loan is the price less the 20\% deposit:
$$PV=0.8\times 19000=15200$$
The loan is repaid monthly over 4 years, so $n=4\times 12=48$ and $r=\dfrac{9\%}{12}=0.0075$.

From the table, the factor is $40.18478$, so
$$PV=M\times 40.18478$$
$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{15200}{40.18478} \\ &=378.25 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$
Total paid is the repayments plus the deposit:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total}&=378.25\times 48+0.2\times 19000 \\ &=\$21956 \end{aligned}$$
This is \$21956.13 if the exact $M$ is used.
criteria: Finds the monthly repayment $M$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Combine halves of empirical rule percentages.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: At the beginning of the Year 2022, 50 000 pairs of gumboots were produced. How many of these pairs of gumboots would you expect to last past the beginning of 2031?

dif.r: Interpret dates as 9 years, then 3 sd tail count.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: iv
parts.latex:
A full refund is provided if a pair of gumboots lasts less than 2 years. Estimate the percentage of purchases that will be refunded?

[A $z$-score table is provided on pages 37 – 38]

dif.r: Compute z-score and read lower tail from table.

figures.cap: blank normal distribution curve with seven tick marks
solution sketch: normal curve labelled 1.8, 3, 4.2, 5.4, 6.6, 7.8, 9

meta.format_note: Figure id kept as in the source solution (1320_q18_s1); the record's sketch_id is 1320_q18_s2. Sketch: normal curve on the given axes, centred at $5.4$, labelled $1.8, 3, 4.2, 5.4, 6.6, 7.8, 9$ at $\mu-3\sigma$ to $\mu+3\sigma$.

solutions.latex:
The interval $3$ to $6.6$ runs from $2$ standard deviations below the mean to $1$ above.

Using the 95\% and 68\% rules:
$$\dfrac{95\%}{2}+\dfrac{68\%}{2}=81.5\%$$

Lasting past the start of 2031 means a life over $9$ years, which is $3$ standard deviations above the mean.

Using the 99.7\% rule, the proportion above $\mu+3\sigma$ is $\dfrac{1-0.997}{2}$:
$$50000\times\dfrac{1-0.997}{2}=75$$
So about 75 pairs.

Here $x=2$, $\mu=5.4$, $\sigma=1.2$.
$$\begin{aligned} z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \\ &=\dfrac{2-5.4}{1.2} \\ &=-2.833\ldots\approx-2.83 \end{aligned}$$
From the $z$-score table, $P(Z<-2.83)=0.23\%$.

$$\therefore\ \text{about } 0.23\% \text{ of purchases could be refunded}$$

questions.stem:
Anthony stands at point A, 230 m due east of the tower OT, of height $h$ metres. The angle of elevation of T from A is $15^\circ$. Brian, at point B, is due south of the tower OT. The angle of elevation to the top of the tower from B is $10^\circ$.

\exfigure{1320_q19_1}
questions.review_note: Figure crop includes the teacher's purple handwritten annotations (N arrow, curved arrow near A) that are part of the page image

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the height of the tower is 61.6 metres correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: Single tan ratio in right-angled triangle.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find how far Brian is from the bottom of the tower. Round your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: Single tan ratio rearranged for adjacent side.

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: What is the bearing of Brian from Anthony?
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: Right-triangle tan then convert angle to a bearing; simpler than sine-rule bearing

figures.cap: tower OT with points A (east) and B (south), angles 15 and 10 degrees

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $OAT$, the angle at $A$ is $15^\circ$, the side opposite is $h$ and the adjacent side is $OA=230$.

Using $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 15^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{230} \\ h&=230\tan 15^\circ \\ &=61.6283\ldots \\ &=61.6 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$

In the right-angled triangle $OBT$, the angle at $B$ is $10^\circ$, the side opposite is $h$ and the adjacent side is $OB$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 10^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OB} \\ OB&=\dfrac{61.6}{\tan 10^\circ} \\ &=349.3509\ldots \\ &=349 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$
This is $350$ m if the exact part (i) answer is used.

Let $\angle OAB=\theta$, where $OB=349$ m (from part (ii)) and $OA=230$ m, in the right-angled triangle $OAB$.
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{349}{230}$$
so $\theta=56.614\ldots^\circ$.

Anthony is due east of $O$, so the bearing of $O$ from $A$ is $270^\circ$. Brian is south of $O$, so $B$ is to the south-west of $A$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 270-56.614\ldots \\ &= 213.38\ldots \\ &\approx 213^\circ \text{ (nearest degree)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of Brian from Anthony is } 213^\circ$$

The solution uses OB=349 from part (ii), which is not shown here. Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Evaluate exactly $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{3}{4x-1}\,dx$.

dif.r: Standard f'/f log integral with coefficient adjustment and exact evaluation

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand so the numerator is the derivative of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{3}{4x-1}\,dx &= \dfrac{3}{4}\int_1^2\dfrac{4}{4x-1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4}\Big[\ln|4x-1|\Big]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4}\left(\ln 7-\ln 3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4}\ln\dfrac{7}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{3}{4}\ln\dfrac{7}{3}$$
criteria: Writes the integral as $\dfrac{3}{4}\ln|4x-1|$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact value of the gradient of the tangent to $y=e^{2x}(x+2)$ at the point where $x=1$.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential, substitute x=1

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=x+2\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2e^{2x}(x+2)+1\cdot e^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}\left(2(x+2)+1\right) \\ &= e^{2x}(2x+5) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= e^2\left(2(1)+5\right) \\ &= 7e^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m_T=7e^2$$
criteria: Applies the product rule with correct $u,\ u',\ v,\ v'$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is $f(x)=\dfrac{x^4}{6}-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}+3x+1$ concave down?

dif.r: Second derivative then solve quadratic inequality

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{4x^3}{6}-\dfrac{6x^2}{3}+3=\dfrac{2x^3}{3}-2x^2+3$$
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{6x^2}{3}-4x=2x^2-4x$$
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2-4x&<0 \\ 2x(x-2)&<0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola $2x(x-2)$ is below the axis between its roots, so
$$\therefore\ 0<x<2$$
criteria: Finds $f''(x)$ and sets up $f''(x)<0$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The function $y=g(x)$ is transformed to the function $y=\dfrac{1}{2}g(3(x-1))+4$. Find the point $P(x,y)$ on $y=g(x)$, if its image point on the transformed function is $P'(-6,5)$.

dif.r: Reverse a combined transformation to find the pre-image point

solutions.latex:
Compare $y=\dfrac{1}{2}g\big(3(x-1)\big)+4$ with $y=kg\big(a(x-b)\big)+c$:
$$a=3,\quad b=1,\quad k=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad c=4$$
A point $(x,y)$ on $y=g(x)$ maps to $\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+1,\ \dfrac{y}{2}+4\right)$.

Matching the $x$ coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{3}+1&=-6 \\ x&=-21 \end{aligned}$$
Matching the $y$ coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y}{2}+4&=5 \\ y&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(-21,2)$$

dif.r: Area between curves with given intersections; routine integration

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: curves y=4-x^2 and y=x^3/4-x with shaded region between them

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=4-x^2$ lies above $y=\dfrac{x^3}{4}-x$ between $x=-2$ and $x=2$, so the area is
$$A=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left[(4-x^2)-\left(\dfrac{x^3}{4}-x\right)\right]dx$$
$$A=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left(4-x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{4}+x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left[4x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{16}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-2}^{2} \\ &= \left[4(2)-\dfrac{2^3}{3}-\dfrac{2^4}{16}+\dfrac{2^2}{2}\right]-\left[4(-2)-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{3}-\dfrac{(-2)^4}{16}+\dfrac{(-2)^2}{2}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{19}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{13}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{32}{3}\ \text{u}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{32}{3}\ \text{u}^2$$
criteria: Finds a correct primitive and substitutes limits, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of the curve $y=3x^3+12x^2+4$ labelling the stationary points, point of inflection and the $y$-intercept. Do NOT determine the $x$-intercepts of the curve.

(Use this page for your working. There is space for the sketch on the next page).

dif.r: Standard cubic sketch: stationary points, nature, inflection; fractional values

parts.label: b
parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does $3x^3+12x^2+4=k$ have 2 solutions?

dif.r: Interpret horizontal lines through turning points as giving two solutions

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=3x^3+12x^2+4

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.
$$y'=9x^2+24x,\qquad y''=18x+24$$
Stationary points: $y'=0$.
$$3x(3x+8)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=-\dfrac{8}{3}$.

At $x=0$, $y=4$, giving $(0,4)$. At $x=-\dfrac{8}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{292}{9}$, giving $\left(-\dfrac{8}{3},\dfrac{292}{9}\right)$.

Nature, using the sign of $y''$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=0:&\quad y''=24>0 &&\text{minimum}\\ x=-\dfrac{8}{3}:&\quad y''=-24<0 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
Point of inflection: $y''=0$.

questions.stem: A tennis ball is dropped from a height of 12 metres. After it first hits the ground, it rebounds to a height of 8 metres. It continues to rebound to a height of two thirds its previous rebound height.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: How high will the ball rise after the $6^{\text{th}}$ time it rebounds from the ground?

dif.r: Geometric term, must identify first term 8 not 12

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: What is the total vertical distance that the ball will eventually travel?

dif.r: Model up-and-down distances, double limiting sum plus initial drop

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The rebound heights form a geometric sequence: $8,\ 5\dfrac{1}{3},\ \ldots$ with $a=8$ and $r=\dfrac{2}{3}$. The 6th rebound is the term $n=6$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n&=ar^{n-1} \\ T_6&=8\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{6-1} \\ &=1.0534\ldots \\ &\approx 1.05 \text{ m (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the 6th rebound is } 1.05 \text{ m high}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The ball falls 12 m, then each rebound height is travelled up and down.
$$S=12+8+8+5\dfrac{1}{3}+5\dfrac{1}{3}+3\dfrac{5}{9}+3\dfrac{5}{9}+\cdots$$
After the first drop, the rebound heights form a geometric series with $a=8$ and $r=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Since $|r|<1$ it has a sum to infinity, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=12+2\left(8+5\dfrac{1}{3}+3\dfrac{5}{9}+\cdots\right) \\ &=12+2\left(\dfrac{8}{1-\frac{2}{3}}\right) \\ &=60 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the ball will travel } 60 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the total distance as $12+2\times$ (sum of rebound heights), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The blood pressure of women who are 50 years old is normally distributed with a mean of 124 and a standard deviation of 18.

Two 50-year-old women are chosen at random. What is the probability that the blood pressure of at least one woman is over 160?

dif.r: Empirical rule tail then complement for at least one of two

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
160 is $\dfrac{160-124}{18}=2$ standard deviations above the mean. About $95\%$ of values lie within 2 standard deviations, so
$$P(X>160)=\dfrac{100\%-95\%}{2}=2.5\%$$
For two women, use the complement of "both are under 160":
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one}>160)&=1-P(\text{both}<160) \\ &=1-(97.5\%\times 97.5\%) \\ &=0.049375 \\ &\approx 4.9\% \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4.9\%$$
criteria: Uses the complement with $P(X<160)=97.5\%$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Sam plays football, a sport where a team can Win, Lose or Draw.

Sam is prone to injury, and plays in 80\% of her team’s games.

When Sam plays, her team has a 73\% chance of winning and a 7\% chance of losing.

When Sam doesn’t play her team has a 55\% chance of winning and a 20\% chance of losing.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: By using a tree diagram or otherwise, show that the probability that Sam’s team wins any given game is 69.4\%.

dif.r: Total probability over two tree branches; answer given

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Given that Sam’s team doesn’t lose in a particular match, what is the probability that Sam played in that match?

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability with complement event 'not lose'

solutions.latex:
Let $S$ be the event that Sam plays, and $W$, $L$, $D$ a win, loss or draw.

\exfigure{1320_q32_s1}

A win happens either way, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(W)&=P(S\cap W)+P(\bar S\cap W) \\ &=(0.8\times 0.73)+(0.2\times 0.55) \\ &=0.584+0.11 \\ &=0.694 \\ &=69.4\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the two winning branches, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $S$ be the event that Sam plays and $\bar L$ the event that the team does not lose. Using conditional probability,
$$P(S\mid\bar L)=\dfrac{P(S\cap\bar L)}{P(\bar L)}$$
Numerator: Sam plays and the team wins or draws, $0.8\times 0.73+0.8\times 0.2$.

Denominator: one minus the probability of losing, $1-\left[0.8\times 0.07+0.2\times 0.2\right]$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(S\mid\bar L)&=\dfrac{(0.8\times 0.73)+(0.8\times 0.2)}{1-\left[0.8\times 0.07+0.2\times 0.2\right]} \\ &=\dfrac{0.744}{0.904} \\ &\approx 82.3\% \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the numerator and denominator, or equivalent merit
Uses $P(S\mid\bar L)=\dfrac{P(S\cap\bar L)}{P(\bar L)}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Maryann invests \$20000 into a superannuation fund at the \textbf{end of each year} to save for her retirement. The interest \textbf{compounds monthly} at a rate of 6 \% p.a.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that after three years, the value of Maryann’s superannuation fund is \$63776.75.

dif.r: Annual deposits with monthly compounding; build recurrence using 1.005^12

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After 10 years, just after her $10^{\text{th}}$ deposit of \$20000, Maryanne withdraws \$100,000 to buy an apartment. Given that she continues to invest \$20000 at the end of each year, find the value of Maryann’s superannuation fund after a \textbf{further} 5 years?

dif.r: Multi-stage annuity: GP sum, withdrawal, growth plus new annuity

criteria: Writes $A_{36}$ as a correct sum of three terms, or equivalent merit
Finds the monthly rate and the yearly growth factor, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $A_{36}=20000\left(1+1.005^{12}+1.005^{24}\right)$. After 10 deposits this is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.005^{12}$ and $n=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{120}&=20000\left(1+1.005^{12}+1.005^{24}+\cdots+1.005^{108}\right) \\ &=20000\left(\dfrac{(1.005^{12})^{10}-1}{1.005^{12}-1}\right) \\ &=\$265702.271\ldots \\ &=\$265702.27 \end{aligned}$$
After the withdrawal of $\$100000$ the value is $\$165702.27$.

Over the further 5 years (60 months) this amount grows to $165702.27(1.005)^{60}$, and the new deposits form a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.005^{12}$ and $n=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{New annuity}&=20000\left(1+1.005^{12}+1.005^{24}+\cdots+1.005^{48}\right) \\ &=20000\left(\dfrac{(1.005^{12})^{5}-1}{1.005^{12}-1}\right) \\ &=\$113120.1455 \end{aligned}$$
Total value:
$$\begin{aligned} &165702.27(1.005)^{60}+113120.1455 \\ &=\$336627.6767\ldots \\ &=\$336627.68 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the fund is worth } \$336627.68$$
criteria: Finds the value of the original amount after 5 years and the new annuity, or equivalent merit
Finds the value after the withdrawal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A car travelling at a constant speed of $v$ km/h consumes fuel at the rate of $\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)$ litres per hour.

Hai hires this car for a rental fee of \$10 per hour. Fuel costs \$2.12/litre and his total trip has a distance of 550 km.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the total cost of the trip in dollars is given by $C=\dfrac{55583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600}$.

dif.r: Build cost model from rates, time 550/v, and fuel price

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the minimum cost Hai will have to pay for his trip.

dif.r: Routine minimisation of given function; awkward numbers, second derivative test

solutions.latex:
Total cost is rental plus fuel, both over the time $t=\dfrac{d}{v}=\dfrac{550}{v}$ hours.
$$\text{Cost}=10t+2.12\times\left[\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)\right]t$$
$$\begin{aligned} C&=10\times\dfrac{550}{v}+2.12\times\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)\times\dfrac{550}{v} \\ &=\dfrac{5500}{v}+\dfrac{583}{10v}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{5500}{v}+\dfrac{583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600} \\ &=\dfrac{55583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes $t=\dfrac{550}{v}$ into the cost expression, or equivalent merit
Writes the cost as rental plus fuel in terms of $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write $C=\dfrac{55583}{10}v^{-1}+\dfrac{583v}{600}$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dv}=-\dfrac{55583}{10}v^{-2}+\dfrac{583}{600}$$
Stationary point: $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{583}{600}&=\dfrac{55583}{10v^2} \\ v^2&=\dfrac{55583\times 600}{10\times 583} \\ &=5720.377\ldots \end{aligned}$$
so $v=75.633\ldots$ km/h (since $v>0$).

Nature: the sign of $C''$ decides.
$$C''=\dfrac{111166}{10}v^{-3}=\dfrac{111166}{10v^3}>0 \text{ for all } v>0$$
so $v=75.633\ldots$ km/h gives the minimum cost.
$$\begin{aligned} C_{\min}&=\dfrac{55583}{10\times 75.633\ldots}+\dfrac{583\times 75.633\ldots}{600} \\ &=\$146.98 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost is } \$146.98$$
criteria: Finds $v$ and tests that it gives a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dC}{dv}$ and sets it to zero, or equivalent merit
