The figure shows three towns $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.

There are three roads out of town $X$ and two roads out of town $Y$.

If they select their ways randomly, what is the probability that they will meet on their way?

dif.r: Interpret road diagram, then multiply two independent probabilities.

can_use: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

figures.cap: roads joining towns X, Y and Z

solutions.latex:
Mr Kent can choose a road that leads to Mr Wayne in 2 of his 3 roads, so the probability is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Mr Wayne must then choose the same road, 1 of his 2 roads, so the probability is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{meet}) &= \dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
A certain function $f(x)$ has the following properties: $f(0) = -1$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = -3$.

Which of the following is possible for all values of $x$?

dif.r: Infer signs of f' and f'' from value and asymptotic behaviour.

solutions.latex:
The function starts at $f(0)=-1$ and tends to $-3$, so it must decrease: $f'(x)<0$.

It approaches a horizontal asymptote, so the decrease slows down, meaning the curve is concave up: $f''(x)>0$.

So $f''(x)>0$ and $f'(x)<0$, which is option D.

parts.latex: Which of the following is $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x}{2x-1}\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Must rewrite improper fraction before integrating to logarithm.

solutions.latex:
Write the numerator in terms of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\int \dfrac{2x}{2x-1}\,dx &= \int \dfrac{(2x-1)+1}{2x-1}\,dx\\ &= \int \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2x-1}\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{2x-1}\right)dx\\ &= x + \dfrac{1}{2}\ln|2x-1| + C\end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: By considering symmetry, which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} x^3 \sin x\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Recognise even integrand and split non-symmetric interval appropriately.

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The function $x^3\sin x$ is even, since $(-x)^3\sin(-x)=x^3\sin x$.

Split the interval at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} = \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} + \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}$$
By even symmetry, $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx = 2\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx$.

So the integral equals $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx + \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx$, which is option C.

parts.latex: Calculate the sum of the arithmetic series $32 + 36 + 40 + \dots + 144$.

dif.r: Find number of terms then apply arithmetic sum formula.

solutions.latex:
The series is arithmetic with first term $a=32$, common difference $d=4$ and last term $T_n=144$.

Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 144 &= 32 + (n-1)\cdot 4 \\ 4n &= 116 \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
Use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{29} &= \dfrac{29}{2}\left[2(32) + 28\times 4\right]\\ &= 14.5\times 176\\ &= 2552\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $x\tan 2x$

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on tan 2x.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}$

dif.r: Quotient or product rule with log; simplify result.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= 1\cdot\tan 2x + x\cdot 2\sec^2 2x\\ &= \tan 2x + 2x\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a product, $\ln x\cdot x^{-2}$, and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^{-2}\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=-2x^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= \dfrac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-2} + \ln x\cdot\left(-2x^{-3}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{x^3} - \dfrac{2\ln x}{x^3}\\ &= \dfrac{1 - 2\ln x}{x^3}\end{aligned}$$
The quotient rule gives the same result.
criteria: Correct use of the product or quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ has a vertex at $(3, 1)$ and passes through $(0, 0)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the other $x$-intercept.

dif.r: Reflect intercept in axis of symmetry.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $a$, $b$ and $c$

dif.r: Use intercept form and vertex to find coefficients.

solutions.latex:
The parabola passes through $(0,0)$ with vertex $(3,1)$, which lies above the origin, so it is concave down.

The axis of symmetry is $x=3$, so the other $x$-intercept is the reflection of $x=0$:
$$\therefore\ x = 6$$

The zeros are $x=0$ and $x=6$, so $y=a(x-0)(x-6)=ax(x-6)$.

The point $(3,1)$ satisfies the equation:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3a(-3) \\ 1 &= -9a \\ a &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y &= -\dfrac{x}{9}(x-6)\\ &= -\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{3}x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{1}{9},\ b = \dfrac{2}{3},\ c = 0$$

questions.stem: Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = p$, $P(B) = 2p$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.42$, and $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $p = 0.15$

dif.r: Substitute into addition rule and solve linear equation.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
By use of a Venn diagram, or otherwise, show that $P(A \cup \tilde{B}) = 0.73$,

where $\tilde{B}$ is the complement of $B$.

dif.r: Reason about union with complement via Venn regions.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that $P(A \cap \tilde{B}) = 0.12$ and hence determine, with reasoning, whether the events $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are independent.

dif.r: Subtract intersection, then test independence with justification.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} p + 2p - 0.03 &= 0.42 \\ 3p &= 0.45 \\ p &= 0.15 \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $P(B)=2p=0.3$, so
$$P(\tilde{B}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$$
$A\cup\tilde{B}$ is everything except the part of $B$ outside $A$, so it is $\tilde{B}$ together with $A\cap B$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup\tilde{B}) &= P(\tilde{B}) + P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.7 + 0.03\\ &= 0.73\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cap\tilde{B}) &= P(A) - P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.15 - 0.03\\ &= 0.12\end{aligned}$$
For independence we need $P(A\cap\tilde{B}) = P(A)\,P(\tilde{B})$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(A)\times P(\tilde{B}) &= 0.15\times 0.7\\ &= 0.105\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.12\ne 0.105$, $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are NOT independent.

figures.cap: tower TP with cables AT and BT, angles 27 and 43 degrees, AB = 25 m

solutions.latex:
In the triangle $ABT$, $\angle ABT$ is the exterior-adjacent angle at $B$:
$$\angle ABT = 180^\circ - 43^\circ = 137^\circ$$
By the angle sum of the triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ATB &= 180^\circ - 27^\circ - 137^\circ\\ &= 16^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule with $AB=25$:
$$\dfrac{AT}{\sin 137^\circ} = \dfrac{25}{\sin 16^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ AT \approx 62 \text{ m}$$

parts.label: c

dif.r: Standard midpoint, perpendicular gradient, then verify point lies on line

figures.cap: quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals meeting at E

solutions.latex:
The diagonal $BD$ passes through $B(7,12)$ and $D(2,-3)$.

The gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_{BD} &= \dfrac{-3 - 12}{2 - 7} \\ &= \dfrac{-15}{-5} \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Using point-gradient form with $B(7,12)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 12 &= 3(x - 7) \\ y - 12 &= 3x - 21 \\ y &= 3x - 9 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of $BD$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down from source rows (gradient; working out the equation).

solutions.latex:
$E$ lies on both diagonals, so substitute $y = 3x - 9$ into $x + 3y = 23$.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3(3x - 9) &= 23 \\ x + 9x - 27 &= 23 \\ 10x &= 50 \\ x &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3\times 5 - 9 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E = (5, 6)$$
criteria: Finds one coordinate, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric was '1/2 for each coordinate; 1 for working'; rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ with gradient perpendicular to $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned} m_{AB} &= \dfrac{12 - 8}{7 - (-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So the gradient of the perpendicular bisector is $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Midpoint of } AB &= \left(\dfrac{-1+7}{2}, \dfrac{8+12}{2}\right) \\ &= (3, 10) \end{aligned}$$
The perpendicular bisector is
$$\begin{aligned} y - 10 &= -2(x - 3) \\ y - 10 &= -2x + 6 \\ 2x + y - 16 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Test $E(5,6)$:
$$2(5) + 6 - 16 = 0$$
Hence $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
criteria: Finds the equation of the perpendicular bisector, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand as a power and use $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x) = 8 - x^3$, $f'(x) = -3x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int x^2\left(8 - x^3\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dx &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int -3x^2\left(8 - x^3\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\left(8 - x^3\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + C \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{8 - x^3} + C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ without changing the question, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$P$ and $Q$ lie on both the line and the circle. Substitute $y = 2x + 5$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 + (2x+5)^2 - 6x - 2(2x+5) - 30 &= 0 \\ x^2 + 4x^2 + 20x + 25 - 6x - 4x - 10 - 30 &= 0 \\ 5x^2 + 10x - 15 &= 0 \\ 5(x^2 + 2x - 3) &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -3$ or $x = 1$. The point $P$ has $x=-3$, so $Q$ has $x = 1$ and
$$y = 2(1) + 5 = 7$$
$$\therefore\ Q = (1, 7)$$

parts.latex:
A roof of a house has a rectangular base 7 m by 10 m.

Each of the four sloping faces make an angle of $50^\circ$ with the horizontal.

The midpoint of $EF$ lies vertically above intersection of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

\exfigure{1341_q30_1}

Calculate the total surface area of the sloping faces, correct to one decimal place.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (sloping roof faces over a rectangular base); now Year 11 Extension 1.

dif.r: 3D hip-roof visualisation; deduce slant height and ridge length

figures.cap: roof with rectangular base ABCD, 10 m by 7 m, ridge EF

solutions.latex:
Each sloping face makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal. Half the width of the base is $3.5$ m.

In the right-angled triangle formed by the roof height $h_R$ and a horizontal run of $3.5$ m:
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{3.5}, \quad\text{so}\quad h_R = 3.5\tan 50^\circ$$
The slant height $h_\triangle$ of the sloping face satisfies
$$\begin{aligned} \sin 50^\circ &= \dfrac{h_R}{h_\triangle} \\ h_\triangle &= \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
The horizontal run $x$ on the end faces satisfies
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{x} = \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{x}, \quad\text{so}\quad x = 3.5$$
Then $EF = 10 - 2\times 3.5 = 3$ m.

The two triangular end faces have base $7$ and slant height $\dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}$. The two trapezium faces have parallel sides $3$ and $10$ and the same slant height.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2 \times 7 + \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 10)\times 2\right) \\ &\approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total area} \approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Correct expression for the total area, or equivalent merit
Finds the slant height and $EF$, or equivalent merit
Finds the slant height or the roof height, or equivalent merit
Sets up a correct trigonometric ratio, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In an online game there are various 'power-ups' that players can discover while progressing through the game. The power-ups come in two sizes, major and minor, and they all belong to one of two categories, either combat or survival.

It is known that 85% of the power-ups in the game are minor and the rest are major.

Of the major power-ups it is known that 60 % are combat power-ups, while of the minor power-ups it is known that 30 % are combat power-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Using the given information, complete the tree diagram below.

\exfigure{1341_q31_1}

dif.r: Fill tree branches using complements

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Power-ups that are discovered in the game occur at random.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the probability that when a power-up is discovered it will be a combat power-up.

dif.r: Sum two tree branch products

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Given that a power-up is a combat power-up, find the probability that it is a major power-up

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability from tree

figures.cap: incomplete tree diagram: minor 0.85, major 0.15, minor-combat 0.30, blanks for the other branches

solutions.latex:
The minor power-ups are $85\%$ and the major ones $15\%$. On the minor branch, $30\%$ are combat, so the rest are survival. On the major branch, $60\%$ are combat.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor}) &= 0.7 \\ P(\text{combat}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.6 \\ P(\text{survival}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.4 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Tree diagram figure is part of the question; the solution gives the missing branch probabilities. Rubric written by us.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the branch values were written as joint probabilities; they are conditional ($P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor})=0.7$, ...).
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the branch values were written as joint probabilities; they are conditional ($P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor})=0.7$, ...).

solutions.latex:
A combat power-up is either minor and combat, or major and combat.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{combat}) &= 0.85 \times 0.3 + 0.15 \times 0.6 \\ &= 0.345 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $A$ be the event that the power-up is major and $B$ the event that it is combat. Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \mid B) &= \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.15\times 0.6}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{0.09}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{23} \\ &\approx 0.2609 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

questions.stem:
Astronomers classify the brightness of stars according to a scale of magnitudes. The difference in magnitude between two stars is defined by the formula

$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right),$$

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the magnitudes of the two stars, and $b_1$ and $b_2$ are the corresponding apparent brightnesses measured in watts per metre squared.

The magnitude of a star is a unitless measure, and its value can be positive or negative.

The star Sirius has a magnitude of $-1.4$ and an apparent brightness of $1.04 \times 10^{-7}$ W/m$^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
The star Acrux has an apparent brightness of $1.42 \times 10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$.

Calculate the magnitude of Acrux, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Substitute into log formula and rearrange for magnitude

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The Sun has a magnitude of $-26.7$.

Calculate the apparent brightness of the Sun, correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Rearrange log formula to exponential form; sign care with magnitudes

solutions.latex:
Take Sirius as star 1 and Acrux as star 2 in the given formula, and make $m_2$ the subject.
$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right)$$
In the source working, $m_1 = -1.4$ is the Sirius magnitude and the quantity sought is the Acrux magnitude; the source writes
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -1.4 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1.04\times 10^{-7}}{1.42\times 10^{-8}}\right) \\ &\approx 0.76 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{magnitude of Acrux} \approx 0.76$$

meta.format_note: Source labelling of $m_1$, $m_2$ is loose; the numeric working is kept as given (0.76 checked). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Take the Sun as star 1 and Sirius as star 2, and make $b_1$ the subject. Let $A = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{2.5}$.

The source working gives $A = 10.12$, so
$$\begin{aligned} b_1 &= b_2 \times 10^A \\ &= 1.04 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{10.12} \\ &\approx 1370 \text{ W/m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes $b_1$ the subject or substitutes correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Doctor Hopper is investigating the population of kangaroos in New South Wales.

The doctor found, based on historical data that the population of kangaroos, $P$, could be modelled by

$$P = 7500 + 500(1.09)^t,$$

where $t$ is the number of years since the start of the year 2000, $t \ge 0$.

Find the rate at which the population of kangaroos is growing at the end of 2021.

Leave your answer correct to two significant figures.

dif.r: Differentiate a^t; interpret end of 2021 as t=22

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right) = a^t\ln a$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 500 \times (1.09)^t \ln 1.09$$
The end of 2021 is $t = 22$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 500 \times (1.09)^{22}\ln 1.09 \\ &\approx 290 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$

The spiral below is formed by connecting semi-circles of increasing radii.

\exfigure{1341_q35_1}

The lengths of each spiral form a geometric sequence, with the length of the first and second spirals being $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ cm and $\pi$ cm respectively.

Show that the sum of the first $n$ spirals is $\dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2}$ cm, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.

dif.r: Identify a and r, apply geometric sum formula

figures.cap: spiral of semicircles on a number line

solutions.latex:
The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and common ratio
$$r = \dfrac{\pi}{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 2$$
Using the sum of a geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{2^n - 1}{2 - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt$

dif.r: Rewrite as 4^{-t}, integrate exponential base, evaluate

solutions.latex:
Write $\dfrac{3}{2^{2t}} = 3\cdot 4^{-t}$ and use $\displaystyle\int a^{kt}\,dt = \dfrac{a^{kt}}{k\ln a}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt &= 3\int_0^1 4^{-t}\,dt \\ &= 3\left[\dfrac{4^{-t}}{-\ln 4}\right]_0^1 \\ &= -3\left[\dfrac{1}{4\ln 4} - \dfrac{1}{\ln 4}\right] \\ &= -3\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{4\ln 4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{4\ln 4} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Kay borrows \$60 000 to set up a clothing pop up shop.

She must pay 12% p.a. interest compounded monthly, with repayments at the end of every six months. Let $\$A_n$ be the amount still owed after the $n$th repayment of $\$M$.

dif.r: Recurrence with monthly compounding but six-monthly repayments

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If it takes 15 years to pay off the loan, find the amount of each repayment, $M$.

dif.r: Generalise to A_30, geometric series with ratio 1.01^6

solutions.latex:
$12\%$ p.a. compounded monthly is $1\%$ per month, and repayments are every $6$ months.

After the 1st month Kay owes $60\,000 \times 1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 5th month she owes $60\,000 \times 1.01^5$.

At the end of the 6th month interest is added and then the repayment is made.
$$A_1 = 60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M$$
At the end of the 7th month Kay owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 11th month she owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01^5$.

At the 12th month, the same process gives
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$15$ years is $30$ repayments, so we need $A_{30}$.

The same step gives the pattern:
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= A_2 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left[60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right)\right]\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{18} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12} + \cdots + 1.01^{174}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.01^6$ and $n = 30$ terms:
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M \times \dfrac{\left(1.01^6\right)^{30} - 1}{1.01^6 - 1}$$
The loan is paid off, so $A_{30} = 0$.
$$M = \dfrac{60\,000 \times 1.01^{180}\left(1.01^6 - 1\right)}{1.01^{180} - 1}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx \$4430.07$$
criteria: Obtains the sum of the geometric series for $A_{30}$, or equivalent merit
Finds $A_3$ or identifies the pattern, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line so that it is $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The acceleration of the particle is given by

$$\ddot{x} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \ \text{ m/s}^2$$

Initially the particle is travelling with a velocity of 3 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the first two times when the particle is stationary.

dif.r: Integrate trig acceleration, find constant, solve cosine equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How far does the particle travel in the first four seconds.

dif.r: Distance needs splitting at turning point and absolute values

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \\ \dot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \\ &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $v = 3$:
$$3 = 2\cos 0 + C, \quad\text{so}\quad C = 1$$
$$\dot{x} = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$$
The particle is stationary when $v = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + 1 &= 0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ and } t = 4$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From (a), $v = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$ is positive for $0 \le t < 2$ and negative for $2 < t \le 4$ (it is zero at $t=2$ and $t=4$). So the particle turns at $t = 2$ and the distance is found in two parts.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \int_0^2 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt + \left|\int_2^4 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt\right| \\ &= \left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_0^2 + \left|\left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_2^4\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \left|4 - \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi} + \left|2 - \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &\approx 4.96 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integrals with absolute value, or equivalent merit
Identifies the change of direction at $t=2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Check: $2+\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{\pi}\approx3.654$, $\left|2-\dfrac{6\sqrt3}{\pi}\right|\approx1.308$, sum $\approx4.96$, matching $\dfrac{9\sqrt3}{\pi}$.

dif.r: Build area function, optimise, check endpoints for least value

figures.cap: rectangle PQRS with P on y=8/x, points (1,8) and (4,2) marked

solutions.latex:
Let $P = (x, y)$ with $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$. The rectangle has sides $6 - x$ and $12 - y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= (6 - x)(12 - y) \\ &= 72 - 6y - 12x + xy \\ &= 72 - \dfrac{48}{x} - 12x + 8 \\ &= 80 - 12x - \dfrac{48}{x} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2}, \qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{96}{x^3}$$
and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$ for $x \in [1, 4]$.

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2} &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 4 \\ x &= 2 \quad (x \in [1, 4]) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$, $x = 2$ gives a maximum, with $A = 32$.

Check the end points:
$$\begin{aligned} x = 1:&\quad A = 20 \\ x = 4:&\quad A = 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest } A = 32 \text{ at } x = 2;\ \text{least } A = 20 \text{ at } x = 1 \text{ and } x = 4$$
criteria: Finds the maximum and tests the end points, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point $x=2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $A$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

On the Richter scale, the magnitude $R$ of an earthquake of intensity $I$ is given by the formula $R = \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, where $I_0$ is a reference intensity used for comparisons.

parts.latex:
The graph of the parabola $y = x^2 - 2x$ is given. The shaded area is equal to:

\exfigure{1342_q6_1}

dif.r: Area split at an x-intercept to handle the region below the axis.

figures.cap: graph of y=x^2-2x with shaded regions between x=0 and x=4

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the axis for $0<x<2$ and above it for $2<x<4$, so the two areas are found separately.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_0^2 (x^2-2x)\,dx\right| + \int_2^4 (x^2-2x)\,dx \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| + \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_2^4 \\ &= \left|\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| + \left(\dfrac{64}{3}-16\right)-\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right) \\ &= \dfrac{4}{3}+\dfrac{16}{3}+\dfrac{4}{3} \\ &= 8 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

solutions.latex:

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are events of a sample space.

Given that $P(B|A) = \sqrt{p}$, $P(A) = p$ and $P(B) = p^2$, which of these is an expression for $P(A|B)$?

dif.r: Conditional probability formula applied twice with symbolic index algebra.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}$:
$$\sqrt{p}=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{p}$$
so $P(B\cap A)=p^{\frac{3}{2}}$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} P(A|B) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{p^{\frac{3}{2}}}{p^2} \\ &= p^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}} \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function, where $k > 0$.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2x\right) & \text{for } -k \le x \le k \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values} \end{cases}$$

Which of the following is true?

dif.r: Recognise the pdf as even cos2x and deduce symmetry.

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
Since $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right)=\cos 2x$, which is an even function, the distribution is symmetric about $x=0$.

Hence $P(X>0.2)=P(X<-0.2)$, which is option B.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of $4x^3-6$, which is $12x^2$, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{12}\int\dfrac{12x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12}\ln|4x^3-6|+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right)$. Answer in the simplest exact form.

dif.r: Quotient rule with trig and exponential, then simplifying.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\tan x & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=\sec^2 x & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right) &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\sec^2 x-2e^{2x}\tan x}{(e^{2x})^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x-2\tan x}{e^{2x}} \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently $\dfrac{(\tan x-1)^2}{e^{2x}}$, which is not required.

questions.stem: Chandra is an enthusiastic gardener. She planted a lemon tree on $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2019, when it was 80 centimetres tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 centimetres tall, that is, it grew 50 centimetres. Each year's growth was then 90% of the growth of the previous year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How tall was the lemon tree after three years?

dif.r: Sum three geometric growth terms and add the initial height.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Assuming the present growth pattern is maintained, explain why the lemon tree will never reach a height of 10 metres?

dif.r: Use a limiting sum in context, including the initial height.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: In which year will the lemon tree reach a height of 5 metres?

dif.r: Set up a geometric sum equation, solve with logs, interpret the year.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Each year's growth is $90\%$ of the previous year's, so the growths in the first three years are $50$, $50\times0.9$ and $50\times0.9^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} H &= 80+(50+50\times0.9+50\times0.9^2) \\ &= 80+(50+45+40.5) \\ &= 215.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Adds the three years' growth to $80$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Removed the source's partial list 'Heights: 80, 130, 175, …' because the third value 175 disagrees with the final working (130 + 45 = 175, consistent; but the line was incomplete and unneeded).

solutions.latex:
The yearly growths form a geometric series with $a=50$ and $r=0.9$. Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{50}{1-0.9} \\ &= 500 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Maximum height $=500+80=580$ cm, which is less than $10$ m.

So the tree will never reach $10$ m.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Height after $n$ years is $80$ plus the sum of $n$ terms of the series. Set this equal to $500$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} 500 &= 80+\dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{1-0.9} \\ 420 &= \dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{0.1} \\ 0.84 &= 1-0.9^n \\ 0.9^n &= 0.16 \\ n &= \dfrac{\log 0.16}{\log 0.9} \\ &\approx 17.3 \end{aligned}$$
So the height is reached during the 18th year, which is 2036.

dif.r: Normal z-score, symmetry, expected count, then justify the target in context.

can_use: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The weight $300$ is two standard deviations below the mean, since $306-2\times3=300$.

By the Empirical rule, $95\%$ of weights lie within two standard deviations, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$P(\text{weight}<300)=\dfrac{0.05}{2}=0.025=2.5\%$$

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score for a packet of weight 300 g, with mean 308 g and standard deviation 3 g, is
$$z=\dfrac{300-308}{3}\approx-2.67$$
By symmetry of the normal distribution:
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z<-2.67)&=1-P(Z<2.67) \\ &=1-0.99621 \\ &\approx 0.0038 \ (0.38\%) \end{aligned}$$
The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets, so
$$\text{Expected number underweight}=0.0038\times4000\approx15.2<20$$
$$\therefore\ \text{They meet the target.}$$
criteria: Finds the $z$-score or the probability of an underweight packet, or equivalent merit

Each day is rainy with probability $0.15$ and not rainy with probability $0.85$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}&=(1^2\times0.255+2^2\times0.0225)-(0.30)^2 \\ &=0.255 \\ &\approx0.26 \end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance:
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\sqrt{0.255} \\ &=0.50497\ldots \\ &\approx0.50 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\sec\theta + 8\cos\theta = 6$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Answer correct to 3 decimal places, where necessary.

dif.r: Convert sec to quadratic in cos, factorise, find four solutions in radians.

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and multiply through by $\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+8\cos\theta&=6 \\ 1+8\cos^2\theta&=6\cos\theta \\ 8\cos^2\theta-6\cos\theta+1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $x=\cos\theta$.
$$(4x-1)(2x-1)=0$$
so $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, and $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ gives $\theta\approx1.318,\ 4.965$.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 1.318,\ 4.965,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $\cos\theta$ and some solutions in radians, or equivalent merit

The table below shows the future values of an annuity of $\$1$ for different rates of interest and for different numbers of compounding periods. The contributions are made at the end of each compounding period.

\exfigure{1342_q24_1}

An annuity account is opened and contributions of $\$500$ are made at the end of every six months for 5 years.

For the first 4 years, the interest rate is $6\%$ per annum, compounding six-monthly. For the $5^{\text{th}}$ year, the interest rate increases to $8\%$ per annum, compounding six-monthly.

Calculate the amount in the account immediately after the last contribution is made.
parts.note: Annuity future value interest-factor table look-up (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only).

dif.r: Combine annuity table with compounding at a changed rate, extra contributions.

figures.cap: Future Value Interest Factors table for 1% to 5%, periods 1 to 8

solutions.latex:
After 4 years there are 8 contributions at $3\%$ per six months. The table factor is $8.8923$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total after 4 years}&=500\times8.8923 \\ &=\$4446.15 \end{aligned}$$
In the 5th year the rate is $4\%$ per six months, so this amount earns interest for 2 periods, and two further contributions are made (the last earning no interest, the first earning one period).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total after 5 years}&=4446.15(1.04)^2+500(2.04) \\ &=\$5828.96 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value after 4 years and the interest on it for the final year, or equivalent merit
Finds the value after 4 years, or equivalent merit

The diagram shows the graph of a particle's velocity, $v$ m/s, at time $t$ seconds.

\exfigure{1342_q25_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals (4 function values) to approximate the distance the particle travels in the first 3 seconds.

dif.r: Read four values from graph, routine trapezoidal rule.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is the estimate for your answer in part a) more than or less than the exact distance that the particle travels in the first 3 seconds? Justify your answer.

dif.r: Justify underestimate using concavity of graph.

solutions.latex:
Using the trapezoidal rule with $h=1$ and the four function values read from the graph:
$$\begin{aligned} D&=\dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(\text{first})+f(\text{last})+2f(\text{middle})\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[8+20+2(15+18)\right] \\ &=47 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct formula or substitution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The estimate is less than the exact distance.

The velocity-time graph is concave down, so the trapeziums have chords lying underneath the graph.

Hence the estimate does not take into account the area between the trapeziums and the graph.
criteria: States less than, with concave down, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the cubic function $y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 3$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

At the point $(1, 8)$ on the curve, the equation of the tangent is given by $y = 2x + 6$.

Determine the values of $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Point and tangent gradient give two simultaneous equations for a, b.

solutions.latex:
The point $(1,8)$ lies on the curve.
$$\begin{aligned} 8&=1+a+b+3 \\ a+b&=4 \end{aligned}\qquad (1)$$
The gradient of the tangent is $2$, and
$$y'=3x^2+2ax+b$$
When $x=1$, $y'=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3+2a+b \\ 2a+b&=-1 \end{aligned}\qquad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=-5$$
Then $-5+b=4$, so $b=9$.
$$\therefore\ a=-5,\ b=9$$
criteria: Finds both equations and $a=-5$, or equivalent merit
Finds both equations, or equivalent merit
Finds one equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $a = 1$.

dif.r: Total probability equals one; integrate a linear-inside power.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf from 0 to x, state piecewise CDF.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the median.

dif.r: Set CDF to one half and solve a simple surd equation.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability must equal 1.
$$\int_0^2\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{a(1+4x)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^2&=1 \\ \dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt9-\dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt1&=1 \\ \dfrac{3a}{2}-\dfrac{a}{2}&=1 \\ a&=1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the total probability integral equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $a=1$, and using a second variable $t$ in the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x(1+4t)^{-\frac12}\,dt \\ &=\left[\dfrac{(1+4t)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4x}}{2}-\dfrac12 \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The complete cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right), & 0\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral with a second variable and limits, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right)&=\dfrac12 \\ \sqrt{1+4x}&=2 \\ 1+4x&=4 \\ x&=\dfrac34 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the median is } \dfrac34$$

parts.latex:
The rate of 'flu infection' in a population of a city is proportional to the number of infected individuals. That is the number of infected people $F$ after $t$ weeks is modelled by the equation $F = F_0 e^{kt}$

where $F_0$ and $k$ are constants. It is known that after 3 weeks, there is twice the number of infections to begin with. If there were 1000 cases of flu infection originally, how many are there after 7 weeks? Express your answer correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Find k from doubling with logs, then substitute t=7.

solutions.latex:
When $t=3$, $F=2F_0$ and $F_0=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000&=1000e^{3k} \\ 2&=e^{3k} \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} F&=1000e^{\frac{7\ln2}{3}} \\ &=5039.68\ldots \\ &\approx5040 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about 5040 cases after 7 weeks}$$
criteria: Finds $k$ and substitutes $t=7$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source printed answer was about 5000, but 5039.68 to 3 significant figures is 5040; corrected to 5040 (source note said the same).

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y = 6 - 8e^{-x}$.

\exfigure{1342_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: On the diagram, sketch the graph of $y = e^x$, which passes through the point $(1, e)$. Show that the $x$ coordinates of the two points of intersection, ($x_1$ and $x_2$, where $x_1 < x_2$), are the solutions of the equation $e^{2x} - 6e^x + 8 = 0$ and solve this equation to find the exact values of $x_1$ and $x_2$.

dif.r: Sketch, form hidden quadratic in e^x, factorise and solve with logs.

skills: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form, the area of the region enclosed by the two curves.

dif.r: Area between exponential curves with log limits needing exact simplification.

figures.cap: graph of y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6
solution sketch: graph of y=e^x added to the diagram, intersecting the given curve at x1 and x2

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1342_q29_s1}

The curves intersect where $e^x=6-8e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=6-\dfrac{8}{e^x} \\ e^{2x}&=6e^x-8 \\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Factorising:
$$(e^x-2)(e^x-4)=0$$
so $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln2,\quad x_2=\ln4$$
criteria: Sketches $y=e^x$, shows the equation and factorises, or equivalent merit
Sketches $y=e^x$ and shows the equation, or equivalent merit
Sketches $y=e^x$ through $(0,1)$ and $(1,e)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: sketch_id 1342_q29_s2 is the sketch asked for; the figure placed is 1342_q29_s1 as in the source. Draw on the given axes the curve y = 6 - 8e^{-x} and y = e^x through (0,1) and (1,e), with intersection points at x = ln 2 (y = 2) and x = ln 4 (y = 4) labelled.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between the curves from $x=\ln2$ to $x=\ln4$, with $y=6-8e^{-x}$ above $y=e^x$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_{\ln2}^{\ln4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} &=\left[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\right]_{\ln2}^{\ln4} \\ &=6(\ln4-\ln2)+8\left(\dfrac14-\dfrac12\right)-(4-2) \\ &=6\ln2-2-2 \\ &=6\ln2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=6\ln2-4 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integral and finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: none needed here; the region is the one between the curves from part (a).

dif.r: Integrate with respect to y and split region between two boundaries.

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: sideways parabola and line with shaded region ABC

solutions.latex:
The line is $x=5-y$. Split the region at $y=2$: the line is the right boundary for $2\le y\le5$ and the parabola for $1\le y\le2$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_2^5(5-y)\,dy+\int_1^2(-y^2+6y-5)\,dy$$
$$\begin{aligned} &=\left[5y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_2^5+\left[-\dfrac{y^3}{3}+3y^2-5y\right]_1^2 \\ &=\dfrac{25}{2}-8+\left(-\dfrac23\right)-\left(-\dfrac73\right) \\ &=4\dfrac12+\dfrac53 \\ &=\dfrac{37}{6} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the triangle $BCD$ with $D(0,2)$ has area $\dfrac12\times3\times3=\dfrac92$, and
$$\int_1^2(-y^2+6y-5)\,dy=\dfrac53$$
so the total is $\dfrac92+\dfrac53=\dfrac{37}{6}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{37}{6} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integral(s) and integrates or substitutes, or equivalent merit
Correct integral set-up, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Karen is retiring next week and her Superannuation Fund contains $\$1\,200\,000$. The Fund is earning $6\%$ p.a. compound interest, compounding monthly. To cover her living expenses in her retirement, Karen wishes to withdraw a regular amount of $\$8\,000$ at the end of each month, after interest has been added.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that after 3 months the amount in her account $A_3$ is given by:

$$A_3 = 1\,200\,000(1.005)^3 - 8\,000\left[(1.005)^2 + (1.005) + 1\right]$$

dif.r: Routine recursive build-up of balance over three months.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By finding a similar expression for the amount remaining after $n$ months, find how many years the money will last.

dif.r: Generalise to A_n with GP sum, set zero, solve with logs.

meta.marker_note: The expanding process must be shown.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern:
$$A_n=1\,200\,000(1.005)^n-8000\left[(1.005)^{n-1}+\cdots+(1.005)+1\right]$$
The bracket is a GP sum with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms.

The money lasts until $A_n=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1\,200\,000(1.005)^n-\dfrac{8000\left((1.005)^n-1\right)}{1.005-1} \\ 1200(1.005)^n&=1600\left((1.005)^n-1\right) \\ 400(1.005)^n&=1600 \\ (1.005)^n&=4 \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln1.005} \\ &=277.95 \text{ months} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the money lasts about 23 years}$$
criteria: Uses the GP sum formula correctly, or equivalent merit
Writes the expression for $A_n$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1342_q32_1}

An open trough of depth $h$ metres and length one metre is constructed out of stainless steel sheeting. The cross-section of the trough is an isosceles trapezium with the acute angles being $45^\circ$ each. The width of the bottom of the trough is $a$ metres. The area of the cross-section measures $60\ \text{m}^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $a = \dfrac{60}{h} - h$.

dif.r: Use 45° geometry and trapezium area to show given relation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the amount of stainless steel, $A$, in $\text{m}^2$, required to construct the trough is given by:

$$A = \dfrac{60}{h} - h + 2h\sqrt{2} + 120.$$

dif.r: Model total surface area of faces, Pythagoras for slant, substitute.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the depth of the trough, to the nearest millimetre (mm), if the amount of stainless steel used is kept to a minimum.

dif.r: Routine derivative of given function, solve, second derivative test.

figures.cap: open trough with trapezium cross-section, depth h, base a, length 1 metre

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, each slanted side makes $45^\circ$ with the base, so the horizontal extension at each end satisfies $\tan45^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x}$, giving $x=h$.

Hence the top width is $b=a+2h$.

Using the area of a trapezium, $\dfrac12h(a+b)=60$:
$$\begin{aligned} 60&=\dfrac12h(2a+2h) \\ 120&=2ah+2h^2 \\ a&=\dfrac{120}{2h}-\dfrac{2h^2}{2h} \\ &=\dfrac{60}{h}-h \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area of the trapezium, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The steel is two trapezium ends, two slanted sides and the base (length 1 m).

Each slanted side has length $\sqrt{h^2+h^2}$ by Pythagoras' theorem.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\times\left(\dfrac12h(2a+2h)\right)+2\times\left(\sqrt{h^2+h^2}\times1\right)+(a\times1) \\ &=h(2a+2h)+2\sqrt2h+a \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $a=\dfrac{60}{h}-h$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2h\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right)+2h^2+2\sqrt2h+\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right) \\ &=120+2h\sqrt2+\dfrac{60}{h}-h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{60}{h}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$$
criteria: Writes the correct expression for $A$, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Possible source slip: part (b) adds the two trapezium ends (area 2 × 60 = 120) to the sides and base, but the trapezium end area is given as 60 m² each, so the working's first line ($2\times\frac12h(2a+2h)$) is consistent with the target. No change made.

solutions.latex:
Write $A=60h^{-1}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dh}=-60h^{-2}-1+2\sqrt2,\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{h^3}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60}{h^2}&=2\sqrt2-1 \\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{60}{2\sqrt2-1}} \\ &\approx5.728 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{(5.728)^3}\approx0.638>0$$
so this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ h\approx5.728 \text{ m}\ (5728 \text{ mm})$$
criteria: Sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground.

It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0 \le t \le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t) = 0.5e^{t}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground. Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.

dif.r: Recognise descent when v=0, solve simple sine equation.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Product rule, tan equation with negative value, choose correct quadrant.

solutions.latex:
The rocket begins to descend when $v=0$.
$$0=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$
Since $0.5e^t\neq0$, we need $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$.

So $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\pi,2\pi,\ldots$ and $\dfrac{t}{10}=0,1,2,\ldots$

The first positive solution is $t=10$.
$$\therefore\ t=10 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and notes $0.5e^t$ is never $0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & w&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & w'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \\ &=0.5e^t\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{10}+\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$ (as $0.5e^t\neq0$):
$$\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$
For $0<t<10$, $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=2.837\ldots$
$$\begin{aligned} t&=2.837\ldots\times\dfrac{10}{\pi} \\ &\approx9.03 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains the tan equation, or equivalent merit
Differentiates and sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The Artful Dodger has three 20 cent coins in his pocket. One of the coins has heads on both sides, another is biased such that it has a 75% chance of landing on heads and the third coin is a fair coin.

A coin is selected at random and tossed.

Given that the coin that was tossed comes up heads, what is the probability that it was the fair coin?

dif.r: Conditional probability over three coins, Bayes-style reverse calculation.

solutions.latex:
By the conditional probability formula, with each coin chosen with probability $\dfrac13$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{fair}\mid\text{heads})&=\dfrac{P(\text{fair}\cap\text{heads})}{P(\text{heads})} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac13\times\frac12}{\left(\frac13\times1\right)+\left(\frac13\times\frac34\right)+\left(\frac13\times\frac12\right)} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac16}{\frac13+\frac14+\frac16} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{4+3+2} \\ &=\dfrac29 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the numerator or the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is the angle of inclination of the line $y=\dfrac{9}{8}x-5$?

dif.r: Direct recall tan(theta) equals gradient, one calculator step.

skills: Angle of inclination of a line

solutions.latex:
The angle of inclination $\theta$ satisfies $\tan\theta=\text{gradient}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{9}{8} \\ \theta&\approx 48^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is positive, so $\theta$ is acute, which matches option B.

look: Read the question and solution against the source page

parts.latex: Which of the following correctly describes the gradient and concavity of the function $f(x)=2x^2+3x-1$ at the origin?

dif.r: Substitute into first and second derivatives of a quadratic.

options.label: A
options.latex: The gradient is positive and the function is concave up

options.label: B
options.latex: The gradient is positive and the function is concave down

options.label: C
options.latex: The gradient is negative and the function is concave up

options.label: D
options.latex: The gradient is negative and the function is concave down

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=4x+3 \\ f'(0)&=3>0 \end{aligned}$$
So the gradient is positive.
$$f''(x)=4>0$$
So the function is concave up, which matches option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an odd function?

dif.r: Recall odd-function definition and test options.

solutions.latex:
An odd function satisfies $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=(-x)^3+(-x) \\ &=-x^3-x \\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$
So $y=x^3+x$ is odd, which matches option C.

parts.latex: The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of a series is given by $T_n=2n^2-4$ for $n\ge 1$. What is the sum of the first three terms?

dif.r: Substitute n=1,2,3 and add.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} T_1&=2(1)^2-4=-2 \\ T_2&=2(2)^2-4=4 \\ T_3&=2(3)^2-4=14 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum}&=-2+4+14 \\ &=16 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=x^2-2x$ and $g(x)=2x+1$, which of the following is a correct expression for $f(g(x))$?

dif.r: Routine composition and expansion.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x))&=f(2x+1) \\ &=(2x+1)^2-2(2x+1) \\ &=4x^2+4x+1-4x-2 \\ &=4x^2-1 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: A ghost gum tree was planted in 2010. The height of the tree $H$, in metres, is a function of the tree's age, in years, after planting. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of $H'(4)=3.2$?

dif.r: Interpret derivative in context; age 4 means start of 2014.

options.label: A
options.latex: Between 2010 and 2014, the height increased at a rate of $3.2$ m per year

options.label: B
options.latex: Between 2010 and 2014, the height increased by $3.2$ m

options.label: C
options.latex: At the start of 2014, the height was increasing at a rate of $3.2$ m per year

options.label: D
options.latex: At the start of 2014, the height was $3.2$ m

solutions.latex:
$H'(4)$ is the instantaneous rate of change of height at age 4 years, which is the start of 2014.

So at the start of 2014 the height was increasing at $3.2$ m per year, which matches option C.

parts.latex: How many solutions does the equation $\sin 3x=0$ have for $0\le x\le\pi$?

dif.r: Adjust domain for 3x, count zeros of sine.

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le\pi$, we have $0\le 3x\le 3\pi$.

$\sin 3x=0$ when
$$3x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ 3\pi$$
That gives 4 solutions, which matches option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the correct simplification of $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$?

dif.r: Several reciprocal-identity steps to simplify to cot.

solutions.latex:
Using $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$:

parts.label: a

parts.note: Correlation and bivariate data are not in 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

parts.label: b
parts.note: Least-squares regression is not in 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

dif.r: Read two points from graph, find line equation.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Use the equation of your regression line from part (b) to predict the number of visitors the website will receive for a week in which \$3000 was spent on advertising.

parts.label: d

figures.cap: scatterplot and regression line, Advertising and Web Traffic

solutions.latex:
$r=0.9$ is close to $1$ and positive.
$$\therefore\ \text{strong positive correlation}$$

Using the points $(2.5,1)$ and $(4.5,3.5)$ on the line, the gradient is
$$m=\dfrac{3.5-1}{4.5-2.5}=1.25$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ with $(2.5,1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1&=1.25(x-2.5)\\ y&=1.25x-2.125\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=1.25x-2.125$$
criteria: Finds the gradient using two points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=3$ (\$3000 is 3 thousand dollars) into the regression line.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1.25\times3-2.125\\ &=1.625\end{aligned}$$
Since $y$ is in hundreds of thousands, this is about $162\,500$ visitors.
$$\therefore\ 162\,500 \text{ visitors}$$

$x=1.5$ lies outside the range of the data, so predicting there is extrapolation and is unreliable.

Alternatively, when $x=1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1.25(1.5)-2.125\\ &=-0.25\end{aligned}$$
This is negative, which makes no sense as the number of visitors cannot be negative.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities on each pair of branches sum to $1$.

So $P(\overline{T})=1-0.2=80\%$.

From $\overline{T}$: $P(R)=40\%$ and $P(\overline{R})=60\%$.

$R$ happens by way of $T$ or $\overline{T}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(R)&=P(T\cap R)+P(\overline{T}\cap R)\\ &=0.2\times0.9+0.8\times0.4\\ &=0.5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(R)=50\%$$

figures.cap: graph of y=sqrt(x) with region shaded up to x=4

solutions.latex:
The area is under $y=\sqrt{x}$ from $x=0$ to $x=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\,dx\\ &=\int_0^4x^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\left(4^{\frac{3}{2}}-0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\times8\\ &=\dfrac{16}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\dfrac{16}{3}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n$. For a particular arithmetic series, $S_8=196$ and $S_9=279$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the value of the $9^{\text{th}}$ term.

dif.r: Must recognise T9 = S9 - S8; one-line calculation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the values of the first term $a$ and the common difference $d$.

dif.r: Standard AP sum and term formulas used in reverse

solutions.latex:
The 9th term is the sum of 9 terms less the sum of 8 terms.
$$\begin{aligned} T_9&=S_9-S_8\\ &=279-196\\ &=83\end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $n=9$ and last term $83$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9}{2}(a+83)&=279\\ a+83&=62\\ a&=-21\end{aligned}$$
Using $T_9=a+8d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 83&=-21+8d\\ 8d&=104\\ d&=13\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=-21,\ d=13$$

questions.stem:
The Richter scale is used to measure the magnitude of earthquakes. The magnitude $R$ of an earthquake is proportional to the logarithm of the ground displacement $d$ caused by the earthquake in millimetres. This relationship can be described by the equation:

$$R=\log_{10}(1000d)$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: In July 2022, an earthquake in the Easter Island region caused a ground displacement of 6310 mm. What was its magnitude on the Richter scale? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: Substitute into a given log formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many times larger is the ground displacement of an earthquake with a magnitude of $3.2$ compared to an earthquake with a magnitude of $1.6$? Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: Convert log to index form, then form a ratio

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=6310$ into the given formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R&=\log_{10}(1000\times6310)\\ &=6.80002\ldots\\ &\approx6.8\end{aligned}$$

Rewrite $R=\log_{10}(1000d)$ in index form, $1000d=10^R$.

For magnitude $3.2$:
$$d_1=\dfrac{10^{3.2}}{1000}$$
For magnitude $1.6$:
$$d_2=\dfrac{10^{1.6}}{1000}$$
The ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d_1}{d_2}&=\dfrac{10^{3.2}}{10^{1.6}}\\ &=10^{1.6}\\ &\approx40\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about 40 times larger}$$
criteria: Writes expressions for $d_1$ and $d_2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The graph of the function $y=\dfrac{x^2+3x}{x^2+3}$ has a horizontal asymptote. Find the equation of this asymptote, clearly showing your working.

dif.r: Routine limit of a rational function at infinity

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator by $x^2$.
$$y=\dfrac{1+\frac{3}{x}}{1+\frac{3}{x^2}}$$
As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{3}{x}\to0$ and $\dfrac{3}{x^2}\to0$, so $y\to1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the horizontal asymptote is } y=1$$

The diagram below shows the graph of a function $f(x)$ with a $y$-intercept of $-3$, a maximum turning point at $A$, and a minimum turning point at $B$. The derivative of the function is $f'(x)=3x^2+2x-8$.

\exfigure{1343_q28_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the equation of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate a polynomial derivative and use the y-intercept for the constant

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of $A$.

dif.r: Factorise the derivative, classify the turning point, substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained by reflecting the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the $x$-axis, shifting 5 units up, and then dilating horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Find the coordinates of the point $A'$, the image of the point $A$, after these successive transformations have been applied.

dif.r: Apply a sequence of transformations to one point

figures.cap: cubic y=f(x) with maximum A, minimum B, y-intercept -3

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f'(x)$:
$$f(x)=x^3+x^2-8x+c$$
The $y$-intercept is $-3$, so $f(0)=-3$ and $c=-3$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3+x^2-8x-3$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} (3x-4)(x+2)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{4}{3}\text{ or }-2\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $f''(x)=6x+2$ decides the nature.
$$f''(-2)=-10<0$$
So there is a maximum at $x=-2$. This agrees with the graph, where $A$ is left of the $y$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-2)&=(-2)^3+(-2)^2-8(-2)-3\\ &=9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A(-2,9)$$
criteria: Identifies $x=-2$ as the maximum, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Apply each transformation to $A(-2,9)$ in order.

Reflect in the $x$-axis: $(-2,-9)$.

Shift 5 units up: $(-2,-4)$.

Dilate horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $x$ is multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{2}$: $(-1,-4)$.
$$\therefore\ A'(-1,-4)$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-4x^2+4x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of a cubic and their nature

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, clearly showing any intercepts and stationary points.

parts.latex: Hence, determine the values of $k$ for which the equation $x^3-4x^2+4x+k=0$ has exactly two solutions.

dif.r: Rewrite as f(x) = -k and read tangencies from the graph

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x^3-4x^2+4x with turning points (2/3, 32/27) and (2,0)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and set the derivative to zero.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2-8x+4 \\ &=(3x-2)(x-2)=0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=2$.
$$f\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=\dfrac{32}{27},\quad f(2)=0$$
Nature: the sign of $f''(x)=6x-8$ decides.
$$f''\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=-4<0$$
so there is a maximum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{32}{27}\right)$.
$$f''(2)=4>0$$
so there is a minimum turning point at $(2,0)$.
criteria: Finds both stationary points and a substantial start to determining nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$- and $y$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1343_q30_s1}
criteria: Maximum at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{32}{27}\right)$ labelled clearly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: graph of y=x^3-4x^2+4x, cubic through origin (0,0) (x-intercept), maximum at (2/3, 32/27), minimum at (2,0) touching the x-axis, also x-intercepts at 0 and 2 only; rises to the right, falls to the left.

solutions.latex:
The equation $x^3-4x^2+4x+k=0$ is $f(x)=-k$.

From the graph, this has exactly two solutions when the line $y=-k$ touches a turning point, that is $-k=0$ or $-k=\dfrac{32}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ k=0 \text{ or } k=-\dfrac{32}{27}$$

questions.stem:
Rectangle $PQRS$ has been inscribed inside an ellipse with equation $x^2+4y^2=36$, as shown in the diagram below. The point $P$ has coordinates $(x,y)$.

\exfigure{1343_q31_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area of the rectangle is $A=2x\sqrt{36-x^2}$.

dif.r: Express rectangle dimensions using the ellipse equation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{72-4x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}$.

dif.r: Product and chain rule, then simplify to a given form

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the maximum possible area of the rectangle.

dif.r: Derivative given; solve, test the maximum, evaluate the area

figures.cap: rectangle PQRS inscribed in ellipse

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2+4y^2=36$, we have $y^2=\dfrac{36-x^2}{4}$.

$P$ is in the first quadrant, so $y>0$ and
$$y=\dfrac{\sqrt{36-x^2}}{2}$$
The rectangle has width $2x$ and height $2y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2x\times 2y \\ &=2x\times 2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{36-x^2}}{2} \\ &=2x\sqrt{36-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $y$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=(36-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(36-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(-2x)=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=2\sqrt{36-x^2}-\dfrac{2x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}} \\ &=\dfrac{2(36-x^2)-2x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}} \\ &=\dfrac{72-4x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A maximum requires $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 72-4x^2&=0 \\ x^2&=18 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=3\sqrt2$ (reject $-3\sqrt2$ since $x>0$).

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side:

questions.stem:
The human heart pumps blood through the body by repeatedly contracting, which pushes blood out of the heart, and then relaxing, which lets new blood flow into the heart. The average human heart contains 50 mL of blood when contracted and 120 mL when relaxed. The total volume $V$ mL of blood in the heart at time $t$ seconds can be modelled by the function

$$V=35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}t\right)+c$$

where $c$ is a constant. The diagram below shows the graph of $V(t)$ for $0\le t\le 4$.

\exfigure{1343_q32_1}

parts.label: a

figures.cap: graph of V(t) for 0 to 4

solutions.latex:
The volume oscillates between $50$ and $120$, so $c$ is the midpoint.
$$c=\dfrac{50+120}{2}=85$$

meta.format_note: Reason line for c added (midpoint of 50 and 120); consistent with source value.

solutions.latex:
The period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$.
$$T=2\pi\div\dfrac{7\pi}{3}=\dfrac{6}{7}$$
The period is $\dfrac{6}{7}$ s.

Differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-35\times\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)$$
When $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt}&=-\dfrac{245\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ &=-\dfrac{245\pi}{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{245\pi}{6} \\ &\approx 128 \text{ mL/s} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and substitution of $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $t=\dfrac{2}{7}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{2}{7}\right)+85 \\ &=35\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+85 \\ &=67.5 \end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{3}{7}$, which is half a period, the volume is at its minimum, $V=50$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Volume pumped out}&=67.5-50 \\ &=17.5 \\ &\approx 18 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the volume at $t=\dfrac{2}{7}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set $V=102.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)&=17.5 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time this occurs is when $\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $t=\dfrac{1}{7}$.

Over $0\le t\le\dfrac{3}{7}$ (half a period), the volume is at least $102.5$ for $0\le t\le\dfrac{1}{7}$.
$$\text{Fraction of time}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{7}}{\frac{3}{7}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

solutions.latex:
The area is split at $x=2$, where the graphs intersect.
$$A=\displaystyle\int_0^2(5-2^x)\,dx+\int_2^3(3-x)^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left[5x-\dfrac{1}{\ln2}2^x\right]_0^2+\left[-\dfrac{3}{4}(3-x)^{\frac{4}{3}}\right]_2^3 \\ &=10-\dfrac{4}{\ln2}+\dfrac{1}{\ln2}-\left(0-\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \\ &=10\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{3}{\ln2} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One correct primitive, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the function $y=kxe^{kx}$ has exactly one stationary point and its $y$-value is independent of $k$, where $k$ is a constant.

dif.r: General show-that with parameter k; uniqueness argument needed

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=kx & v&=e^{kx}\\ u'&=k & v'&=ke^{kx}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=ke^{kx}+k^2xe^{kx} \\ &=ke^{kx}(1+kx) \end{aligned}$$
For $y'=0$: $ke^{kx}\ne0$, so $1+kx=0$ and $x=-\dfrac{1}{k}$ is the only stationary point.

When $x=-\dfrac{1}{k}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=k\left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)e^{k\left(-\frac{1}{k}\right)} \\ &=-e^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
which is independent of $k$.
criteria: Finds the $x$-value of the stationary point, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

Arthur's bag contains 4 green marbles and 2 red marbles. Beatrice's bag contains 3 green marbles and 3 red marbles. One of their bags is randomly selected, and then two marbles are removed in succession without replacement.

What is the probability that Arthur's bag was selected, given that the two marbles were the same colour?

dif.r: Two-stage tree with reversed conditional probability

solutions.latex:
Using the definition of conditional probability:
$$P(A\mid\text{same colour})=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and same colour})}{P(\text{same colour})}$$
For Arthur's bag (both red or both green):
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\text{ and same})&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{6}\times\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{30} \end{aligned}$$
For Beatrice's bag:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\text{ and same})&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{same colour})=\dfrac{7}{30}+\dfrac{6}{30}=\dfrac{13}{30}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\mid\text{same colour})&=\dfrac{\frac{7}{30}}{\frac{13}{30}} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{13} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates a necessary probability correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3}{7}$ and $90^\circ<\theta<180^\circ$, what is the value of $\tan\theta$?

dif.r: Pythagoras plus quadrant sign for tan

solutions.latex:
Since $90^\circ<\theta<180^\circ$, $\theta$ is in the second quadrant, where $\sin\theta>0$, $\cos\theta<0$ and $\tan\theta<0$.

In a right-angled triangle with opposite side $3$ and hypotenuse $7$, Pythagoras' theorem gives the adjacent side:
$$\sqrt{7^2-3^2}=\sqrt{40}$$
So $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt{40}}{7}$.
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\frac{3}{7}}{-\frac{\sqrt{40}}{7}}=-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{40}}$$
This is negative, so the answer is option A.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=P-|x|$ is a triangle above the $x$-axis between $x=-P$ and $x=P$, with apex $(0,P)$. The $y$-intercept is positive, so $P>0$. This rules out options C and D.

The integral is the area of this triangle, with base $2P$ and height $P$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-P}^{P}(P-|x|)\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2P\times P \\ &= P^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $P^2=16$, and with $P>0$:
$$P=4$$
The answer is option A.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

options.label: A
options.latex: At $t=2$, the particle is to the left of the origin, and travelling towards the origin.

options.label: B
options.latex: At $t=5$, the particle is at the origin, and at rest.

options.label: C

options.latex: At $t=15$, the particle is at the origin, and travelling from left to right.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph of a particle for 0 to 16 seconds

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the gradient of the displacement graph, and displacement is the signed area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis. The particle is at rest when $v=0$.

From the graph:
$$\begin{aligned} v&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<2 &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for } 2<t<10 &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 10<t<16 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Option A: at $t=2$, $v=0$, so the particle is at rest, not travelling towards the origin. False.

Option B: at $t=5$, $v$ is at its maximum and positive, so the particle is moving, not at rest. False.

Option D: at $t=15$, $v<0$, so the particle is travelling from right to left. False.

Option C: at $t=10$, $v=0$, so the particle is at rest. The positive area for $2<t<10$ is much larger than the negative area for $0<t<2$, so the displacement at $t=10$ is positive and the particle is to the right of the origin. True.

The answer is option C.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{x^2}\right)&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}\times x^2-2x\,e^{3x}}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x\,e^{3x}(3x-2)}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{e^{3x}(3x-2)}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Consider the region enclosed by the curve $y=12+4x-x^2$ and the coordinate axes.

\exfigure{1344_q19_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the exact area of the region

dif.r: Find roots then definite integral of quadratic

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule and 5 function values to estimate the area of the region.

dif.r: Direct trapezoidal rule with given function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence find the percentage error between the exact area and the estimation from part (b).

dif.r: Simple percentage error from two found values

figures.cap: shaded region under y = 12 + 4x - x^2 between x = -2 and x = 6, above the x-axis

solutions.latex:
The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ and $x=6$, so the area is

$$\int_{-2}^{6}(12+4x-x^2)\,dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-2}^{6}(12+4x-x^2)\,dx&=\left[12x+2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{6} \\ &=\left(12\times 6+2\times 6^2-\dfrac{6^3}{3}\right)-\left(12\times(-2)+2\times 2^2-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{3}\right) \\ &=72-\left(-\dfrac{40}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{256}{3} \\ &=85\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Limits $-2$ and $6$ are the roots of $12+4x-x^2$; taken from the source working.

solutions.latex:
\extable{Ts5369_1}

Five function values give 4 strips, so

$$h=\dfrac{6-(-2)}{4}=2$$

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big(y_0+y_4+2(y_1+y_2+y_3)\big)$:

$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}\Big(0+0+2(12+16+12)\Big) \\ &=80 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the function values, or applies the trapezoidal rule with correct $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Table not visible; $x=-2,0,2,4,6$ taken from the working.

solutions.latex:
The error is the exact area less the estimate.

$$\text{Error}=85\dfrac{1}{3}-80=5\dfrac{1}{3}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error}&=\dfrac{5\frac{1}{3}}{85\frac{1}{3}}\times 100\% \\ &=6.25\% \end{aligned}$$

The estimate is an underestimate by $6.25\%$.

parts.latex:
A bag contains 4 red liquorice and 6 black liquorice lollies. Reese picks a lolly at random. If it is a red liquorice lolly, she will eat it and pick another. If it is a black liquorice lolly, she will replace it in the bag and choose another.

By drawing a tree diagram or otherwise, find the probability that after two draws, she chooses a red lolly and a black lolly, in any order.

dif.r: Two-branch tree with replacement depending on first colour

solutions.latex:
If the first lolly is red, it is not replaced, so the second draw is from 9 lollies (3 red, 6 black).

If the first lolly is black, it is replaced, so the second draw is from 10 lollies (4 red, 6 black).

The two orders are $RB$ and $BR$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(RB\text{ or }BR)&=\dfrac{4}{10}\times\dfrac{6}{9}+\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac{4}{10} \\ &=\dfrac{38}{75} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of one order correctly, or equivalent merit

$$\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx$$

dif.r: Reverse derivative result to integrate ln x, then log simplification

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\ln x+x\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &=\ln x+1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule with correct $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$. Integrate both sides from $e$ to $2e$:

$$\int_e^{2e}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)\,dx=\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx+\int_e^{2e}1\,dx$$

$$\big[x\ln x\big]_e^{2e}=\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx+\big[x\big]_e^{2e}$$

Rearranging:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx&=\big[x\ln x\big]_e^{2e}-\big[x\big]_e^{2e} \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e\ln e-(2e-e) \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e\ln e-e \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e-e \\ &=2e\ln 2e-2e \\ &=2e(\ln 2+\ln e)-2e \\ &=2e\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rearranges to express $\displaystyle\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx$ using $\big[x\ln x\big]$ and $\big[x\big]$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In a circle, an arc length of 30cm subtends $80^\circ$ at the centre of that circle. Find its radius.

solutions.latex:
The arc length is $l = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$ with $\theta = 80$.
$$\begin{aligned} 30 &= \dfrac{80}{360}\times 2\pi r \\ &= \dfrac{4}{9}\pi r \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \pi r &= \dfrac{30\times 9}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{135}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{135}{2\pi} \\ &\approx 21.5 \text{ cm (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r \approx 21.5 \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the arc length formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$

dif.r: Trig equation with adjusted compound-angle domain, exact values

solutions.latex:
Since $0\le x\le 2\pi$, adjust the range of the angle one step at a time.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi \\ 0&\le \dfrac{x}{2}\le \pi &&(\text{divide by } 2)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}&\le \dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \dfrac{3\pi}{4} &&(\text{subtract } \dfrac{\pi}{4})\end{aligned}$$
We need $\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

In the range $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \theta\le \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ the only solution is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ \dfrac{x}{2} &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \\ x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Finds the correct range for the angle and the solution $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

dif.r: Set derivative zero at given point to find constant

parts.label: b

dif.r: Routine stationary point and inflection test for cubic

solution sketch: sketch of y = -f(x)+3: max (0,3), inflexion (1,-1), min (2,-5)

solutions.latex:
A maximum turning point at $(2,8)$ means $f'(2)=0$.

Expanding, $f(x)=2kx^2-2x^3$, so $f'(x)=4kx-6x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 4k\times 2-6\times 2^2 \\ 0 &= 8k-24 \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, use $f(2)=8$:
$$\begin{aligned} 8 &= 2\times 2^2(k-2) \\ 8 &= 8(k-2) \\ 1 &= k-2 \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=3$$

meta.format_note: Source line '0 = 2k - 6' (after 4k×2 - 6×2²) skipped a step; written as 0 = 8k - 24, same result k = 3. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
With $k=3$, $f(x)=6x^2-2x^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 12x-6x^2 \\ &= 6x(2-x) \end{aligned}$$
The stationary points are at $x=0$ and $x=2$. Since $(2,8)$ is the maximum, $(0,0)$ is the minimum turning point.

For inflexions, find where $f''(x)=0$.
$$f''(x)=12-12x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 12-12x \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts5383_1}

The concavity changes from concave up to concave down, so $(1,4)$ is a point of inflexion.

Alternatively, $x=1$ lies between the maximum $(2,8)$ and the minimum $(0,0)$, so the curve changes concavity there.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum turning point } (0,0),\ \text{inflexion point } (1,4)$$
criteria: Finds the minimum turning point and $x=1$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A survey of where students choose to read the current news revealed that, on a regular basis, 33% read the news on Instagram, 45% read the news on Facebook and 44% do not read the news at all.

parts.latex: A student is selected at random. Given that this student does read the news on a regular basis, find the probability that this student gets their news from Facebook.

solutions.latex:
Let $F$ = Facebook and $I$ = Instagram. $P(\text{neither})=44\%$, so $P(F\cup I)=56\%$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(F\cap I) &= 33+45-56 \\ &= 22\% \end{aligned}$$
Venn diagram: Facebook only $23\%$, both $22\%$, Instagram only $11\%$, neither $44\%$.
$$\therefore\ P(F\cap I)=22\%$$

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, with $\text{News}$ meaning the student reads the news:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Fb}\mid\text{News}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{Fb}\cap\text{News})}{P(\text{News})} \\ &= \dfrac{23+22}{23+22+11} \\ &= \dfrac{45}{56} \\ &\approx 80.4\% \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P \approx 80.4\%$$

questions.stem: Rumour spreading at a school can be modelled by $N=2\times 1.61^{0.7t}$ where $N$ is the number of students who have heard the rumour and $t$ is the number of hours after it first started.

parts.label: b
