dif.r: Solve exponential equation using logarithms

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7\times 6} \\ &= 14.78\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 14 \text{ or } 15 \text{ students (both accepted)}$$

meta.marker_note: Both 14 and 15 students accepted.
meta.format_note: Source criterion 'Both 14 and 15 students accepted' moved to marker_note.

solutions.latex:
Set $N=165$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 165 &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7t} \\ \dfrac{165}{2} &= 1.61^{0.7t} \end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{165}{2}\right) &= \ln\left(1.61^{0.7t}\right) \\ &= 0.7t\ln 1.61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{165}{2}\right)}{0.7\ln 1.61} \\ &= 13.23\ldots \\ &\approx 13.24 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 13.24 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Takes logarithms to obtain $\ln\left(\dfrac{165}{2}\right)=0.7t\ln 1.61$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\displaystyle \int_0^1 \left(8kx-4kx^3\right)dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[4kx^2-kx^4\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ 4k-k-(0-0) &= 1 \\ 3k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}x-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3$$
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2$$
The mode is the maximum of $f(x)$, so solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2 \\ 4x^2 &= \dfrac{8}{3} \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le x\le 1$, $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.

This is a maximum, as $f'(x)$ is a downward parabola, positive before and negative after $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}\approx 0.82 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Differentiates $f(x)$ and sets $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with $C=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(4-x)^2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(16-8x+x^2)\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(16x-8x^2+x^3+48-24x+3x^2\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(x^3-5x^2-8x+48\right) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3x^2-10x-8 \\ &= (3x+2)(x-4) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=4$.

As $(4-x)^2$ is a length, $x\ne 4$. Hence $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

By the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:

$$\therefore\ QR=19.79\ldots\approx 19.8 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$

parts.latex:
The parabola $f(x)=x^2-mx+n$ has a minimum at $(-2,-4)$.

What are the values of $m$ and $n$?

dif.r: Vertex formula then substitute point; two linked steps.

solutions.latex:
The vertex of $f(x)=x^2-mx+n$ is at $x=\dfrac{m}{2}$. The minimum is at $x=-2$, so
$$\dfrac{m}{2}=-2$$
$$m=-4$$
The point $(-2,-4)$ lies on the curve, so $f(-2)=-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} (-2)^2-(-4)(-2)+n &= -4\\ 4-8+n &= -4\\ n &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=-4 \text{ and } n=0$$
This matches option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the derivative of $y=\dfrac{3x^2-4}{4x^2-3}$?

dif.r: Quotient rule with algebraic simplification to match options.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x^2-4 & v&=4x^2-3\\ u'&=6x & v'&=8x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{6x(4x^2-3)-8x(3x^2-4)}{(4x^2-3)^2}\\ &= \dfrac{24x^3-18x-24x^3+32x}{(4x^2-3)^2}\\ &= \dfrac{14x}{(4x^2-3)^2} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

solutions.latex:
For $f(x)$ increasing we need $f'(x)>0$.
$$f'(x)=2x-6x^2$$
Solve
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-6x^2&>0\\ 2x(1-3x)&>0\end{aligned}$$
The critical values are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$, and the parabola $2x-6x^2$ is concave down, so it is positive between them.
$$\therefore\ 0<x<\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Factorises and finds the critical values, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)=-\operatorname{cosec}x\cot x$

solutions.latex:
Write $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1 & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=0 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)&=\dfrac{\sin x\times 0-\cos x}{(\sin x)^2}\\ &=-\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct quotient rule derivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A piece of wire of length 24 cm is to be cut into two pieces. One piece is to be bent to form a square of side $x$ cm and the other piece is to be bent to form an equilateral triangle of side $y$ cm. Let $A_1(x)$ and $A_2(y)$ be the respective areas of the square and equilateral triangle.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: With the aid of a diagram, show that $A_2(y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2$.

dif.r: Direct use of half ab sin C with 60 degrees.

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the sum $S$ of the two areas is given by $S=x^2+\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)^2$.

dif.r: Set up length constraint and substitute to build given expression.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, determine the exact value of $x$ so that $S$ is at its minimum.

dif.r: Optimise given function; messy surd algebra and nature test.

solutions.latex:
The 24 cm wire is cut into lengths $4x$ (square) and $3y$ (triangle).

Diagram: a square of side $x$; an equilateral triangle of side $y$ with each angle $60^\circ$.

Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with two sides $y$ and included angle $60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2(y)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times y^2\times\sin 60^\circ\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times y^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Diagrams, or uses $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source diagrams are described only in words; question asks for a diagram but none is drawn here.

solutions.latex:
The total length of wire is 24 cm:
$$4x+3y=24$$
So $3y=24-4x$, hence
$$y=\dfrac{4}{3}(6-x)$$
Substitute into $S=A_1+A_2=x^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=x^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left[\dfrac{4}{3}(6-x)\right]^2\\ &=x^2+\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dS}{dx}=2x-\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dS}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)=\dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3}-\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}x\\ \left(2+\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\right)x&=\dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3}\\ x&=\dfrac{24\sqrt{3}}{9+4\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2S}{dx^2}=2+\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}>0$$
So $S$ is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{24\sqrt{3}}{9+4\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ and shows the second derivative is positive, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Fish are introduced into a small dam. The size of the population, $N$, of fish can be modelled can be modelled by the function

$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24e^{-0.5t}}$$

where $t$ is the time in months after the fish are introduced into the dam.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population is given by

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}$$

dif.r: Show-that derivative via quotient rule with exponential.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the range of the function $N$, justifying your answer.

dif.r: Range needs initial value, limit and monotonicity justification combined.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=500 & v&=1+24e^{-0.5t}\\ u'&=0 & v'&=-12e^{-0.5t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt}&=\dfrac{(1+24e^{-0.5t})\cdot 0-500\times(-12e^{-0.5t})}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Quotient rule working with one error, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No marks are awarded for the final line, but the statement must be written.

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24}=20$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so
$$N\to\dfrac{500}{1+24\times 0}=500$$
Since $\dfrac{dN}{dt}>0$ for all $t$, $N$ is always increasing, so it rises from 20 towards 500 without reaching it.
$$\therefore\ 20\le N<500$$
criteria: Finds the limiting value $N=500$, or equivalent merit

Let $L=a+b$, where the two parts of the tube satisfy
$$a=\dfrac{3}{\cos\alpha},\qquad b=\dfrac{4}{\sin\alpha}$$
$$L=3(\cos\alpha)^{-1}+4(\sin\alpha)^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}=\dfrac{3\sin\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha}-\dfrac{4\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}=\dfrac{3\sin^3\alpha-4\cos^3\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\alpha}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin^3\alpha-4\cos^3\alpha&=0\\ \tan^3\alpha&=\dfrac{4}{3}\\ \tan\alpha&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&<0 &&\text{at } \alpha=47^\circ\\ \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&=0 &&\text{at } \alpha\approx 47.7^\circ\\ \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&>0 &&\text{at } \alpha=48^\circ\end{aligned}$$
So $L$ is a minimum at $\alpha=47.74^\circ$. The longest tube that fits round the corner has this minimum length:
$$L=\dfrac{3}{\cos 47.74^\circ}+\dfrac{4}{\sin 47.74^\circ}\approx 9.87\text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum length}\approx 9.87\text{ m (2 dp)}$$

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int e^{2x}-e\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
Integrate each term, using $\displaystyle \int e^{ax}\,dx=\dfrac{e^{ax}}{a}$ and noting $e$ is a constant.
$$\int \left(e^{2x}-e\right)dx=\dfrac{e^{2x}}{2}-ex+c$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: What is the expression for the obtuse angle subtended by the line $x+y=1$, and the positive direction of the $x$-axis?

skills: Angle of inclination of a line

solutions.latex:
Rearranging, $y=-x+1$, so the gradient is $-1$.

Then $\tan\theta=-1$ with $\theta$ obtuse.

The acute reference angle is $\tan^{-1}1$, so
$$\theta=\pi-\tan^{-1}1$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
Consider a curve with the following properties:

$f(x)$ is odd.

$f(5)=0$ and $f'(2)=0$.

$f'(x)>0$ for $x>2$.

Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)$?

dif.r: Combine odd symmetry, intercept and derivative info to pick graph

figures.cap: option A: graph option A
option B: graph option B
option C: graph option C
option D: graph option D

solutions.latex:
Odd function: $f(-x)=-f(x)$, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin.

$f(5)=0$ gives an $x$-intercept at $x=5$, and so also at $x=-5$.

$f'(2)=0$ gives a stationary point at $x=2$, and $f'(x)>0$ for $x>2$ means the curve is increasing after $x=2$.

Option C is the graph with all of these features.

parts.latex: Which expression is NOT equal to $\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)$?

dif.r: Check four expressions with log laws and change of base

solutions.latex:
Use the change of base rule, $\log_2 b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln 2}$.

Option B: $\dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{8}}{\ln 2}=\log_2\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Option C: $\log_2 1-\log_2 8=\log_2\dfrac{1}{8}$ by the log law for quotients.

Option D: $\dfrac{\ln 1-\ln 8}{\ln 2}=\dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{8}}{\ln 2}$, which is equal.

Option A is the reciprocal $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln\frac{1}{8}}=\dfrac{1}{-3}$, while $\log_2\dfrac{1}{8}=-3$, so A is not equal.

The answer is option A.

parts.latex: What values of $k$ result in $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin kx\,dx=0$, where $k$ is an integer?

dif.r: Integrate with general k, then solve cos kπ = 1

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}\sin kx\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{\cos kx}{k}\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= -\dfrac{\cos k\pi}{k}+\dfrac{1}{k} \end{aligned}$$

Since $P(B')=0.8$,
$$P(B)=1-0.8=0.2$$

$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=0.1$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find stationary points.
$$f'(x)=4x^3+6x^2=2x^2(2x+3)$$
Setting $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Substituting, $f(0)=1$ and $f\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=-\dfrac{11}{16}$.

Stationary points: $(0,1)$ and $\left(-\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$.

For points of inflection, solve $f''(x)=0$.
$$f''(x)=12x^2+12x=12x(x+1)$$
So $x=0$ or $x=-1$.

Test the sign of $f''$ either side of each root.
$$\begin{aligned} f''&>0 &&\text{for } x<-1 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''&<0 &&\text{for } -1<x<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''&>0 &&\text{for } x>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
Concavity changes at both, so $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are points of inflection.
criteria: Finds the stationary points and solves $f''(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $v=3(t-1)(t-3)$ and $\ddot{x}=6(t-2)$

dif.r: Product rule twice with factorising to given forms

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when the particle is moving towards O.

dif.r: Interpret towards O as v<0 since x≥0

can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find when the particle is moving towards O and slowing down.

dif.r: Combine sign conditions on velocity and acceleration for slowing down

parts.label: d
parts.latex: How far has the particle travelled in the first 4 seconds?

dif.r: Distance not displacement; must track two direction changes

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $x=t(t-3)^2$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=(t-3)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(t-3)^2+2t(t-3) \\ &=(t-3)(t-3+2t) \\ &=(t-3)(3t-3) \\ &=3(t-1)(t-3) \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, again by the product rule with $u=t-1$, $v=t-3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=3\big((t-1)\cdot 1+(t-3)\cdot 1\big) \\ &=3(2t-4) \\ &=6(t-2) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $x=t(t-3)^2\ge 0$ for $t\ge 0$, the particle is never left of O, so it moves towards O when $v<0$.
$$3(t-1)(t-3)<0$$
This parabola opens upward, so it is negative between the roots.
$$\therefore\ 1<t<3$$

The particle slows down when $v$ and $\ddot{x}$ have opposite signs. Moving towards O means $v<0$, so we need $\ddot{x}>0$.
$$6(t-2)>0$$
Hence $t>2$.

From part (b), $v<0$ for $1<t<3$.

Therefore both conditions hold when
$$2<t<3$$

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: none needed for this part (sketch_id 1036_q14_s1 not used). Reasoning for $v<0$ taken from part (b) as $1<t<3$ since $v=3(t-1)(t-3)$.

solutions.latex:
The particle may change direction where $v=0$, so find the positions at the endpoints and turning points.
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\quad x=0\\ t=4:&\quad x=4 \end{aligned}$$
From $v=3(t-1)(t-3)=0$, the particle is at rest at $t=1$ and $t=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=1:&\quad x=4\\ t=3:&\quad x=0 \end{aligned}$$
The particle goes from $0$ to $4$, back to $0$, then to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 4+4+4\\ &= 12 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the positions at the turning points and endpoints, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given $\sec\theta=-\dfrac{37}{12}$ for $0<\theta<\pi$, find the exact value of $\text{cosec}\,\theta$.

dif.r: Reciprocal ratios with Pythagorean triple and quadrant sign

solutions.latex:
Since $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$,
$$\cos\theta=-\dfrac{12}{37}$$
In a right-angled triangle with adjacent $12$ and hypotenuse $37$, Pythagoras' theorem gives opposite side $\sqrt{37^2-12^2}=35$.

For $0<\theta<\pi$, $\sin\theta>0$, and $\cos\theta<0$ places $\theta$ in the second quadrant, so
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{35}{37}$$
Since $\text{cosec}\,\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$,
$$\therefore\ \text{cosec}\,\theta=\dfrac{37}{35}$$
criteria: Finds the ratio $\sin\theta=\dfrac{35}{37}$ without the correct sign, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_3 x^4\right)$

dif.r: Log law then change of base before differentiating

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\log_3 x^4=4\log_3 x$, then the change of base rule $\log_3 x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_3 x^4\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(4\log_3 x\right)\\ &= 4\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{4}{\ln 3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{x\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the change of base rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The probability distribution below has a mean of $1.5$.

\extable{1036_q17_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the value of $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Two simultaneous equations from probability sum and mean

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, calculate the variance of the data.

dif.r: Standard variance formula with found values

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+a+0.3+b&=1\\ a+b&=0.4 &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
The mean is $1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0+1\cdot a+2(0.3)+3b&=1.5\\ a+3b&=0.9 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 2b&=0.5\\ b&=0.25 \end{aligned}$$
Then $a=0.4-0.25=0.15$.
$$\therefore\ a=0.15,\ b=0.25$$
criteria: Writes two correct equations, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $e^{2\ln x}=2x+3$.

dif.r: Simplify e^(2ln x), solve quadratic, reject using domain

solutions.latex:
The logarithm needs $x>0$. Using $e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$:
$$e^{2\ln x}=e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=2x+3\\ x^2-2x-3&=0\\ (x-3)(x+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=3$ or $x=-1$. Since $x>0$, reject $x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=3$$

questions.stem:
On any given day, the depth of water in a lake is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\le t\le 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $t$ for which $h(t)=10$.

dif.r: Trig equation in context with adjusted domain, two quadrants

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What rate is the depth of the river changing at 1:00 pm?

dif.r: Chain rule derivative, convert 1 pm to t=7

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch $h(t)$ showing all important features.

\exfigure{1036_q19_1}

dif.r: Sketch sine with given amplitude, centre and period

figures.cap: blank axes for sketch of h(t)
solution sketch: worked sketch of h(t)

solutions.latex:
Setting $h(t)=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=10\\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-4\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$
criteria: Finds one correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h'(t)&=8\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from 6 am, so 1:00 pm is $t=7$.
$$h'(7)=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)\text{ m/h}$$
$$\therefore\ h'(7)\approx -0.54 \text{ m/h}$$

meta.format_note: Added numerical value $-0.54$ m/h (computed: $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos 105^\circ\approx -0.542$); source gave exact form only.

solutions.latex:
The period is
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}}=24$$
The centre line is $h=14$ and the amplitude is $8$, so the maximum is $22$ and the minimum is $6$.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx$

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3-3x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|3x-x^3\right|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the perimeter of region G, is given by $P=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r}$.

dif.r: Build perimeter and area from sectors, eliminate θ

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the minimum value of $P$.

dif.r: Routine minimisation of simple given function

figures.cap: baseball field diagram showing sectors XAB (radius 4r) and XDC (radius 3r), region G

solutions.latex:
The arc length of a sector of radius $R$ and angle $\theta$ is $R\theta$, so arc $AB=4r\theta$ and arc $CD=3r\theta$. Also $AD=BC=4r-3r=r$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=AD+AB+BC+CD\\ &=r+4r\theta+r+3r\theta\\ &=2r+7r\theta &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
The area of $G$ is the large sector minus the small sector, using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}R^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(4r)^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}(3r)^2\theta&=5000\\ \dfrac{7r^2\theta}{2}&=5000\\ \theta&=\dfrac{10000}{7r^2} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=2r+7r\cdot\dfrac{10000}{7r^2}\\ &=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the perimeter in terms of $r$ and $\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source: line drawn from perimeter with straight sides AD and BC each of length $r$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $P=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r}$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dr}=2-\dfrac{10000}{r^2}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} r^2&=5000\\ r&=50\sqrt{2} &&(r>0) \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{20000}{r^3}>0 \text{ since } r>0$$
So $r=50\sqrt{2}$ gives a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min}&=100\sqrt{2}+\dfrac{10000}{50\sqrt{2}}\\ &=100\sqrt{2}+100\sqrt{2}\\ &=200\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows the stationary point is a minimum, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Tangent, intercepts, then curve area minus triangle; multi-stage

figures.cap: curve y=(2x-1)^4, tangent at B(1,1), shaded region R

solutions.latex:
Differentiating the curve:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=8(2x-1)^3$$
At $B(1,1)$ the gradient is $8$, so the tangent is
$$y-1=8(x-1)$$
When $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&=8(x-1)\\ x&=\dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The region $R$ is the area under the curve from $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $x=1$, minus the triangle under the tangent with base $1-\dfrac{7}{8}=\dfrac{1}{8}$ and height $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of } R&=\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}(2x-1)^4\,dx-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{8}\times 1\\ &=\left[\dfrac{(2x-1)^5}{10}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}-\dfrac{1}{16}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{10}-0-\dfrac{1}{16}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{80} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the area as integral minus triangle, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-intercept of the tangent, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient at $B$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Alice, Brett and Chris are all going to see the Eiffel Tower. Alice is due north of the tower, Chris is due east and Brett is on the line of sight between them. The angles of elevation to the top of the tower from Alice, Brett and Chris are $23^\circ$, $25^\circ$ and $32^\circ$ respectively.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the angle between the Eiffel Tower, Alice and Chris is represented by

$$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D visualisation, express distances via h, then ratio

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the bearing of Brett from the Eiffel Tower?
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D bearings with ambiguous sine rule case resolved geometrically

solutions.latex:
Let $D$ be the base of the tower, $E$ its top and $h=DE$. Let $\theta=\angle DAC$, the angle between the tower, Alice and Chris. Since Alice is due north and Chris due east of the tower, $\angle ADC=90^\circ$.

In right-angled triangle $CDE$:
$$h=CD\tan 32^\circ,\quad\text{so } CD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADE$:
$$h=AD\tan 23^\circ,\quad\text{so } AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{CD}{AD}\\ &=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}\div\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &=\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}\approx 34.2^\circ$$
criteria: Expresses $CD$ and $AD$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source opening had an unfinished phrase ('and $\angle DAE$...'); removed it. Diagram for the solution (key 1036_q24_s1) is not added here.

solutions.latex:
In triangle $ADB$ (right-angled at the elevation triangles): $AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$ and $BD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 25^\circ}$. Also $\angle DAB=\theta\approx 34.2^\circ$, with $\angle ABD=\alpha$ and $\angle ADB=\beta$.

By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{AD}&=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{BD}\\ \sin\alpha&=\sin\theta\times\dfrac{\tan 25^\circ}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &\approx 0.61729 \end{aligned}$$
So $\alpha\approx 38^\circ$ or $\alpha\approx 142^\circ$ (ambiguous case).

If $\alpha=38^\circ$:
$$\beta=180^\circ-38^\circ-34^\circ=108^\circ$$
This is not valid, because $B$ lies between $A$ and $C$ so $0<\beta<90^\circ$.

Therefore $\alpha=142^\circ$, and
$$\beta=180^\circ-34^\circ-142^\circ\approx 4^\circ$$
Brett is $4^\circ$ east of north from the tower.
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is about } 004^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Rejects the ambiguous case, or equivalent merit
Applies the sine rule to find $\sin\alpha$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A sector with perimeter 28 cm contains an angle of 1.5 radians at the centre of a circle with radius $r$ cm. What is the value of $r$?

dif.r: Sector perimeter formula used in reverse to find radius.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is the arc length plus two radii, with arc length $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.5r+2r&=28\\ \dfrac{7}{2}r&=28\\ r&=8 \end{aligned}$$
So $r=8$, which is option B.

parts.latex: Consider the functions $f(x)=x^2$ and $g(x)=x+2$. Which of the following expressions is equal to $f(g(x))-g(f(x))$?

dif.r: Direct composition of two simple functions and expansion.

solutions.latex:
Substitute one function into the other.
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x))-g(f(x))&=(x+2)^2-(x^2+2)\\ &=x^2+4x+4-x^2-2\\ &=4x+2 \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option A.

parts.latex:
A and B are two independent events with $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{3}{8}$ and $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

What is the value of $P(B)$?

dif.r: Addition rule combined with independence, then solve linear equation.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
For independent events, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, so
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$$
Substituting,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{8}&=\dfrac{1}{4}+P(B)\left(1-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\\ \dfrac{3}{4}P(B)&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ P(B)&=\dfrac{1}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option D.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_{10}3x$?

dif.r: Change of base, differentiate, then recognise 1/ln10 as log10 e.

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_{10}3x=\log_{10}3+\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\log_{10}3x&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_{10}3+\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 10} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{\ln 10}=\log_{10}e$, this equals $\dfrac{\log_{10}e}{x}$.

So the answer is option D.

meta.format_note: The source's last step was an over-complicated chain (with extra factors of $\log_{10}e$) that simplified to $\dfrac{\log_{10}e}{x}$; replaced by the direct step $\dfrac{1}{\ln 10}=\log_{10}e$. Same result.

parts.latex:
The marks on a test are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

2.5% of the marks are 34 or less and 16% of the marks are 70 or more. What is the value of $\mu$?

dif.r: Translate percentages to empirical-rule z-values, solve simultaneous equations.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
For a normal distribution, 2.5% of scores lie at or below 2 standard deviations below the mean, and 16% lie at or above 1 standard deviation above the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \mu-2\sigma&=34\\ \mu+\sigma&=70 \end{aligned}$$
Double the second equation and add it to the first.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\mu&=34+2\times70=174\\ \mu&=58 \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx$?

dif.r: Combine fractions and Pythagorean identity before integrating sec squared.

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator, then use $1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx&=\int\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2x}\,dx\\ &=\int\dfrac{2}{\cos^2x}\,dx\\ &=2\int\sec^2x\,dx\\ &=2\tan x+c \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option C.

parts.latex: A single lump sum investment of $\$P$ earns an amount of interest $\$I$ after 2 years with a rate of interest of 6% p.a. compounded monthly. Which of the following is an expression for $P$?

dif.r: Compound interest formula rearranged for principal from interest earned.

solutions.latex:
Interest is the final amount minus the principal. The monthly rate is $\dfrac{0.06}{12}=0.005$ and there are $24$ months.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(1+\dfrac{0.06}{12}\right)^{24}-P&=I\\ P\left\{(1.005)^{24}-1\right\}&=I\\ P&=\dfrac{I}{(1.005)^{24}-1} \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
If $x>0$ what is the limiting sum of the series

$\log_2 x-\log_4 x+\log_{16}x-\log_{256}x+\dots+(-1)^{n+1}\log_{2^{\left(2^{n-1}\right)}}x+\dots$ ?

dif.r: Recognise log series as geometric via change of base; non-routine.

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, the $n$th term is
$$T_n=(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac{\log_2x}{\log_2 2^{\left(2^{n-1}\right)}}=(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac{\log_2x}{2^{n-1}}$$
Hence the series is geometric with $a=\log_2x$ and $r=-\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{\log_2x}{1+\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\log_2x \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option A.

parts.latex: A circle has equation $x^2+y^2-6x+4y+k=0$ for some constant $k$. Find the set of possible values of $k$.

dif.r: Complete squares then reason radius squared must be positive.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+y^2-6x+4y+k&=0\\ x^2-6x+9+y^2+4y+4&=13-k\\ (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2&=13-k \end{aligned}$$
Hence $r^2=13-k$. A circle needs $r^2>0$, so $13-k>0$.
$$\therefore\ k<13$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure with one error in algebra, or quotes $k\le 13$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $A(-1,-5)$ and $B(5,-1)$ are two points. Find in general form the equation of the straight line through the midpoint of $AB$ and perpendicular to $AB$.

dif.r: Midpoint, gradient, perpendicular gradient, point-gradient form; all routine.

solutions.latex:
The midpoint of $AB$ is
$$\left(\dfrac{-1+5}{2},\dfrac{-5-1}{2}\right)=(2,-3)$$
The gradient of $AB$ is
$$\dfrac{-1-(-5)}{5-(-1)}=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
The perpendicular gradient is $-\dfrac{3}{2}$, so the perpendicular bisector is
$$\begin{aligned} y+3&=-\dfrac{3}{2}(x-2)\\ 2y+6&=-3x+6\\ 3x+2y&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 3x+2y=0$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure but with one error, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the point on the curve $y=2\sqrt{x}$ where the tangent to the curve is parallel to the line $2x-y-2=0$.

dif.r: Differentiate root, equate to line gradient, solve for point.

solutions.latex:
The line $2x-y-2=0$ is $y=2x-2$, which has gradient $2$.

Differentiate the curve.
$$y=2\sqrt{x},\quad \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$$
The tangent is parallel to the line when the gradients are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}&=2\\ \sqrt{x}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=2\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}}=1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the point is }\left(\dfrac{1}{4},1\right)$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure but with one error, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} a&=ab-b^2\\ b^2&=ab-a\\ b^2&=a(b-1)\\ a&=\dfrac{b^2}{b-1} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sin x+x\cos x$$
At $x=1$ (radians),
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sin 1+\cos 1\approx1.38$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the gradient is }1.38$$

parts.latex: Find the values of any constant $A$ such that $\displaystyle\int_0^3 (x^2+A)\,dx=2A^2$.

dif.r: Routine definite integral then solve a factorable quadratic in A

solutions.latex:
Integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3(x^2+A)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^3+Ax\right]_0^3 \\ &= 9+3A \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $2A^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9+3A &= 2A^2 \\ 2A^2-3A-9 &= 0 \\ (2A+3)(A-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=3 \text{ or } A=-\dfrac{3}{2}$$
criteria: Integrates to find a quadratic equation for $A$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the value of the constant $k>0$ such that $\displaystyle\int_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx=\ln 10$.

dif.r: Logarithmic limits need careful log-law simplification before solving

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then substitute the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx &= \Big[x+\ln x\Big]_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2} \\ &= (\ln k^2-\ln k)+\big(\ln(\ln k^2)-\ln(\ln k)\big) \\ &= 2\ln k-\ln k+\ln(2\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln k+\ln 2+\ln(\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln 2k \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\ln 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln 2k &= \ln 10 \\ 2k &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=5$$
criteria: Evaluates and partially simplifies the definite integral in terms of $k$, or equivalent merit
Evaluates the definite integral in terms of $k$ without simplification, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.

dif.r: Standard quotient rule stationary points with sign test

solutions.latex:
Use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x-2\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=8$.

Stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,8)$.

The sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ decides the nature (the curve is undefined at $x=2$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x<0 &&\text{increasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=0 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<2 \text{ and } 2<x<4 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=4 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>4 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the nature of one of them, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Applies the quotient rule for differentiation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At time $t$ hours after midnight on a particular day the depth $D$ metres of water in the Oztown harbour is given by the function $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 24$.

questions.stem: An item is purchased for \$20 000. It appreciates in value so that after $t$ years its value $\$V$ is given by the formula $V=20000p^t$ for some constant $p>1$. After 9 years its value is \$32 000.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $p$ correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Substitute and take ninth root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find correct to the nearest \$10 per year the rate at which the item is appreciating in value after 9 years.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential base p and evaluate at t=9

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=9$, $V=32000$ into $V=20000p^t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 32000 &= 20000p^9 \\ p^9 &= \dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=(1.6)^{\frac{1}{9}}\approx 1.0536$$
criteria: Writes and simplifies a numerical expression for $p^9$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $V=20000p^t$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=20000\ln p\cdot p^t$$
At $t=9$, $\ln p=\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6$ and $p^9=\dfrac{8}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 20000\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6\right)\times\dfrac{8}{5} \\ &\approx 1670 \end{aligned}$$
The item is appreciating at \$1670 per year (nearest \$10 per year).
criteria: Differentiates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At the start of year 2000 a colony of 600 animals was established in a sanctuary. Each year the population size grows at a rate of 10% per year and at the end of each year 50 of the animals are released into the wild. The population size $P_n$ at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year can be determined using the recurrence relation $P_n=1.1\times P_{n-1}-50$ where $n=1,2,3,\dots$ and $P_0=600$.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Write down expressions for $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ in terms of $P_0$ and hence show that

$P_n=100\times(1.1)^n+500$.

dif.r: Generalise recurrence into GP sum and simplify to closed form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the year in which the growth in population size from the beginning of that year to the start of the next year first exceeds 100.

dif.r: Set up difference inequality, solve with logs, interpret calendar year

criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. process correct but one error, or simplification not completed, or equivalent merit
Finds expressions for $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
We need the least integer $n$ such that $P_n-P_{n-1}>100$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100\left\{(1.1)^n-(1.1)^{n-1}\right\} &> 100 \\ (1.1)^{n-1}(1.1-1) &> 1 \\ (1.1)^{n-1} &> 10 \\ (n-1)\log_{10}(1.1) &> 1 \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{1}{\log_{10}(1.1)}\approx 24.16 \end{aligned}$$
So $n-1=25,26,27,\dots$, and the least $n$ is $26$.

Year $n$ is the calendar year $1999+n$ ($P_0$ is the start of 2000), so $n=26$ is 2025.

The required year is 2025.
criteria: Correct procedure with one error in calculation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity and use initial condition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when and where the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Set v=0, solve surd equation, substitute into displacement

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds of its motion.

dif.r: Distance requires accounting for change of direction

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9 \\ x &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $0=2+c$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$
criteria: Integrates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9 &= 0 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=8$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(9)(3)-72-2 \\ &= -20 \end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $v=-3$, so the particle initially moves in the negative direction.

The particle is at rest at $t=8$ seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in its initial direction of travel.

When $t=24$, $x=32$.

The particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=-20$ (at rest at $t=8$), then to $x=32$ by $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 20+(20+32) \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The cost $\$C$ per hour when employees work $x$ hours per day to complete a project is given by $C=ax^3+d$ for some constants $a$ and $d$. The time $T$ hours to complete the project is given by $T=\dfrac{120}{x}$. In order to complete the project, the cost would be \$248 per hour when employees work 4 hours per day on the project and \$472 per hour when employees work 8 hours per day on the project.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write down two equations in $a$ and $d$ and solve these equations to find the values of $a$ and $d$.

dif.r: Substitute two cases and solve linear simultaneous equations

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the total cost $\$S$ of completing the project when employees work $x$ hours per day on the project is given by $S=60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x}$.

dif.r: Recognise total cost equals time times hourly cost

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Use differentiation to find the minimum total cost of completing the project.

dif.r: Standard optimisation of given function with nature test

solutions.latex:
Substitute the two given cases into $C=ax^3+d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 248 &= 64a+d &&(1)\\ 472 &= 512a+d &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2).
$$\begin{aligned} 224 &= 448a \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 248-64\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 216 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2},\ d=216$$
criteria: Writes correct simultaneous equations but makes one error in solution, or equivalent merit
Writes one of the equations correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Total cost is time multiplied by cost per hour, $S=TC$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{120}{x}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{2}+216\right) \\ &= 60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate $S$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 120x-\dfrac{25\,920}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{120}{x^2}\left(x^3-216\right) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary point: $\dfrac{dS}{dx}=0$ gives $x^3=216$, so $x=6$.

The sign of $\dfrac{dS}{dx}$ decides the nature:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<6 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=6 \\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>6 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ gives a minimum.
$$S=60(36)+\dfrac{25\,920}{6}=6480$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum cost is } \$6480$$
criteria: Correct procedure with one error or omission, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

dif.r: Check non-negativity and integrate to 1

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ of the random variable $X$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf to get piecewise CDF

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that if $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ are the quartiles of the distribution of $X$ then $\dfrac{1}{Q_1},\dfrac{1}{Q_2},\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.

dif.r: Find three quartiles from CDF and verify common difference

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
A probability density function needs $f(x)\ge 0$ and total area $1$.

For $1\le x\le 2$, $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}>0$, and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 f(x)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{x}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -1+2 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds and evaluates the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 2$, integrate the density from $1$ to $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x \dfrac{2}{t^2}\,dt \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{t}\right]_1^x \\ &= 2-\dfrac{2}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<1\\[6pt] 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right), & 1\le x\le 2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$
criteria: Correct procedure with one error or omission, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source integrand used $x$ as both limit and variable; written with dummy variable $t$ (same mathematics).

solutions.latex:
Each quartile $Q$ satisfies $F(Q)=\dfrac{1}{4},\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{3}{4}$, with $F(x)=2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.

First quartile:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_1}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= \dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
Median:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Third quartile:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_3}\right) &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3} &= \dfrac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$$
Check the differences:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{Q_2}-\dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= \dfrac{6}{8}-\dfrac{7}{8}=-\dfrac{1}{8} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3}-\dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= \dfrac{5}{8}-\dfrac{6}{8}=-\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $-\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Therefore $\dfrac{1}{Q_1},\dfrac{1}{Q_2},\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.
criteria: Correct procedure with an error in execution, or AP not verified, or equivalent merit
Finds one of the quartiles or its reciprocal correctly, or equivalent merit

\exfigure{1052_q33_1}

The diagram shows the graphs of the curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ where $f(x)=e^x$ and $g(x)=6-8e^{-x}$.
questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State a sequence of dilations, reflections, translations that would transform the graph of the curve $y=f(x)$ into the graph of the curve $y=g(x)$.

dif.r: Describe dilation, two reflections and translation in valid order

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinates ($x_1$ and $x_2$ where $x_1<x_2$) of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $e^{2x}-6e^x+8=0$ and solve this equation to find the exact values of $x_1$ and $x_2$.

dif.r: Equate curves, multiply by e^x, solve quadratic in e^x

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form the area of the region enclosed by the two curves.

dif.r: Area between exponential curves with log limits, exact simplification

figures.cap: graphs of y=e^x and y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6

solutions.latex:
Start with $y=e^x$.

A vertical dilation by factor $8$ gives $y=8e^x$.

Reflecting in the $y$ axis gives $y=8e^{-x}$.

Reflecting in the $x$ axis gives $y=-8e^{-x}$.

A vertical translation up by $6$ units gives $y=6-8e^{-x}$.

So: a vertical dilation by factor $8$, then reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axes, followed by a vertical translation upwards by $6$ units.
criteria: Identifies one or two correct transformations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x &= 6-8e^{-x} \\ e^{2x} &= 6e^x-8 \\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8 &= 0 \\ (e^x-2)(e^x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln 2,\ x_2=\ln 4$$
criteria: Finds the equation and the values of $e^x$, or equivalent merit
Obtains the required equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Between the intersections $g(x)\ge f(x)$, so the area is
$$\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
Integrate and substitute the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \Big[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= 6(\ln 4-\ln 2)+8\left(e^{-\ln 4}-e^{-\ln 2}\right)-\left(e^{\ln 4}-e^{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= 6\ln 2+8\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-(4-2) \\ &= 6\ln 2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area is } (6\ln 2-4) \text{ square units}$$
criteria: Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative with partial evaluation, or equivalent merit
Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}\right)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}\right)&=\dfrac{x^2\cos x-2x\sin x}{(x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{x\cos x-2\sin x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is D.

parts.latex:
$X$ is a continuous random variable whose probability density function is $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$ for $0\le x\le\sqrt{e-1}$ and zero otherwise.

Find the probability that $X<e-2$.

dif.r: Must find region where pdf below value, then integrate; non-routine

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The probability is found by integrating the density over the values of $x$ where $f(x)<e-2$, namely $0\le x\le e-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{e-2}\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx&=\Big[\ln(x^2+1)\Big]_0^{e-2}\\ &=\ln\big((e-2)^2+1\big)-\ln 1\\ &=\ln(e^2-4e+5) \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is C.

The time taken ($t$ days) to paint a house varies inversely with the number of painters ($N$) on the job.

Which of the following best represents the relationship between the number of painters and the time taken to paint a house, given that it takes 4 painters 18 days to paint the same house?

dif.r: Recognise hyperbola for inverse variation through given point

figures.cap: option A: option A graph
option B: option B graph
option C: option C graph

solutions.latex:
Inverse variation gives a hyperbola of the form $t=\dfrac{k}{N}$, which rules out A and D.

The hyperbola must pass through $(4,18)$, since 4 painters take 18 days.

Hence the correct option is B.

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int 6x^2\,(4x^3-5)^3\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Reverse chain rule with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
The factor $12x^2$ is the derivative of $4x^3-5$, so write the integrand with this factor.
$$\begin{aligned} \int 6x^2(4x^3-5)^3\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 12x^2(4x^3-5)^3\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(4x^3-5)^4}{4}+C\\ &=\dfrac{(4x^3-5)^4}{8}+C \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is A.

parts.latex: Which is the complete solution set to the equation $\sin^2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, for the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$?

dif.r: Squared trig equation, plus/minus cases, phase shift, domain checking

solutions.latex:
Taking square roots gives
$$\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$
Since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, there are solutions in all four quadrants:
$$x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4},\ \ldots$$
Subtracting $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{25\pi}{12},\ \ldots$$
For $0\le x\le 2\pi$ the solutions are $\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{12}$.

Hence the correct option is C.

dif.r: Routine linear equation with one fraction

solutions.latex:
Multiply both sides by 3 to clear the fraction.
$$\begin{aligned} 4x-\dfrac{2x+1}{3}&=5\\ 12x-(2x+1)&=15\\ 10x-1&=15\\ 10x&=16\\ x&=1.6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1.6$$
criteria: Correct answer with no working, or working towards the correct answer with one small error

figures.cap: right triangle with cables from A and B to top of building

solutions.latex:
Let the second cable have length $c$. In the triangle formed by the two cables, the angle between the 80 m cable and the 20 m side at $A$ is $60^\circ$, so apply the cosine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} c^2&=20^2+80^2-2\times 20\times 80\cos 60^\circ\\ &=5200\\ c&=\sqrt{5200}\\ &=72.11102551\ldots\\ &\approx 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, showing all steps to the approximated answer
Correct substitution into the cosine rule with a small calculation error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $O$ be the base of the building.

Method 1 (right-angled trigonometry). In the right-angled triangle with $A$, $O$ and the top of the building:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ&=\dfrac{69.2}{AO}\\ AO&=\dfrac{69.2}{\tan 60^\circ}\\ &=39.9526\ldots\\ &\approx 40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the 80 m cable as hypotenuse:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{80}\\ AO&=80\cos 60^\circ=40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (Pythagoras). In the right-angled triangle with $B$ and $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} 72^2&=OB^2+69.2^2\\ OB^2&=395.36\\ OB&=19.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
So $AO\approx 20+19.9=39.9\approx 40$ m.

The distance from $A$ to the base of the building is approximately 40 metres.
criteria: Correct answer with all necessary calculations, using Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry
Progress towards the correct answer with a small error, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^2e^{2x+1}\right)=6xe^{2x+1}(x+1)$.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential chain, then factorise to given form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx$.

dif.r: Hence integral using given derivative, constant factor, evaluate limits

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x^2 & v&=e^{2x+1}\\ u'&=6x & v'&=2e^{2x+1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^2e^{2x+1}\right)&=6x\cdot e^{2x+1}+3x^2\cdot 2e^{2x+1}\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}+6x^2e^{2x+1}\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}(1+x)\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct application of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $6x(x+1)e^{2x+1}$ is the derivative of $3x^2e^{2x+1}$, so write the integrand with the factor 6.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int_1^2 6x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\Big[3x^2e^{2x+1}\Big]_1^2\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\left(3(2)^2e^{5}-3(1)^2e^{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\left(12e^5-3e^3\right)\\ &=2e^5-\dfrac{1}{2}e^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct application of the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Express $\dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}$ as a single algebraic fraction, in simplest form.

dif.r: Factorise denominators, cancel, combine and simplify algebraic fractions

solutions.latex:
Factorise each denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}&=\dfrac{2x}{(x-2)(x+2)}-\dfrac{x+1}{(x-2)(x+1)}\\ &=\dfrac{2x}{(x-2)(x+2)}-\dfrac{1}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{2x-(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-2)}\\ &=\dfrac{x-2}{(x+2)(x-2)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x+2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct factorisation and manipulation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle moves on the $x$-axis so that it’s displacement in metres from the origin at a time $t$ seconds is given by the equation $x=\ln(t^2+6)$.

The particle starts from rest at the point $x=\ln(6)$ and accelerates in a positive direction as shown in the distance-time graph below.

\exfigure{1547_q15_1}

Determine when the acceleration of the particle becomes zero and find the velocity at this time.

dif.r: Differentiate log twice with quotient rule, solve, substitute back

figures.cap: graph of x = ln(t^2+6) starting at ln(6)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity.
$$\dot{x}=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+6}$$
Differentiate using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & v&=t^2+6\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2t \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{2(t^2+6)-2t\cdot 2t}{(t^2+6)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{12-2t^2}{(t^2+6)^2} \end{aligned}$$
The acceleration is zero when $12-2t^2=0$, so $t^2=6$.

Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\sqrt{6}$.

The velocity at this time is
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{(\sqrt{6})^2+6}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\sqrt{6}\text{ s and } v=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\text{ m/s}$$
criteria: Correct equations for $\dot{x}$ and $\ddot{x}$, or equivalent merit
Correct equation for $\dot{x}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^4-3x^2+18x+24$ at the point where $x=-2$.

dif.r: Standard normal equation: point, derivative, perpendicular gradient

solutions.latex:
Find the point of contact.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-2)^4-3(-2)^2+18(-2)+24\\ &=16-12-36+24\\ &=-8 \end{aligned}$$
Find the gradient of the tangent.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=4x^3-6x+18\\ \text{at } x=-2:\ y'&=-32+12+18\\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent has gradient $m_1=-2$, so the normal has gradient $m_2=\dfrac{1}{2}$, since $m_1m_2=-1$.

Equation of the normal through $(-2,-8)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(-8)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(x-(-2)\big)\\ 2y+16&=x+2\\ x-2y-14&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x-2y-14=0\ \left(\text{or } y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-7\right)$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal and the point of contact, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of the tangent and the point of contact, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of the tangent or the point of contact, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The results on a class task are normally distributed with a mean of 40.

Two students, Dixie and Chloe, both receive their results on the task.

Dixie is told that she scored a mark of 50 and that this converted to a $z$-score of 2.

Chloe is only told that her $z$-score was 2.5.

By first finding the standard deviation, determine what mark Chloe scored on the task.

dif.r: z-score formula used in reverse twice

solutions.latex:
Use the $z$-score formula $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with Dixie's result to find $\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\dfrac{50-40}{\sigma}\\ \sigma&=5 \end{aligned}$$
Now use Chloe's $z$-score.
$$\begin{aligned} 2.5&=\dfrac{x-40}{5}\\ 12.5&=x-40\\ x&=52.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Chloe scored } 52.5$$
criteria: Correct standard deviation only, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
An artist has two boxes of paints beside his easel. The first box contains 15 tubes which contain green, red or blue paint and the second contains four tubes which have only red or blue paint.

The artist chooses one tube of paint from each box.

The tree diagram below shows the probabilities of him choosing a given colour.

\exfigure{1547_q18_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that the tubes he chooses are red and blue?

dif.r: Two tree branches summed for either order

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that the tubes he chooses are not the same colour?

dif.r: Complement of same-colour outcomes from tree

figures.cap: two-stage probability tree diagram

solutions.latex:
The colours red and blue can occur in two orders, red then blue or blue then red.
$$\begin{aligned} P(R\text{ and }B)&=P(RB)+P(BR)\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{60}+\dfrac{3}{20}\\ &=\dfrac{16}{60}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$

Find the probability that the colours are the same, then subtract from 1.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same})&=P(RR)+P(BB)\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{3}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{20}+\dfrac{1}{20}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{not same})&=1-\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some progress towards the correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the greatest and least values of the function $f(x)=10x^2e^{-x}$ in the domain $[0,4]$.

dif.r: Product rule stationary points with endpoint comparison, standard method

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=10x^2 & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=20x & v'&=-e^{-x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=-10x^2e^{-x}+20xe^{-x}\\ &=10xe^{-x}(2-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$ when $x=0$ or $x=2$.

Test $x=2$ (the factor $2-x$ decides the sign, as $10xe^{-x}>0$ for $x>0$):
$$\begin{aligned} f'(1)&=10e^{-1}>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ f'(3)&=-30e^{-3}<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2$ is a local maximum.
$$f(2)=10(2)^2e^{-2}=\dfrac{40}{e^2}\approx 5.4$$
Compare with the end points.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=0\\ f(4)&=10(4)^2e^{-4}\approx 2.93 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)>0$, the least value is at $x=0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{greatest value } \dfrac{40}{e^2}\approx 5.4,\ \text{least value } 0$$
criteria: Finds the turning points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int(10x-15)\,(x^2-3x)^4\,dx$.

dif.r: Reverse chain rule after spotting factor 5 times derivative of inner function.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator so that it is a multiple of the derivative of $x^2-3x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(10x-15)(x^2-3x)^4\,dx&=\int5(2x-3)(x^2-3x)^4\,dx\\&=5\cdot\dfrac{1}{5}(x^2-3x)^5+c\\&=(x^2-3x)^5+c\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Answer which includes $(x^2-3x)^5$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{4x^3+x^2\,dx}{3x^4+x^3}$.

dif.r: Standard f'/f log integral with constant adjustment, then evaluate limits.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x^4+x^3)=12x^3+3x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^2\dfrac{4x^3+x^2}{3x^4+x^3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_1^2\dfrac{12x^3+3x^2}{3x^4+x^3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\ln(3x^4+x^3)\Big]_1^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\ln 56-\ln 4\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln 14\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Answer which includes the log integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The arm span (in metres) for a group of 1200 residents of a town are normally distributed with a mean of 1.68 metres and a standard deviation of 0.24 metres.

By first calculating $z$-scores, use the table above to determine how many of the residents will have an arm span greater than 1.5 metres.

figures.cap: normal curve with shaded area between -z and z

solutions.latex:
From the table, $P(-0.5<z<0.5)=0.3829$ and $P(-1.25<z<1.25)=0.7887$.

By symmetry, each half of these intervals has half the probability.
$$\begin{aligned}P(-0.5<z<1.25)&=\dfrac{0.3829}{2}+\dfrac{0.7887}{2}\\&=0.19145+0.39435\\&=0.5858\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the correct relevant probabilities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Calculate the $z$-score for 1.5 m.
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\&=\dfrac{1.5-1.68}{0.24}\\&=-0.75\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $P(-0.75<z<0.75)=0.5467$, so by symmetry the area to the right of $-0.75$ is this half plus the right half of the curve.
$$P(z>-0.75)=\dfrac{0.5467}{2}+0.5=0.77335 \text{ (or } 77.335\%)$$
Number of residents:
$$\begin{aligned}0.77335\times1200&=928.02\\&\approx 928\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 928 \text{ residents}$$
criteria: Finds the correct $z$-score, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use calculus to determine and verify the nature of the stationary points, find local maxima and minima and points of inflection (horizontal or otherwise) and hence sketch the graph of the function $y=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3$. Accurate values for all $x$-intercepts are not required.

dif.r: Full quintic curve sketch: stationary points, three inflections including horizontal one.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3 with key points

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3\\y'&=60x^4-60x^3-120x^2\\&=60x^2(x-2)(x+1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=0,\ 2,\ -1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y''&=240x^3-180x^2-240x\\&=60x(4x^2-3x-4)\end{aligned}$$
Test each stationary point using $y''$.
$$\begin{aligned}x=0&: y''=0 &&\text{(possible inflection)}\\x=2&: y''=720>0 &&\text{(concave up, minimum)}\\x=-1&: y''=-180<0 &&\text{(concave down, maximum)}\end{aligned}$$
Possible inflections occur when $y''=0$: $x=0$ or $4x^2-3x-4=0$, giving
$$x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{73}}{8}\approx-0.69 \text{ or } 1.44$$
Test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned}x=-0.5&: y''=45>0\\x=1&: y''=-180<0\end{aligned}$$
Concavity changes at each of these, so all are points of inflection. At $x=0$ the gradient is also zero, so it is a horizontal inflection.

Key points: local maximum $(-1,13)$, point of inflection $(-0.693,7.935)$, horizontal inflection $(0,0)$, point of inflection $(1.443,-110.143)$, local minimum $(2,-176)$.

\exfigure{1547_q23_s1}

parts.latex:
For the first 5 years following retirement, Harrison was able to withdraw \$36 000 at the end of each year to pay his remaining mortgage and living expenses.

Show that the present value of a \$36 000 annuity for 5 years is \$169 686.
parts.note: Annuity present value interest factor table look-up (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only)

dif.r: Multiply withdrawal by table factor; one routine step.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Harrison wants to reduce his withdrawal to \$20 000 per year for the next 10 years, starting 5 years after his retirement.

If the amount he deposited when he opened the account was \$340 000, would he be able to make these planned withdrawals over the ten years? (Justify your answer with calculations)
parts.note: Annuity present value interest factor table look-up (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only)

dif.r: Deferred annuity via difference of factors, combine and justify sufficiency.

solutions.latex:
The present value of an annuity is the withdrawal times the factor from the table, using $r=0.02$ and $N=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=\$36\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$169\,686\end{aligned}$$

The ten years of withdrawals start after year 5, so take the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 15 years and subtract the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 5 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=20\,000\times12.8493-20\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$162\,716\end{aligned}$$
The total required is this plus the $\$169\,686$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=\$162\,716+\$169\,686\\&=\$332\,402\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \$340\,000 \text{ would be enough}$$
criteria: Working towards the correct amount for the ten year period, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Daria adds together the integers, which are not multiples of 2 or 3, between 1 and 300 inclusive.

So, $1+5+7+11+\ldots\ldots\,295+299$.

Eva adds together all the powers of 2 between 1 and 10 000 inclusive.

So, $1+2+4+8+\ldots\,4\,096+8\,192$

Who will achieve the larger answer and what is the difference?

dif.r: Non-routine inclusion-exclusion with arithmetic series, plus GP term count and comparison.

solutions.latex:
Daria: add all integers to 300, then remove multiples of 2 and of 3, adding back multiples of 6 (removed twice). Each is an arithmetic series.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{All integers}&=\dfrac{300}{2}(1+300)=45150\\\text{Multiples of 2}&=\dfrac{150}{2}(2+300)=22650\\\text{Multiples of 3}&=\dfrac{100}{2}(3+300)=15150\\\text{Multiples of 6}&=\dfrac{50}{2}(6+300)=7650\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Required sum}&=45150-(22650+15150-7650)\\&=15000\end{aligned}$$
Eva: the powers of 2 form a GP with $a=1$, $r=2$. Find $n$ from the last term.
$$ar^{n-1}=2^{n-1}=8192=2^{13}$$
so $n=14$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_{14}&=\dfrac{1(2^{14}-1)}{2-1}\\&=16383\end{aligned}$$
Eva's sum is larger, and the difference is
$$16383-15000=1383$$
criteria: Required working with only a minor error (e.g. using $n=13$ or $15$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right)$ and hence find the expected value, $E(x)$, of the function.

figures.cap: graph of f(x)=1-e^{-x} with shaded area to x=t

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^t(1-e^{-x})\,dx&=1\\\Big[x+e^{-x}\Big]_0^t&=1\\t+e^{-t}-1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=x+e^{-x}-1$$
Substitute $t=1.84$:
$$1.84+e^{-1.84}-1=0.99881743\approx1$$
So the area under the curve is 1, correct to 2 decimal places.

Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right)&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}\\&=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
The expected value is $E(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{1.84}x\,f(x)\,dx$. Using the result above, $\displaystyle\int -xe^{-x}\,dx=xe^{-x}+e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(x)&=\int_0^{1.84}(x-xe^{-x})\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right]_0^{1.84}\\&=2.14384149-1\\&=1.14384149\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and progress toward the definite integral, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the area of the triangle in terms of $x$ can written as:

$$A=(20-x)\,(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

dif.r: Set up area using perimeter and Pythagoras; simple algebraic show-that.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Use calculus to find the values of $x$ and $y$ which give a maximum area and find this area.

dif.r: Product and chain rule on surd, solve, verify maximum, compute area.

figures.cap: isosceles triangle with sides x, base 2y, height h

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $2x+2y=40$, so $y=20-x$.

Let $h$ be the height. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $y$, $h$, $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{x^2-y^2}\\&=\sqrt{x^2-(20-x)^2}\\&=\sqrt{40x-400}\end{aligned}$$
The area is
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot2y\cdot h\\&=(20-x)(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Working which has an error in reasoning or is incomplete, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=20-x & v&=(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\u'&=-1 & v'&=20(40x-400)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dx}&=(20-x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}(40x-400)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot40-(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{800-60x}{(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$x=\dfrac{80}{6}=13\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side.
$$\begin{aligned}x=13&: \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx1.82>0\\x=14&: \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx-3.16<0\end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum at $x=13\dfrac{1}{3}$, and then $y=20-x=6\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left(20-\dfrac{40}{3}\right)\left(40\times\dfrac{40}{3}-400\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&\approx76.98\\&\approx77\text{ cm}^2 \text{ (2 s.f.)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates and solves to find the maximum with a minor error, or equivalent merit
Some relevant working toward maximising, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that: $\;\sin^2 x+\cot^2 x=\operatorname{cosec}^2 x-\cos^2 x$.

dif.r: Multi-step identity proof needing non-obvious Pythagorean substitutions.

solutions.latex:
Start from the left-hand side and write $\cot^2x=\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\sin^2x+\cot^2x\\&=\sin^2x+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cdot\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Use $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$ in the first term of the numerator.
$$\begin{aligned}&=\dfrac{\sin^2x(1-\cos^2x)+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Use $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}&=\dfrac{1-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}-\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\operatorname{cosec}^2x-\cos^2x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Almost complete proof with a minor logical error or incomplete, or equivalent merit
Some relevant trig relations derived from the given statement, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Area between curves split at sign change across two intervals.

figures.cap: cubic and quadratic curves with shaded regions between them

solutions.latex:
The curves cross at $x=0,\ 2,\ 5$, so the area is found in two parts. The difference of the curves is $(x^3-4x^2+12)-(3x^2-10x+12)=x^3-7x^2+10x$, which changes sign at $x=2$.
$$\text{Area}=\left|\int_0^2(x^3-7x^2+10x)\,dx\right|+\left|\int_2^5(x^3-7x^2+10x)\,dx\right|$$
Integrate each part.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{7x^3}{3}+5x^2\right]_0^2\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{7x^3}{3}+5x^2\right]_2^5\right|\\&=\left|5\dfrac{1}{3}\right|+\left|-10\dfrac{5}{12}-5\dfrac{1}{3}\right|\\&=5\dfrac{1}{3}+15\dfrac{3}{4}\\&=21\dfrac{1}{12}\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Done without separating the integrals (answer is then $10\dfrac{5}{12}$), or equivalent merit
Some relevant calculations relating to integrals, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Bree borrows \$20 000 to buy a car. She is charged interest at 4.8\% pa, calculated at the end of each month, and she repays regular monthly instalments of \$$P$ after the interest is added.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the amount owing after $n$ months is given by the equation

$A_n=20000\times1.004^n-P\left(1.004^{n-1}+1.004^{n-2}+\cdots\ldots+1.004^2+1.004+1\right)$.

dif.r: Build recurrence for first few months and generalise pattern.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
After paying the loan for 12 months, she still owes \$17 055.80 on the loan.

Find the amount of the monthly instalment, \$$P$.

dif.r: Sum GP in formula and solve linear equation for repayment.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the number of months required to pay off the loan completely (the term of the loan).

dif.r: Set balance zero, isolate exponential, solve with logs, round up.

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{0.048}{12}=0.004$, so each month the balance is multiplied by $1.004$ and then $P$ is subtracted.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=20000\times1.004-P\\A_2&=A_1\times1.004-P\\&=20000\times1.004^2-P(1.004+1)\\A_3&=A_2\times1.004-P\\&=20000\times1.004^3-P(1.004^2+1.004+1)\end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_n=20000\times1.004^n-P\left(1.004^{n-1}+1.004^{n-2}+\cdots+1.004^2+1.004+1\right)$$
criteria: Working toward the result, or equivalent merit
Recognises and uses the sum of a geometric series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$, with $P=320$.
$$\begin{aligned}20000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{320(1.004^n-1)}{0.004}&=0\\20000(1.004)^n&=80000(1.004^n-1)\\60000(1.004)^n&=80000\\(1.004)^n&=\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms.
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}{\ln(1.004)}\\&\approx72.06\end{aligned}$$
Since a whole number of instalments is needed, the loan is paid completely after 73 months.
criteria: Working toward the term of the loan, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Pasta boxes are labelled with a net weight of 375 g. The business selling the pasta boxes fills the boxes to a net weight of 380 g, to avoid customer complaints. The weight of the pasta boxes follows a normal distribution with a mean weight of 380 g and a standard deviation of 2.5 g.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that a box selected randomly will contain less than 375 g of pasta?

dif.r: z-score then empirical rule tail probability.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The business sets a target of less than $16\%$ of all boxes will contain more than 385 g of pasta. The business can change the mean weight of the boxes to meet this target. What is mean weight required to meet the target if the standard deviation remains at 2.5?

dif.r: Empirical rule in reverse to find required mean.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Find the $z$-score of $375$.
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \dfrac{375 - 380}{2.5} = -2$$
About $95\%$ of scores lie between $z = -2$ and $z = 2$, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$5\% \div 2 = 2.5\%$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The probability a box has less than 375 g is } 2.5\%$$
criteria: Finds the $z$-score of $375$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
About $68\%$ of scores lie between $z = -1$ and $z = 1$, so $16\%$ lie above $z = 1$. This is the target, so $385$ must correspond to $z = 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{385 - \mu}{2.5} \\ \mu &= 385 - 2.5 \\ &= 382.5 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The mean weight is } 382.5 \text{ g}$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $|5 - 3x| \ge 11$

dif.r: Absolute value inequality, two cases with sign reversal.

solutions.latex:
For $|A| \ge k$, we need $A \ge k$ or $A \le -k$.

So $5 - 3x \ge 11$ or $5 - 3x \le -11$.

First case:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x &\ge 6 \\ x &\le -2 &&(\text{divide by } -3, \text{ reverse the inequality}) \end{aligned}$$
Second case:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x &\le -16 \\ x &\ge \dfrac{16}{3} &&(\text{divide by } -3, \text{ reverse the inequality}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \le -2 \text{ or } x \ge \dfrac{16}{3}$$
criteria: Finds one answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $x^3e^{2x}$ with respect to $x$.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential chain rule.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^3e^{2x}\right) &= 3x^2e^{2x} + 2x^3e^{2x} \\ &= x^2e^{2x}(2x + 3) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule with at least 2 correct terms, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the initial acceleration of the particle?

dif.r: Differentiate velocity and substitute t=0.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: When is the particle first at rest?

dif.r: Set velocity zero, solve sin t = 1/2, first solution.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Given that the particle is initially at the origin, find an equation for the displacement ($x$), at a time $t$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity, use initial condition for constant.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled between the first two times when the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Distance from displacements at rest times, exact values, no sign change.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$$
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos t$$
Initially $t = 0$:
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos 0 = -16$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Initially the acceleration is } 16 \text{ m/s}^2 \text{ towards the left}$$

The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 - 16\sin t &= 0 \\ 16\sin t &= 8 \\ \sin t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The particle is first at rest after } \dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ seconds}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \displaystyle\int (8 - 16\sin t)\,dt = 8t + 16\cos t + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$ (initially at the origin):
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 8 \times 0 + 16\cos 0 + C \\ C &= -16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 8t + 16\cos t - 16$$

The particle is at rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, so find the displacement at each time using the result of part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
The velocity is not zero between these times, so the distance is the size of the change in displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \left|\left(\dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16\right)-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16\right)\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{16\pi}{3}-16\sqrt{3}\right| \\ &= 16\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{16\pi}{3} \ (\approx 10.96) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes some progress, or equivalent merit
