questions.stem:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & 1 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the value of $k$?

dif.r: Integrate pdf over domain, set equal to one.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $F(t)$ the cumulative distribution function.

dif.r: Integrate pdf from lower limit for piecewise CDF.

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^4 (4kx-kx^2)\,dx &= 1 \\ k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] &= 1 \\ 9k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{9}$$
criteria: Provides correct equation stating that the integral equals one, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{9}$, the density is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
For $1\le t\le 4$, $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$, so the integral starts at 1.
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^t f(x)\,dx \\ &= \int_1^t \dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\int_1^t (4x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^t \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[\left(2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}-\dfrac{5}{3}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{27}(6t^2-t^3-5) \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{27}(6x^2-x^3-5) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Makes significant progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit
Provides correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression, in terms of $n$, for the number of sticks required to make a similar arrangement of $n$ squares in the $n$th row.

dif.r: Recognise arithmetic sequence, write general term.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: James continues to make squares following the same pattern. He makes 4 squares in the 4th row and so on until he has completed 10 rows. Find the total number of sticks James uses in making these 10 rows.

dif.r: Direct arithmetic series sum formula.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: James started with 1750 sticks. Given that James continues the pattern to complete $k$ rows but does not have sufficient sticks to complete the $(k+1)$th row, show that $k$ satisfies $(3k - 100)(k + 35) < 0$.

dif.r: Model condition as sum inequality, rearrange and factorise.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What is the value of $k$?

dif.r: Solve quadratic inequality, pick largest positive integer.

figures.cap: rows of 1, 2 and 3 squares labelled Row 1 to Row 3
solution sketch: parabola with x-intercepts -35 and 100/3

solutions.latex:
The numbers of sticks form the sequence $4, 7, 10, \ldots$

This is an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=4$ and common difference $d=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 4+3(n-1) \\ &= 3n+1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the formula for the $n$th term of an AP with one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic series $4, 7, 10, \ldots$ with $a=4$, $d=3$, $n=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right] \\ S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left[2\times 4+(10-1)\times 3\right] \\ &= 175 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 175 \text{ sticks}$$

The number of sticks used in $k$ rows must be less than 1750 (there are not enough for row $k+1$ is handled in part (d)).
$$S_k<1750$$
Using the sum of an arithmetic series,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\left[2\times 4+3(k-1)\right] &< 1750 \\ k(8+3k-3) &< 3500 \\ 3k^2+5k-3500 &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
Factorising,
$$(3k-100)(k+35)<0$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wording said only the number of sticks is less than 1750; I kept the meaning and removed nothing mathematical.

solutions.latex:
Find where the quadratic is zero.
$$(3k-100)(k+35)=0$$
$$k=\dfrac{100}{3}\text{ or }k=-35$$
\exfigure{1302_q20_s1}

The product is negative between the roots, so $-35<k<\dfrac{100}{3}$.

The value of $k$ is a positive whole number of rows, and $\dfrac{100}{3}=33 \cdot \dot{3}$.
$$\therefore\ k=33$$

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the intercepts.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the curve with the equation $y = f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine product rule, factorise quadratic, second-derivative test for nature.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What are the coordinates of any points of inflexion?

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change; standard two-step.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$ over a suitable domain.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using found stationary and inflexion points plus intercepts.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=(x+3)(x-1)^2

solutions.latex:
For the $x$-intercepts, put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= (x+3)(x-1)^2 \\ x &= -3 \text{ or } x=1 \end{aligned}$$
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= (0+3)(0-1)^2 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\text{ intercepts are }(-3,0),\ (1,0)\text{ and }(0,3)$$
criteria: Finds either the $x$ or $y$ intercepts, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+3) & v&=(x-1)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= (x+3)\cdot 2(x-1)+(x-1)^2\times 1 \\ &= 3x^2+2x-5 \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x)=6x+2$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2+2x-5 &= 0 \\ (3x+5)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$x=-\dfrac{5}{3}\text{ or }x=1$$
When $x=-\dfrac{5}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{256}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=0$.

The stationary points are $\left(-\dfrac{5}{3},\dfrac{256}{27}\right)$ and $(1,0)$.

The sign of $f''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{5}{3}:\ f''&=6\times\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}\right)+2=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times 1+2=8>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A possible point of inflexion occurs where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+2 &= 0 \\ x &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{128}{27}$.

Test for a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-1)&=6\times(-1)+2=-4<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(0)&=6\times 0+2=2>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so
$$\therefore\text{ the point of inflexion is }\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{128}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the point of inflexion without testing for change in concavity, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous function $y = f(x)$ defined in the domain $[-4, 5]$. The function consists of a line segment, a quarter of a circle centred at $(0, 0)$ with radius 2 and a logarithmic function $f(x) = \ln(x - 1)$ in the domain $[2, 5]$

\exfigure{1302_q22_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the exact area bounded by the function $y = f(x)$ and the $x$-axis in the domain $[-4, 2]$

dif.r: Area from triangle and quarter circle formulas read off graph.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_2^5 \ln(x - 1)\,dx$

given that $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^5 f(x)\,dx = 4\ln 4 - 7 - \pi$

dif.r: Must split integral and use negative signed area below axis.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): line segment, quarter circle and logarithmic curve

solutions.latex:
In $[-4,2]$ the line segment from $(-4,0)$ to $(0,-2)$ forms a triangle with the $x$-axis, and the quarter circle of radius 2 gives a quarter-circle region.

Triangle (base 4, height 2):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}bh \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 2 \\ &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Quarter circle:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{4}\pi r^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times 2^2 \\ &= \pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Total area}=(4+\pi)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Calculates area of one region or shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Triangle vertices inferred from base 4 and height 2 in the source working; figure not visible here.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the line segment was said to end at $(0,2)$; the graph has it at $(0,-2)$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the line segment was said to end at $(0,2)$; the graph has it at $(0,-2)$.

solutions.latex:
Split the given integral at $x=2$.
$$\int_{-4}^5 f(x)\,dx=\int_{-4}^2 f(x)\,dx+\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx$$
The region on $[-4,2]$ lies below the $x$-axis, so its integral is $-(4+\pi)$.
$$4\ln 4-7-\pi=-(4+\pi)+\int_2^5 \ln(x-1)\,dx$$
$$\therefore\ \int_2^5 \ln(x-1)\,dx=4\ln 4-3$$
criteria: Writes an equation that equates the integral and the area, or shows understanding, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The curve $C$ has the equation $y = f(x)$, $x \ne 0$, and the point $P(2, 1)$ lies on $C$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $f(x)$ given $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6 - \dfrac{8}{x^2}$.

dif.r: Integrate negative powers then find constant from point.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an equation for the tangent to $C$ at the point $P$. Express your answer in general form.

dif.r: Derivative given; substitute for gradient and write tangent.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite with negative powers, then integrate term by term.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6-8x^{-2}$$
$$f(x)=x^3-6x+8x^{-1}+C$$
The point $P(2,1)$ lies on $C$, so $f(2)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2^3-6\times 2+8\times 2^{-1}+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-6x+\dfrac{8}{x}+1$$
criteria: Finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent at $P(2,1)$ is $f'(2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= f'(2) \\ &= 3\times 2^2 - 6 - 8\times 2^{-2} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Using the point-gradient form $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= 4(x-2) \\ y - 1 &= 4x - 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4x-y-7=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent at $P(2,1)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $X$ be a normally distributed random variable with mean 6 and variance 9 and let $Z$ be the random variable with the standard normal distribution.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $P(X > 6)$.

dif.r: Direct recall: half the normal distribution lies above mean.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $b$ such that $P(X > 8) = P(Z < b)$.

dif.r: Z-score plus symmetry to convert upper tail to lower tail.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Here $\mu = 6$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$ (so $\sigma = 3$).

The normal distribution is symmetric about the mean, so
$$P(X>6)=P(X>\mu)=0.5$$

By symmetry about the mean $6$, $P(X>8)=P(X<4)$.

Convert to a $z$-score:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \\ &= \dfrac{4-6}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $P(X>8)=P\left(Z<-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$.
$$\therefore\ b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\sin x + 1 + \cos x\cot x - \operatorname{cosec} x = 1$

dif.r: Short identity proof: common denominator and Pythagorean identity.

solutions.latex:
Using $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec} x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \sin x + 1 + \cos x\cdot\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} - \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 x + \sin x + \cos^2 x - 1}{\sin x} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x + \sin x - 1}{\sin x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\sin x-1}{\sin x} \quad (\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1) \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x} \\ &= 1 \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes significant progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

$P = P_0e^{-kt}$

where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants, and $t$ is the number of days after the application of the pesticide.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Once in the soil, the half-life of the pesticide is the time taken for its concentration to be reduced to one half of its initial value. If the half-life of the pesticide is 25 days, find the value of $k$. Answer correct to 2 significant figures.

criteria: Uses the exponential decay formula with one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $k=0.028$ and $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{-0.028\times 80} \\ &= 0.1064\ldots P_0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage decrease} &= 1-0.1064\ldots \\ &= 0.8936\ldots \\ &\approx 89\% \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx = \dfrac{10}{3}$, $0 \le a < \pi$, calculate the value of $a$.

dif.r: Integrate, solve cos3a=-1, restrict solutions to domain.

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then apply the limits:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ \left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos 3x\right]_0^a &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ -\dfrac{5}{3}(\cos 3a-\cos 0) &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ \cos 3a-\cos 0 &= -2 \\ \cos 3a &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $3a=\pi, 3\pi,\ldots$, and since $0\le a<\pi$ we need $0\le 3a<3\pi$, giving $3a=\pi$.

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: line $y=mx$ with $m=-\dfrac{e}{3}$ through the origin, tangent to the curve $y=-e^{\frac{x}{3}}$ at $P(3,-e)$. The curve lies below the $x$-axis, passes through $(0,-1)$, decreasing, approaching $y=0$ as $x\to-\infty$. Label $P(3,-e)$, the $y$-intercept $(0,-1)$ and the asymptote $y=0$.

solutions.latex:
At $P$ the line and curve have the same $y$-value:
$$mx=-e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \qquad (1)$$
At $P$ the line's gradient equals the gradient of the curve:
$$m=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \qquad (2)$$
From (1), $-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}=mx$, so substituting into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{3}mx \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$y=-e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3}=-e$$
$$\therefore\ P=(3,-e)$$
criteria: Finds one of the coordinates or shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $P$, $mx=-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ with $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3m &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3} \\ 3m &= -e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=-\dfrac{e}{3}$$

Show that the total length, $l$ m, of rods is given by:

$$l = 3x + \dfrac{48}{x}$$

dif.r: Interpret diagram for rod count and fabric area constraint.

dif.r: Standard differentiate, solve, second-derivative check for minimum.

parts.latex: What is the minimum cost of the frame?

dif.r: Substitute x=4 and multiply by cost per metre.

figures.cap: open-ended tent frame with edges x and y

solutions.latex:
The sheet is a rectangle with dimensions $x$ and $2y$, so
$$\begin{aligned} x\times 2y &= 24 \\ y &= \dfrac{24}{2x} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The frame has three rods of length $x$ and four of length $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} l &= 3x+4y \\ &= 3x+4\times\dfrac{12}{x} \\ &= 3x+\dfrac{48}{x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dl}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3-\dfrac{48}{x^2} &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 16 \\ x &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x$ is a length, $x=-4$ is rejected.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2l}{dx^2}=\dfrac{96}{x^3}=\dfrac{96}{4^3}>0 \text{ at } x=4$$
So $l$ has a minimum at $x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The minimum length of rods occurs at $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} l &= 3\times 4+\dfrac{48}{4} \\ &= 24 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 24\times 9.50 \\ &= \$228 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost of the frame is } \$228$$
criteria: Finds the minimum length of rods, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{3}x^3-4x^2-9x+5$ has a local maximum turning point at:

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary points.

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2-8x-9\\ &= (x-9)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

So $y'=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x=9$.

The second derivative decides the nature.

$$y''=2x-8$$

At $x=-1$, $y''=-10<0$, so there is a local maximum.

The $y$-value there is

$$\begin{aligned} y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-4+9+5\\ &= 9\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The local maximum is at $\left(-1,\ 9\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$, which is option A.

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities
can_use: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

figures.cap: graph of y=x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2

solutions.latex:
The factors $(x-2)^2$ and $(x+2)^2$ are never negative.

So the sign of $x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2$ is the sign of $x$, except where a squared factor is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &> 0 &&\text{for } x>0, x\neq 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &= 0 &&\text{for } x=-2,\ 0,\ 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &< 0 &&\text{for } x<0, x\neq -2 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the expression is $\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$ and at $x=-2$.

This is option A.

parts.latex:
A ball thrown upwards from a building attains a height above the ground given by the function $h(t)=8t-2t^2+12$, where $t$ is the time in seconds and $h$ is in metres.

Find the value for $t$ for which $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$ and hence find the maximum height above the ground the ball reaches.

solutions.latex:
The maximum height occurs where $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 8-4t = 0\\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2h}{dt^2}=-4<0$$

So the graph is concave down and this is a maximum.

$$\begin{aligned} h(2) &= 8(2)-2(2)^2+12\\ &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ and the maximum height is } 20 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex: Find the first and second derivative of the function $f(x)=(x^2-4)^3$.

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule for the first derivative.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3(x^2-4)^2\times 2x\\ &= 6x(x^2-4)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=6x & v&=(x^2-4)^2\\ u'&=6 & v'&=4x(x^2-4)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 6(x^2-4)^2+6x\times 4x(x^2-4)\\ &= 6(x^2-4)\left[(x^2-4)+4x^2\right]\\ &= 6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6x(x^2-4)^2 \text{ and } f''(x)=6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4)$$
criteria: Finds $f'(x)$ and applies the product rule for $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Lucy contemplates playing a new game which involves tossing three coins simultaneously. She will receive \$10 if she obtains 3 heads, \$5 if she obtains 2 heads and \$3.00 if she obtains 1 head. However, if she obtains no heads, she must pay \$20. She must also pay \$5 for each game she plays.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is Lucy's expected gain?
skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is this a fair game? Why?

solutions.latex:
The gain $X$ for 0, 1, 2, 3 heads, with each probability from three tosses, is:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} X & -20 & 3 & 5 & 10\\ \hline P(X) & \dfrac{1}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{1}{8}\end{array}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= -20\times\dfrac{1}{8}+3\times\dfrac{3}{8}+5\times\dfrac{3}{8}+10\times\dfrac{1}{8}\\ &= \$1.75 \end{aligned}$$

This is before the \$5 fee.

$$\therefore\ E(X)=\$1.75$$

meta.format_note: Source's expected value of \$1.75 is before the \$5 fee; part (b) uses the fee.

solutions.latex:
It costs \$5 to play, so the expected gain per game is

$$\begin{aligned} 1.75-5 &= -3.25 \end{aligned}$$

Lucy can expect to lose \$3.25 per game on average.

A fair game has an expected gain of 0.

$$\therefore\ \text{It is not a fair game, as Lucy loses money.}$$

questions.stem:
Consider the cone with a slant side of 9 cm below.

\exfigure{154_q9d_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If the height is $x$ cm, show that the radius, $r$, is $\sqrt{81-x^2}$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(81x-x^3\right)$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the height of the cone when the volume is maximum.

figures.cap: cone with slant side 9 cm, height and radius

solutions.latex:
The cone's height, radius and slant side form a right-angled triangle.

By Pythagoras' theorem, with slant side 9 and height $x$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2+x^2 &= 9^2\\ r^2 &= 81-x^2 \end{aligned}$$

Since $r>0$,

$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt{81-x^2}$$

The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$, with $h=x$ and $r^2=81-x^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(81-x^2)x\\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(81x-x^3\right) \end{aligned}$$

Expand and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 27\pi x-\dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^3\\ \dfrac{dV}{dx} &= 27\pi-\pi x^2 \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$.

$$x^2=27$$

Since $x>0$, $x=\sqrt{27}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-2\pi x=-2\pi\sqrt{27}<0$$

So this is a maximum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the height for maximum volume is } \sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$$

parts.latex: If $f(x)=(x+1)^2$ and $g(x)=x-2$ then find function $F$ defined as $f(g(x))$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)=x-2$ into $f$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x)) &= \left((x-2)+1\right)^2\\ &= (x-1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ F(x)=(x-1)^2$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: worked sketch of y=x^4-3x^2 on [-3,3]

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 4x^3-6x\\ &= 2x(2x^2-3) \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$.

$$f(0)=0$$

$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right) &= \dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{9}{2}\\ &= -2\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points: } (0,0),\ \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right),\ \left(-\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$

Use the second derivative to test the nature.

$$f''(x)=12x^2-6$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ f''\left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right) &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum turning point at } (0,0);\ \text{minimum turning points at } \left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Determines the nature of one type of point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Intercepts: put $y=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^4-3x^2 &= 0\\ x^2(x^2-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{intercepts: } (0,0),\ (-\sqrt{3},0),\ (\sqrt{3},0)$$
criteria: Finds one correct set of intercepts, or equivalent merit
Shows the endpoints and intercepts, or equivalent merit
Shows the endpoints or the intercepts, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The probability distribution of $X$ is given by the formula $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$, where $x=1,2,3,4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the table below

\extable{154_q10c_t1}

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the expected value of $X$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find $P(X<\mu)$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute each value of $x$ into $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \hline P(X=x) & \dfrac{1}{30} & \dfrac{4}{30} & \dfrac{9}{30} & \dfrac{16}{30}\end{array}$$

The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\times\dfrac{1}{30}+2\times\dfrac{4}{30}+3\times\dfrac{9}{30}+4\times\dfrac{16}{30}\\ &= \dfrac{100}{30}\\ &= 3\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$

From part (b), $\mu=\dfrac{100}{30}=3\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $X<\mu$ means $X=1,2,3$.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(X<3\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{30}+\dfrac{4}{30}+\dfrac{9}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{14}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X<\mu)=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

meta.format_note: Added the value of mu = 100/30 from part (b) (sum of x^3/30), which is consistent with the source's 3 1/3.

questions.stem:
The surface area of an \textbf{open} cylindrical can is 300 cm$^2$.

\exfigure{154_q11a_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If the radius of the base is $x$ cm, show that the volume is $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(300x-\pi x^3\right)$ cm$^3$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the maximum volume.

figures.cap: open cylindrical can with base radius x cm

solutions.latex:
Let the height be $h$ cm. The volume of a cylinder is
$$V=\pi x^2h \quad (1)$$
The can is open, so the surface area is the base plus the curved surface.
$$300=\pi x^2+2\pi xh$$
Hence
$$2\pi xh=300-\pi x^2$$
$$h=\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right) \quad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\pi x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(300x-\pi x^3\right) \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $h$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit
Writes the surface area equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the volume as a function of $x$ and differentiate.
$$V=150x-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x^3$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=150-\dfrac{3}{2}\pi x^2$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$.
$$\pi x^2=100$$
Since $x>0$,
$$x=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-3\pi x<0 \text{ for } x>0$$
So this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3000}{\sqrt{\pi}}-\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}} \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum volume}=\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}} \text{ cm}^3$$
criteria: Finds $x=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}$ and shows it gives a maximum, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Find the general primitive, $F$, of the following functions.

solutions.latex:
Increase each power by 1 and divide by the new power.
$$F(x)=\dfrac{x^9}{9}-\dfrac{x^8}{8}+10x+c$$

Split the fraction and use index laws.
$$\begin{aligned} f(t)&=\dfrac{t^4}{t^2}-\dfrac{1}{t^2}\\ &=t^2-t^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
Integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned} F(t)&=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-\dfrac{t^{-1}}{-1}+c\\ &=\dfrac{t^3}{3}+\dfrac{1}{t}+c \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $s$ in terms of $t$ if $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=u+at$, given that $u$ and $a$ are constants and $s=0$ when $t=0$.

solutions.latex:
Integrate with respect to $t$.
$$s=ut+\dfrac{at^2}{2}+c$$
When $t=0$, $s=0$, so $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}at^2$$
criteria: Integrates and finds $c=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Complete the table with $xp(x)$ and $x^2p(x)$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} x & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 & \text{Total}\\ \hline p(x) & \dfrac{4}{25} & \dfrac{5}{25} & \dfrac{7}{25} & \dfrac{6}{25} & \dfrac{2}{25} & \dfrac{1}{25} & 1\\ xp(x) & \dfrac{20}{25} & \dfrac{30}{25} & \dfrac{49}{25} & \dfrac{48}{25} & \dfrac{18}{25} & \dfrac{10}{25} & \dfrac{175}{25}\\ x^2p(x) & \dfrac{100}{25} & \dfrac{180}{25} & \dfrac{343}{25} & \dfrac{384}{25} & \dfrac{162}{25} & \dfrac{100}{25} & \dfrac{1269}{25}\end{array}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{9}{x^{2.}-4}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Is this function odd, even or neither?

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.latex: In the space below sketch the function. There is no need to find $x$ intercepts.

figures.cap: solution sketch: worked sketch of y=9/(x^2-4)

solutions.latex:
A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{9}{(-x)^2-4}\\ &=\dfrac{9}{x^2-4}\\ &=f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f \text{ is an even function}$$

meta.format_note: The question prints the function as x^{2.}-4 (stray full stop); the solution uses x^2-4.

solutions.latex:
As $x\to\pm\infty$, the denominator grows without bound, so $f(x)\to 0$.

Horizontal asymptote: $y=0$.

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero.
$$x^2-4=0$$
$$x=\pm 2$$
criteria: Finds the horizontal asymptote or the vertical asymptotes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\therefore\ \left(0,-\dfrac{9}{4}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point}$$

questions.stem: The cost of running a train at a constant speed $v$ km/h is $C=50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ dollars per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for an 800 km journey in terms of $v$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find an expression for the cost of an 800 km journey.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the most economical speed for this journey.

solutions.latex:
Use speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$.
$$v=\dfrac{800}{t}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{800}{v} \text{ hours}$$

The cost of the journey is the cost per hour multiplied by the time.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost}&=\left(50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}\right)\times\dfrac{800}{v}\\ &=\dfrac{40000}{v}+8v \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the product of cost per hour and time, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the cost with respect to $v$.
$$\text{Cost}=40000v^{-1}+8v$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dv}(\text{Cost})=-40000v^{-2}+8$$
Set the derivative to zero.
$$v^2=5000$$
Since $v>0$,
$$v=\sqrt{5000}\approx 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2}{dv^2}(\text{Cost})=\dfrac{80000}{v^3}>0 \text{ for } v>0$$
So this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is about } 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$
criteria: Solves for $v$ and tests for a minimum, or equivalent merit
Differentiates and sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Janet is a biologist completing research on bee hives on the river called \textit{Bend}. The river follows the curve $y=x^2-1,\ x\ge 0$ as shown below. All lengths are measured in kilometres.

Janet's research station is located at $(0,0)$ and the Bee hive ($P$) is located at $(0,1)$.

Janet was interested in a Bee hive ($R$) located on the \textit{Bend} river.

\exfigure{154_q13b_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Using the distance formula, if the bee hive is at the point $R\ (s,t)$ show that the length ($L$) in kilometres in a straight line from $P$ to the bee hive located at $R$ is given by

$L=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}$.

$\left[\text{Distance formula: }\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\right]$

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
If the Bee hive ($R$) is located at a point closet to the beehive ($P$).

Find $\dfrac{dL}{ds}$ and hence find the coordinates of the Bee hive ($R$).

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the length ($L$), in kilometres, the direct line between the Bee hives.

figures.cap: curve y=x^2-1 with bee hives P(0,1) and R(s,t), research station at origin

solutions.latex:
$R$ lies on $y=x^2-1$, so $t=s^2-1$ and $R=(s,s^2-1)$.

Use the distance formula between $P(0,1)$ and $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=\sqrt{(s-0)^2+\left((s^2-1)-1\right)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+(s^2-2)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+s^4-4s^2+4}\\ &=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the coordinates of $R$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=(s^4-3s^2+4)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{4s^3-6s}{2\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}}\\ &=\dfrac{2s^3-3s}{\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}} \end{aligned}$$
The denominator is positive, so $\dfrac{dL}{ds}=0$ when the numerator is zero.
$$s(2s^2-3)=0$$
Since $s>0$,
$$s=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$$
Then
$$t=\dfrac{3}{2}-1=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Test the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} s=1:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ s=2:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{8}}>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $L$ is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ R=\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

Substitute $s^2=\dfrac{3}{2}$ into $L=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2-3\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)+4}\\ &=\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{18}{4}+\dfrac{16}{4}}\\ &=\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{4}}\\ &\approx 1.32 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the value of $s^2$, or equivalent merit

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: graph of y=-e^x(x+1), intercepts -1 and -1

solutions.latex:
Solutions of $-e^x(x+1)=x^2-1$ are the intersections of $y=-e^x(x+1)$ with the parabola $y=x^2-1$.

Both pass through $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$, since $x^2-1=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x^2-1=-1$ at $x=0$.

So $x=-1$ and $x=0$ are solutions. We check there are no others by comparing the two sides on each interval.

For $x>0$: $e^x\ge 1+x$, so $-e^x(x+1)\le-(x+1)^2$, and
$$-(x+1)^2-(x^2-1)=-2x(x+1)<0$$
so the exponential curve is below the parabola: no solution.

For $x<-1$: put $t=-x>1$. The equation $e^{-t}(t-1)=(t-1)(t+1)$ needs $e^{-t}=t+1$, impossible since $e^{-t}<1<t+1$: no solution.

For $-1<x<0$: divide by $x+1>0$ to get $-e^x=x-1$, that is $e^x+x-1=0$. The function $e^x+x-1$ is increasing and equals $0$ only at $x=0$, so there is no solution in this interval.

Therefore there are exactly $2$ solutions, option B.

figures.cap: graph of y=a cos bx with shaded area from 0 to pi/4, zero at pi/4, and 3pi/4

solutions.latex:
The graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, so one half-period of the curve between the crossings is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

By symmetry about $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (a quarter-period shape, as for $\cos$), the area below the axis from $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ to $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is twice the shaded area from $0$ to $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\text{Area below the axis}=2\times\dfrac{1}{2}=1$$
The integral gives the area above the axis minus the area below it:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}(a\cos bx)\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}-1 \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}|x-1|\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
The expression $|x-1|$ equals $1-x$ for $x<1$ and $x-1$ for $x\ge1$, so split the integral at $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-2}^{3}|x-1|\,dx &= \int_{-2}^{1}(1-x)\,dx+\int_{1}^{3}(x-1)\,dx \\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-2}^{1}+\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-(-4)\right)+\left(\dfrac{3}{2}-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{2}+2 \\ &= \dfrac{13}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=2x\tan x$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2\tan x + 2x\sec^2 x \\ &= 2(\tan x + x\sec^2 x) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{e^{2x}}{5x}$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=5x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{5x(2e^{2x})-e^{2x}\times 5}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10xe^{2x}-5e^{2x}}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{5e^{2x}(2x-1)}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{2x}(2x-1)}{5x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin 2x\,dx.$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{3x^4-2x^3+x^2}{x^2}\,dx$

solutions.latex:

The graph of $y=2x$ and $y=6x-x^2$ intersect at the origin and at point $B$.

parts.label: a

parts.latex: Find the shaded area bounded by $y=2x$ and $y=6x-x^2$.

figures.cap: line y=2x and parabola y=6x-x^2 meeting at O and B, region between shaded

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-x^2 &= 2x \\ x^2-4x &= 0 \\ x(x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=4$, $y=2\times 4=8$.
$$\therefore\ B=(4,8)$$

Between $x=0$ and $x=4$ the parabola is above the line.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^4(6x-x^2-2x)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^4(-x^2+4x)\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2\right]_0^4 \\ &= -\dfrac{64}{3}+32 \\ &= \dfrac{32}{3} \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If $y=e^{2x}+e^{8x}$, prove that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-10\dfrac{dy}{dx}+16y=0.$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x}+8e^{8x}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}$$
Substitute into the left-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= 4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}-10(2e^{2x}+8e^{8x})+16(e^{2x}+e^{8x}) \\ &= 4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}-20e^{2x}-80e^{8x}+16e^{2x}+16e^{8x} \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Finds both derivatives, or equivalent merit
Finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $f(x)$ given $f'(x)=\sec^2 2x$ and the curve passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).$

So $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac12\tan 2x$$

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx=\dfrac{10}{3},\quad 0\le a<\pi,$ calculate the value of $a$.

Integrating:
$$\left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos 3x\right]_0^a=\dfrac{10}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{5}{3}(\cos 3a-\cos 0)&=\dfrac{10}{3}\\ \cos 3a-1&=-2\\ \cos 3a&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le a<\pi$, we have $0\le 3a<3\pi$, so $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=1+e^x.$

Show that $f(x)\times f(-x)=f(x)+f(-x).$

solutions.latex:
Left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+e^x)(1+e^{-x})\\ &=1+e^{-x}+e^x+e^0\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
Right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=(1+e^x)+(1+e^{-x})\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)\times f(-x)=f(x)+f(-x)$$
criteria: Expands the LHS correctly, or equivalent merit

The denominator is zero when $3-3^x=0$, that is at $x=1$.

parts.latex:
Find the area enclosed between the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=3$.

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: graph of y=sqrt(x+1) with region between curve, y-axis and y=0, y=3 shaded

solutions.latex:
Make $x$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\sqrt{x+1}\\ y^2&=x+1\\ x&=y^2-1\end{aligned}$$
The region lies between the $y$-axis and the curve for $0\le y\le 3$. For $0\le y<1$ the curve is left of the $y$-axis ($x<0$), so that part is taken as an absolute value.
$$A=\int_1^3(y^2-1)\,dy+\left|\int_0^1(y^2-1)\,dy\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_1^3+\left|\left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_0^1\right|\\ &=\left(\dfrac{27}{3}-3\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right)+\left|\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|\\ &=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{22}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=7\dfrac{1}{3}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution, or equivalent merit
Correct integrals (with absolute value for the negative part), or equivalent merit

$$\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ y\text{-intercept }\dfrac{1}{2},\ \text{no }x\text{-intercept}$$
criteria: Finds the $y$-intercept or shows no $x$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=e^x+1\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{(e^x+1)e^x-e^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x(e^x+1-e^x)}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$:
$$\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are no stationary points}$$

As $x\to\infty$, $e^x$ becomes very large, so $y\to 1$ from below.

As $x\to-\infty$, $e^x\to 0$, so $y\to 0$ from above.
$$\therefore\ y\to 1^{-}\text{ as }x\to\infty,\quad y\to 0^{+}\text{ as }x\to-\infty$$
criteria: Correct behaviour in one direction, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The trapezium has parallel sides $AD=\dfrac{1}{e}$ and $BC=e$, and height $AB=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(2)\left(\dfrac{1}{e}+e\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1+e^2}{e}\end{aligned}$$

The shaded area is the trapezium less the area under the curve.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\dfrac{e^2+1}{e}-\int_{-1}^{1}e^x\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{e^2+1}{e}-\Big[e^x\Big]_{-1}^{1}\\ &=\dfrac{e^2+1}{e}-e+e^{-1}\\ &=e+\dfrac{1}{e}-e+\dfrac{1}{e}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{e}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{2}{e}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Trapezium area minus integral, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a rectangle $OABC$ inscribed in the region bounded by the curve $y=e^{-x}$ and the $x$ and $y$ axes. The point $B(x,y)$ represents a point on the curve.

\exfigure{155_q13c_1}

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the dimensions of the rectangle so that its area is a maximum.

figures.cap: rectangle OABC under y=e^{-x} with B(x,y) on the curve

solutions.latex:
The rectangle has length $x$ and width $y=e^{-x}$.
$$A=x\cdot e^{-x}=xe^{-x}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=x(-e^{-x})+e^{-x}(1)=e^{-x}(1-x)$$
For stationary points $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x}>0$, this gives $1-x=0$, so $x=1$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0&1&2\\\hline \dfrac{dA}{dx}&1&0&-0.135\end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $x=1$ gives a maximum.

At $x=1$, $y=e^{-1}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{length }1,\ \text{width }e^{-1}$$
criteria: Tests the nature (maximum), or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative and $x=1$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the value of $x$ for which $9^{3-5x} = 27^{2x}$?

solutions.latex:
Write both sides as powers of $3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9^{3-5x}&=27^{2x}\\ 3^{2(3-5x)}&=3^{3(2x)}\end{aligned}$$
Equal bases, so equate the indices.
$$\begin{aligned} 2(3-5x)&=3(2x)\\ 6-10x&=6x\\ 16x&=6\\ x&=\dfrac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value $\tan x$ of given that $\sin x = \dfrac{2}{5}$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \pi$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\sin x=\dfrac{2}{5}$, the adjacent side is found by Pythagoras' theorem.
$$\sqrt{5^2-2^2}=\sqrt{21}$$
In the second quadrant $\tan x<0$, so
$$\tan x=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{21}}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
Given that $O$ is the centre of the circle and $OQ = 8\,cm$, what is the area of the shaded segment?

\exfigure{156_q3_1}

figures.cap: circle with centre O, chord PQ, angle POQ = pi/4, radius 8 cm, shaded segment

solutions.latex:
The shaded segment is the sector minus the triangle, with $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $r=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 8\times\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ &=32\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What is the domain and range of a circle with the equation $x^2 + 10x + y^2 = 11$?

solutions.latex:
Complete the square.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+10x+y^2&=11\\ x^2+10x+25+y^2&=11+25\\ (x+5)^2+y^2&=36\end{aligned}$$
The circle has centre $(-5,0)$ and radius $6$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Domain: } & -11\le x\le 1\\ \text{Range: } & -6\le y\le 6\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the change in amplitude and period when the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 6x$ is transformed into $g(x) = \sin 3x$.

options.label: A
options.latex: The amplitude is halved and the period is halved.

options.label: B
options.latex: The amplitude is halved and the period is doubled.

options.label: C
options.latex: The amplitude is doubled and the period is halved.

options.label: D
options.latex: The amplitude is doubled and the period is doubled.

solutions.latex:
Amplitude changes from $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $1$, so it is doubled.

Period changes from $\dfrac{2\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so it is doubled.

Hence the answer is option D.

figures.cap: cosine graph with x-intercept A marked

solutions.latex:
The function has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ and is translated $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to the right.

The point $A$ is a zero of the cosine curve, shifted by $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\dfrac{3\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following statements is true for the function $f(x) = e^{|x|} + 3$

options.label: A
options.latex: The function is an even function.

options.label: B
options.latex: The function is not continuous at $x = 0$.

options.label: C
options.latex: The function has a stationary point at $x = 0$.

options.label: D
options.latex: The function has an asymptote at $y = 3$.

solutions.latex:
$$f(-x)=e^{|-x|}+3=e^{|x|}+3=f(x)$$
So $f$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis, hence an even function.

Hence the answer is option A.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \dfrac{2x}{x^2+8}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the primitive is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4\dfrac{2x}{x^2+8}\,dx&=\Big[\ln(x^2+8)\Big]_0^4\\ &=\ln 24-\ln 8\\ &=\ln 3\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}\right)\right)$. Give your answer in simplest form.

(Hint: Use your log laws to help with the differentiation).

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$, rewrite the expression.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\ln(\sin x)-\ln(1+\cos x)\Big)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\dfrac{-\sin x}{1+\cos x}$$
Combine over a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} &=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)+\sin^2x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{\cos x+\cos^2x+\sin^2x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates both terms correctly and forms a common denominator, or equivalent merit
Correct derivatives of both terms, or equivalent merit
Uses log laws, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A surveyor who is $y$ metres due south of a tower sees the top of it with an angle of elevation $8^\circ$.

A second surveyor is $x$ metres due east of the tower.

From her position the angle of elevation is $10^\circ$ to the top of the tower.

The two surveyors are 940 m apart.

\exfigure{156_q11g_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $y = \dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (two surveyors and a tower): now Year 11 Extension 1.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the height ($h$) of the tower to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (two surveyors and a tower): now Year 11 Extension 1.

figures.cap: tower of height h, surveyors S (south, distance y, angle 8 degrees) and E (east, distance x, angle 10 degrees), SE = 940 m

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the tower (height $h$), the base and the surveyor, the angle of elevation is $8^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 8^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{y}\\ y&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\end{aligned}$$

Similarly, for the second surveyor, $x=\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}$.

The surveyors and the base of the tower form a right-angled triangle (right angle at the base), so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$x^2+y^2=940^2$$
Substitute.
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}\right)^2&=940^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ\right)&=940^2\\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{940^2}{\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ}}\\ &\approx 103.3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The height of the tower is $103$ m, to the nearest metre.
criteria: Correct expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $\displaystyle\int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 8$, find $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{-1} 2f(x+4)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=f(x+4)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ translated $4$ units to the left, so the area is unchanged.
$$\int_{-4}^{-1}f(x+4)\,dx=\int_0^3f(x)\,dx=8$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{-1}2f(x+4)\,dx&=2\int_{-4}^{-1}f(x+4)\,dx\\ &=2\times 8\\ &=16\end{aligned}$$

From a group of 15 hockey players at a game of hockey, 13 played on the field, 7 sat on the bench and 5 both played and sat on the bench. A hockey player is chosen at random from the team.

Find $P(A \mid B)$.

solutions.latex:
Here $A\cap B$ is the event 'played and sat on the bench'.
$$P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{5}{15},\qquad P(B)=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

parts.latex:
A function is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{2x-1}{3x+2}$.

Find the gradient of the normal at the point where $x = -1$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x-1 & v&=3x+2\\ u'&=2 & v'&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{2(3x+2)-3(2x-1)}{(3x+2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{(3x+2)^2}\end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x=-1$ is
$$f'(-1)=\dfrac{7}{(3\times(-1)+2)^2}=7$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent.
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-\dfrac{1}{7}$$
The gradient of the normal at $(-1,3)$ is $-\dfrac{1}{7}$.
criteria: Gradient of the tangent $7$, or equivalent merit
Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Calculate the $\text{Var}(X)$ correct to 2 decimal places. Show all working.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1, and $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times a+1\times b+2\times0.3 \\ 0.8&=b+0.6 \\ b&=0.2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a+b+0.3&=1 \\ a+0.2+0.3&=1 \\ a&=0.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a=0.5,\ b=0.2$$

Using $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\big[E(X)\big]^2$, first find $E(X^2)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=0^2\times0.5+1^2\times0.2+2^2\times0.3 \\ &=1.4 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X)&=1.4-0.8^2 \\ &=0.76 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By solving $f(x) = 0$ show that $x$-intercepts are $-2$, 0 and 2.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Prove that $f(x)$ is an even function.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that $f'\left(\sqrt{2}\right) = 0$.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Given that $\left(\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is a maximum turning point, explain in words why $\left(-\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is also a maximum turning point.

solutions.latex:
Solve $f(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2-x^4&=0 \\ x^2(4-x^2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x^2=0$ or $4-x^2=0$.

$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\pm2$$

A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=4(-x)^2-(-x)^4 \\ &=4x^2-x^4 \\ &=f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is an even function}$$

Differentiate term by term.

$$f'(x)=8x-4x^3$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\sqrt2\right)&=8\sqrt2-4\left(\sqrt2\right)^3 \\ &=8\sqrt2-4\times2\sqrt2 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

Since $f$ is even, its graph is a reflection of itself in the $y$-axis.

So every stationary point on the right of the $y$-axis has a matching stationary point of the same type on the left.

$$\therefore\ \left(-\sqrt2,4\right) \text{ is also a maximum turning point}$$

questions.stem:
A city is suffering through a drought and adopts a plan to import water from another city.

It is given that the volume of water imported in the $1^{\text{st}}$ year since the start of the plan is $1.8\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$. In subsequent years, the volume of water imported each year is 90% of the volume of water imported in the previous year

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Find how much water was imported in the $4^{\text{th}}$ year.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the total volume of water imported in the first 10 years.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Explain why the total volume of water imported since the start of the plan will never exceed $1.9\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^3$.

solutions.latex:
The yearly volumes form a geometric sequence with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$ and $n=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_4&=ar^{n-1} \\ &=1.8\times10^9\times0.9^{3} \\ &\approx1.3\times10^9 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the geometric sequence, $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$, with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$, $n=10$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9\left(0.9^{10}-1\right)}{0.9-1} \\ &=1.172378808\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ S_{10}\approx1.2\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Correct value of $S_{10}$ before rounding, or equivalent merit
Correct sum formula substitution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $|r|=0.9<1$, the series has a limiting sum.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9}{1-0.9} \\ &=1.8\times10^{10} \end{aligned}$$

The total can never exceed $1.8\times10^{10}$, and $1.8\times10^{10}<1.9\times10^{10}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the total never exceeds } 1.9\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3$$
criteria: Finds the limiting sum $1.8\times10^{10}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $e^{2\ln x} = 4x + 21$

solutions.latex:
Use $e^{2\ln x}=e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$, valid for $x>0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=4x+21 \\ x^2-4x-21&=0 \\ (x-7)(x+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=7$ or $x=-3$.

The original equation needs $x>0$ for $\ln x$, so $x=-3$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ x=7$$

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The function $y=3\sin x$ is odd, and the limits are symmetric about $0$.

$$\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}3\sin x\,dx=0$$

questions.stem: The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that the velocity is the rate of change of the displacement, find an expression for the velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the two times when the object is stationary.
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find an expression for the acceleration of the object.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.

$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{t^2}-2t^2\right)$$

$$v=2te^{t^2}-4t$$
criteria: Differentiates one term correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The object is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2te^{t^2}-4t&=0 \\ 2t\left(e^{t^2}-2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=0$ or $e^{t^2}=2$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^{t^2}&=2 \\ t^2&=\ln2 \\ t&=\pm\sqrt{\ln2} \end{aligned}$$

Time cannot be negative, so $t\ge0$ and $t=-\sqrt{\ln2}$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ s or } t=\sqrt{\ln2} \text{ s}$$
criteria: Solves one factor and finds both candidate times, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Differentiate $2te^{t^2}$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & w&=e^{t^2} \\ u'&=2 & w'&=2te^{t^2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a&=2e^{t^2}+2t\times2te^{t^2}-4 \\ &=2e^{t^2}+4t^2e^{t^2}-4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $A$ and $b$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Between what times in the first day can the ship sail?

figures.cap: graph of h(t) in metres against t in hours: minimum 12 at t=0, maximum 18 near t=6, minimum near t=12

solutions.latex:
The mean level is $15$, the low is $12$ and the high is $18$.

The amplitude is $3$. The curve is at its minimum when $t=0$ (7 am), so $A=-3$.

Low tide is at 7 am and high tide at 1 pm, so half a period is $6$ hours and the period is $12$.

$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

$$\therefore\ A=-3,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave only $y(t)=-3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+15$; derivation written with $t$ in hours from 7 am, as the source implies. Figure not visible, so this is assumed.

solutions.latex:
The ship needs $h\ge13.5$. First solve $h=13.5$.

$$\begin{aligned} 13.5&=-3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+15 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)&=\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

In one 12-hour cycle, $\dfrac{\pi t}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, so $t=2$ or $t=10$.

Between these times the cosine is above $\dfrac12$, so $h<13.5$ is not the case; checking the middle, at $t=6$, $h=18>13.5$, so the ship can sail for $2\le t\le10$.

With $t$ measured from 7 am, $t=2$ is 9 am and $t=10$ is 5 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can sail between 9 am and 5 pm}$$

meta.format_note: Question asks for the first day; source gives only the one interval 9 am to 5 pm, kept. Replaced a loose inequality comment by a check at $t=6$.

questions.stem: The population of an ant colony is modelled by the equation $P = 1000e^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the initial population.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
After 10 weeks the population is 25 000.

Show that $k = 0.3219$, correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: During which week will the population exceed 80 000 for the first time?

solutions.latex:
The initial population is at $t=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} P&=1000e^{0} \\ &=1000 \end{aligned}$$

Solve $P=80000$ using $k=0.3219$.

$$\begin{aligned} 80000&=1000e^{0.3219t} \\ 80&=e^{0.3219t} \\ 0.3219t&=\ln80 \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln80}{0.3219} \\ &\approx13.613 \end{aligned}$$

The population passes 80 000 after 13.613 weeks, which is during the 14th week.

$$\therefore\ \text{14th week}$$

questions.stem: An artist posted a song online. Each day there were $2^n + 3n$ downloads, where $n$ is the number of days after the song was posted.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the number of downloads on the third day after the song was posted.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the total number of times the song was downloaded in the first 20 days after it was posted?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Substitute $n=3$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=2^3+3(3) \\ &=17 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 17 \text{ downloads}$$

The total is the sum of two parts: a geometric series from $2^n$ and an arithmetic series from $3n$.

Geometric part: $a=2$, $r=2$, $n=20$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{2\left(2^{20}-1\right)}{2-1} \\ &=2\,097\,150 \end{aligned}$$

Arithmetic part: $a=3$, $d=3$, $n=20$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2\times3+(20-1)\times3\big) \\ &=630 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total}&=2\,097\,150+630 \\ &=2\,097\,780 \text{ downloads} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both sums, or equivalent merit
Finds one sum correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area is given by $A = 3x\sqrt{9-x}$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $x$ that will maximise the area, showing why this is the maximum.

figures.cap: right-angled triangle against a wall of height h, base x metres

solutions.latex:
The fencing covers the side $x$ and the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is $18-x$ m.

In the right-angled triangle, the side along the wall $h$ satisfies Pythagoras' theorem.

$$\begin{aligned} h&=\sqrt{(18-x)^2-x^2} \\ &=\sqrt{324-36x} \\ &=\sqrt{36(9-x)} \\ &=6\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

The area is half base times height.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac12\times x\times6\sqrt{9-x} \\ &=3x\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

Write $A=3x(9-x)^{\frac12}$ and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x & v&=(9-x)^{\frac12} \\ u'&=3 & v'&=-\dfrac12(9-x)^{-\frac12} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=3(9-x)^{\frac12}-\dfrac{3x}{2}(9-x)^{-\frac12} \\ &=\dfrac{6(9-x)-3x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{54-9x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 54-9x&=0 \\ x&=6 \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=6$; the denominator is positive for $x<9$, so the numerator $54-9x$ decides the sign.

\extable{Ts5767_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $x=6$ gives a maximum.

Alternatively, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{-9(12-x)}{4(9-x)^{\frac32}}$, and at $x=6$ this is approximately $-2.598<0$, so a maximum.

$$\therefore\ x=6 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the simplified derivative, or equivalent merit
Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A block of ice in the form of a cube melts in such a way that the block remains cubic. After a time $t$ hours the volume of the block is $V\ \text{m}^3$. Initially the cube has edge length of 4 metres and after 9 hours the cube has edge length of 1 metre.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If the rate of change of volume, $R\ \text{m}^3$ per hour, is given by $R = -k$ for some constant $k > 0$, show that $V = 64 - 7t$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when the cube has edge length 2 metres.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of volume is constant.

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-k$$

Integrating gives

$$V=-kt+c$$

Initially the edge is $4$ m, so when $t=0$, $V=4^3=64$.

$$V=64-kt$$

After 9 hours the edge is $1$ m, so $V=1$ when $t=9$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1&=64-9k \\ 9k&=63 \\ k&=7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ V=64-7t$$
criteria: Finds $V=64-kt$ and uses $t=9$, $V=1$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's alternative (constant rate $k=\dfrac{64-1}{9}=7$) omitted as equivalent.

solutions.latex:
An edge length of 2 m gives volume $2^3=8 \text{ m}^3$.

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=64-7t \\ 7t&=56 \\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the edge length is 2 m after 8 hours}$$

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum of a geometric series $a + ar + ar^2 + \cdots$ exists only when the terms shrink to zero, that is when $r^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

This happens when $|r|<1$, which is the same as
$$-1<r<1$$
Option A, $r>1$, and option B, $|r|>1$, make the terms grow. Option D, $r<1$, includes $r=-2$, where the terms grow.

solutions.latex:
The square root is defined only when the expression under it is not negative.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x^2 &\ge 0 \\ x^2 &\le 1 &&(\text{add } x^2 \text{ to both sides}) \\ -1 &\le x \le 1 \end{aligned}$$
The end points are included, since $f(\pm 1)=\sqrt{0}=0$ is defined.

questions.review_note: scan path default review

parts.latex: Which of the following pairs of transformations commute?

options.label: C
options.latex: Reflection in the $y$ -axis and reflection in the $x$ -axis.

solutions.latex:
Two transformations commute when applying them in either order gives the same result. Test each pair on a point $(x,y)$.

Option C: reflection in the $y$-axis is $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$ and reflection in the $x$-axis is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$.
$$(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y) \qquad (x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$$
The results are the same in either order, so these commute.

The other pairs do not commute. For a vertical reflection and a vertical translation by $k$:
$$\text{reflect then translate: } -y+k \qquad \text{translate then reflect: } -(y+k)=-y-k$$
For a vertical translation by $k$ and a vertical dilation by factor $2$:
$$\text{translate then dilate: } 2(y+k) \qquad \text{dilate then translate: } 2y+k$$
A horizontal translation and a horizontal dilation fail in the same way.

So the correct option is C.

meta.self_check: Tested each pair on a general point; only the two axis reflections give the same image in either order.
meta.generated_note: Working written to accompany the keyed answer C.

parts.latex: Consider the series $\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{45}+\sqrt{125}+\cdots+z=225\sqrt{5}$, the value of $z$ is:

solutions.latex:
Dividing every term by $\sqrt5$ (since $\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt{125}=5\sqrt5$), the series is
$$\sqrt5+3\sqrt5+5\sqrt5+\cdots+z=225\sqrt5$$
so $1+3+5+\cdots+\ell=225$, an arithmetic series with $a=1$, $d=2$.

The last term is
$$\begin{aligned} \ell&=a+(n-1)d \\ &=1+(n-1)\times 2 \\ &=2n-1 \end{aligned}$$
Using the sum formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+\ell)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 225&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[1+2n-1\right] \\ 225&=n^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $n=\pm15$, and since $n>0$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned} z&=(2n-1)\sqrt5 \\ &=(2\times15-1)\sqrt5 \\ &=29\sqrt5 \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.label: c

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The sequence $24, 29, 34, \dots$ is arithmetic with $a=24$, $d=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_8&=a+(n-1)d \\ &=24+(8-1)\times 5 \\ &=59 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 8^{th} \text{ row has } 59 \text{ plants}$$

The number of plants in row $n$ is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=24$, $d=5$. We need $T_n>150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 24+(n-1)\times 5&>150 \\ (n-1)\times 5&>126 \\ n-1&>\dfrac{126}{5} \\ n&>25.2+1=26.2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, $n=27$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 27^{th} \text{ row is the first with more than 150 plants}$$

meta.format_note: Source line $24+(n-1)d>150$ had d unsubstituted; substituted $d=5$ for clarity.

solutions.latex:
The total number of plants is the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, with $a=24$, $d=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2895&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(48+5n-5\right) \\ 5790&=n(43+5n) \\ 5n^2+43n-5790&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\dfrac{-43\pm\sqrt{43^2-4\times5\times(-5790)}}{10} \\ &=\dfrac{-43\pm343}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=30$.
$$\therefore\ 30 \text{ rows were planted}$$

parts.latex: In a geometric progression $S_4=30$, while the sum to infinity is 32. Find the first three terms.

solutions.latex:
For a geometric series, $S_4=\dfrac{a(1-r^4)}{1-r}=30$ and $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=32$.

From the second, $a=32(1-r)$. Substituting into the first:
$$\begin{aligned} 30&=\dfrac{32(1-r)(1-r^4)}{1-r} \\ 1-r^4&=\dfrac{30}{32} \\ r^4&=1-\dfrac{30}{32} \\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}$$
So $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$, and both satisfy $|r|<1$.

For $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$32=\dfrac{a}{1-\frac{1}{2}}$$
so $a=16$, and the terms are $16, 8, 4,\dots$

For $r=-\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$32=\dfrac{a}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{2a}{3}$$
so $a=48$, and the terms are $48, -24, 12,\dots$
$$\therefore\ 16, 8, 4 \text{ or } 48, -24, 12$$
criteria: Finds the two values of $r$, or equivalent merit
Finds $a$ in terms of $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
For a given arithmetic sequence, the ratio of the sum of the first $m$ terms to the sum of first $n$ terms is $m^2:n^2$, where $m\neq n$.

Prove that the ratio of the $m^{th}$ term to the $n^{th}$ term is $(2m-1):(2n-1)$.

solutions.latex:
The ratio of the sums of the first $m$ and $n$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, is
$$\dfrac{\frac{m}{2}\left(2a+(m-1)d\right)}{\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)}=\dfrac{m^2}{n^2}$$
Cancelling $\dfrac{m}{n}$ on both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2a+(m-1)d}{2a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{m}{n} \\ 2an+mnd-nd&=2am+mnd-md \\ 2an-2am&=nd-md \\ 2a(n-m)&=d(n-m) \end{aligned}$$
Since $m\ne n$, we may divide by $n-m$:
$$d=2a \qquad (1)$$
The ratio of the $m^{th}$ to the $n^{th}$ term is, using (1),
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a+(m-1)d}{a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{a+(m-1)2a}{a+(n-1)2a} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2(m-1)}{1+2(n-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2m-2}{1+2n-2} \\ &=\dfrac{2m-1}{2n-1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_m:T_n=(2m-1):(2n-1)$$
criteria: Significant progress towards the proof, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source criterion said 'showing $a=2d$' but the working shows $d=2a$; criterion changed to $d=2a$ to match the working.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{3}{x}\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
Integrating $\dfrac{3}{x}$ gives a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{3}{x}\,dx &= \Big[3\ln x\Big]_1^2 \\ &= 3(\ln 2-\ln 1) \\ &= 3\ln 2 \\ &= \ln 2^3 \\ &= \log_e 8 \end{aligned}$$
Hence option B.

parts.latex: What is the solution of $4^m = 27$ ?

solutions.latex:
Take logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_e 4^m &= \log_e 3^3 \\ m\cdot 2\log_e 2 &= 3\log_e 3 \\ m &= \dfrac{3\log_e 3}{2\log_e 2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence option D.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\left(e^{3x+2}\right)^6$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using index laws, $\left(e^{3x+2}\right)^6=e^{18x+12}$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{18x+12}\right)=18e^{18x+12}=18\left(e^{3x+2}\right)^6$$
Hence option A.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3x}$ ?

solutions.latex:
Write $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}x^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times(-1)x^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence option C.

parts.latex: What is the stationary point on the curve $y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 12x + 2$ ?

solutions.latex:
A stationary point occurs where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2-12x+12 = 0 \\ 3(x-2)^2 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2$, and then
$$y=8-24+24+2=10$$
The stationary point is $(2,10)$, option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\dfrac{2x}{e^x}$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{2x}{e^x}\right) &= \dfrac{2e^x-2xe^x}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{2-2x}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$
Hence option A.

parts.latex: If $f(x) = \tan\left(\sqrt{x}-2\right)$, what is $f'(x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule, with inner function $\sqrt{x}-2$ whose derivative is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^2\left(\sqrt{x}-2\right)$$
Hence option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $f(x) = e^{\cos x}$

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule, with inner function $\cos x$ whose derivative is $-\sin x$:
$$f'(x)=-\sin x\, e^{\cos x}$$
Hence option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{(2-x^2)^4}\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $2-x^2$, which is $-2x$, so write
$$\begin{aligned} \int x(2-x^2)^{-4}\,dx &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{(2-x^2)^{-3}}{-3}+C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6(2-x^2)^3}+C \end{aligned}$$
Hence option B.

solutions.latex:
The curve is above the $x$-axis on $0\le x\le 1$, so that integral is positive.

The curve is below the $x$-axis on $1\le x\le 2$, so that integral is negative and needs the absolute value to give an area.

The area is therefore

parts.latex: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 15\cos(4x)\,dx$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 15\cos 4x\,dx &= \dfrac{15}{4}\Big[\sin 4x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{4}\left(\sin 2\pi-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{15}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{15}{4}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{15} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The function $f(x)$ is defined by the rule $f(x) = x^2(6-x)$ in the domain $-1 \le x \le 6$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$. Showing all intercepts and stationary points.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: State the range of $f(x)$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x^2(6-x) on -1<=x<=6

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= 6x^2-x^3 \\ f'(x) &= 12x-3x^2 \\ &= 3x(4-x) \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=4^2(6-4)=32$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,32)$.

To find their nature, use the second derivative.
$$f''(x)=12-6x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=12>0 &&\text{so }(0,0)\text{ is a minimum}\\ f''(4)&=-12<0 &&\text{so }(4,32)\text{ is a maximum}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the coordinates of both stationary points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{(3x-1)^2}$.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate.
$$\begin{aligned} \int(3x-1)^{-2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{(3x-1)^{-1}}{-1}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3(3x-1)}+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3x}{x^2+1}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $x^2+1$, which is $2x$, so
$$\int\dfrac{3x}{x^2+1}\,dx=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+1)+C$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^3-x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Divide each term by $x^2$, then integrate.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^3-x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx &= \int\left(x-1+x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-x-\dfrac{1}{x}+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Divides term by term, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int_3^5 \dfrac{e^x}{e^x-7}\,dx$. State your answer as an exact value in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^5\dfrac{e^x}{e^x-7}\,dx &= \Big[\ln\left(e^x-7\right)\Big]_3^5 \\ &= \ln\left(e^5-7\right)-\ln\left(e^3-7\right) \\ &= \ln\dfrac{e^5-7}{e^3-7} \end{aligned}$$
This is approximately $2.38$.
criteria: Identifies the logarithm, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = \ln\dfrac{x\left(x^2-1\right)}{x+1}$.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator, $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, and cancel $x+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \ln\dfrac{x(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1} \\ &= \ln\left[x(x-1)\right] \\ &= \ln x+\ln(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x-1} \\ &= \dfrac{2x-1}{x(x-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{2x-1}{x^2-x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies to the log form and obtains $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = x\cos x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x-x\sin x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{3-\sqrt3\pi}{6} \\ &\approx -0.407 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$y-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{3-\sqrt3\pi}{6}\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximation to $\displaystyle\int_2^4 \ln x\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

solutions.latex:
Two applications means $n=2$ strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{4-2}{2}=1$$
The function values at $x=2,3,4$ are
$$f(2)=\ln 2\approx 0.693,\quad f(3)=\ln 3\approx 1.097,\quad f(4)=\ln 4\approx 1.386$$
Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_2^4 \ln x\,dx &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(2)+2f(3)+f(4)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[0.693+2(1.097)+1.386\right] \\ &\approx 2.14 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution of function values, or equivalent merit
Correct application of the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Prove that $\tan\theta(\sec\theta-\sin\theta\tan\theta)=\sin\theta$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence: Solve $2\tan\theta(\sec\theta-\sin\theta\tan\theta)=1$ for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Writing in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\left[\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}-\dfrac{\sin\theta\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines into a single fraction, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a), the equation becomes
$$2\sin\theta=1$$
so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

In $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$, sine is positive in the first and second quadrants.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx$. State your answer as an exact value in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is the derivative of $2+\sin x$, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln(2+\sin x)\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \ln\left(2+\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(2+\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \\ &= \ln 3-\ln 1 \\ &= \ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the volumes of the cylinder of maximum volume and the cone, are in the ratio 4:9.

figures.cap: cylinder inscribed in a cone, points A, B, C, D, E, radius r, height h

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, $AB=18$ is the height of the cone, so $AD=18-h$.

In $\triangle ADE$ and $\triangle ABC$: $\angle ADE=\angle ABC=90^\circ$ and $\angle AED=\angle ACB$ (corresponding angles, $DE\parallel BC$).

Hence $\triangle ADE$ is similar to $\triangle ABC$, and corresponding sides are in proportion:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AD}{AB} &= \dfrac{DE}{BC} \\ \dfrac{18-h}{18} &= \dfrac{r}{9} \\ 18-h &= 2r \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=18-2r$$
criteria: Establishes similar triangles and the proportion, or equivalent merit
Identifies $AD=18-h$ or a pair of similar triangles, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us. Triangle labels A, B, C, D, E refer to the question's figure.

solutions.latex:
The volume of the cylinder, using $h=18-2r$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \pi r^2h \\ &= \pi r^2(18-2r) \\ &= 18\pi r^2-2\pi r^3 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} V' &= 36\pi r-6\pi r^2 \\ &= 6\pi r(6-r) \end{aligned}$$
$V'=0$ gives $r=0$ or $r=6$. Since $r\ne 0$, $r=6$, and this is a maximum.

Then $h=18-2(6)=6$, so
$$V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi(6)^2(6)=216\pi$$
$$V_{\text{cone}}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(81)(18)=486\pi$$
$$\therefore\ V_{\text{cyl}}:V_{\text{cone}}=216:486=4:9$$
criteria: Solves $V'=0$ and selects $r=6$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the domain for $y=\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{x+2}}$

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $x+2 \ge 0$, and it is in the denominator, so it cannot be zero.

Hence $x+2>0$.
$$x>-2$$

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with horizontal asymptote y=1
option A: option A sketch
option B: option B sketch
option C: option C sketch
option D: option D sketch

solutions.latex:
The graph of $f$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis with a smooth maximum at $x=0$, and it levels off towards $y=1$ as $x \to \pm\infty$. Reading the gradient:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &> 0 &&\text{for } x<0 &&\text{increasing}\\ f'(0) &= 0 &&\text{at the maximum} &&\text{stationary}\\ f'(x) &< 0 &&\text{for } x>0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
Also $f'(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ since the curve flattens, so $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f'$.

The graph of $f'$ is therefore odd, positive for $x<0$, passing through the origin, and negative for $x>0$, with asymptote $y=0$.

Option A is undefined at $x=0$, but $f'(0)=0$. Option C crosses the $x$-axis away from the origin, which would mean extra stationary points. Option D has no asymptote $y=0$.

Hence the answer is option B.

meta.self_check: Gradient sign of f on each side of the maximum and asymptote of f'.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\cos(\ln x)$, where $x>0$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\ln x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos u = -\sin u\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(\ln x) &= -\sin(\ln x)\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sin(\ln x)}{x} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option A.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with shaded regions R1 and R2

solutions.latex:
$R_1$ and $R_2$ lie below the $x$-axis, so their integrals are negative:
$$\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx=-2, \qquad \int_{3}^{4} f(x)\,dx=-3$$
Split the given integral at $x=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3 f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx - \int_3^4 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 10-(-3) \\ &= 13 \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{3} f(x)\,dx &= \int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_0^3 f(x)\,dx \\ &= -2+13 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Which statement is true for an ungrouped data set with no outliers?
parts.note: Interquartile range and outliers of a data set are removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

options.label: A
options.latex: The largest possible range is 2 times the interquartile range

options.label: B
options.latex: The largest possible range is 3 times the interquartile range

options.label: C
options.latex: The largest possible range is 4 times the interquartile range

options.label: D
options.latex: The largest possible range is 5 times the interquartile range

solutions.latex:
A value is an outlier if it lies more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$.

With no outliers, the smallest and largest scores lie within these fences, so the range is greatest when the data extend to the fences.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{largest range} &= (Q_3+1.5\,IQR)-(Q_1-1.5\,IQR) \\ &= (Q_3-Q_1)+3\,IQR \\ &= IQR+3\,IQR \\ &= 4\,IQR \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.
