questions.stem:
Jasper records the number of Year 12 students who studied for at least one hour each day for each of the past ten days, the results were as follows:

15, 18, 20, 20, 22, 26, 28, 32, 34, 47

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the mean correct to one decimal place.
parts.note: Mean of a raw data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the interquartile range.
parts.note: Interquartile range of a data set is removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Is 47 an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.note: Outliers (1.5 x IQR test) are removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

solutions.latex:
The mean is the sum of the scores divided by the number of scores.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean} &= \dfrac{262}{10} \\ &= 26.2 \end{aligned}$$

The interquartile range is $Q_3 - Q_1$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 - Q_1 &= 32 - 20 \\ &= 12 \end{aligned}$$

An outlier lies above the upper fence $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper fence} &= 32 + 1.5 \times 12 \\ &= 50 \end{aligned}$$
Since $47 < 50$, 47 is not an outlier.

questions.stem: Annabelle takes 2 cans, without replacement, from a refrigerator that contains 8 cans of Pepsi, 4 cans of Coke and 3 cans of Sprite. Find the probability that Annabelle gets:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: 2 of the same drink

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At least one Pepsi

solutions.latex:
Add the probabilities of two Pepsi, two Coke and two Sprite (15 cans in total, no replacement).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{8}{15}\times\dfrac{7}{14} + \dfrac{4}{15}\times\dfrac{3}{14} + \dfrac{3}{15}\times\dfrac{2}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{105} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: at least one Pepsi is the opposite of no Pepsi (7 of the 15 cans are not Pepsi).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1 - P(\text{no Pepsi}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{6}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

Case 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 7x - 12 &\le -16 \\ 7x &\le -4 \\ x &\le -\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \le -\dfrac{4}{7} \text{ or } x \ge 4$$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The business sets a target of less than 16% of all blocks will have more than 80. The business can change the mean weight of the boxes to meet this target. What is mean amount of screws required to meet the target if the standard deviation is 2?
skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The standard deviation is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
$$z = \dfrac{75 - 79}{2} = -2$$
By the 68-95-99.7 rule, 95% lie within 2 standard deviations, so 2.5% lie below $z=-2$.
$$\therefore\ P = 2.5\%$$

About 16% of values lie more than one standard deviation above the mean.

So 80 must be one standard deviation above the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= 80 - 2 \\ &= 78 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx &= \int \cos\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{180} + C \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin x^{\circ} + C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $2x^2+1$, which is $4x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int_1^2 \dfrac{4x}{2x^2+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\Big[\ln(2x^2+1)\Big]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\ln 9 - \ln 3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=(3x-4)\sqrt{5-2x}$

solutions.latex:
Write $y = (3x-4)(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x - 4 & v &= (5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} - \dfrac{3x-4}{(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{3(5-2x) - (3x-4)}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{19 - 9x}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Working re-set in the u, u', v, v' grid; $v'=\dfrac{1}{2}(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-2)$ simplified; same result as the source.

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \sin x & v &= 1 + \cos x \\ u' &= \cos x & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{(1+\cos x)\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + 1}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find how much Jasmine earned in the first year of her job and by how much her pay increases each year.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How much will Jasmine have earned in total after working at her job for 15 years?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Bree started a job at the same time, and with the same starting salary as Jasmine. Bree's salary, however, increased by 2% per annum. With the use of logarithms, show in which year will her income first be greater than \$100 000?

solutions.latex:
The salary forms an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, so $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} a + 3d &= 81\,000 \\ a + 8d &= 98\,500 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned} 5d &= 17\,500 \\ d &= 3500 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 10\,500 &= 81\,000 \\ a &= 70\,500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{first year pay is } \$70\,500 \text{, with an annual increase of } \$3500$$

meta.format_note: Fixed the id: part (a) working had $T_4$ and $T_9$ equations unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$, with $n = 15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 70\,500 + 14\times 3500\right) \\ &= \$1\,425\,000 \end{aligned}$$

Bree's salary is a geometric sequence with $a = 70\,500$ and $r = 1.02$, so $T_n = 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1} &> 100\,000 \\ 1.02^{n-1} &> \dfrac{200}{141} \end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms of both sides (the base $1.02>1$, so the inequality is unchanged):
$$\begin{aligned} n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{200}{141}\right)}{\log 1.02} \\ n - 1 &> 17.65\ldots \\ n &> 18.65\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ she first earns more than $\$100\,000$ in her 19th year at the job.
criteria: Uses logarithms to solve for $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\tan\theta=\sec\theta$

solutions.latex:
Express $\tan\theta$ as $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and use a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes over a common denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A school has two History classes that sit an exam. Andy's class has 16 students and has a mean mark of 65%, whilst Juliana's class has 24 students. The combined mean for the 2 classes is 68.6%. Find the mean for the Juliana's class.

$$\therefore\ \text{the mean of Juliana's class is } 71\%$$

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?
skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability over the domain is 1.
$$\int_1^{14} \dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^{14} \dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14} &= 1 \\ k\left(\ln 27 - \ln 1\right) &= 2 \\ k\ln 27 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$
criteria: Sets the total area equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $T$ days be the time at which the cumulative probability is 0.75.
$$\int_1^{T} \dfrac{\frac{2}{\ln 27}}{2t-1}\,dt = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 27}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{T} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \ln(2T-1) &= \dfrac{3\ln 27}{4} \\ 2T - 1 &= e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} \\ T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} + 1}{2} \\ &\approx 6.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 7 days}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to 0.75, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rounded up to 7 days since 6.4 days is not yet a full day with 75% chance.

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\sqrt{\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}}\right]=\dfrac{2}{4-x^2}$

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws to rewrite the function, then differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2+x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2-x)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2+x}+\dfrac{1}{2-x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2-x+2+x}{(2+x)(2-x)}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4}{4-x^2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{4-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the values of $Q_0$ and $k$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how long will one-eighth of the initial dose remain?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=Q_0$, so $Q_0=6$.

After 15 hours the amount is half the initial dose, so $Q=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 6e^{15k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{15k} \\ 15k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$k = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{15}$$

One-eighth of the initial dose is $\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4} &= 6e^{kt} \\ \dfrac{1}{8} &= e^{kt} \\ kt &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k$ from part (a).
$$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\div 15} = 45 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Sets up equation for one-eighth of the dose, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Kloe has taken up golf, each year she plays 30 rounds of golf. In 2011 she totalled 3300 shots, in 2021 she totalled 2760 shots. The number of shots she took each year decreased by the same amount. To make it as a professional golfer she needs to get under 2115 shots in her 30 rounds. If this trend continues, in what year can she become a professional golfer?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The yearly totals form an arithmetic progression. From 2011 to 2021 is 10 years, so with $a=3300$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+10d &= 2760 \\ 10d &= -540 \\ d &= -54 \end{aligned}$$
She needs fewer than 2115 shots.
$$\begin{aligned} a+(n-1)d &< 2115 \\ 3300+54-54n &< 2115 \\ -54n &< -1239 \\ n &> 22.944\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $n=23$ years, and Kloe can be a professional golfer in 2033.
criteria: Finds the common difference, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\tan x+\cot x$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the equation of the tangent to $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\tan x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \cot x+\tan x \end{aligned}$$
which is the required result.
criteria: Finds the derivative $\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The gradient is the derivative from part (a) at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= 1+1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_e\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \log_e 1 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} y-0 &= 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ y &= 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $y=4x^3-x^4$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature and find any points of inflection

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of the function, clearly showing the stationary points and intercepts with the coordinate axes.

\exfigure{1303_q35_1}

figures.cap: blank grid for sketching
solution sketch: sketch of y=4x^3-x^4 with (0,0), (2,16), (3,27), (4,0)

solutions.latex:
$$y'=12x^2-4x^3 \qquad y''=24x-12x^2$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-4x^3 &= 0 \\ 4x^2(3-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$, giving the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

At $x=0$, $y''=0$, so the test is inconclusive and $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.

At $x=3$, $y''=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

For points of inflexion, $y''=0$.
$$12x(2-x)=0$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$. Test the concavity either side of each.
$$\begin{aligned} x=1 &: y''=12>0 \\ x=2 &: y''=0 \\ x=2.5 &: y''=-15<0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(2,16)$ is a point of inflexion.
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1 &: y''=-36<0 \\ x=0 &: y''=0 \\ x=1 &: y''=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes and $y'=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
criteria: Completes all but one of the points of inflexion with test, or equivalent merit
Finds stationary points and their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

criteria: Sketch with some correct features, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Aurelia cuts rectangles of equal height from a strip of paper and arranges them in a row. The first rectangle has a length of 10 cm. The second rectangle has a length of 9.6 cm. The length of each subsequent rectangle is 96% of the length of the previous rectangle.

\exfigure{1303_q36_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the length of the $5^{\text{th}}$ rectangular strip, correct to 3 significant figures
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the length required to make the first 10 rectangles, correct to 3 significant figures
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If Aurelia had a strip of paper 2.4 m in length, explain with working, if this is sufficient to make an unlimited number of rectangles.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: strip of paper cut into rectangles, first of length 10 cm

solutions.latex:
The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a=10$ and ratio $r=0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5 &= 10\times 0.96^4 \\ &\approx 8.49 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Using the sum of a GP, $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ with $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10(1-0.96^{10})}{1-0.96} \\ &\approx 83.8 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{10}{1-0.96} \\ &= 250 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Now $2.4 \text{ m}=240 \text{ cm}<250 \text{ cm}$.

So 2.4 m is not sufficient to make an unlimited number of rectangles.

questions.stem:
A cylindrical water tank holds 4000 litres of water, making its volume 4 cubic metres as shown in the diagram (not to scale).

\exfigure{1303_q37_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the surface area is given by $S=2\pi r^2+8r^{-1}$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the radius that would give the smallest possible surface area.

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r metres, height h metres, volume 4 m^3

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$, with $V=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= \pi r^2h \\ h &= \dfrac{4}{\pi r^2} \end{aligned}$$
The closed cylinder has surface area $S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{4}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2+\dfrac{8}{r} \\ &= 2\pi r^2+8r^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a minimum, set $S'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} S' &= 4\pi r-8r^{-2} = 0 \\ 4\pi r-\dfrac{8}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3-8 &= 0 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{8}{4\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$S''=4\pi+\dfrac{16}{r^3}$$
Since $r>0$, $S''>0$, so this is a minimum area.
$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}} \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the radius, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Simultaneously solve the equations $\log_{10}(2-x)-\log_{10}y=1-\log_{10}2$ and $\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y$

solutions.latex:
Rearrange the first equation using log laws.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(2-x)+\log_{10}2-1 &= \log_{10}y \\ \log_{10}(4-2x)-1 &= \log_{10}y \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
$$\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4-2x}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4-2x}{2x} &= 10 \\ 4-2x &= 20x \\ x &= \dfrac{2}{11} \end{aligned}$$
From (2), $y=2x=\dfrac{4}{11}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2}{11},\ y=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

questions.stem: Max borrows \$250 000 to purchase a house. He repays his loan in equal monthly instalments of \$$M$ for 25 years. Interest is charged at 3% p.a., compounded monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By first finding expressions for $A_1,A_2$ and $A_3$ (the amount owing after 1 month, 2 months and 3 months), find an expression for $A_n$ (the amount owing after $n$ months).

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the amount of each monthly instalment, \$$M$, and hence calculate the amount of interest Max pays on the loan.

criteria: Finds expressions for $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid after $25\times 12=300$ months, so $A_{300}=0$.
$$250000(1.0025)^{300}-M\left(1+1.0025+\cdots+1.0025^{299}\right)=0$$
The bracket is a GP sum with $a=1$, $r=1.0025$, $n=300$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= \dfrac{250000(1.0025)^{300}}{\left(\frac{1.0025^{300}-1}{1.0025-1}\right)} \\ &= \$1185.53 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= 300M-250000 \\ &= \$105\,658.49 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the monthly instalment, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the displacement, $x$, of the particle in terms of $t$.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\dot{x}=\displaystyle\int 4\cos 2t\,dt=2\sin 2t+C$$
When $t=0$, $\dot{x}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2\sin 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 2t+1 &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time $2t>0$ with $\sin 2t=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2\sin 2t+1)\,dt=-\cos 2t+t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -\cos 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-\cos 2t+t+1$$

parts.latex: What is the exact value of $\sin\theta$ such that $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2}{3}$, where $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \pi$?

solutions.latex:
Draw a right-angled triangle with adjacent side 2 and hypotenuse 3. By Pythagoras' theorem, the opposite side is $\sqrt{3^2-2^2}=\sqrt{5}$.

In the second quadrant $\sin\theta>0$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following options is the same as $\sin(\pi - \theta)$?

solutions.latex:
Since $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta$ (complementary angles),
$$\sin(\pi-\theta)=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Two students work independently on a mathematical problem. Each student has a probability of 0.8 of solving it. What is the probability that both students solve the problem?

solutions.latex:
The students work independently, so the probabilities multiply.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both}) &= 0.8\times 0.8 \\ &= 0.64 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: If $P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.6, P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, then which of the following option is a true statement?
skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B) \\ &= 0.5+0.6-0.8 \\ &= 0.3 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: The fourth term of an arithmetic series is 27, and the seventeenth term is -38. What is the common difference?

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.

From $T_4=27$:
$$a+3d=27 \quad (1)$$
From $T_{17}=-38$:
$$a+16d=-38 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 13d &= -65 \\ d &= -5 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Determine the number of terms in the series $3(2)^{20} + 3(2)^{21} + \ldots + 3(2)^{k-1} + \ldots + 3(2)^{62}$.

solutions.latex:
The powers of 2 run from $20$ to $62$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{number of terms} &= 62-20+1 \\ &= 43 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

questions.stem: A standard die is rolled twice. The sum $X$ of the numbers that are upwards-facing is calculated.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to 5.
skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: It is known that a 4 appears on the die at least once in the two throws. What is the probability that $X$ is greater than 9?
skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Using a table of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 10 outcomes give $X\le 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 5) &= \dfrac{10}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{18} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct sample space or count of favourable outcomes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Outcomes with at least one 4: $36-25=11$.

Of these, the sums greater than 9 are $(4,6)$ and $(6,4)$, which is 2 outcomes.
$$P(X>9\mid \text{a 4 on a die})=\dfrac{2}{11}$$

meta.format_note: Working for the counts 11 and 2 added by us; source gave answer only.

parts.latex:
Chemistry, Physics and Biology are three of the subjects students may decide to study. For a group of 50 students, the following is known:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 students study neither Chemistry nor Physics nor Biology
\item 20 students study Chemistry
\item 25 students study Physics
\item 15 students study Biology
\item 9 students study both Chemistry and Physics
\item 10 students study both Chemistry and Biology
\item 11 students study both Physics and Biology
\end{itemize}

A student is chosen at random. By drawing a Venn diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that the student studies all three subjects.

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three subjects.

The number studying none is 12, so
$$n(\text{at least one subject})=50-12=38$$
Adding the three subject totals gives $20+25+15=60$, and $60-38=22$.

From the Venn diagram regions:
$$\begin{aligned} (9-x)+(10-x)+(11-x)+2x &= 22 \\ 30-x &= 22 \\ x &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{all three})=\dfrac{8}{50}=\dfrac{4}{25}$$
Alternatively, using
$$P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-\big[P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap C)+P(B\cap C)\big]+P(A\cap B\cap C)$$
we get
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B\cap C) &= \dfrac{38}{50}-\dfrac{20+25+15}{50}+\dfrac{9+10+11}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{25} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct Venn diagram or equation for the overlap, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+b+0.3 &= 1 \\ b &= 0.6 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\mu=\sum x\,P(X=x)=25$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10(0.1)+a(0.6)+30(0.3) &= 25 \\ 1+0.6a+9 &= 25 \\ 0.6a &= 15 \\ a &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One value correct, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A bag contains three white balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Construct the probability distribution table.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Leaving your answers as fractions and in exact form, determine:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: the expected value of $X$.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: the variance of $X$.

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: the standard deviation.

criteria: Some correct probabilities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{8}{7} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= 0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)+1^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)+2^2\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)-\left(\dfrac{8}{7}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{20}{49} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation} &= \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{49}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{7} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\cos\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1$, where $0 \le x \le 2\pi$

solutions.latex:
From $0\le x\le 2\pi$ we get $0\le 2x\le 4\pi$, so
$$-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \dfrac{15\pi}{4}$$
In this range, $\cos^{-1}(-1)$ gives
$$2x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\pi,\ 3\pi$$
$$2x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{4}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{8}$$
criteria: One solution or correct extended range for the angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$

solutions.latex:
Writing in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{1-\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the first term of the geometric sequence $3, 3\sqrt{2}, 6, 6\sqrt{2}, \ldots$ which exceeds 800?

solutions.latex:
The sequence is geometric with $a=3$ and $r=\sqrt{2}$, so $T_n=3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1}$.

We need $T_n>800$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> 800 \\ (\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> \dfrac{800}{3} \\ (n-1)\log(\sqrt{2}) &> \log\left(\dfrac{800}{3}\right) \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{800}{3}\right)}{\log(\sqrt{2})} \approx 16.11 \\ n &> 17.11 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, the 18th term is the first to exceed 800.
criteria: Correct inequality in $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In an arithmetic series, the fourth term is 6 and the sum of the first 16 terms is 120. Find the common difference.

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(2a+(n-1)d)$.

From $T_4=6$:
$$a+3d=6,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+6d=12 \quad (1)$$
From $S_{16}=120$:
$$\dfrac{16}{2}(2a+15d)=120,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+15d=15 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$9d=3$$
$$\therefore\ d=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Both equations and progress, or equivalent merit
One correct equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given that $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, show that the limiting sum of the series

$$\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos^4\theta + \sin\theta\cos^6\theta + \ldots$$

is equal to $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$. Explain why you can find the limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=\sin\theta$ and $r=\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} \\ &= \operatorname{cosec}\theta \end{aligned}$$
A limiting sum exists when $-1<r<1$. For $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0<\cos^2\theta<1$, so the limiting sum can be found.
criteria: Shows the sum equals $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The first five terms of a sequence are $3, 7, 11, 15, 19, \dots$

Which of the following recurrence relations could generate this sequence?

solutions.latex:
The differences between consecutive terms are all $4$, so each term is the previous term plus $4$.

Hence $T_1 = 3,\ T_n = T_{n-1} + 4$ generates the sequence, which is option B.

parts.latex: Which expression is a term of the geometric series $2x - 6x^2 + 18x^3 - \cdots$?

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a = 2x$ and the common ratio is
$$r = \dfrac{-6x^2}{2x} = -3x$$
Using $T_n = ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_8 &= (2x)(-3x)^7 \\ &= -4374x^8 \end{aligned}$$
Also $T_7 = (2x)(-3x)^6 = 1458x^7$, which is not an option.

Hence the term is $-4374x^8$, which is option A.

questions.review_note: Options A and B are printed identically as x = 1/3 (a minus sign appears to have been lost in A); transcribed as printed

parts.latex:
For the series $x + \dfrac{x}{5} + \dfrac{x}{25} + \cdots$

What is the value of $x$ for which the series has a limiting sum of $\dfrac{5}{6}$?

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a = x$ and the common ratio is
$$r = \dfrac{x}{5} \div x = \dfrac{1}{5}$$
Using the limiting sum formula:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{1 - \frac{1}{5}} \\ &= \dfrac{5x}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{5}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5x}{4} &= \dfrac{5}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{4}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

meta.format_note: Options A and B in the source are identical ($x=\dfrac{1}{3}$); kept as given, does not affect the key.

parts.latex: Which of the following will produce a positive value?

solutions.latex:
Check the sign of each option:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 150^\circ &< 0 &&(\text{second quadrant})\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) &= -1 \\ \cos(-30^\circ) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} > 0 \\ \sin \pi &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence only $\cos(-30^\circ)$ is positive, which is option C.

meta.format_note: Working written by us as the source had only the answer.

parts.latex: What is the exact value of $\text{cosec}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{cosec}\dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\cot\theta$, given that $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$ ?

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$, $\theta$ is in the second quadrant, so $\cos\theta<0$ and $\sin\theta>0$.

In the reference triangle the hypotenuse is $3$ and the adjacent side is $2$. By Pythagoras' theorem, the opposite side is
$$\sqrt{9-4} = \sqrt{5}$$
Then
$$\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{5}}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the correct set of solutions for $\sin x = -\cos x$ for $-\pi < x < \pi$?

solutions.latex:
Dividing $\sin x = -\cos x$ by $\cos x$ gives $\tan x = -1$.

Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, with reference angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \quad\text{or}\quad x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
Both lie in $-\pi < x < \pi$, so the answer is option B.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\ln(\ln(x))$, where $x > 1$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y = \ln(\ln x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln x} \times \dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x\ln x} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\sec x$ ?

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and differentiate:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x) &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec x \tan x \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $e^{\sin x}$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $u=\sin x$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx} e^{\sin x} = \cos x \, e^{\sin x}$$
Hence the answer is option A.

questions.stem: A clerk is employed at an initial salary of \$18\,320 per annum and after each year of service he receives an increase of \$780 per year.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: What is his salary for the second year of employment?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: What is his salary for the tenth year of employment?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: What are his total earnings over ten years of employment?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The salary rises by $\$780$ after the first year.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Salary} &= \$18\,320 + \$780 \\ &= \$19\,100 \end{aligned}$$

The salaries form an arithmetic sequence with $a = 18\,320$ and $d = 780$, so the tenth term is $a + 9d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= \$(18\,320 + 9 \times 780) \\ &= \$25\,340 \end{aligned}$$

Using the arithmetic series sum $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$ with $n=10$, $a = 18\,320$ and $l = 25\,340$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}(18\,320 + 25\,340) \\ &= \$218\,300 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: $x$, $x^2$ and $7x$ are the first three consecutive terms of an arithmetic series.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $x(x-4) = 0$
skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, find the first 3 terms of this series if all the terms are positive integers.
skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
In an arithmetic series the common difference is constant, so $T_2 - T_1 = T_3 - T_2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - x &= 7x - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 8x &= 0 \\ 2x(x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(x-4) = 0$$
criteria: Correct equation from the common difference, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (i), $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

The terms are positive, so $x \ne 0$ and $x = 4$.

The terms are $4,\ 16,\ 28$.

parts.latex: Show that the sequence $\log_{10} 3,\ \log_{10} 9,\ \log_{10} 81, \dots$ is a geometric sequence.
skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
A sequence is geometric if consecutive ratios are equal. Using $\log_{10} 9 = 2\log_{10} 3$ and $\log_{10} 81 = 4\log_{10} 3$:
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 9}{\log_{10} 3} = 2$$
$$\dfrac{T_3}{T_2} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 81}{\log_{10} 9} = 2$$
Since $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$, the sequence is geometric.
criteria: Finds one ratio, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many terms of the series $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \cdots$ give a sum of $\dfrac{2047}{2048}$?

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2047}{2048} &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\right)}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{1}{2^n} \end{aligned}$$
So $2^n = 2048 = 2^{11}$, hence $n = 11$.

There are $11$ terms.
criteria: Correct equation for $S_n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Calculate the sum of all the numbers between 100 and 400 (non-inclusive), which are not divisible by 7.

solutions.latex:
First find the sum of all the integers from 101 to 399, an arithmetic series with $n = 299$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{299}{2}(101 + 399) \\ &= 74\,750 \end{aligned}$$
The multiples of 7 in this range are $105, 112, 119, \cdots, 399$. Find how many there are using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 399 &= 105 + (n-1)\times 7 \\ n &= 43 \end{aligned}$$
Their sum is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{43}{2}(105 + 399) \\ &= 10\,836 \end{aligned}$$
Subtract the multiples of 7 from the total.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum} &= 74\,750 - 10\,836 \\ &= 63\,914 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the sum is } 63\,914$$
criteria: Finds the sum of the multiples of 7, or equivalent merit
Finds the number of multiples of 7, or equivalent merit
Finds the sum of all numbers from 101 to 399, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Using the formula for the limiting sum of a geometric series, convert the recurring decimal $4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5}$ into a mixed fraction.

solutions.latex:
Write the decimal as a whole number plus a geometric series.
$$4.353535\ldots = 4 + 0.35 + 0.0035 + 0.000035 + \cdots$$
The terms after $4$ form a geometric series with $a = 0.35$ and $r = 0.01$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ applies.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} &= 4 + \dfrac{0.35}{1 - 0.01} \\ &= 4 + \dfrac{35}{99} \\ &= 4\dfrac{35}{99} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} = 4\dfrac{35}{99}$$
criteria: Finds correct $a$ and $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact values of $\theta$ such that $2\sin^2\theta = 1 - \sin\theta$, where $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\sin\theta$.
$$2\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta - 1 = 0$$
Factorising (or using the quadratic formula):
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2 - 4(2)(-1)}}{2\times 2} \\ &= -1 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $\sin\theta = -1$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
For $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $\sin\theta$, or equivalent merit
Writes the correct quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $(1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) = \sec^2 x$

solutions.latex:
Use the identities $1 + \cot^2 x = \text{cosec}^2 x$ and $\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) \\ &= \text{cosec}^2 x \times \tan^2 x \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}\times\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec^2 x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the identities correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\cos 2x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ in the domain $[0, 360^\circ]$

solutions.latex:
Let $u = 2x$. Since $0 \le x \le 360^\circ$, we have $0 \le u \le 720^\circ$.
$$\cos u = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
The reference angle is $30^\circ$, and cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants. Two full rotations are covered.
$$u = 30^\circ, 330^\circ, 390^\circ, 690^\circ$$
Dividing by 2:
$$x = 15^\circ, 165^\circ, 195^\circ, 345^\circ$$
criteria: Finds some correct solutions or correct values of $u$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the initial population.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the minimum number of salmon in the farm at any time?

parts.label: c
parts.latex: How many days will it take for salmon population to first reach 1150?

solutions.latex:
The initial population is at $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 500\cos(0) + 900 \\ &= 1400 \end{aligned}$$

The minimum occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) = -1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min} &= -500 + 900 \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$

Set $P = 1150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1150 &= 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For the first time, take the smallest positive angle.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ days}$$

questions.stem: Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $y = \tan^3 x$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y = (\tan x)^3$:
$$y' = 3\tan^2 x \times \sec^2 x$$
criteria: Partially correct use of the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^4 & v&=2^x\\ u'&=4x^3 & v'&=2^x\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 \times 2^x + (2^x \ln 2)x^4 \\ &= 2^x x^3(4 + x\ln 2) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct product rule set-up, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By first simplifying the expression, differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{2}} + e^{-x}}{e^x}$ with respect to $x$.

solutions.latex:
Simplify first using index laws.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{2}}}{e^x} + \dfrac{e^{-x}}{e^x} \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2} - x} + e^{-x-x} \\ &= e^{-\frac{x}{2}} + e^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$y' = -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}} - 2e^{-2x}$$

questions.stem: Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $g(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2x-3}\right)$

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $y = \sin(x^\circ)$

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ first.
$$g(x) = \ln(x+1) - \ln(2x-3)$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x+1} - \dfrac{2}{2x-3} \\ &= \dfrac{2x - 3 - 2x - 2}{(x+1)(2x-3)} \\ &= \dfrac{-5}{(x+1)(2x-3)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses log laws correctly or finds one correct term, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(e^{2x}+4)^2 \times 2e^{2x} \\ &= 6e^{2x}(e^{2x}+4)^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Partially correct use of the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians, since $x^\circ = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$ radians.
$$y = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos x^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Converts to radians, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $y = \dfrac{x}{\ln x}$, show that $y^2 - xy + x^2 y' = 0$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$y' = \dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2}$$
Substitute into the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= y^2 - xy + x^2 y' \\ &= \left(\dfrac{x}{\ln x}\right)^2 - x\times\dfrac{x}{\ln x} + x^2\,\dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - x^2\ln x + x^2\ln x - x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= 0 \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Determine the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ at the point where $x = \pi$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the tangent gradient.
$$y' = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$m_{\text{tangent}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The normal is perpendicular, so $m_{\text{normal}} = 2$.

At $x = \pi$, $y = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 0 &= 2(x - \pi) \\ y &= 2x - 2\pi \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct normal gradient, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

1595_q4a_1.notes: Increasing concave-down curve from O, drawn as y=A(1-e^{-0.75x}) and fitted to the crop's point at x=1 and its end point. 1595_q4c_s1.notes: Both branches of y=3+1/(x+2) are drawn from the equation (0.9pt, arrows where the crop has them). I used one x scale (81 px/unit) and one y scale (65 px/unit) chosen to split the error between the crop's asymptote and intercept positions. The teacher's sketch is not to scale: intercepts sit about 13 px from the crop and the asymptotes about 10-13 px. The crossings at 7/2 and -7/3 are the true crossings of the drawn curve. Fractions are stacked. Left out: the teacher's working in the top right and the stray '2'. Blue becomes black dashed. The score is low mainly from the dropped working text, the handwriting and the teacher's curve hugging the asymptotes less closely than the true function. Rules 1, 6, 9, 16, 17, 23.

1595_q4d_1.notes: The curve is smooth Bezier pieces through (-6,0), (-4,5), (0,0), (2,-2), (4,0), flat at both turning points, on one uniform scale (32 px/unit in x, 17.5 px/unit in y). Each turning point therefore sits at its true coordinate: the crop draws the max about 15 px right of where uniform scaling puts it. There are arrows at both ends, filled house heads instead of the crop's open axis chevrons and bold heads. Labels are in maths font with a proper minus sign. The remaining colour is label glyph differences and the crop's heavy arrowheads. Rules 1, 4, 9, 16.

I moved the y-axis about 20 px right so the intercepts and turning points sit at true coordinates on one uniform scale: the teacher's sketch puts the axis at about x=-1. The y-axis is redrawn with its arrow at the top and a y label. The teacher's downward arrowhead at the bottom was dropped, but the long axis length is kept. The score is low from handwriting, the scan strokes and the moved axis. Rules 1, 4, 9, 16, 17. | 20 Nov checker: "Make the curve smoother and make it the actual graph": The hand-placed Bezier curve is replaced by a TikZ plot (100 samples, smooth) of a degree-7 polynomial through the true x-intercepts -10, 2, 10 and the turning points (-6,5) and (6,-2) with zero slope there and no other turning points, so the curve is the true transformed graph at the same scale, with axes, ticks, labels, dots and end arrows unchanged.

Tick labels are a little larger than the crop's tiny scan text so they can be read. The overlay is below 0.85 only because of the removed scribble, the hand-drawn arrowheads and axis letters, label font differences and the y-axis being about 1 px off.
